News.title: Keeping Nigel Farage out of Downing Street is 'moral responsibility', Lib Dem leader says
News.content:
Keeping Nigel Farage out of Downing Street is 'moral responsibility', Lib Dem leader says

EXCLUSIVE: Sir Ed Davey raised concerns over the recent £72million donated to Reform by Crypto billionaires Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, and vowed his party would be a 'firewall'f against Reform

View 2 Images Ed Davey vowed to stop Nigel Farage becoming PM (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Keeping Nigel Farage out of Downing Street is a “moral responsibility”, and the “most serious” task of his political career, the Lib Dem leader has claimed.

‌



Sir Ed Davey raised concerns over the recent £72million donated to Reform by Crypto billionaires Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, and vowed his party would be a “firewall” against Reform.

‌



Earlier this year ministers brought in a £100,000 ceiling on the sum of money that can be donated to political parties by anyone living abroad, which would also be enforced for the first 12 months after British expats come back to the UK.

‌



Addressing the recent donations scandal, the Kingston and Surbiton MP said: “With this new money, it is deeply threatening.

View 2 Images Ed Davey said the Lib Dems were a 'firewall' against Reform (Image: Getty Images)

‌



“Having dismantled the blue wall at the last election, we now have an orange wall, which we want to defend and expand. That, I think, is the way to keep the Tories out and stop Reform.

“I deeply worry about Reform, who increasingly are openly racist and dividing our country, and one thing I hope Burnham will do is to focus a little bit more on where that populism and extremism is at its worst.

“I feel a heavy responsibility on me and our party, because I genuinely think we are a firewall against Reform in areas where Labour just aren't playing. It's a moral responsibility and I don't think I've had anything more serious to do in my political career.”

‌



His intervention comes as the UK elections watchdog announced political spending limits will be reviewed.

Vijay Rangarajan - the head of the Electoral Commission - said the rules needed to be "fit for purpose" and maintain public confidence in campaign financing.

He told the Sunday Times: "Our review will look across the campaign spending framework as a whole, including spending limits, the interaction between party and candidate spending, and the reporting requirements that support public confidence in the system."

‌



He was tasked to set up the review in July by ministers.

Under existing restrictions, parties standing candidates in Britain must not spend more than £34 million in the year before a general election.

Elsewhere at the Lib Dem conference, Sir Ed urged the PM to cut fuel duty by 10p a litre at least until Christmas to ease cost-of-living pressures.

Article continues below

The party also wants to slash bus fares to £1, cut rail fares by 10% and make driving electric cars cheaper by cutting VAT on public charging.

News.title: More than £100,000 raised for family of Noah Woods after toddler's tragic death
News.content:
More than £100,000 raised for family of Noah Woods after toddler's tragic death

Noah Woods' body was tragically found in a pond on Wednesday after he went missing - over £100,000 has been raised for his grieving family

View 3 Images Over £100,000 has been raised for the family of Noah Woods (Image: Suffolk Police / SWNS)

The fundraiser for the devastated family of three-year-old Noah Woods, who was tragically found dead in a pond, has surpassed £100,000.

‌



The toddler became separated from a relative after visiting a playground in, Brantham, on Tuesday afternoon, Suffolk Police said. Around 1,300 members of the public joined a search to find Noah, who police said was non-verbal, partially deaf and had been undergoing an assessment for autism. Met Police divers recovered his body from a lake, known locally as Decoy Pond, on Wednesday afternoon and Suffolk Police said his death was not being treated as suspicious.

‌



A JustGiving page set up by Good Dads Club, a community of fathers based in Colchester, Essex, had received more than £105,000 in donations from more than 6,300 supporters by Sunday evening.

‌



Premier League star Leif Davis pays tribute to Noah Woods after kind donation READ MORE :

View 3 Images Members of the public helping during the search for Noah (Image: James Linsell Clark / SWNS)

Fundraisers organisers confirmed the money would go to help the toddler's family. A message on the JustGiving page said: "In light of the news regarding three-year-old Noah Woods, Good Dads Club is calling on our community to give whatever they can to ease the overwhelming burden on his family during this heartbreaking time.

"While no amount of money can undo these life altering events, every single financial contribution will go directly toward helping Noah’s family's expenses, navigate daily bills, and take the necessary time off work to grieve without the added strain of financial worry.

‌



"Please consider donating today, no contribution is too small and share this campaign so we can surround Noah's loved ones with the solidarity they desperately need."

View 3 Images Noah's body was found on Wednesday (Image: Suffolk Police / SWNS)

Noah's father Rhys Woods, on Thursday, paid tribute to his son in a message shared on a community Facebook group. He wrote: "There are no words to describe the pain of this loss, we are all absolutely heartbroken, Noah was the sweetest and most innocent little boy, with nothing but love to give, and we are going to miss him so very much."

Article continues below

Suffolk Police said on Thursday that the body of the child recovered by police divers had been formally identified as Noah Woods, aged three and from Brantham, subject to confirmation at formal inquest proceedings.

The force said that his death was not being treated as suspicious but that police still have a number of inquiries to complete before submitting a file for the coroner.

The fundraiser can be found HERE.

News.title: Call to shut down 'Jenrick hotels' in attack on Tory turncoat Reform MP Robert Jenrick
News.content:
Call to shut down 'Jenrick hotels' in attack on Tory turncoat Reform MP Robert Jenrick

EXCLUSIVE: In a fiery attack on Reform's Robert Jenrick, senior Lib Dem Max Wilkinson will urge ministers to look to Europe to shut down 'Jenrick's hotels' - pointing to the MP's 2022 brag

Robert Jenrick speaks about 'ramping up' asylum hotels in 2022

Dozens of "Jenrick's hotels" housing thousands of asylum seekers must finally be shut, ministers will be urged today in a fiery attack on the Reform MP.

‌



Lib Dem frontbencher Max Wilkinson will lash out at Tory turncoat Robert Jenrick, who famously bragged about securing hotels when he was Immigration Minister. In a keynote speech, Mr Wilkinson, the Lib Dem home affairs spokesman, will tell the Lib Dem conference that the Reform MP and his colleagues are "shamelessly" exploiting a small boat crisis they helped to create.

‌



He will call on the government to look to sign up to a new EU migration pact to clear up the mess left by Mr Jenrick and co. Mr Wilkinson is expected to say: "Was it not Robert Jenrick himself who bragged about opening up more asylum hotels when he was Immigration Minister?

‌



230 most dangerous areas for knife crime in UK identified with plans to increase CCTV and police patrols READ MORE :

View 2 Images Lib Dem Max Wilkinson will launch a scathing attack on Robert Jenrick's record on Monday (Image: Getty Images)

"And was it not the Tories in the Home Office who stopped processing asylum cases leaving taxpayers to foot the bill for a huge backlog? We have seen their politicians visit Dover and Calais over and over and over again to shamelessly point at the mess that they created."

In an interview in 2022, as the asylum backlog grew, Mr Jenrick told Sky News: "More hotels have been coming online almost every month throughout the whole of this year. So, (fellow Reform defector) Suella Braverman and her predecessor, Priti Patel, were procuring more hotels.

‌



"What I have done in my short tenure is ramp that up and procure even more because November, historically, has been one of the highest months of the year for migrants illegally crossing the Channel."

Nigel Farage later branded Mr Jenrick a "fraud" when sharing the quote on X. But this did not stop Mr Jenrick defecting to Reform in January after being sacked from the shadow cabinet by Kemi Badenoch, who got wind of his plan.

Blaming Brexit for the small boats crisis, Mr Wilkinson will call for the UK to join the EU's Migration and Asylum Pact, which sees participating nations agree to co-operate on screening and returns. Other countries that are not part of the bloc, including Switzerland, Norway and Iceland, have adopted elements of the agreement.

‌



Mr Wilkinson will say: "Before the (Brexit) referendum, not a single small boat crossed the Channel. Since then, more than 200,000 people have tried to make that dangerous journey - some, tragically, never making it to safety on those flimsy rubber dinghies.

View 2 Images Mr Wilkinson will turn his fire on Robert Jenrick, who defected to Reform in January (Image: Getty Images)

"The new status quo created by the Tories and Reform and then weaponised by them has led directly to the unrest and mistrust we see across the nation.

‌



"There is a solution: to enter EU's landmark new Migration and Asylum Pact. To put a stop to dangerous Channel crossings and the criminal gangs’ business model once and for all.

"And to close down Jenrick’s hotels, which never worked for communities or asylum seekers, despite costing taxpayers a fortune. This is the solution we need to build an asylum system British people can trust - that is fair and effective for all."

Last week Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said the pact should not be viewed as a "silver bullet", telling MPs: "It is a real mistake to think that that pact is the future and if we were in that, this problem would go away - because I promise you it would not."

Article continues below

Since leaving the EU, Britain has not had a Europe-wide returns agreement, but last summer Keir Starmer reached a one-in-one-out deal with France. This has seen around 1,400 small boat arrivals returned so far in exchange for people deemed to have legitimate claims coming the other way.

Labour has vowed to close the remaining asylum hotels by the general election by shifting people onto large sites while their applications are processed. At its peak there were over 56,000 people living in around 400 hotels.

At the end of June there were 16,021 in under 160 venues.

News.title: Two men 'armed with machete' seen in Merseyside town before man stabbed in flat
News.content:
Two men 'armed with machete' seen in Merseyside town before man stabbed in flat

A man in his 20s was stabbed in a flat in Prescot, Merseyside, with a witness saying they saw two men armed with a 'machete' enter the building beforehand

View 2 Images Police outside Fairhurst Terrace flats on Scotchbarn Lane in Prescot (Image: Liverpool Echo)

A man has been stabbed in a flat in a Merseyside town, with a witness saying they saw two men armed with a "machete" enter the building before the incident.

Emergency services were called to Fairhurst Terrace on Scotchbarn Lane in Prescot at around 2.20pm on Sunday following reports of a disturbance.

Merseyside Police said officers attended and found evidence of an assault. A man in his 20s was taken to hospital with injuries consistent with those caused by a bladed weapon. A force spokesperson said his condition was still being assessed.

A resident told the Liverpool Echo they saw two men wearing balaclavas enter the flat armed with a "machete" before fleeing.

They said: "I believe [the victim's] mum took him to Whiston Hospital with severe stab wounds. There's blood all over the walls and his bedroom. They left the knife at the scene but escaped over the fences at the back onto St James Road. They had balaclavas on and one spoke with a Liverpool accent."

View 2 Images Police described the incident as a 'targeted attack' (Image: Liverpool Echo)

A police cordon remained in place at the scene on Sunday evening as detectives continued their investigation. Several police vehicles lined the residential road while officers conducted door-to-door enquiries, including on Lavender Crescent.

Detective Inspector Leanne Toole said: "We initially believe that this was a targeted attack which took place inside a premises. Nonetheless. I completely recognise the impact this might have on people in the area when hearing what has happened, especially those neighbours who may have heard or seen something.

"In addition to our extensive work in the area, it is important that anyone living, working or passing by the area who we may not yet have been able to reach checks in case they hold any evidence.

"We are particularly looking for anyone who saw or otherwise captured anyone leaving the area on foot or in a vehicle at around 2.20pm this afternoon. Come forward and we will do all we can to swiftly identify and remove from the community those responsible, and indeed anyone who is involved in violent offences."

Anyone with information is asked to contact Merseyside Police's social media desk via X or Facebook. Information can also be reported via the force's website or by calling 101, quoting incident reference 26000772391.

Alternatively, information can be passed anonymously to the independent charity Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111 or via its website.

News.title: Three sisters who died off Brighton beach drowned say police in new statement
News.content:
Three sisters who died off Brighton beach drowned say police in new statement

Sisters Jane Adetoro, 36, Christina Walters, 32, and Rebecca Walters, 31, who were recovered from the sea off Brighton, died by drowning, Sussex Police said

View 3 Images L-R: Joseph Jacobson and his daughters Jane Adetoro, Christina Walters and Rebecca Walters (Image: Family Handout/PA Wire)

The three sisters whose bodies were recovered from the sea off the coast of Brighton died by drowning, with police finding no evidence of criminality or third-party involvement.

‌



Jane Adetoro, 36, Christina Walters, 32, and Rebecca Walters, 31, were recovered from the water near Madeira Drive on May 13. The women, who were from the Uxbridge area of London, were named by Sussex Police.

‌



An inquest into their deaths opened in May at Brighton and Hove Coroner's Court and is expected to resume in early October. The inquest previously heard that post-mortem examinations had given a provisional cause of death as "yet to be ascertained". On Sunday, Sussex Police said post-mortem examinations had confirmed that "all three women died by drowning".

‌



View 3 Images Flowers left at the scene where the bodies of three sisters were recovered from the sea off Brighton beach (Image: Anahita Hossein-Pour/PA Wire)

The force also said the police investigation into the sisters' deaths had concluded, finding no evidence of criminality or third-party involvement.

During the investigation, Sussex Police officers, supported by other forces, reviewed hundreds of hours of CCTV footage, took statements from witnesses across the country and conducted further enquiries to establish the sisters' movements before their deaths.

‌



The investigation found the three women were dropped off by taxi at Madeira Drive at 10.20pm on May 12. Police found no evidence that they visited any nightclubs or businesses in the area that evening.

The women were found to have entered the water close to the area where their bodies were recovered the following morning, "wearing everyday clothing".

With the police investigation now concluded, the inquest will resume to determine the facts surrounding where, when and how the three sisters died.

‌



An inquest hearing in May was told that Ms Adetoro was brought ashore by an RNLI crew and pronounced dead by a paramedic at the scene.

View 3 Images Floral tributes for the sisters (Image: Adam Gerrard/Daily Mirror)

Christina Walters was recovered from the sea by an RNLI lifeboat, while Rebecca Walters was washed ashore on Brighton beach. Both were also pronounced dead by paramedics.

‌



Following the sisters' deaths, their father, Joseph Jacobson, said there were days when the grief felt "unbearable", but he held on to the memories they shared and "the bond that death can never take away".

Chief Superintendent Adam Hays said: "From the outset of this complex and challenging investigation, we have been acutely aware of the speculation surrounding this incident, the public’s unanswered questions and their desire for answers.

"Our priority throughout has been uncovering the truth for the loved ones of Jane, Rebecca and Christina, because at this incident’s core there has always been a grieving family coming to terms with an unthinkable tragedy and loss. Our investigation has been thorough.

Article continues below

"Our extensive enquiries intentionally considered concerns raised by black communities surrounding the deaths of black people in or near bodies of water, as we worked to understand who the three women were, and the factors that could have led to them being found on the beach that morning.

"However, our enquiries have now concluded, pending any new information coming to light. Jane, Rebecca and Christina’s tragic deaths sparked a national outpouring of grief, and I would like to thank everyone who supported our investigation by coming forward with information.

"We will now support the coronial process and ask that the sisters’ family continue to be given privacy to come to terms with their loss."

News.title: RNLI warned of cyber attack after volunteers abused for saving migrants by far-right thugs
News.content:
RNLI warned of cyber attack after volunteers abused for saving migrants by far-right thugs

Online security experts have warned that the identities of RNLI members could have been leaked or fallen into the wrong hands

View 2 Images RNLI volunteers were labelled as traitors online by far-right thugs for rescuing asylum seekers in the Channel (Image: Barry Williams/PA Wire)

RNLI members have been warned they may have been hit with a cyberattack amid a heightened threat from far-Right agitators.

‌



Volunteers for the organisation were told their data may have been stolen by hackers - just days after they suffered online and physical abuse for rescuing 120 migrants from a dinghy in the English Channel.

‌



Online security experts have warned that the identities of RNLI members could have been leaked or fallen into the wrong hands after a cyber-attack on a third-party software provider. In a letter accompanying the autumn copy of its Lifeboat magazine, the charity warned supporters that their "name, contact details and records of interactions with the RNLI" could have been breached in the raid on Beacon CRM.

‌



View 2 Images Balaclava-clad followers have protested in both Dover and Portsmouth in recent weeks

NHS says 20 women had breasts removed unnecessarily as hundreds of cancer patients suffer significant harm READ MORE :

Orlando Bloom begs for international aid at world's largest refugee camp as cuts fuel crisis READ MORE :

The RNLI said it was advised last month by the provider to "assume that data held within its systems was taken" in a cyber-attack that affected around 1,500 charities in late July.

"At this stage we're not aware of any misuse of your personal information and have no evidence that your information has been published or shared," the charity added.

‌



The RNLI has suspended its services in Portsmouth since its staff were subjected to relentless abuse and branded "traitors" by anti-migrant protesters.

Peter Sparkes, the charity's chief executive, condemned abuse of its volunteers as "wholly unacceptable in civilised society", adding that the RNLI worked to save lives at sea irrespective of whose they are.

The latest data breach has fuelled concerns that lifeboat volunteers will face "doxxing", which involves the publication online of a person's home address.

‌



Dr William Allchorn, a senior research fellow at Anglia Ruskin University's International Policing and Public Protection Research Institute, said that those on the far-Right could exploit the data breach.

He told the Sunday Telegraph: "They use open source maritime tracking and endto-end encryption, but beyond that I don't know how sophisticated their set up is."

"It is the chill effect," he added. "For those on the fringes of the movement this information could be quite key."

‌



Andy Burnham hit out at "appalling" abuse directed at hero crews after they were labelled as traitors online by far-right thugs for rescuing asylum seekers in the Channel and bringing a dinghy to safety in Portsmouth, Hants.

Hundreds of protesters blocked roads overnight on September 6 and vowed to stop migrants from leaving the port.

The boat, reported to be carrying about 140 migrants, is thought to have made one of the longest journeys of any small boat and landings as far west as Hampshire are rare.

‌



The Mirror later revealed two RNLI heroes were named and pictured online by Portsmouth protestors who condemned them as "collaborators" and "traitors" for rescuing asylum seekers.

The RNLI issued security advice warning volunteers and staff not to wear the charity’s branding because of “unacceptable abuse”.

A spokesman for the RNLI said: "Beacon CRM works with many charities and organisations across the UK and Ireland, and while they cannot confirm exactly which records were accessed or downloaded, it advised all affected organisations, including the RNLI, to assume that data held within its systems was taken.

Article continues below

"At this stage, there is no evidence that information relating to RNLI supporters has been published, shared online or otherwise misused."

News.title: Earl Spencer in tears as he admits pictures of Diana 'break him'
News.content:
Earl Spencer in tears as he admits pictures of Diana 'break him'

Diana, Princess of Wales' brother, Earl Charles Spencer, became visibly emotional during a new interview as he was interrogated about his late sister and their memories

View 4 Images Earl Spencer became emotional as he spoke about Diana, Princess of Wales (Image: Jeff Overs/BBC/PA Wire)

Earl Spencer was left in tears as he spoke candidly about his late sister, Diana, Princess of Wales. In recent days, the Earl, 62, has made a string of allegations against his former in-laws, the Royal Family, including King Charles.

‌



In a new interview, the aristocrat was asked by Laura Kuenssberg about his late sister following claims that His Majesty said Diana "would soon be forgotten," following her tragic death in 1997. Buckingham Palace, in a rare statement, strongly refuted Charles's claims.

‌



During his interview with Kuenssberg at his ancestral home, Althorp, the Earl paused and became emotional when asked about the childhood memories he shares with Diana.

‌



View 4 Images The Earl spoke about growing up at Sandringham with the late Princess (Image: Jeff Overs/BBC/PA Wire)

He said: "My memories of Diana tend to be from our happy childhood days, in our home before this, which was Park House in Sandringham, in Norfolk. Even though we had the rupture of my parents' divorce, it was such a happy home. Just those days there, carefree days… not an instance, but a period of life."

Diana and Charles' parents, John, Eighth Earl Spencer, and The Honourable Frances Shand Kydd, rented Park House on the late Queen Elizabeth's private Sandringham estate. John had a close tie to the late Queen, having served as an equerry to her and her father, King George VI. They moved to Althorp in 1975, when John inherited the title of Earl from his father.

‌



Charles went on to add: "It really breaks me up when I look at old photographs of Diana as a child, and then think what happened to her, it's terribly sad." When asked how much he misses his sister, he told Laura: "Every day. That's the thing with sibling loss. You never get over it."

View 4 Images Charles said he has 'never' gotten over the death of Diana (Image: Channel 4)

It was at this moment that Charles' eyes started to fill with tears as Laura brought the interview to a halt. Earlier this week, Charles' book, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, which is currently being serialised ahead of its release on Tuesday, has made a string of claims against The House of Windsor.

‌



He also suggests that his nephews, Diana's sons, Princes William and Harry, will not be shocked by his book. He said: "I don't like to talk about what I've been speaking about to William and Harry but this will not be a surprise to them I will tell you that. These words will not be a surprise to them."

Charles also addressed the two princes, walking behind Diana's coffin ahead of her funeral. William was just 15, and Harry was 12, just weeks before his 13th birthday. He claims to have argued with the then-Prince Charles, Diana's former husband, over the decision.

View 4 Images The Earl has made a series of allegations about his former brother-in-law, the now King Charles (Image: John Stillwell/PA Wire)

‌



He claimed: "I said, 'Well, of course not, sir, she wouldn't want it'. And then he said, 'Well, I walked behind Lord Mountbatten's coffin.' And I said, 'Yes, but you were 30, and he wasn't your mother'."

Following the claims that His Majesty said people would "soon forget" the late Princess, Buckingham Palace said: "While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss."

In retaliation, the Earl claimed to have been "gaslit" by His Majesty, adding that the statement was a "poor imitation of the 'recollections may vary,'" quote which Her Late Majesty famously used during the fallout from Harry and Meghan's infamous Oprah Winfrey interview.

Article continues below

Earl Spencer insists he is "telling the truth" in the book, adding that as a historian, it is his "duty as an eyewitness to history", to share the story of his sister.

News.title: Earl Spencer drags Harry and William into Charles row with astonishing claim - 'this will not be a surprise'
News.content:
Earl Spencer drags Harry and William into Charles row with astonishing claim - 'this will not be a surprise'

Diana's brother Earl Charles Spencer has made a series of fresh claims in a new TV interview, and this time he has weighed in on his nephews, Prince William and Prince Harry

Earl Spencer mentions Harry and William in Diana row

Earl Spencer has hit out at the royals with more claims against King Charles as he drags Prince William and Prince Harry into the explosive Diana row.

‌



Lady Diana's brother is due to release his controversial memoir, called 'Swan Song: Diana, My Sister' next week, nearly 30 years after the Princess was killed in a car crash. The aristocrat has stirred up controversy with several TV interviews in which he made a series of claims against his former brother-in-law.

‌



Buckingham Palace responded to an explosive claim, from earlier this week, that King Charles said "we'll forget her soon enough" after Diana's death. In response, the Palace said "the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason".

‌



Earl Spencer claims Prince Harry and Meghan Markle's treatment echoes what happened to Diana READ MORE :

View 3 Images Earl Spencer, Prince William, Prince Harry and King Charles at Diana's funeral (Image: Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images)

Earl Charles Spencer, in an interview with the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg released in full on Sunday, opened up about his sister's death while also commenting on his nephews Prince William and Prince Harry. Here are several bombshell claims from Earl Spencer's TV interview:

Charles had a 'giddy tone' after Diana died

Earl Spencer claimed the then-Prince Charles had a "giddy tone" and sounded like a "lottery winner"

‌



"He was telling me how he had told the boys, William and Harry, at Balmoral and broken the news to them. And, I felt, as I say in the book actually, I felt there was a sort of giddy tone. I had a lot of calls that day from people who cared, who were stunned like we all were and I just felt there was a lightness in his tone about Diana's death that really jarred with me."

When asked about claims in his book that the King was "giddily elated like a lottery winner", the Earl said: "I'm reporting, every word of this book, I report exactly as I saw it and felt it at the time and I was surprised at the giddiness of his tone. That's what I am recording there."

View 3 Images Earl Spencer claimed Charles had a 'giddy tone' in a call after Diana's death (Image: PA)

‌



Earl initially told crash was 'not too serious'

The Earl said he had been living in Cape Town, South Africa, at the time and was called in the middle of the night by his sister Lady Jane Fellows and told Diana was in a crash.

He said: "I got a call in the middle of the night and it was my sister Jane and she said 'don't worry Diana's been in a car crash but it's not too serious'."

Earl Spencer said he watched the news throughout the nice and got more "distressing" calls from home until his sister's husband, who worked as the late-Queen's private secretary, revealed Diana had died. He said: "It started... as a little prang, and then it became a broken leg, perhaps a head injury, and then death."

‌



View 3 Images Lady Diana and Earl Spencer as children (Image: Getty Images)

Book will 'not be a surprise to William and Harry'

The Earl suggested Diana's sons would not be "surprised" over the claims and contents in his soon-to-be released memoir.

Earl Spencer said: "I don't like to talk about what I've been speaking about to William and Harry but this will not be a surprise to them I will tell you that. These words will not be a surprise to them."

‌



On the two Princes, the Earl also claimed Diana "wouldn't have wanted" her young sons to walk behind her coffin at her funeral. Earl Spencer also claimed he argued with the then-Prince Charles over this decision over a phone call.

In the BBC interview, he claimed: "I said, 'Well, of course not, sir, she wouldn't want it'. And then he said, 'Well, I walked behind Lord Mountbatten's coffin.' And I said, 'Yes, but you were 30 and he wasn't your mother'."

Coverage of Harry & Meghan having 'cancerous influence'

Earl Spencer claimed the treatment of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex bears "echoes" of what his sister experienced.

‌



He said his sister was "really brought low" by "criticism" she received from the media. He added it was a "pity" to see "echoes of that" in the coverage of Harry and Meghan.

Earl Spencer added: "I'm not here to speak for Harry and Meghan, but for anyone who's being destroyed in this way daily, it must be such a cancerous influence in their life."

'I know lots of things about Charles not in the book'

The Earl revealed his motivations behind writing this book nearly 30 years after Diana's death and said he felt he had a "duty" and was an "eyewitness to history".

‌



"This was very much a spur for me to write this now. Both of my parents died in their 60s, I'm in my 60s. I'm aware of mortality and I wanted to just put things down once and for all which were true."

Earl Spencer, adding it was not a threat, said: "I know lots of things about the King which I chose not to include in the book because they were not relevant."

Earl hopes 'William and Harry resolve now'

Earl Spencer said he did not take sides between his nephews and said: "I hope one day it's resolved, but I don't know all.

Article continues below

" I certainly don't know what's been done in the finer detail and so I would feel intrusive if I got more involved than to say of course a mother would want her two sons to be happy together and love each other."

Buckingham Palace, on Wednesday, in response to the Earl earlier claims said: "While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss."

News.title: Key takeaways from BBC interview as Earl Spencer defends claims about King
News.content:
Earl Spencer has told the BBC writing his book about sister Princess Diana, which has made headlines for its criticism of King Charles, was his "duty...as an eyewitness to history".

In an interview with the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg ahead of the memoir's release on Tuesday, Earl Spencer said he wanted "to put things down once and for all that were true".

Among claims made in Swan Song about the King, who was then the Prince of Wales, was that he said "we'll forget her soon enough" during an argument over whether Princes William and Harry should walk in Diana's funeral procession.

In a strongly worded response, Buckingham Palace said the King was "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss".

Here are the key moments from Earl Spencer's interview, which include his first account of how he was told about Diana's death and criticism of press coverage of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex.

News.title: Watch: Emotional Earl Spencer says he misses sister Diana every day
News.content:
Earl Spencer, brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, said he misses his sister every day during an interview with the BBC.

"That's the thing with sibling loss, you never get over it," he told Laura Kuenssberg.

His book, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, is due to be published on Tuesday and is expected to be highly critical of the Royal Family.

He said one of the reasons the book is called Swan Song is because it is his "sign off" as Diana's brother and "final take on the situation".

"This is my swan song too. I'm not here to bang on about Diana, this is my final word, celebration of her," he added.

The full interview, Princess Diana: My Sister's Story, is available on BBC iPlayer and will be broadcast on BBC One at 18:30 BST on Sunday.

News.title: Specialist courts for rape cases to be rolled out across England and Wales
News.content:
Labour promised in its 2024 manifesto to halve violence against women and girls within a decade.

"For too long, victims of rape and serious sexual offences have felt let down by our justice system," Burnham said.

"Prosecution rates for rape remain shamefully low, with many victims waiting years for justice. This is not good enough."

The changes were "long overdue" and would make a "significant difference" but focusing on prosecution alone would not be enough, he added.

"So as well as ensuring victims get justice, we will step up action to prevent these horrific crimes from happening in the first place," the prime minister said.

Nichols spoke publicly for the first time about being raped when she accused the then Justice Secretary, David Lammy, of using crime victims as a "cudgel" to push through his reforms of the legal system.

She was criticising the Courts and Tribunals Bill's plans to limit jury trials to cases with a likely prison sentence of three years or more.

She said she had waited 1,088 days to go to court, with every day being "agony" and the "trauma" made worse by her role in public life.

Her attacker, she said, was acquitted at crown court but subsequently ordered to pay compensation after she won a civil case against him.

"It is because I have been raped that I am as passionate as I am about what it means for a justice system to be truly victim-focused," she said.

"It is because I have endured every indignity that our broken criminal justice system could mete out that I care what kind of reform will actually deliver justice for survivors and victims of crime more widely."

Responding to news of the specialist courts being rolled out, the Conservatives said tackling delays to criminal rape trials was "long overdue" and they pushed Labour to commit to scrapping plans to restrict jury trials.

"The fact that victims have been withdrawing their cases because they have taken too long has been a disgrace," said shadow justice secretary Nick Timothy.

"Labour need to get courts sitting throughout the year, end the delays and clear the backlog â not undermine our right to a trial by jury."

Last year another charity, the Salford Survivor Project, said victims of rape and sexual assault were being "failed by the system" as court backlogs reached a record high.

The long delays for cases to go to trial were having a serious impact on victims' mental health, it said.

Also last year, a woman who says she was sexually assaulted by a taxi driver on her 21st birthday told BBC News she had dropped the case because of court delays.

She reported the alleged incident in early 2022 and gave evidence in court in December 2023 but the case was adjourned until September 2024 when the judge fell ill.

"I made the decision, even though I hate the statement, to drop the case," she said. "I couldn't let this hurt me further."

The Crown Prosecution Service said that, without her testimony, the case had been dropped because of insufficient evidence.

News.title: Burnham hails Greenland deal ahead of expected first Trump meeting
News.content:
"Donald Trump is trying to claim he's got a success in Greenland, but actually, all he's got is almost a carbon copy of the agreement that's persisted since the 1950s," he said at a Q&A with members at party conference.

"So let Donald Trump try to pretend he's had a victory. The truth is, Europe, Nato, countries like Canada stood up to him and won."

Trump had tried for months to purchase or annex the semi-autonomous territory, arguing that it was vulnerable to adversaries, including Russia and China.

In the wake of the deal, Frederiksen said she was "pleased that there is a prospect of a good agreement" for all three parties, which was expected to be signed at the UN General Assembly next week.

The deal "strengthens our common security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic area" while also recognising "the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination", she said in a joint statement with Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen.

The agreement would still need to go through "the necessary parliamentary procedures to enter into force" once signed, the statement noted.

Burnham has spoken with Trump at least twice since entering Downing Street and No 10 said he intends to use the UNGA to "drive forward work on issues that matter to people at home" including the cost of living and the war in Ukraine.

News.title: Kelsey Parker welcomes baby after 'devastating' stillbirth last year
News.content:
Kelsey Parker, the widow of The Wanted singer Tom Parker, has welcomed a baby after last year announcing a "devastating" stillbirth.

The podcaster and author, 35, had two children with British boy band star Tom Parker before he died in 2022, aged 33, after being diagnosed with terminal brain cancer.

She is now in a relationship with Will Lindsay and last June revealed the "earth-shattering news" that they had lost their baby Phoenix.

On Sunday, a post on her Instagram account showed a photo of a newborn baby's arm next to a pink sign with the word River. "Welcome to the world, River. Our little bit of hope," the caption said.

Celebrities including The Saturdays singer Rochelle Humes, TV presenter Susanna Reid and reality TV star Holly Hagan-Blyth have congratulated Kelsey Parker on social media.

"Congratulations angel," Rochelle Humes wrote.

"Oh my goodness â this is so wonderful â welcome River," Susanna Reid said.

Hagan-Blyth commented "I am SO happy for you xxxx".

Kelsey Parker's Instagram bio says "turning life's hardest moments into hope".

Last year she posted a poem online after the loss of her stillborn baby.

It was called Born Sleeping, Forever Loved, and began "the world grew quiet as you arrived, So loved, so longed for, yet not alive. Our precious boy, our angel light, Born with wings, took silent flight".

News.title: Neville calls Man Utd 'pathetic' - but Carrick maintains belief
News.content:
Cunha also mentioned the "noise" around United when he spoke to BBC Match of the Day.

Neville is a significant part of that noise, either directly or through his growing media empire.

Carrick has previously said he can shut it out.

It cannot be quite so easy though when United fans - who usually back their team through disappointment - followed up chants on Wednesday in disgust at the Brighton debacle by here booing Carrick's decision to take off popular England midfielder Kobbie Mainoo 11 minutes from time.

"There's always going to be certain reactions when you're making changes," said Carrick. "I've spoken to Kobbie after the game and he's absolutely fine.

"I understand at times when we are chasing the game, everyone's a little bit emotional. The supporters are, as well they should be, desperate for us to do the right thing.

"But I don't take any negatives or offence to it. I think we've just got to try and keep doing the right things to get back into the game.

"The supporters were unbelievable today, I have to say, all the way through, and stuck with the boys and supported them. At least we've given them something small at the end to take from it, and I'm sure there's more to come."

And that is the key point.

A draw at Fulham is "something small" considering the home side started the game at the foot of the Premier League - and have now swapped places with Tottenham.

Five points from five games leaves United 12th, an incredible 10 points behind pacesetters Manchester City already.

Their Â£70m summer signing Carlos Baleba is still to make his debut, and long-term injury victim Matthijs de Ligt was not involved at all, even though both were part of the squad that travelled south on Saturday.

Striker Benjamin Sesko also missed the game after suffering a recurrence of the shin problem against Brighton that he was troubled by for an extended period last season before submitting to a recovery programme that ruled him out for more than three months.

Carrick says "at this point" the extent of the damage is unknown.

This would all be pretty underwhelming were it not for the ticketing issues instigated by the club's touting crackdown that has annoyed so many in the fanbase.

On Wednesday, United will release their full-year financial results to 30 June, around which the full extent of their current debt will be revealed.

Then there is the general debate about the wisdom of new stadium, which is set to cost in excess of Â£2bn, with planning permission potentially submitted with the main Old Trafford masterplan, which is earmarked for late 2027 or early 2028.

Little wonder, after leading United back to the Champions League so unexpectedly last season, Carrick is presiding over a club whose supporters feel deflated, even if he does not recognise that.

"It's still a big season ahead," he said. "It's a long season and you're going to have spells through a season. That's part of the journey.

"It's not a sprint, it's a long effort.

"I'm not playing it down, you know. We wanted more points, so I'm not saying everything's great. I understand the frustration. We wanted to be better and we wanted to do other things.

"But deflation is certainly not what we have within the club and within the group. The players didn't have that on the pitch today and that's what will carry us through the season without a doubt."

News.title: Kuenssberg: I asked Earl Spencer who we should believe - him or the King?
News.content:
When I arrived at Althorp on Thursday to speak to Charles, Earl Spencer, only a handful of people were in evidence in the vast stately home, where Princess Diana had once tapdanced in the hall and rollerskated in the cavernous library.

It was only hours after Buckingham Palace had sent out its blistering statement in response to the explosive claims made in a new book by Earl Spencer. From the particularly English peace of this grand countryside setting, Diana's brother had provoked a storm.

That Palace statement, questioning Earl Spencer's account of the days after his sister's death, was a total contrast to its normal "never explain, never complain" mantra. But it meant that as we sat down, with oil paintings of Earl Spencer's aristocratic ancestors staring down at our TV lights, the interview was not just about his recollections of his sister. It had become about whether the earl, or the King himself, was telling the truth. As we asked Earl Spencer: which Charles are we meant to believe?

News.title: Watch: Earl Spencer says he felt Charles had 'giddy tone' during call after Diana's death
News.content:
Earl Spencer has said he felt there was a "lightness" in the tone of the then-Prince Charles during a phone call following the death of his sister, Diana, Princess of Wales.

In an interview with the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg, he said he took a call at his home in Cape Town from Charles, who told him how he had broken the news to Princes William and Harry at Balmoral Castle.

"I felt there was a sort of giddy tone," Earl Spencer told the BBC. "I'd had a lot of calls that day from people who cared, who were stunned... and I just felt there was a lightness in his tone about Diana's death that really jarred with me."

Buckingham Palace released a rare statement on Wednesday in response to claims made by Earl Spencer in his book Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, which is due to be published on Tuesday.

It said the King was "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss".

The full interview, Princess Diana: My Sister's Story, is available on BBC iPlayer and will be broadcast on BBC One at 18:30 BST on Sunday.

News.title: Homes evacuated over fears fire at seaside hotel weakened building's structure
News.content:
Speaking to the BBC, John Dighton, who was evacuated from Pavilion Court, said that he was told to leave his flat at about 19:00 on Saturday.

The 50-year-old said: "We don't know how long we will be out for but we have grabbed stuff for a couple of days.

"The worst thing is the not knowing. We are at a hotel over the road from the flats."

Ross Honeycomb, 39, was staying at the hotel with his family and told the BBC on Saturday how they were woken by fire alarms at about 01:00.

He said: "I thought I was dreaming, it was horrifying.

"We looked out and there was smoke billowing from the underground car park. Later we started hearing explosions."

Kevin Crawford, 91, and his wife Kathleen, 82, said they had booked in for a two-week stay at the hotel.

The couple, from London, told the BBC that they were in their room on the sixth floor when they heard a fire alarm.

"We saw the fire but we thought the fire brigade had it under control," said Kevin.

"We managed to sleep through it. At the time, we didn't realise how bad the fire was."

The council's chief executive, Susan Priest, said on Saturday: "The extent of support of organisations, including Three Hills, Morrisons and the Salvation Army, has been amazing and helped to ensure that visitors and residents were looked after, supported and had food and hot drinks.

"This was an extremely difficult day, firstly for the hotel guests and this evening for our residents who have had to move out of their homes."

News.title: The deadly new drugs making Scotland's fight against addiction even harder
News.content:
Efforts to bring down Scotland's sky-high rate of drug deaths are being frustrated by the arrival of hundreds of powerful new synthetic substances that experts warn are making the deadly drugs crisis even more dangerous.

In the past three years, there has been an explosion in the supply of new synthetic cannabinoids and opioids, transforming the illicit drugs trade and increasing the risk of fatal overdoses.

Annual figures to be released on Wednesday are expected to show a rise in the number of drug-related deaths in Scotland, which already has an unenviable record as the drugs death capital of Europe.

"The illicit drug supply in Scotland is getting more and more dangerous," said Dr Lorna Nisbet of Dundee University's Leverhulme Research Centre for Forensic Science.

News.title: Billionaire Man United owner loses moral high ground after tax exile, Labour chair says
News.content:
The Labour Party chair has said Sir Jim Ratcliffe loses "the moral high ground" by making statements about the UK while living in tax exile.

Speaking to Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Bridget Phillipson said she would take the billionaire businessman's comments that the UK was "on the slide" with a "pinch of salt".

Sir Jim, the founder of petrochemical giant Ineos and Manchester United's co-owner, told the BBC he has lost confidence in the UK due to a combination of high taxes and high immigration.

He has been a tax resident in Monaco since 2020 and said "things would have to get better" in the UK for him to return.

When questioned over the remarks, Phillipson said Sir Jim loses "the moral high ground" by "making these kinds of pronouncements while choosing to make decisions, that he is within his rights to make, to become a tax exile".

Pushed on whether it bothers her that people who create jobs and pay a lot of tax were leaving the UK, the minister said she was "optimistic about our country's prospects".

Other high profile billionaires have left the UK, including including steel tycoon Lakshmi Mittal and most recently the UK's third biggest taxpayer, hedge-fund boss Chris Rokos.

But, Philipson argued the country was in a good position ahead of the Budget next month, and Andy Burnham has shown a "sense of hope and optimism whilst recognising that many families are still struggling and there is more to do."

"Of course, there are challenges, including big international headwinds, but I fundamentally believe that we are in a strong position going into this budget because of the decisions taken over the last two years, and I believe our country's best days lie ahead of us," she said.

Philipson declined to speculate over whether there would be tax rises in the Budget on 28 October, and said the government remained committed to being disciplined about its spending rules.

News.title: Tens of thousands of fridge freezers left at docks as household collections suspended
News.content:
People have reported storing broken fridges and freezers in their gardens for months because some council collections have been suspended.

It follows the closure of specialist treatment facilities and a wider shortage of capacity to process cooling appliances, the Local Government Authority (LGA) said.

Recycling company Unimetals, which had dozens of sites in the UK, filed for liquidation in 2025 leaving tens of thousands of fridge freezers at Newport Docks.

The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said it was working to manage the capacity shortages.

Almost a quarter of Welsh councils say they have suspended household collections of fridge-freezers due to a shortage of space at disposal sites.

Cardiff is one of these and Lee Young, who lives in the city, has been trying to get rid of his broken fridge-freezer for two months.

"I tried to take it to the recycling centre in July but was told it wasn't accepted. Someone said the council would collect it, but they won't either."

It has been sitting in his back garden ever since and he does not know when council collections will resume.

News.title: Human extinction fears make me want to flee AI and live on an island
News.content:
Since headlines broke about claims AI advancement could lead to human extinction, James Downs has felt his anxiety rising.

"It makes me almost feel powerless. Like, what can I do as an individual?" said the mental health campaigner from Cardiff.

This sense of fear has led him to check his phone for more news.

"And the more you look at it the more your attention's drawn to the negative or scary things and the worse and worse it can seem," said the 37-year-old.

Earlier this month, a top safety researcher at Anthropic warned AI was advancing so quickly he believed there was a greater than 10% chance it "could kill all humans" within the next decade.

Then computer scientist and Nobel Prize winner Geoffrey Hinton, known as the "Godfather of AI", told the BBC that the claim was "not unreasonable", external.

On Tuesday, amid rising public concerns about the risks, the boss of ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said people should have more faith in AI firms to keep the tech safe.

News.title: Ed Davey calls for immediate 10p cut to fuel duty
News.content:
Sir Ed Davey is calling on the government to immediately cut fuel duty by 10p a litre until Christmas as part of a package of policies aimed at cutting the cost of living.

The Liberal Democrat leader is also urging the government to scrap a permanent increase in fuel duty which is set to take effect in January.

Fuel duty was frozen under the Conservatives in March 2022 and Sir Keir Starmer's government continued the freeze, deciding in May to push back a planned 3p increase in September until the end of this year.

The Lib Dems claim cutting 10p from fuel duty now would mean fuel would drop by 12p per litre at the pump.

Sir Ed claimed drivers should be supported and a temporary three-month fuel duty cut would pay for itself by stimulating the economy.

"Petrol and diesel prices are higher than they've been for a long time because of Trump's mad war with Iran, and people need help now," he said.

The policy would cost about Â£2bn, he said, adding: "It's a three-month package, a temporary package, but if you look at the extra money the government will get through the energy profits levy, from gas taxes, from VAT and fuel duty, it's self-funding."

In a speech to his party's conference on Tuesday, Sir Ed will make further calls to cut the bus fare cap from Â£3 to Â£1, and reduce rail fares by 10%.

He will also call for VAT to be dropped from public charging points for electric vehicles and a review of network costs the Lib Dems have labelled unfair.

Chancellor John Healey is under pressure to raise taxes or cut spending at his Budget next month, amid soaring government borrowing costs.

Asked about Sir Ed's call for a fuel duty cut, Labour Party chair Bridget Phillipson told Laura Kuenssberg: "I'm sure John Healey will be open to any and all suggestions ahead of the budget but actually this is an area where the Labour government has taken action on fuel duty already.

"Whilst I recognise what the Lib Dems have to say on this topic, this is the element of politics about it - they've got their conference, they're making their pitch, good luck to them."

Sir Ed also ruled out scrapping the state pension triple lock after party grandee and former business secretary Sir Vince Cable said at a fringe event it was unsustainable and should be "phased out".

Speaking at Q&A on the conference stage, Sir Ed said the policy had been introduced by the Lib Dems during the Conservative coalition to address inequalities and there was still work to do to tackle pensioner poverty.

"It has not finished the job," he told party members, who were split in a show of hands about whether the triple lock should be scrapped if the Lib Dems win power.

The triple lock guarantees that the state pension goes up each year in line with either inflation, wage increases or 2.5% - whichever is the highest - but critics say it is unaffordable and unfair to younger people.

News.title: JLR suppliers call for shift to aerospace
News.content:
Major Jaguar Land Rover suppliers have urged the government to help automotive manufacturers move into aerospace and defence, warning that large-scale car production in the UK faces long-term decline.

In an open letter to the prime minister, chancellor and West Midlands Mayor Richard Parker, industry leaders argued Britain's automotive supply chain was "not in decline" but "in the wrong market".

The intervention comes nearly a fortnight after JLR announced plans to cut 4,000 jobs.

The Treasury said it recognised the uncertainty facing workers and was supporting the automotive sector through grants, lower energy costs and investment in electric vehicle production.

JLR has its global headquarters in Coventry and plants in Solihull, Wolverhampton and Halewood.

Signatories to the letter said the redundancies were "the first visible crack" in a UK automotive supply chain supporting about 183,000 manufacturing jobs.

News.title: Maddy Cusack 'more than a number on a shirt' as anniversary falls during inquest delay
News.content:
Sitting on a bench dedicated to her memory, Maddy Cusack's sister and cousin fondly remember her as their sunshine and someone with a real sense of fun.

Olivia Cusack says her big sister was the person "I looked up to my whole life", while for Emily Reilly, her cousin Maddy's the one who "used to get us in trouble with my dad".

But as they come to remember the former Sheffield United footballer on the third anniversary of her death, they're still waiting for answers.

An inquest examining what happened to Maddy Cusack, who was 27 when she was found unconscious at her home in Derbyshire, started in June and should've finished in July.

But it has been paused for months while her former club Sheffield United looks for documents linked to her medical records.

It means her family will have to wait until at least December to hear more evidence, a wait Olivia describes as "extremely overwhelming".

"It is very emotional and you can find yourself frustrated at times," she tells BBC Newsbeat.

"They're very difficult days."

A federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent reportedly shot and wounded a man in Austin, Texas, early Sunday afternoon during the latest instance of government violence allegedly tied to President Donald Trump's mass deportation campaign.

The unidentified victim was hit once in the torso and rushed to a local trauma center, where he’s in serious but stable condition, Austin-Travis County EMS Chief Robert Luckritz said during a news conference.

Officials said city police officers weren’t present during the shooting, which took place near a highway overpass in the 800 block of Anderson Square around 12:55 p.m. local time.

Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis said she was told the shooter “is an ICE agent,” and Mayor Kirk Watson said he was “very angry about this.”

“Part of what makes me angry about this, part of what makes me so unhappy about it, is that we live in a time where there's a politics of fear, where people are trying to create fear,” Watson said.

open image in gallery A car at the scene appears to have bullet holes in it ( Reuters )

Watson said there was “no reason for us to be surprised” by the shooting, given “the nature of ICE and how it’s doing its business” in other cities. He also called for an independent, third-party investigation, saying it “would not be appropriate” to let ICE conduct the probe.

Spokespersons for ICE and the Department of Homeland Security didn’t immediately return inquiries from The Independent.

Photographs taken at the scene show a dark blue Toyota Corolla with damage along its passenger side and what appear to be two bullet holes in the rear window.

The police chief said she couldn’t confirm a report that the car was sideswiped and that the ICE agent fired multiple shots through its rear windshield.

“That's not what I'm hearing. I'm hearing that it was out on foot...there was a small foot pursuit,” she said, adding that “this is all very preliminary” and that she hadn’t been briefed by federal officials.

Democratic U.S. Rep. Greg Casar, whose district covers the shooting scene, said, “I think the obvious should be said, that there is a reason that people in Austin and across the country are deeply suspicious of anything that ICE has said.”

“People in the community don't know all the facts, but people are hurting and upset because they see how ICE has shot and, in some cases, even killed people with impunity in other parts of the country,” he said.

Casar also called on ICE to end what he called its “surge of officers here” and to instead “be focused on transparently working on issues of crime, not what they've been doing consistently here in Austin before this event.”

The mayor said local officials “have seen an increase, we believe, in the number of incidents where ICE has detained somebody, stopped somebody, those sorts of instances.”

“And it happened in a relatively brief period of time,” Watson said. “I think in one week we saw it go from: count them on one hand to in the thirties, and that happened in less than a couple of days.”

This is a developing story. More follows...

I’ve driven the Skoda Peaq before, but this time there was an important difference: the camouflage had gone, the prototype status had gone and I was driving the production car that customers will actually be able to buy. And the more time I spent with it, the more impressed I became.

In fact, there’s something slightly unexpected about the Peaq. For me, this feels like Skoda’s cut-price answer to the Range Rover Electric. Clearly the badge on the bonnet will mean very different things to different buyers and the two cars aren’t direct price rivals, but there are similarities in the way the Peaq looks and feels. Even the rear lights, which seem to disappear into the dark trim until they’re illuminated, remind me of the hidden-until-lit treatment on the Range Rover.

The Peaq is Skoda’s new electric flagship, its biggest production car yet and its first large seven-seat EV. At 4,874mm long with a 2,965mm wheelbase, it’s a substantial thing, but one of the biggest surprises from driving it through German towns and tighter urban streets is that it rarely feels intimidatingly large.

You sit high, the view out is excellent and the controls give you confidence. Add in the cameras and assistance technology and there’s none of the slight apprehension you can sometimes get when threading a big SUV through narrow streets. My supermarket car-park test confirmed it, too: this is a big seven-seater you can actually imagine living with every day, rather than nervously abandoning at the far end of the car park.

It looks smart, too. Skoda’s Modern Solid design language gives it a clean, unfussy appearance, with slim T-shaped lighting, the glossy Tech-Deck Face and, for the first time on a production Skoda, flush door handles. There’s presence without the designers having felt the need to throw every crease, vent and styling gimmick they could find at it.

The bigger step forward is inside. This feels like a flagship in a way no previous Skoda has. The design is stylish, the quality is really good, it’s tremendously spacious and, crucially, it’s all very usable. Nothing feels as though it’s been made more complicated simply to appear clever.

And after driving the finished car rather than the prototype, my view has strengthened rather than softened. This is a seriously impressive Skoda and, for me, the best large all-electric SUV in the Volkswagen Group. I’d consider buying one myself, which probably tells you quite a lot.

How we tested

After an initial drive of a pre-production Peaq while judging German Car of the Year, I drove the production Skoda Peaq extensively in Germany on motorways, urban streets and town roads, testing its ride, steering, technology, practicality, visibility and manoeuvrability, including my usual supermarket car-park test.

open image in gallery I drove the production version of the Skoda Peaq in Germany, popping into Aldi for my usual car park test ( Skoda )

Independent rating: 9/10

Pros: Exceptional space, genuinely usable seven seats, superb interior quality, best Skoda tech yet, impressive comfort and refinement, surprisingly easy to manoeuvre

Exceptional space, genuinely usable seven seats, superb interior quality, best Skoda tech yet, impressive comfort and refinement, surprisingly easy to manoeuvre Cons: Price starts at more than £50,000, rapid charging isn’t among the very fastest

Skoda Peaq specs

Price: £51,980

£51,980 Battery size: 86kWh

86kWh Maximum claimed range: 390 miles

390 miles Miles per kWh: 4.6

4.6 Charging : 199kW, 10-80 per cent in 28 minutes

Battery, range, charging, performance and drive

Every Peaq gets an 86kWh usable battery, the largest yet fitted to a Skoda EV, with two powertrain choices. The rear-wheel-drive Peaq 90 produces 282bhp, while the Peaq 90x adds all-wheel drive and increases power to 295bhp. The 90x gets from 0-62mph in 6.8 seconds, so there’s more performance than anyone’s ever likely to need in a big family SUV – let’s be honest, you’re not trying to convince everybody on board that they’ve accidentally bought tickets for a rollercoaster.

open image in gallery The Peaq looks good and drives well, with a hint of Range Rover about it ( Škoda )

The rear-wheel-drive 90 offers the longest maximum claimed range at 390 miles, which equates to around 4.5 miles/kWh. DC rapid charging peaks at 199kW, with Skoda quoting around 28 minutes for a 10 to 80 per cent charge on a suitable charger. Those numbers are perfectly respectable, although 199kW isn’t especially remarkable now that some rivals are pushing charging speeds considerably higher.

There’s Vehicle-to-Load, so the Peaq can use energy from its battery to power external electrical equipment, plus one-pedal driving that I enjoyed using, and an available heat pump. SportLine cars also get paddles behind the steering wheel to alter the regenerative braking.

The numbers only tell half the story, though, because the production Peaq drives better than the prototype I tried previously. The ride seems slightly more forgiving now. There’s still enough control to stop such a large car becoming floaty, but sharp surfaces are dealt with more calmly and the whole thing feels more settled.

That improvement suits the car perfectly. The Peaq isn’t trying to be a giant hot hatch and nor should it. It feels happiest flowing along comfortably, quietly and confidently, whether you’re on town roads or covering ground quickly on the motorway.

The steering is good, too. There’s enough weight and accuracy to place the car confidently without adding unnecessary effort, and that combines with the elevated seating position and excellent visibility to disguise the Peaq’s size remarkably well. Even on narrower urban roads I never felt as though I was piloting something enormous.

open image in gallery At just under five meters long, the Škoda Peaq is a rival for more expensive seven-seat EVs like the Kia EV9, Hyundai Ioniq 9 and Volvo EX90 ( Škoda )

Then there’s manoeuvrability. I was impressed by this on the earlier car and the production Peaq confirmed it. You can wind on plenty of steering lock, which helps enormously in tight spaces, while the camera technology takes much of the guesswork out of parking. I deliberately took it into the sort of supermarket car park owners will use all the time rather than just admiring the technology on an empty launch-site car park, and it passed the test very comfortably.

At higher motorway speeds it feels planted, quiet and secure. So the Peaq does something a good large SUV should do: it feels substantial when you want reassurance, but not enormous when you’re squeezing past parked cars.

Interior, practicality and boot space

Space is one of the Peaq’s great strengths and this really is a proper seven-seater, rather than a five-seat SUV with two occasional chairs hidden under the boot floor. The 2,965mm wheelbase gives Skoda plenty to work with and it’s used extremely well.

open image in gallery Even the third row in the Škoda Peaq gets room for adults - just ( Skoda )

The second row is generously proportioned, but it’s the third row that impressed me most. I’m close to 6ft tall and I can get back there and sit reasonably comfortably, provided the second-row seats are moved forward a little. Do that and there’s still decent space for the people in the middle row, so you’re not simply transferring discomfort from one set of passengers to another.

That makes a big difference in the real world. Plenty of seven-seat SUVs are fine if seats six and seven are occupied by smaller children, but the Peaq’s rearmost seats are genuinely usable. There’s good headroom as well, and the cabin doesn’t leave those in the back feeling as if they’ve been posted into a dark cupboard.

The interior itself is excellent. It looks stylish, it feels beautifully made and the quality is really good throughout. There’s a maturity to the design that suits the Peaq’s flagship status without losing the straightforward usability that Skoda buyers tend to expect.

Five interior Design Selections are available, ranging from Loft and Lodge through to the two Suite treatments and SportLine. The lighter Ceramic interior uses Techtona, Skoda’s leather alternative, while Suite Black combines leather and artificial leather. SportLine brings a darker look with Suedia and Techtona, sports seats and a three-spoke steering wheel.

There’s plenty of clever thinking, too. The optional Relax Package brings electrically adjustable heated seats with ventilation, massage functions and legrests, plus cushions, a folding table and a wellbeing app that can coordinate things such as the climate control, ambient lighting and seat massage.

Boot space is equally impressive. Even with all seven seats being used there are 299l available. Fold the third row and that becomes 890l, while dropping both rear rows creates a huge 2,075l space.

And there’s more under the bonnet: 37l of storage for charging cables or the parcel shelf. I still prefer my own name for it – a froot rather than a frunk – but whatever you call it, it’s useful.

Skoda has scattered its usual Simply Clever ideas around the Peaq as well. There’s a display cleaner, ticket holder, a USB connection near the rear-view mirror if you want to fit your own dash cam, extra charging for passengers further back and wipers with the washer jets built directly into them.

open image in gallery The Škoda Peaq gets a boot with 299 litres, 890 litres, or 2,075 litres with seven, five or two seats in place ( Steve Fowler )

The huge panoramic roof adds to the feeling of space. It’s the largest fitted to a Skoda and uses Dynamic Shade Control rather than an ordinary blind, with nine sections that can alter how much light comes through. The result is a cabin that feels expensive, spacious and thoughtfully designed rather than merely big.

Technology, stereo and infotainment

For me, this is the best technology we’ve yet seen in a Skoda. There’s plenty of it, as you’d expect in the company’s flagship, but what impressed me is how well it has been integrated rather than simply how long the equipment list is.

open image in gallery The new Škoda Peaq gets a high-quality interior with a great touchscreen, plus plenty of traditional Škoda 'simply clever' features including a fold-out table ( Škoda )

The centrepiece is the 13.6-inch portrait touchscreen, the first vertically mounted infotainment display in a Skoda. I’m a fan. Portrait screens can make a lot of sense in a car because they leave more room to display navigation information ahead of you, while keeping the controls you use most regularly lower down.

Skoda has thought about the physical ergonomics, too. The centre armrest is positioned so you can support your elbow while operating the touchscreen, rather than holding your whole arm in mid-air and hoping your finger lands on the right icon as the car moves. It’s one of those wonderfully obvious ideas once somebody has actually done it.

There are still proper controls where you want them. The centre console has temperature toggles, a separate control for fan speed and a physical volume wheel, while the steering wheel gets conventional buttons rather than asking you to swipe and prod your way around everything.

open image in gallery The Skoda Peaq's rear lights – like the Range Rover's – stay hidden until lit ( Škoda )

The Android-based infotainment system is quick and clear in use and includes Skoda’s own applications alongside services such as Spotify, YouTube and Google Maps. A 10-inch digital display sits in front of the driver, while wireless phone charging can deliver up to 25W to two devices. Magnets help hold the phones in exactly the right position, something I particularly liked when I first saw the Peaq, and it takes the guesswork out of phone positioning on wireless chargers.

There’s plenty of assistance technology without it feeling as though the car is constantly fighting you. Standard equipment includes traffic sign recognition, front assist, turn assist, crosstraffic assist, blind-spot monitoring and predictive adaptive cruise control, while higher specifications add features including the area view camera, remote park assist and trained parking. The latter can repeat a previously learned parking manoeuvre, which could be useful if your driveway requires the sort of steering routine normally associated with docking a ferry.

And then there’s the Sonos system. The optional 16-speaker, 755W set-up was developed specifically for the Peaq, and having now spent more time listening to it I’m impressed. There’s a lovely richness to the sound, plenty of punch from the bass and good separation, so individual parts of a track remain clear rather than being mashed together into one loud noise.

open image in gallery The first Sonos sound system in a Skoda is an impressive audio system - I enjoyed it ( Škoda )

It would be even nicer if a future software-over-the-air update could add Dolby Atmos. There’s no suggestion here that it currently has it, but it’s something I’d like to see added to an already excellent system.

There’s a neat Sonos connection for early buyers, too, with the first Peaq customers able to get a free Sonos Play speaker. It’s a nice extra, although the in-car set-up is probably the more convincing advert for the partnership.

Prices and running costs

And here we arrive at the Peaq’s biggest problem: the price starts with a five rather than a four. The range begins at £51,980 for the rear-wheel-drive Peaq SE L 90. That’s a lot of money for a Skoda, even allowing for the fact that this is the biggest, most spacious and most sophisticated model the company has built.

open image in gallery The Škoda Peaq hides its size well both in terms of design and how it feels to drive ( Škoda )

You do get plenty for it. SE L comes with 19-inch alloy wheels, LED headlights, the powered tailgate with virtual pedal operation, heated front and rear seats, a heated windscreen, the 13.6-inch infotainment display, digital instruments, wireless phone charging and the mobile digital key.

Move to the Edition 90 and the price rises to £55,130, while the all-wheel-drive Edition 90x costs £57,230. Edition adds the Suite interior, matrix LED headlights, the illuminated light band, area view camera, remote park assist and trained parking.

SportLine starts at £58,280 in rear-wheel-drive 90 form and £60,380 as the 90x. It brings 20-inch wheels, the darker exterior treatment, sports seats, three-spoke heated steering wheel and dynamic chassis control. There are options beyond that, including the Relax Package with its massage seats and legrests, panoramic roof and the Sonos audio system, which is available after launch.

I can see some buyers looking at £51,980 and wishing Skoda had somehow found a way to make the first number a four. I do, too – £49,995 would have been better psychologically. But the Peaq makes a strong case for itself once you spend time with it. The space is exceptional, the third row actually works, the cabin quality is excellent and the technology feels like a genuine step forward rather than an excuse to fill the dashboard with bigger screens.

open image in gallery Physical controls mean the touchscreen doesn't have to take care of everything ( Škoda )

I also think it’s a way better car than the Peugeot 5008. The Kia EV9 and Hyundai Ioniq 9 are tougher rivals, but the Peaq has its own combination of usability, size, range and quality. And while the Range Rover Electric sits in very different territory financially, the Peaq gives you some of that big, calm, expensive-feeling electric-SUV experience for considerably less.

The verdict: Škoda Peaq

The Peaq is another winner from Skoda – it’s a seriously impressive flagship: spacious, beautifully made, easy to use and surprisingly manageable. It’s a nine for now, with 10/10 possible after a UK drive.

Škoda Peaq rivals

FAQs

How long does it take to charge?

The Skoda Peaq can charge its 86kWh battery from 10 to 80 per cent in around 28 minutes on a suitable rapid charger, with peak DC charging of up to 199kW. That’s a perfectly usable figure for long-distance driving, although some rivals now offer higher peak charging speeds.

How much does it cost and is it worth it?

The Peaq starts from £51,980 for the rear-wheel-drive SE L 90, rising to £60,380 for the all-wheel-drive SportLine 90x. I’d dearly like that starting price to begin with a four rather than a five, but you get a seriously impressive seven-seat electric SUV for the money. The space, quality, technology, 390-mile maximum claimed range and genuinely usable third row are all major strengths. Having driven the finished production car, I’d consider buying one myself.

Does Skoda replace batteries for free?

Škoda will cover the battery for any faults for eight years, while the standard warranty of three years is less than rivals like Kia and Hyundai offer.
