Neville said: "I've never seen a Man Utd team walk out of possession as much as that. Michael has just said there was nothing wrong with the team's energy.

"Michael has got to stop defending them. I get why he's defending them; he's loyal, he wants his players to work for him, and obviously there's a long way to go in the season.

Image: Manchester United's numbers out of possession

"Both teams were the same. I called them mannequins. I've never seen a United team walk around as much as that. No alertness, no aliveness. No 'on your toes'. You should always be on your toes.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Gary Neville was unhappy with the lack of running from the Manchester United team out of possession during their draw with Fulham in the Premier League.

"Always shifting up two or three yards. They were just walking when Fulham were in possession. Fulham had 46 passes in the first couple of minutes to get their first shot.

"I don't know how many over-10-pass sequences Fulham had in that game, but the international break has come at a great time. There needs to be a rebalance.

"Very rarely do I say a team doesn't work hard or is lacking in effort. That's the ultimate criticism you can give a group of players.

"I'm always very careful to say that, but in those first 15 minutes of that second half, Man Utd and generally for the first 60 minutes, were a genuine disgrace. Nowhere near good enough without the ball.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player FREE TO WATCH: Highlights from the Premier League match between Fulham and Manchester United.

"Michael is of course saying something different to us than he is saying privately. That would've really worried me. People will ask questions about him, but he knew that when he took the job.

"But there's no panic in that sense - no one is putting pressure on Carrick - but if those types of performances continue, he will find himself in a lot of trouble. They've got to work harder than that for him."

A joint-worst start to a Premier League season for Man Utd Manchester United have won just five points from five league games this season – their joint-fewest at this stage of a Premier League campaign (also 5 in 2014-15).

Neville also elaborated on how United's personnel is causing Carrick a headache. He said: "I wish he could play all of those attacking players, but they are going to kill him defensively.

"It's not just the defence and the back four that are causing him a problem - Mbeumo and Rashford are too high and wide. They don't narrow back in. You've got Tielmans and Mainoo in midfield who are a little bit one-paced. Baleba will probably come in there. Bruno floats around a little bit, and then Cunha floats around a little bit.

"You've got these five or six players who are better with the ball than without the ball.

"It would be great to see them score loads of goals and maybe concede one or two and go and win games, but there is going to have to be a reset from the point of view of defensive structure because there are far too many of them walking on the pitch."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Fulham boss Álvaro Arbeloa said there were key decisions that didn't go his side's way, and felt that the referee 'didn't like' to let Manchester United lose.

Cunha: They put in more energy than us - we cannot accept this

Cunha also said Man Utd lacked energy at Craven Cottage, telling Sky Sports: "It is frustrating for us. After the goal, we played much better and had a lot of character. It needs to be from the start. It is only one point but we should never play for one point.

"It is hard. They put in more energy than us, we cannot accept this. We need to do our best. We need to improve in every single position. It is only the beginning. Last season was the same, with noise around, but we finished third."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Manchester United boss Michael Carrick reflects on their draw with Fulham in the Premier League.

However, Carrick did not subscribe to the same view, adding to Sky Sports: "I didn't think we did [look passive]. Did you think we were passive? Football is a difficult game.

"We controlled a lot of the first half and we played a lot of good football today. There is going to be spells when you don't have it go your own way.

"The goal they scored, and arguably there is a foul at one point on Matheus [Cunha], and it is two deflections. It goes their way. To expect total dominance for the whole game, I don't think anyone gets that in this league."

Sports.title: Ireland blow 19-point lead to lose to USA in WXV Global Series
Sports.content:
Freda Tafuna of the United States starred against Ireland

Ireland blew a 19-point lead to suffer a 40-36 loss to the USA in their opening game of the WXV Global Series.

The hosts romped to a 17-0 lead in the first 20 minutes in Dublin, with Vicky Elmes Kinlan opening the scoring and Dannah O'Brien scoring a conversion.

Tries from Cliodhna Moloney-MacDonald and Aoife Wafer made it 24-12 at half-time.

Early in the second half Ireland extended their advantage to 19 points, leading 31-12.

But the visitors, led by a player-of-the-match performance from Freda Tafuna, patiently clawed their way back into the clash with four successive tries from Kathryn Treder, twice, Hallie Taufoou and Tafuna.

Tafuna's try, scored while Kinlan was in the sin-bin, set the tone for the USA's first win over Ireland since 2018.

Scott Bemand's side are back in action next weekend away to Japan on Sunday at the Dexcom Stadium.

Sports.title: 'Might be time to wrap it up' - O'Neill to consider Celtic future
Sports.content:
Martin O'Neill will take stock as his future as Celtic boss comes under further scrutiny following the 1-0 defeat by Rangers at Parkhead.

The Light Blues cruised to a 3-0 League Cup win over the Hoops at Ibrox last Sunday and, in the Scottish Premiership rematch, a first-half strike by Ryan Naderi took Derek McInnes' side to within two points of the Hoops at the top of the table going into the international break.

In his second spell as permanent manager after two stints as interim boss last season, O'Neill was under growing pressure going into the game after the 3-1 loss to Ferencvaros at Parkhead on Thursday night.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Ryan Naderi fired Rangers to victory at Celtic Park

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the Scottish Premiership match between Celtic and Rangers.

Following another poor performance, the 74-year-old spoke about entering a period of self-reflection.

"I genuinely will reflect and see," the Northern Irishman said. "It's a matter of whether I can help the team. The manager is supposed to be able to do that. I will look at that this week.

"I think every single time something crops up and things don't go so well, age plays a part. And, do you know what, they might be right. I'll be 110 in two years' time so it might be time to wrap it up.

"I will reflect on the games and speak to the board. You never know, they may well want to speak to me. I'll try to get a couple of days away and see how it goes."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player O'Neill felt the latest Old Firm defeat was a close game but he was shut down by former striker Chris Sutton who was left disappointed by the loss

Asked what would happen if he reflected, then decided he could not improve the team, O'Neill replied: "By that time, I will promise you, I'll let you know.

"I don't know. I'll have a look."

O'Neill addressed the growing negativity within the Hoops support, saying: "Well, I think they're absolutely entitled.

"I mentioned this to you on Friday, absolutely entitled to, of course.

"And I'm not immune from criticism. Far from it. Absolutely and utterly far from it.

"I think there's every reason to ask, 'can you turn this round? Can you change the whole thing?'

"We are, as I said, two points clear, so I have to kind of look at the bigger picture at this minute.

"But I knew that we were in a big, big fight anyway, with both ourselves, Rangers, and Hearts again, who are far from out of anything.

"It's a long season ahead. It's not the first time I've been questioned about my managerial time. So, yeah, I'll have a look at it. I will reflect and see."

'Celtic have big problems'

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Kris Boyd and Neil Lennon on Celtic's dismal display against Rangers

Former Celtic manager Neil Lennon on Sky Sports:

"He's [Martin O'Neill] changed formation, he made four changes midweek. He's trying to find a recipe to get some fluidity.

"Rangers were the far superior team, not just in physical attributes and running power, but football.

"They played all the football. Celtic were a lot better than they have been in the first half, without being brilliant.

"But second half, totally disjointed, totally outplayed. Outworked, which is the worst thing you can label at a team. Really disjointed, battered, actually battered.

"All the best players were in a blue shirt today. Celtic have a lot to ponder and a lot to work out.

"They've got an international break, which is probably coming at a good time for them. I know a lot of them may be away playing for their countries but there needs to be a total reset because the last three performances in the space of a week have been very poor."

Sky Sports' Chris Sutton:

"Knowing Martin, he'll be greatly concerned. I don't like to disagree with him but it wasn't a close game. There was a massive gulf between the teams.

"I can't actually remember a Celtic team getting such a doing at Celtic Park from a Rangers team, which happened today.

"It looked like Celtic were making it up as they went along. Rangers were better in every department.

"Celtic have got big problems. They were smashed by Rangers and that's a concern."

Sports.title: Heath bounces back after blowing lead to win first LET event
Sports.content:
England's Charlotte Heath secured her maiden Ladies European Tour title in dramatic fashion, holding off a host of challengers to claim victory at the La Sella Open in Denia, Alicante.

The 24-year-old rookie started the final round with a four-shot advantage and, despite seeing her lead disappear during a tense Sunday afternoon, she held her composure to card a final-round 73 and finish at 10 under par, two shots clear of the field.

After three weather-affected days, gusting winds continued to add an extra layer of difficulty, and set the stage for a thrilling finale at one of the LET's premier events.

Heath's front nine featured a solitary bogey at the fifth as she turned in 37, while Germany's Helen Briem mounted a strong challenge and briefly drew level at nine under par through 13 holes. However, Briem immediately dropped a shot at the next, allowing Heath to reclaim the outright lead.

As Briem and Shannon Tan of Singapore slipped back on the closing stretch, Italy's Alessandra Fanali posted the clubhouse target at eight under par.

The strongest challenge ultimately came from Englishwoman Alice Hewson, who surged into contention with a birdie finish. Standing over an eagle putt on the 18th that would have tied the lead, Hewson narrowly missed before tapping in for birdie, joining Fanali at eight under par.

Image: Heath bounced back after losing a four-shot lead before going on to win by two strokes

Heath was left needing a composed finish to seal the biggest victory of her career.

On the final hole, Heath split the fairway with her drive before finding a difficult position to the right of the green with her second shot. Unfazed, she pitched to nine feet and confidently rolled in a birdie putt to cap a remarkable week, ending her week with two birdies and two bogeys across the back nine.

The victory earns Heath her first LET title, a £128,722 (€150,000) winner's cheque and an unforgettable breakthrough moment in her rookie season.

"It's incredible," said Heath. "This year, I've gone out in the leading group twice before, so I guess it's third-time lucky.

"It was incredible having Alex [Long] on the bag. He kept me so calm and just reminded me that I'd played good golf all week. When the pressure is on, negative thoughts can creep in, so I'm very, very happy to get it done."

Heath admitted the mental challenge was as demanding as any shot she faced.

"You probably didn't want to be in my head on that golf course today," she said. "I was thinking I was going to shank it, hook it, pull it. You never know. Alex kept the ship steady all day."

Hewson, meanwhile, reflected on another strong performance at a venue she has long enjoyed.

Image: England's Alice Hewson finished tied for second at eight under par

"It's been a really solid week," she said. "I played some nice golf out there and probably didn't hole as many putts as I would have liked.

"La Sella is always one of my favourite stops on tour and having my whole family here made it even more special."

What's coming up next?

The LET travels to Italy for the Buccellati Ladies Italian Open at Golf Club Milano, which will be played from September 25-27.

Sports.title: Cunha strikes late to deny Fulham and salvage point for Manchester United
Sports.content:
To paraphrase a former Manchester United manager, Michael Carrick knew that the storm would come. Everything went a little too perfectly for him in the second half of last season. There would be ill winds at some point. Which was what Carrick could feel before this visit to Fulham. What were his emotions afterwards?

Relief was surely the main thing. Because after the derby defeat by Manchester City last Sunday and the midweek Carabao Cup exit against Brighton – both at Old Trafford – Carrick was starring at an unwanted hat-trick. All this on the back of other wobbles since the opening weekend when United lost at Hull. It is all extremely angsty and edgy.

It was a darkly comic own goal by Lisandro Martínez that raised Fulham’s hopes of a first Premier League win under Álvaro Arbeloa; an episode in which the United goalkeeper, Senne Lammens, emerged with zero credit. Put it down as a colossal mess. United have almost always won in this corner of south‑west London in recent seasons. A crash against the team that started the day at the foot of the table was unthinkable.

Carrick and his side averted disaster when they caught a huge break with time almost up. There was little on for Matheus Cunha on the edge of the area, to the left of centre, and so he took on the shot for the near corner. The Fulham goalkeeper, Bernd Leno, looked to have it covered. Cue an almighty deflection off David Affengruber that sent the ball spinning into the opposite corner. United escaped.

It was true that Fulham invited pressure after the own goal. They sank back and came to lack an out‑ball. But it did not look as though United would find the required moment. Carrick’s players were too slow. Their moves were predictable. They could not get in behind in the second half, their only efforts coming from outside the area. Thankfully for Carrick, Cunha got one to work.

There was plenty to like about Fulham, who remain a work in progress under Arbeloa. He appears to have concluded that he needs greater security in central midfield – hence Sander Berge and Shea Charles, with Alex Iwobi moved out to the left wing. There were round pegs in round holes for Fulham, which was not completely the case for United, albeit they were able to welcome back Luke Shaw on the left side of their defence.

With no Benjamin Sesko because of a recurrence of his shin issue, Carrick was without his only pure No 9. His solution, once again, was to use Cunha as a false 9 and ask Bruno Fernandes to play close to him. It was a box midfield, with Youri Tielemans and Kobbie Mainoo further back.

View image in fullscreen Lisandro Martínez and Senne Lammens rue handing Fulham the lead. Photograph: Peter Cziborra/Action Images/Reuters

Arbeloa got his wingers, Oscar Bobb and Iwobi, to come inside to good effect. The battle for control of the middle of the pitch pulsed, with Josh King a major part of it.

The No 10 threatened during a first half in which Fulham were the more urgent and creative team. King worked Lammens in the 32nd minute after buying a yard of space from Shaw and it was not the only time that United felt their hearts skip.

Fulham had to be annoyed that they did not score before the interval. Twice, Gonzalo García fluffed his finish when well placed; on the second occasion, Berge extended Lammens on the second phase of the move. There was also the moment when Bobb spun into a seam of space only to drag wide. King wanted a free‑kick on the edge of the area in the 45th minute after running into Harry Maguire but he was looking for the contact and was booked correctly for diving.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

United hit the woodwork twice in the first half and had other flickers. They got into some good positions only to lack composure. Cunha did well to wriggle clear of Affengruber on the right and pull back for Fernandes, who flicked against the far post. Cunha also saw his first deflected shot of the day loop high and drop down against the outside of the upright. Martínez forced Leno into a decent save early on. Marcus Rashford lifted a good chance high.

United lost their way after the restart. They lacked energy and could get nothing going. It was as if they hit a wall, and then came the gut punch of the own goal. It started when Cunha failed to hold up the ball in a deep midfield position. He was outmuscled by Calvin Bassey, who simply wanted it more. The Fulham captain pushed on to the edge of the area and when he unloaded, United’s problems were about to deepen.

Lammens’s parry was unconvincing and Martínez was ponderous. He could not set his feet properly and merely jabbed the ball towards his own goal – whereupon Lammens, perhaps wondering whether it was a back pass, tried to clear with his feet and got it all wrong.

United could feel the red panic lights flashing. They fought to stabilise and the plus point for Carrick was that his players kept going. Bryan Mbeumo and Cunha forced Leno into fine saves with curlers from distance. The key point was that they were from distance. Fulham looked poised to keep United at bay; they also went close to a second goal when Kevin, on as a substitute, forced Lammens into a save. Enter Cunha. He was the United saviour. The fault-lines for his team remain pronounced.

Sports.title: Semenyo helps chaotic Manchester City beat Sunderland despite Brobbey hat-trick
Sports.content:
Manchester City sent a message to Arsenal with this chaotic victory that takes Enzo Maresca’s team three points clear as leaders during the three-week international break.

Until the Premier League resumes on 10 October City can enjoy their status while Mikel Arteta’s champions have to stew following Saturday’s 3-0 humbling at Brighton.

Maresca will review this match because City lacked control and may not have enjoyed a 5-3 win that featured two Antoine Semenyo strikes for them, a Brian Brobbey hat-trick for Sunderland, with Enzo Fernández, Rayan Cherki and Erling Haaland the other scorers.

Maresca’s side are entertaining for the neutral and heart-palpitating for the manager. When the normally calm Rúben Dias hit the ball towards his goal and scrambled to hoof off the line, this was City in microcosm, versus Régis Le Bris’ potent visitors. The conclusion, though, from the season opening phase is that City will compete with the Gunners to the end of the title race – providing they become less fragile.

Sunderland conceded first by allowing a break at a corner that ended in Dayann Methalie chopping down Iliman Ndiaye. Next came a moment of Fernández skill from a free-kick along the right-hand edge of the box. City’s £125m deadline-day acquisition from Chelsea asked Ndiaye to alter position in the area, then guided the ball straight home, on the near side, his instruction to the winger hoodwinking Robin Roefs, Sunderland’s goalkeeper, who ended up on his backside. It was a first goal for Fernández since his equaliser in the World Cup semi-final for Argentina against England.

Having been excellent, City fell asleep seconds later. Enzo Le Fée is one of Sunderland’s star acts and the pinpoint pass into Brobbey that split Dias and Matheus Nunes showed why. The No 9’s first touch was smart, allowing him to then beat, with the outside of his right boot, the onrushing Gianluigi Donnarumma.

Maresca had billed the contest as City’s toughest so far and you saw now that this was not regulation respectful manager-speak. Le Bris’ side pinged the ball about and were quick to fire it into the danger area. Yet, when feeling too comfortable while playing out from the back, City pounced again. Kevin Danso’s loose pass from his area was nabbed by Ndiaye and the ball went instantly to Haaland near the penalty spot. Semenyo took over, tapped to Cherki and the Frenchman made space and threaded in.

That made it 2-1 to City with half an hour gone. Three minutes later a breathless opening period had another twist. Le Fée slipped in Thomas Meunier, the wide right forward crossed, and Brobbey could not miss. Following a prolonged video assistant referee check Sunderland’s second stood: Brobbey and Meunier being offside was the question and it appeared marginal.

Again, Maresca’s side suffered due to naivety. And, again, they roved upfield and breached their visitors’ rearguard. This time Cherki hit Marc Guéhi with a chip from the right that provoked a scramble in Sunderland’s area. The ball came out to Semenyo who powered in to restore City’s lead.

By the interval it should have been 4-2 but the normally lethal Haaland splayed wide after Ndiaye teed him up. The last bit of action had a mis-hit Brobbey effort nearly chipping Donnarumma who needed his 6ft 5in to tip over.

Maresca wanted the match slowed down in the second half, with the ball at City feet. Yet still holes were punched in them as when Elliot Anderson was caught upfield and Noah Sadiki ran into space and ballooned over.

View image in fullscreen Brian Brobbey gets to take the match ball home but the Sunderland striker looks dejected after the defeat. Photograph: Matt West/Shutterstock

Another goal looked to be needed because Sunderland were relentless. Cherki’s curving pass right to Ndiaye created a chance for the fourth but the winger’s touch was clumsy. Better was Semenyo’s decisiveness that made it 4-2. Cherki’s pass caused Nordi Mukiele a problem, the ball went to City’s Ghanaian international, and he arrowed into the far right corner.

Could City breathe? No was the answer. Anderson may have been lucky not to concede a penalty when the ball struck a hand in the area – another indication of City’s scruffiness: afterwards Le Bris stated this should have been a penalty, and you could see why.

Brobbey’s third arrived when Granit Xhaka delivered from the right, Nilson Angulo helped the ball on, and the Dutchman converted. This was seven goals before the hour mark in what was a basketball-like affair packed with incident that, next, included Haaland’s late fifth.

Jérémy Doku, on for Ndiaye, had Josko Gvardiol slaloming along the left, the defender’s cross to the far post slid beyond Roefs by the Norwegian. Initially flagged as offside, the VAR overturned the assistant referee’s call and that was 5-3 – the end of the scoring on an afternoon that will not be forgotten soon.

“Collectively we did what we could, fought together and got the three points,” Semenyo said. It also made it five wins from five for last season’s runners-up who, for now, are back in the box seat.

Sports.title: Isak pounces to give Liverpool victory on Iraola’s return to Bournemouth
Sports.content:
At the final whistle, victory secured, Andoni Iraola embraced both his current players and those he guided to new heights at Bournemouth last season. Liverpool are not yet the overwhelming, suffocating force Iraola wants them to become but they did enough to claim three points here, Alexander Isak capping a peculiar performance with a simple finish.

Cody Gakpo was again the architect, the Dutchman the supplier for all four of Isak’s goals this season. Isak’s only other shot before scoring was to balloon a first-time effort high and wide but his second-half strike was sufficient to return Liverpool to winning ways in the Premier League.

Perhaps it was inevitable that these teams would neutralise each other. On Iraola’s final day at Bournemouth’s training base he spent an hour in the company of his successor, Marco Rose, who is yet to taste victory in the Premier League. The pair stopped talking only because Tiago Pinto, Bournemouth’s sporting director, interrupted to remind them there were other things on the agenda.

“We knew what we were going to get, they knew what they were going to get and maybe you could see it,” Rose said. “It is mostly the same after our games; I sit here after a good performance, but you don’t get points for good performances. You have to force wins.”

Amine Adli, sidelined because of a calf injury, scored a 95th-minute winner in a 3-2 victory for Bournemouth in this fixture last season but there was no such chaos to this game. The only clear sight of goal arrived approaching the hour when Gakpo bypassed Adrien Truffert down the right flank and squared, the ball trickling towards Isak on the edge of the six-yard box.

A few minutes earlier Isak had sent Iraola retreating to the away dugout. “Yes, yes,” Iraola said, encouraging Isak as the Sweden striker made tracks on the wing, white shirts attacking the box, only for his wayward cross to end up with the ball flying towards the scaffolding structure in a corner of this ground, part of Bournemouth’s ongoing stadium upgrade.

View image in fullscreen Andoni Iraola applauds the fans after victory at the Vitality Stadium. Photograph: Ian Walton/AP

In midweek, Iraola was rooting for his former club on their European bow but promised a businesslike return to Bournemouth and stepped off one of the two Liverpool team coaches with a game face. Tommy Elphick, who captained Bournemouth to the Premier League in 2015 and followed Iraola to Liverpool, embraced old colleagues pitchside before the warm-up.

“I love it because I love this club and it is growing,” Iraola said after Liverpool extended their unbeaten start to seven games in all competitions. “They will enjoy European nights here. This stadium will become a lot nicer. I was delighted to see a lot of the people I appreciate so much.”

All the niceties, Iraola said, could wait until afterwards. Pablo de la Torre, his fitness coach who was part of his Bournemouth staff, made that clear within the opening 30 seconds, wresting the ball away from Adam Smith to delay the hosts taking a quick throw‑in. Bournemouth were intent on building on their history‑making win on Thursday in the Basque Country and had the best chance of the first half, Alisson’s smart right-hand save preventing Evanilson’s front-post flick squeezing in at his near post.

Dominik Szoboszlai dropped a typically vicious free-kick wide of Djordje Petrovic’s post and Petrovic saved a deflected Bradley Barcola shot, but Liverpool spent much of the first half containing Bournemouth’s threats. Iraola conceded that his side were slow out of the blocks.

“We didn’t start with the intensity that is required to win here,” he said. “You never play comfortably here – Bournemouth put you under pressure and you have to adapt.”

Liverpool only teased glimpses of quality. Florian Wirtz saw a disguised pass for Isak cut out and Bournemouth flew forward, the alert and again impressive Jérémy Jacquet extinguishing the danger as Ryan Christie flung his body to connect with a low cross. Christie chopped inside Szoboszlai close to the touchline and Scott switched play with a pinged diagonal pass.

Bournemouth seemed to be growing in confidence but then Gakpo breezed past Truffert, usually such a dependable performer who last week was given a France recall. Gakpo crossed from the right and while James Hill dived in to stop the threat of Wirtz at the front post, the ball dropped to an unmarked Isak on the edge of the six‑yard box to stroke the ball in.

It was not a nerveless finale. Iraola hopped on the touchline as Scott, poised to make his England debut in this international window, lined up a 90th-minute free‑kick. After Liverpool won a free-kick deep into four minutes of stoppage time, Iraola crossed his hands and frantically pointed his players towards the scoreboard showing there were only a matter of seconds remaining. Moments later, it was a case of job done. “I think in life you always get what you deserve,” a phlegmatic Rose said. “One error is too much, that’s the point.”

Sports.title: Rangers and Ryan Naderi finish off Celtic’s horror week with Old Firm victory
Sports.content:
If ever a stadium can be rocked by silence, this was the moment. With no visiting fans allowed at any of this season’s Glasgow derbies, Ryan Naderi’s winning goal was met with nothing but the banging of fists of the clear plastic of the Rangers bench, and the shouting of the broadcast commentators. A screaming void of apathy and atrophy, the sound of a beckoning abyss, of a title race blowing open and a team slowly breaking apart.

That Rangers were unable to celebrate this triumph with their fans in the stadium was, of course, a source of lament, as well as a measure of just how ugly this fixture has become over the years.

It has become a day that is no longer relished but dreaded, a failure not just of the two fanbases themselves but the authorities who have allowed the ugliness to fester, who have talked a tough game on sectarianism but done little in practice to combat it at source.

But nothing could spoil the mood of Derek McInnes’s team, humming after a tough start to the season and now able to toast a second victory over their rivals in the space of a week. For Celtic, sitting on three straight defeats, the silence will be filled with plenty of noises and voices over the coming international break: awkward questions and painful decisions that last season’s dramatic double may have forestalled but which can no longer be avoided.

The drop in standards over the opening weeks of this season has been alarming, and at 74 years of age Martin O’Neill is wise enough and self-aware enough to know that he may be as much part of the problem as part of the solution. For him, the next few weeks will be a time of “self-reflection” on his role and his future, on whether he truly has the energy in him for one last fight.

“It’s a matter of whether I can help the team, and I’ll have a look at that this week,” he said. “Every time things don’t go so well, age plays a part, and you know what, they may be right. I’m 110 in two years’ time. That may be time to wrap it up. But I’ll see how it goes.

View image in fullscreen Tempers flare between Rangers manager Derek McInnes (right) and his opposite number, Martin O’Neill, at Celtic Park. Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PA

“Let me generalise a little bit. I got an opportunity to come back last October which I never thought would happen in my life. Winning the league, the game against Hearts, was one of the great moments of my managerial time. But even then, I was still thinking about whether you can still have the energy, the desire. There’s nothing great about getting old, I’ll tell you that.”

What is true of O’Neill may also be true of a few of his players. Is Callum McGregor, club legend but now 33 years of age and increasingly off the pace, still fit for purpose? Does Liam Scales need replacing? Does Kieran Tierney still have the legs? What exactly is James Forrest still doing about the place? And in the meantime, would you remotely trust the Celtic board – still essentially hollow of footballing expertise – to oversee the required transition?

Not on this evidence. The summer signings – Kasper Høgh, Mika Baur, Camilo Durán – largely disappeared from view.
