Quick Guide Roundup: Vrancken bewildered by VAR as Hearts frustrated at Kilmarnock Show Wouter Vrancken was left bewildered by the “strange” video assistant referee decision to rule out an early Hearts goal in their 1-1 draw at bottom-placed Kilmarnock. The Jambos thought they had gone ahead in the 11th minute when Laurent Mendy’s effort – which appeared to be going wide – was diverted into the net by the Killie defender Cathal McCarthy. But the VAR, Matthew MacDermid, advised Duncan Nicolson to rule it out as the ball had accidentally struck Mendy’s hand. Killie went ahead a few minutes later through a Jamie McCart own goal before Stephen Kingsley equalised in the 86th minute (pictured). But Vrancken cited similarities with the recent incident involving Manchester United’s Harry Maguire against Ipswich and felt Mendy’s inadvertent handball should have been rendered irrelevant by McCarthy heading the ball into the net. “For me, when it’s such a clear situation, it’s strange that the VAR comes in between and rules wrong,” said the Belgian. “We had a meeting last week about the laws of the game and the refs did their explanation but when you don’t see them applied in the game, then I’m thinking this is strange." Martin Boyle ended Hibernian’s losing streak at home after they fought back to claim a point in a 1-1 draw against Aberdeen. The Dons went ahead in the 17th minute with a composed finish from former Hibs striker Kevin Nisbet. Managerless Hibs – with John Potter in interim charge after David Gray’s midweek sacking – looked bereft of confidence for long spells. However, the Leith side – who had lost six successive games at Easter Road – earned a share of the spoils when Boyle levelled from the penalty spot in the 62nd minute after Jack Milne dragged Jason Kerr to the ground. Steven Pressley praised Joe Westley for the bravery he showed by playing in Dundee's 2-1 home win over Motherwell. The former Burnley striker fractured his cheekbone against Hearts a fortnight ago but declared himself available after deciding against having surgery. Instead, he played wearing a protective mask and nett Dundee’s opening goal from the penalty spot before Bradley Fink doubled their advantage. Alex Lowry pulled one back for the visitors just before the break but the home side held on. Pressley said: “Joe showed great courage. But he gave a wonderful performance, without any trepidation. Joe was fearless in everything he did and to score a goal is really important for him because he lives off them." Jim Goodwin hailed his side’s performance as the perfect tonic as Dundee United defeated St Mirren 3-0 in a one-sided contest in Paisley, with first-half goals from Jesse Randall, Lyall Cameron and Kevin Ciubotaru. It was Goodwin’s first appearance in the dugout since a recent health scare and the United manager said: “On a personal note, it was great to be back. Certainly the best medicine that I could have hoped for was that type of result and performance." A stunning set-piece strike from Enes Alic in the sixth minute of stoppage time secured a dramatic 1-1 draw for 10-man St Johnstone against Falkirk. Falkirk took advantage of Cheick Diabaté’s 54th-minute red card to seize the lead through Ethan Ross on the hour. But Alic found the top corner from 25 yards to move Simo Valakari’s side up to sixth place. Press Association Photograph: Mark Runnacles/Shutterstock Editorial Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

There was fury here but precious little focus, plenty of passion but no real patterns of play, no order to the chaos, no real idea of how to keep the ball or fashion a chance. Rangers dominated the central areas, where Dan Neil and Nicolas Raskin are already forging a formidable partnership and James Penrice merrily stomped all over the place.

O’Neill gambled on a back five, on Luke McCowan in a sort of withdrawn winger role, discarded both at half-time, rolled through his substitutions, but the plan never really emerged from the fog. Celtic are basically like the tangled ball of printer cables and headphone wires in the bottom drawer, where you’re never quite sure whether you’re unpicking the knots or making them tighter.

Naderi’s goal, bundled in from close range after Kim Min-su’s long-range effort was parried helpfully into his path by Viljami Sinisalo, was simply the most consequential emblem of Rangers’ superiority here. Emmanuel Fernandez got a rough ride early on, Tierney clipped the bar from distance and Ivor Pandur made a fine save from Colby Donovan early in the second half. That was basically it, as far as explicit threat went. Donovan’s header was the only Celtic shot on target.

“For a young team, it’s brilliant that they can take the good from this,” said McInnes. “Coming to places like this, it won’t get much more difficult. It’s only three points, but in the context of the season it was important for lots of reasons.” He knows, of course, that Rangers are not the finished article. But right now there is a power vacuum at the top of Scottish football and his improving side may as well be the one to fill it.

Sports.title: Jonathan David earns Atlético precious win over 10-man Real Madrid in fractious derby
Sports.content:
Diego Simeone said it had been a special week in Madrid, a “tremendous energy about the city”, and it closed the way he wanted. He had enjoyed the Formula One, he said, and he had enjoyed going to see Shakira. He enjoyed this even more, at least he did by the time the last of many, many blows on the referee’s whistle brought it to an end, sending him sprinting up the tunnel punching the air. Two-nil up against 10 men through goals from Álex Grimaldo and Jonathan David, seemingly in control, a late strike from Antonio Rüdiger awoke old ghosts and brought tension to the final minutes, but they had done it.

“A lot has happened in Madrid this week but this was the only thing that mattered in his mind and mine,” Atlético’s goalkeeper, Jan Oblak, said. José Mourinho’s first derby back ended in defeat and recriminations: he turned up at the press conference with a picture of two moments in which he felt that Atlético players – Lee Kang-in and Cristian Romero – should have been sent off, and insisting that the story of the derby was there. And yet there are other questions: over the way Dean Huijsen gave away the penalty and got the red card that tilted the game against them, and the way Real played. How little they did until that moment when, briefly, they appeared to have a lifeline.

A familiar foe had defeated him. It is 13 years since these managers met in this fixture, their last time the day that Atlético finally broke a curse and won the Copa del Rey at the Santiago Bernabéu. That night, Mourinho was sent off and didn’t go to get his runner’s-up medal from the king as Atlético won their first derby in 13 years. His return to Real Madrid has been driven in part by nostalgia and it was like old times in the press room. At times in the first half here it was like old times too. Which were not always good. Mourinho and Simeone are “companions of war”, the Real manager had said, and so it was.

Twenty minutes passed before the first shot, Aurélien Tchouaméni striking over from 25 yards, and it wasn’t until the 39th that there was one on target. That came, perhaps inevitably, from outside the area and Oblak pushed Arda Guler’s effort away. Otherwise, not a huge amount else was happening. Not when it came to actual football, anyway: it had been heating up almost from the beginning, Guler the first to confront the referee after he was fouled by Álex Baena. To which he would respond by fouling Baena back.

From the bench, something was said and Simeone was booked; the scene was set. This was a battle played out down there as much as out on the pitch, where it was tough and tight. When Lee went looking for David with a cross towards the back post after quarter of an hour, it was the closest anyone had got, physically, to either goal, and immediately Real broke up the right. The roar that greeted Marc Pubill’s tackle to take out Kylian Mbappé said something about the fear it was in transition that Atlético would be caught. The fear or, from Mourinho’s point of view, the hope. The plan, in fact, and they would wait for the moment.

The hosts had more of the ball and the territory but they tended to approach with caution. The lines of white shirts before them didn’t offer them the space to run into, so they were inclined to go to wide, which almost always meant the right wing. Another advance on that side led to a moment soon after when Ibrahima Konaté’s moment of doubt saw David take the ball from him inside the area, leading to Giuliano Simeone flashing wide. Then Thibaut Courtois had to dive to push a Lee cross away. At the other end Vinícius Júnior shot over twice – both over, both from distance – before the half’s most significant moment. Which, appropriately, wasn’t about the play.

Instead, Jude Bellingham slid in to tackle Romero and the referee showed him a red. Bellingham was incensed, his teammates and Real Madrid’s bench were too, and the video assistant referee was engaged. The referee, Miguel Ángel Ortiz, who was struggling to control this, was called to the screen to watch it again. There, he saw Romero’s studs hit Bellingham’s knee. The decision was rescinded, the Englishman’s card taken away. Atlético felt it should have been red. When Lee’s studs went in on Federico Valverde, Real did too.

Confrontations continued, angry words were exchanged, but as they went off at half-time, chances didn’t come with them. Two red cards did now: at half-time Atlético’s goalkeeper coach and Real’s assistant were sent off.

View image in fullscreen Real Madrid’s Dean Huijsen fouls Giuliano Simeone leading to a penalty and a red card for the defender. Photograph: Juan Carlos Lucas/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock

The second half began with Koke introduced and Baena immediately forcing a save. It was Atlético’s first shot on target, and it was the start of an entirely different game. Their second shot soon after would give them the lead, and an advantage that was even bigger than that. A long ball over the top from David Hancko dropped out of the sky and into the run of Simeone and, as he tried to bring it down and head into the area, Dean Huijsen dragged him down. Ortiz pointed to the spot; he was also called to the VAR screen again. Not to overturn the penalty, that could not have been clearer, but to change the colour of the card. Huijsen walked, Grimaldo scored and the Metropolitano exploded.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

You suspected that Mourinho would too. First, he removed Guler and Vinícius to introduce Yan Diomandé and Rüdiger. Vinícius had done little, racking up just 22 touches, and a readjustment was required but there have been times when decisions like that – the Brazilian’s removal late in last year’s clásico, on a night that Real Madrid actually won, was the beginning of the end for Xabi Alonso – have caused splits. What this does is yet to be seen. The change didn’t have any real impact, either. Instead, Atlético doubled the lead. Again, it came from the right where Lee, who was outstanding, worked it to Simeone. His low cross, bent behind Madrid’s back four, was perfect. Six yards out, David turned it in.

Quick Guide European football: Milan and Juventus back to winning ways Show In Serie A Christian Pulisic marked his first start of the season with his first Milan goal of 2026, making the breakthrough against Lecce in the 14th minute with an exquisite finish. He plucked a long pass out of the air with a deft first touch before finishing calmly. Adrien Rabiot scored at the end of a flowing move after the break, before substitute Diego Moreira struck with his third goal in two league games. The comfortable victory relieved pressure on the Milan head coach, Ruben Amorim, after a three-match winless run in all competitions had stalled his side’s early progress. Juventus returned to form with a 2-0 home win over Atalanta as Francisco Conceição and Gleison Bremer struck either side of half-time. The Bianconeri had picked up one point in their previous two league games but went in front in the 28th minute when Conceição scored his first goal of the season with a low shot. Bremer sealed the three points by guiding home a header from a corner with 13 minutes remaining as Juventus inflicted a third straight defeat on their former coach Maurizio Sarri. Earlier, Fiorentina maintained their unbeaten run under Paolo Vanoli with a 1-1 draw against Napoli. Billy Gilmour put Napoli in front with a cushioned volley after Fiorentina hit the woodwork twice early on, but the home side drew level through a deflected Alex Jimenez strike in the second half. Como had the chance to move joint-top when they travelled to newly-promoted Frosinone, but Cesc Fàbregas’s side suffered their first loss of the season as a 2-0 reverse ended their four-match winning run in all competitions. First-half goals from Giacomo Calo and Giorgi Kvernadze, and a heroic goalkeeping display by Lorenzo Palmisani, sealed a famous win for the hosts. Parma beat Genoa 2-1 to claim their first victory of the season and leave Daniele De Rossi’s side winless after five games. Elsewhere in La Liga, Valencia stay in the bottom three after losing 3-2 at home to Real Sociedad. Luka Sucic gave the visitors a 26th-minute lead and Aaron Mayol levelled the scores 12 minutes after half-time. In a hectic final quarter of the match Carlos Soler put Sociedad ahead from the spot before a Luken Beitia own goal made it 2-2. The visitors then grabbed the points with a late goal from Ander Barrenetxea before having Orri Óskarsson sent off in the sixth minute of added time. Meanwhile, Getafe beat Málaga 1-0, Deportivo A Coruña drew 1-1 with Real Betis and Villarreal defeated Levante 3-1. In Ligue 1, Angry Marseille fans displayed banners hostile to the club's American owner, Frank McCourt, at their match against Paris Saint-Germain. Marseille hosted their bitter rivals on Sunday night on the back of four consecutive losses in all competitions and fans mocked the “Champions Project” of McCourt, who aimed to return the club to the European elite when he took over the club 10 years ago . The banners read: "2016: Champions Project. 2026: Ligue 2 Project? McCourt Out." PSG finished 2-1 winners with goals from Ferran Torres and Marquinhos while Angel Gomes was on target for the home side, who had Timohty Weah sent off in the 77th minute. Bayer Leverkusen defender Miguel Gutíerrez scored a goal and set up another as they beat RB Leipzig 2-0 on Sunday for their second win of the Bundesliga season. Gutíerrez provided an assist for Patrik Schick just before the break and scored himself after 57 minutes. Schalke and Elversberg ‌had to settle for a point after a 0-0 draw in their first ever top-flight meeting while Paderborn eased past Hoffenheim 3-1. Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

David was withdrawn immediately, Julián Alvarez replacing him to whistles from the home fans. Still Atlético came, and the Argentinian so nearly had the third when Courtois made an extraordinary save from Romero and as the ball dropped Konaté rescued Madrid twice, the second time clearing off the line from Alvarez. Simeone smelt blood – Ademola Lookman was introduced too. Real Madrid, it seemed, could do nothing. Oblak barely saw them. Not once in that second half did Real touch the ball in his area, until they scored in the 89th minute. Kylian Mbappé barely touched the ball anywhere. Inside Atlético’s half, a pigeon sat pecking at the grass for a good few minutes, uninterrupted by even the briefest of counterattacks.

When Diomandé at last got away with 15 minutes to go, Oblak saved a shot that was hit straight at him, the opportunity to maybe make a match of the final minutes wasted. Or so it seemed. From a dead ball, Rüdiger headed in to give them a hope, a few minutes of a rebellion that was brief and incomplete, unlike Simeone’s week.

Sports.title: ‘Mixed emotions’ for Farke as Leeds stay unbeaten with Crystal Palace stalemate
Sports.content:
Perhaps it is testament to the progress Leeds have made since returning to the Premier League just over a year ago that there was frustration at failing to move up to third after drawing with Crystal Palace. Instead, Daniel Farke’s team enter the prolonged international break in fifth and unbeaten, which is a fine achievement in itself.

Apart from Tyrick Mitchell’s disallowed goal, neither side gave much impression they would secure the points. For Palace, it was a first clean sheet of the season, having conceded at least twice in their opening four games, relieving pressure on Pierre Sage, while the hosts endured their first blank.

A victory by two clear goals would have meant a best-ever start to a Premier League campaign for Leeds but they were blunt in the final third. There was even a level of discontent amid a ponderous performance with fans chanting “forward” as they failed to replicate the thrashing of Newcastle on Monday.

“Mixed emotions,” Farke said. “We would have preferred to win, but the reality is it is 38 game days. It is not always magic nights under the floodlights, champagne football, you overrun the opponent and score goals for fun. Sometimes it is a scruffy Sunday afternoon when you have to dig in. This was one of these games.”

Farke is into the final year of his contract and signing a new deal is a priority for him and the club. His stature has grown over the past 10 months, with Leeds the fifth-best performing team in the division since December 2025 and the German will likely be rewarded in the coming weeks for bringing stability to the club as Leeds aim to build on strong foundations.

The most notable moment of the opening quarter here came when Walter Benítez took too long to distribute the ball. The referee, Adam Herczeg – making his Premier League debut and fully aware of the rules – awarded Leeds a corner as punishment. It was a tentative game in the autumn sunshine, lacking intensity and quality, with Ao Tanaka snatching at a shot the closest anyone got to threatening a goal.

Around the half-hour something akin to a football match broke out as nervousness was replaced by urgency. Jørgen Strand Larsen and Quinten Timber engineered a chance for Palace which was blocked and allowed Leeds to break through Noah Okafor down the left, although his cross was turned behind.

Palace had the greater quality, with Adam Wharton and Timber comfortable in possession in the middle of the park, while Yéremy Pino whizzed around in the hope of finding an opener. It was controlled play, as the visitors took their time in the buildup, although there was often very little at the end of it as James Trafford was left unthreatened.

View image in fullscreen James Justin stretches to block an effort from Eddie Nketiah. Photograph: Greig Cowie/Shutterstock

Leeds on the other hand would burst into life for brief moments as the full-backs flew forward, changing the dynamic in an instant but Palace’s centre-backs and wing-backs were built to deal with these rapid transitions, leaving Dominic Calvert-Lewin starved of service. Benítez could relax and re-read the laws of the game, having failed to face a single shot on target in the opening 40 minutes.

Palace pushed the fast-forward button at the break and Mitchell put the ball in the back of the net from a fine move down the right. The glory turned to anguish when the video assistant referee intervened to show Anan Khalaili was offside in the buildup, causing an eruption inside Elland Road.

Leeds were sluggish but the warning from Mitchell caused a reaction and they were almost ahead when Calvert-Lewin’s only real chance was saved by Benítez. The England striker was given too much space to get on the end of a cross but his sidefooted volley was weak.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

There was a touch of menace in the game as Tanaka and Wharton were booked in quick succession, the first for a cynical foul and the latter after lunging in late without a hope of winning the ball, ensuring Herczeg was far busier than the two goalkeepers.

Leeds were completely ineffective in open play, Ethan Ampadu engaged in a long-throwathon. Every few minutes he would trot to a sidelineto pick up the ball and hurl it into the box but Palace were alive to the danger. “We had many set pieces today, but also today we didn’t have the best quality of the delivery,” Farke said.

Palace edged the match and Daichi Kamada could have won it late on but his header drifted inches wide. Sage will be relieved to see his defence so well organised and untroubled after conceding 11 in the first four games, leading to plenty of early scrutiny on his appointment. “Especially when I read the social media, there’s a big pressure.” Sage said.

“But you know, I don’t care about that. I do my job with honesty, I give my best with my skills and my limits. And in the end, I have no regrets with what I do.”

Sports.title: Andros Townsend avoids injury after bizarre pitch roller incident in Thailand
Sports.content:
The former England winger Andros Townsend has joked Stoke away “wasn’t so bad after all” following a bizarre incident in Thailand where he was run over by a pitch roller.

The former Tottenham and Crystal Palace attacker currently plays in Thai League 1 for PT Prachuap and made headlines on Saturday night when a clip emerged on social media which showed the 35-year-old being taken out before a fixture at Pattani.

Townsend was warming up when a member of staff at Pattani appeared to lose control of the pitch roller and it crashed into the 13-cap England international. The left leg of the Prachuap player briefly got stuck under the vehicle, but he did feature off the bench late on in the 3-0 win.

Regular ITV pundit Townsend later took to Instagram to make light of the incident, referencing one of his recent posts in which he contrasted a sun-drenched Thai away trip with previous visits to Stoke’s windswept stadium.

Townsend said on his Instagram story: “It turns out Stoke away wasn’t so bad after all. Swipe to see why.”

Another post described Townsend as ‘The King of Memes in Thai League history’ and he replied “trust me” with four laughing emojis.

Sports.title: Holmberg rescues point for Arsenal but Manchester United off the mark in WSL
Sports.content:
Arsenal were mightily relieved as a 95th-minute Smilla Holmberg volley rescued a point at home to a much-improved Manchester United side, but the draw will not be enough to eradicate concerns about how far behind the leaders Manchester City Renée Slegers’ team are slipping already and how frequently they seem to struggle to break down a low block.

A defiant Manchester United stunned the north Londoners as Eva Olid’s side claimed the first point of her tenure with a performance that defied all of the pre-match scripts, but it was very nearly a victory, had it not been for Holmberg’s last-gasp back-post finish from Leah Williamson’s deep, diagonal ball into the box, which finally broke the visitors’ stubborn resistance.

Widely criticised for their dismal displays in their opening two defeats against London City Lionesses and Chelsea, Manchester United were heavily tipped to struggle again at the Emirates but an encouraging defensive effort and an against-the-run-of-play Julia Zigiotti Olme strike gave them a precious lead in a display that will buy the former Hearts manager Olid plenty of time to continue working on her style on the training ground and quieten those doubting her.

Instead it will be Arsenal now facing scrutiny as they failed to win at home for a second straight game and slipped four points behind the defending champions, Manchester City, after just three rounds of fixtures. Last term, Manchester City dropped points in only four games and the early-season leaders have a 100% record so far. Arsenal’s next two WSL games are away to Chelsea and Manchester City.

Quick Guide Spurs put seven past Crystal Palace Show Olivia Holdt struck a second-half hat-trick as Tottenham continued their promising start to the new Women’s Super League season by thrashing 10-player Crystal Palace 7-0 at Selhurst Park. The Eagles had midfielder Fuka Tsunoda sent off after only eight minutes for a late foul on Cathinka Tandberg. Spurs – who drew at Liverpool last week after opening with a win over West Ham – had twice struck the woodwork in the first half before Denmark forward Holdt’s treble took the game away from the home side. Summer signing Victoria Pelova, substitute Shekiera Martinez and Amanda Nilden all scored in the closing stages. Netherlands midfielder Pelova then slotted in a seventh during added time to leave Martin Ho’s side second in the table. Everton snatched a 1-0 win at West Ham after a stoppage-time own goal from Irons defender Laia Codina. Both sides looked set for a point before Codina nodded into her own net from a free-kick by Yuka Momiki as the Toffees moved up to fifth. Lynn Wilms scored an 89th-minute equaliser as Aston Villa snatched a 1-1 draw against Brighton, who had gone ahead in the first half through Gabby George, leaving each club still in search of a first WSL win. Press Association Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

“It’s not ideal, it’s not what we wanted at all, four lost points,” Slegers admitted, reflected on consecutive home draws, but she added: “It’s round three in the WSL, there are a lot of games left to play. Let’s see in May, how it ends. Not converting dominance into wins, that’s something we have to look at. We believe in the quality of the squad. When that starts clicking, it’s going to be really good.”

In truth, this was a result that Arsenal could ill-afford, especially after last weekend’s goalless draw at home to the newly promoted side Crystal Palace, where the north Londoners were surprisingly wasteful in the final third. Slegers’ team had scored just one goal from 43 shots across their opening two league fixtures. Surely, therefore, a home match against a side who conceded five goals last time out was the perfect opportunity to banish any concerns of a lack of clinical quality in the final third? Think again.

View image in fullscreen Manchester United’s Julia Zigiotti Olme celebrates scoring against Arsenal. Photograph: Paul Harding/WSL/WSL Football/Getty Images

The hosts did create good openings and looked to have control of the midfield. Their winger Lisa Baum shot straight at Phallon Tullis-Joyce early on and was providing dangerous crosses from the left. Mariona Caldentey also went close, curling just wide and Tullis-Joyce made a fine save to keep out Stina Blackstenius’ header. Nevertheless, it had been United’s Elisabeth Terland who went closest in the first half, being thwarted by two excellent Misa Rodríguez saves in quick succession.

Arsenal stepped up the pressure after half-time but Georgia Stanway – one of Arsenal’s better performers for the rest of the game – made a costly error as she tried to play a simple pass back towards the centre-back Steph Catley that carelessly rolled the ball into the path of Zigiotti Olme instead. The grateful Manchester United midfielder confidently stepped the ball around Catley and slotted through the legs of Rodríguez. The Emirates was astonished. The United bench, jubilant.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Phallon Tullis-Joyce leaping up to make a crucial save to keep Arsenal at bay. Photograph: Nina Farooqi/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock

From then on, it was ‘backs to the wall’ for the visitors, much like it was during the majority of this fixture last term, which ended goalless. Tullis-Joyce dived low and strong to keep out a Cailtin Foord effort and United battled well to clear the danger from several set pieces as the home side grew increasingly frustrated. The crowd eventually erupted as the substitute Holmberg earned them a point and Manchester United’s players fell to their knees.

Quick Guide WSL Saturday roundup: Chelsea's Potter and Malard sink Birmingham Show Chelsea and London City Lionesses climbed the Women’s Super League table with respective victories over Birmingham and Charlton. After thumping Manchester United 5-0 last weekend, Chelsea won again as Lexi Potter and Melvine Malard secured a 2-0 win. Potter found the roof of the net in the eighth minute (the celebrations pictured above) and in the 71st minute the France star Malard made a quick impact from the bench with her first goal at Stamford Bridge. Chelsea moved up to second and with their goal difference were likely to stay there. London City lost 2-1 to West Ham last time out but impressed in a 4-1 triumph at promoted Charlton. Isobel Goodwin’s double had London City two goals ahead after 15 minutes and, despite Jodie Hutton halving the deficit in the 39th minute with a fine finish, Jana Fernández restored their advantage before half-time. The German forward Nicole Anyomi made sure the outcome was no longer in doubt with the Lionesses’ fourth after 76 minutes. They sit third, a point behind Chelsea. Press Association Photograph: Yaroslav Dunka/Shutterstock Editorial Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Olid was pleased with their display, though, explaining: “After losing 5-0, the focus this week was the defensive shape, because I think the attack will come. Implementing a new style of play needs time. But the effort, the hard work, the intensity, that can never be missing. It was so important to see that today. That is the minimum. Now, from here, little-by-little, we will improve the attacking style.”

Sports.title: Raheem Sterling vows to be 'better than yesterday' as former England footballer, 31, breaks his silence after pleading guilty to dangerous driving and drug possession following £270,000 Lamborghini car crash
Sports.content:
Raheem Sterling says he is seeking 'progress over perfection' after pleading guilty to dangerous driving and drug possession.

In his first Instagram post since bodycam footage of his May arrest was released, Sterling says his goal is to 'be better than yesterday'.

On Tuesday, Sterling pleaded guilty at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court after crashing his £270,000 Lamborghini while driving under the influence of laughing gas.

Sterling told police he had 'a problem' with the drug after submitting rush hour motorists to a terrifying 90 minutes of dangerous driving, in which he zig-zagged on the M25 and M3 motorways before swerving onto a slip road and crashing into a metal gate.

The 31-year-old former England international was arrested by police who claim he tried to hide nitrous oxide, or laughing gas, from them by moving it to the back seat of his black Lamborghini Urus SUV.

Police bodycam footage shows the moment that Sterling was arrested with canisters and a deflated balloon on his lap. An officer can be heard saying 'you can put that down' to the footballer after opening his car door.

He can then be seen taking the items from his lap and putting them behind his seat.

Raheem Sterling says he is seeking 'progress over perfection' following his court case

Sterling pleaded guilty to dangerous driving and drug possession after crashing his £270,000 Lamborghini in May

The 31-year-old was charged with dangerous driving and possession of laughing gas after swerving his car on the M25 and M3

Sterling is asked 'can you jump out for me' and who was at the wheel at the time of the crash, but does not reply.

The officer adds: 'So you refuse to answer, okay.'

Sterling is told to get out of the car, asked his name and age at the roadside and to 'put the phone down, stop playing games. Stop tensing up.'

The former Manchester City and Chelsea star, who won the PFA Young Player of the Year award in 2018-19, is then read his rights as he is arrested after being asked to put his arms behind his back.

His arrest, near the Minley interchange on the M3 in Hampshire, happened four weeks after he had returned to the UK following the end of an abortive attempt to revive his football career at Dutch club Feyenoord. He remains without a club.

Sterling, from Berkshire, pleaded guilty on Tuesday to dangerous driving, possession of nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation and failing to provide a specimen after a single vehicle collision at 8.45am on May 28. Police found six cannisters of nitrous oxide in his car.

Basingstoke Magistrates' Court heard that Sterling was so impaired by the laughing gas that he was unable to perform basic police station tests like placing his finger on his nose or placing one foot in front of another.

Barrister Simon Jones, prosecuting, said of Sterling: 'He appeared to be quiet, withdrawn and lethargic and actively fidgeting. Eye lids drooping consistent with fatigue or drug impairment. He said he was feeling very cold, despite this being in the middle of a heatwave with 33-degree temperatures.'

Motorist Fiona Jennings told police she had looked across to witness the driver of the Lamborghini with a balloon in front of his face which was so big she thought it was an air bag.

Image issued by the Crown Prosecution Service shows the damage to the Lamborghini Urus being driven by Sterling

The former England international was pictured arriving in court today to face charges following a car crash in May

Sterling, from Berkshire, pleaded guilty on Tuesday to dangerous driving, possession of nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation and failing to provide a specimen

It was so big that 'she had no idea how the driver would have been able to see the road ahead,' Mr Jones said. Ms Jennings described Sterling's driving as 'absolutely horrendous' and expressed 'genuine concern that the driver may kill someone.'

Evidence presented to court suggested Sterling was also inhaling laughing gas while at the wheel of the Lamborghini a full seven hours before his arrest.

A concerned witness called police after seeing the driver of the same car entering a McDonalds car park alarmingly fast at 1.10am the same morning and seeing the driver holding up 'a pink, inflated balloon.'

By 7.45am that morning, another motorist concerned by the Lamborghini erratically changing lanes, saw the driver placing a white balloon to his mouth and inhaling its contents. For 30 minutes, that motorist watched the vehicle weave from inside to outside lane and back and come close to smashing into the central reservation.

It was after Sterling had left the M3 near Farnborough, Hampshire, hit the gate and come to halt with the tyres of his wheels ripped up, that police found him sitting in T-shirt and shorts in the passenger seat of the car.

One officer told him to 'stop tensing up' after he had stepped out of the car. Sterling replied: 'I'm not tensing up.' Sterling provided breath tests, which established he was not under the influence of cannabis, cocaine or alcohol. But he later refused requests for a blood test, insisting that a lawyer of his choosing must be present, having rejected the offer of a duty solicitor. He also refused to answer any police questions.

Mr Jones said of Sterling's conduct: 'He was attempting to impose a condition on provision of a specimen. He was told the investigation could not be delayed for that reason. At the roadside, there was cooperation without the need for legal advice. When the search for the presence of drugs started, the cooperation ended.'

Sterling's barrister, Jason Bartfeld QC, told the court that there was 'extensive personal mitigation' in his case and that the footballer had taken 'voluntary steps to mitigate his difficulties.'

Mr Bartfeld agreed that this was a 'top category case' because it was a prolonged period of dangerous driving and Sterling was suffering 'serious impairment'. But he said the nitrous oxide would only have caused impairment in 'short periods' and that the chemical did not pose the same risks as cannabis or alcohol.

He claimed police had left Sterling confused about the blood sample. Sterling later told police in a statement: 'I asked for a solicitor. I did not fully understand I had not slept all night and was tired and confused.'

Sterling could face a maximum two years' imprisonment. The case was adjourned until November for pre-sentencing reports.

Sports.title: Celtic supporters' bus bursts into FLAMES: Emergency services rush to scene in Glasgow to evacuate fans after Old Firm derby
Sports.content:
A group of football fans suffered a major scare as their coach went up in flames following Sunday's Old Firm derby.

As frustrated Celtic fans headed for home having seen their side lose 1-0 at Parkhead to their bitterest rivals Rangers, the biggest concern of the day was still to come.

As a group of Celtic fans travelled home the rear of their coach caught fire on the A728 near to the Emirates Arena.

Thick black smoke soon dominated the Glasgow sky as fans were quickly evacuated and moved to safety as emergency services rushed to the scene in the east end of the city.

Police Scotland have confirmed nobody was injured.

But in a latest twist, McLean's Coaches, who own, the coach, believe 'vandalism' caused the fire.

A group of Celtic fans were evacuated as their coach home burst into flames after the match

A statement from McLean's Coaches, shared by the Daily Record, after the fire claimed: 'We are aware of an incident involving one of our coaches on the Clyde Gateway earlier today. Based on the initial information and images we have received, we have reason to believe the incident may have been caused by vandalism.

'The matter has been reported to the relevant authorities, who are investigating the circumstances. The vehicle has been recovered and will undergo a full inspection.'

Two fire engines were seen on site with the Clyde Gateway brought to a standstill as the blaze was tackled and eventually halted with stunned fans watching on from the side of the road.

It marked the end to a disappointing day for those rooting for Celtic after they were narrowly beaten.

Ryan Naderi's first half strike was enough by the time the final whistle sounded as Celtic's misery was compounded by the fact that they have now lost to Rangers twice in the space of eight days.

Sports.title: Jamie Carragher insists £116m Liverpool star Florian Wirtz must be DROPPED by Andoni Iraola after his 'poorest performance' in a Reds shirt against Bournemouth
Sports.content:
Jamie Carragher insists £116m Liverpool star Florian Wirtz must be DROPPED by Andoni Iraola after his 'poorest performance' in a Reds shirt against Bournemouth

Jamie Carragher believes Florian Wirtz must be dropped by Liverpool after 'one of his poorest' performances in a red shirt at Bournemouth.

The £116million attacker has flattered to deceive since pitching up from Bayer Leverkusen and Liverpool legend Carragher was left totally unimpressed with his showing on the south coast.

'That was one of the poorest I've ever seen him in a Liverpool shirt,' Carragher, said, speaking on the new Jamie Carragher Podcast.

'I've been critical of the fact that he hasn't got the numbers. But normally when you watch Wirtz, he's neat and tidy, he keeps possession, there's things that you like. He gets out of a tight situation where you're normally expecting your player to lose the ball.

'But the reason I worry is, I don't think Wirtz is in poor form since he came to Liverpool. I actually think what we're seeing is what he is.'

Carragher's comments laid bare just how little Wirtz has done to convince of his talents in England, with the Sky pundit adding that he simply doesn't see 'how he's going to hurt' teams.

Florian Wirtz (left) needs to be dropped when Liverpool face Man City, says Jamie Carragher

Wirtz (right) once again struggled to exert any influence when Liverpool faced Bournemouth

'The gap he's got to get to almost justify what people were expecting, I almost think is too big. You can't get there,' Carragher added as part of his damning assessment.

'Even if he improves a bit and gets there, it's still not what Liverpool thought they were getting.

'And it's not just Wirtz, it's the knock-on effect. So when he plays at No 10, it means Dominik Szoboszlai has to play central midfield. I don't think Szoboszlai is a central-midfield player, I don't.'

Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola now goes into a three-week international break with plenty ponder ahead of a return to action against league leaders Manchester City on October 11.

'I think going forward Iraola's got a decision to make here. Wirtz would not be in my Liverpool team,' Carragher added.

'I thought this Bournemouth game was a big game for Wirtz. Because if he doesn't produce [against Bournemouth], he's then going to have a three-week break.

'By the time we come back, we're into October. Before you know it, it'll be Christmas in six to eight weeks, or it'll feel like we're getting to Christmas. He has to do something!

'Wirtz wouldn't be in my Liverpool team. Manchester City at home, for me, he can't be in the team.'

Sports.title: How Led Zeppelin-loving anglophile from Los Angeles, who worships Jeremy Clarkson, beat Rory McIlroy to land PGA title, as Spanish outsider chokes to miss out on £1.3m prize
Sports.content:
For JJ Spaun, the Led Zeppelin-loving anglophile from Los Angeles, there was a fairway to heaven at the BMW Championship. For Rory McIlroy, a resident on the Wentworth estate, there was a near miss and a short journey home to process it.

Whatever difficulties McIlroy is experiencing with his swing, he was sufficiently grooved to card a 68 and a 15-under-par finish that left the world No2 two strokes behind Spaun.

If there were frustrations about his proximity to victory, then they were nothing compared to the plight of Manuel Elvira. Heard of him? If you hadn’t then that would make most of us.

Ranked 296th in the world, and without a win of any description in his eight years as a professional, the Spaniard, 30, had the DP World Tour’s flagship event in the palm of his hands. And then he suffered one of those gut-squeezing chokes that crop up in this maddening game.

His dramas came on the fairway of the 18th hole, a par five, where he stood at 17 under par. His drive had left 228 yards to the front of the green and this hole had been a birdie-fest all week. With Spaun already in the clubhouse, a par would have guaranteed Elvira a play-off; a four would be worth £1.3million and more than the rest of his journeyman career combined.

What followed was somewhat soul destroying. Having made the nervy decision to lay-up short of the creek, Elvira committed the cardinal sin of missing the fairway and finding a bunker. From there, it got so much worse – he flew his recovery to the foot of the 18th grandstand, where his ball nearly hit a group of journalists, and Elvira then proceeded to duff his fourth into another bunker.

On his victory, Spaun said: ‘It means so much. I've kind of blossomed into this player I never thought I could be'

JJ Spaun's wife Melody accompanied his final round with a Jeremy Clarkson mask on a stick

Rory McIroy's second place means he is only just behind Patrick Reed in the Race to Dubai

By the time his ball disappeared below ground, after his seventh stroke, the series of blunders had cost him around £800,000. A cheque of approximately £500,000 for a share of second place with McIlroy, Aaron Rai and Adam Scott is nothing to be sniffed at, but the tears of his wife at greenside told their own story.

His reaction after signing for a 70: ‘Devastated.’

The spoils instead went to a man who admitted he was playing with a ‘chip on my shoulder’. That was Spaun, the 2025 US Open champion who recently incurred the surprise indignity of being left out of the American team for the Presidents Cup.

Channelling his energies on a trip to Surrey, the late-blooming 36-year-old made his point emphatically with this performance – his closing 67 started with a bogey and not a single blemish followed. Finishing with four birdies in his final five holes, he sealed the deal in style.

That it occurred in England was notable for the fact he is besotted with this country. He and his wife regularly spend holidays in the Cotswolds and more recently he has become addicted to watching Clarkson’s Farm on Amazon Prime – his wife Melody accompanied his final round with a Jeremy Clarkson mask on the end of a stick. Each to their own.

On his victory, Spaun said: ‘It means so much. I've kind of blossomed into this player I never thought I could be. England is a place that's dear to my family's heart and the stars kind of aligned this week for me to come out on top.’

Detailing the Clarkson infatuation, Spaun added: ‘We've grown fond of him, along with the English culture. We take holidays in December in the Cotswolds, and we really enjoy his show. I went to his pub, The Farmer's Dog, with the hopes to catch a glimpse of him but he wasn't around.

‘My wife said we would have a surprise guest following us this week if I competed in the tournament and sure enough on Friday morning I saw the face of Jeremy Clarkson and her holding it. Jeremy was there in spirit and I think he brought me good fortune.’

Golf is nothing if not utterly mystifying. In McIlroy’s case, that extends to understanding his swing, which he warned might take five or six months to fix but looked pretty handy here. His tie for second place means he is only marginally behind Patrick Reed in the Race to Dubai standings for the final two months of the season. If McIlroy can pass the American, he will win the order of merit for an eighth time, equalling Colin Montgomerie.

‘I had my chances out there,’ McIlroy said. ‘I putted OK for the most part this week but I missed a lot of putts. I wish I had some of those putts back but I have to be encouraged with where my game is at.

‘I hit the ball really well today and I’m encouraged with the signs. I just have to keep working at it.

‘I have three events until the end of my DP World Tour season. I'm not sure what Patrick's schedule looks like coming up, but I feel like I have enough opportunities. It would be obviously amazing to match Monty's record.’

Sports.title: Only a late stroke of luck spared dismal Man United defeat at struggling Fulham, but it's Sir Jim Ratcliffe - not Michael Carrick - who must take the blame for his club's worsening crisis, writes OLIVER HOLT
Sports.content:
There is a pub on Fulham High Street called The Eight Bells.

Paper signs on the windows say that it is reserved for away fans only and on Sunday afternoon, the strains of Manchester United supporters singing in support of their team drifted into the afternoon sunshine before the game.

It is reputed to be Fulham's oldest pub. In fact, there are unsubstantiated claims it is even older than United's back-four. It might have been more appropriate if it was called The Seven Bells, because that is what United got knocked out of them for much of their clash with Alvaro Arbeloa's side at Craven Cottage.

They were outplayed for long periods of the match but escaped with a 1-1 draw after a stroke of luck in the dying minutes brought them a last-gasp equaliser.

They salvaged a little pride but not much. They have five points from their opening five games against Hull City, Ipswich Town, Everton, Manchester City and Fulham.

A season that began with some hopes of them challenging for the title has collapsed into a situation where they are 10 points behind Manchester City before we have even entered the last week of September. Sir Jim Ratcliffe, their minority owner, is an expert on once great things now 'on the slide'. He has added United to his portfolio.

Manchester United are facing more questions than answers after a 1-1 draw away at Fulham

Michael Carrick watched on in dismay as his side looked second best away against Fulham

'It is quite difficult to see how we arrest it,' Sir Jim said of the UK's travails. That sounds like a dispiritingly familiar refrain to United fans.

It is 13 years since they last won the Premier League title and it will be 14 in May. They are too far behind City and Arsenal already to have any chance of ending their drought.

They had some momentum coming into this campaign. Now they have none.

Manager Michael Carrick will get some of the blame for that but this is not his fault. The horror show that is unfolding now is the fault of Sir Jim and his band of hapless executives who masterminded a dreadful summer transfer window that has left United hopelessly adrift of their rivals.

Knocked out of the Carabao Cup by Brighton last week, spurned by the greatest of their young talents, JJ Gabriel, and at war with their own supporters, United had chances and hit the woodwork twice but they looked more predictable and more weary than Fulham.

This was a Fulham, by the way, that were bottom of the table at the start of play but looked more imaginative, more optimistic, more youthful and more coherent than their opponents.

Fulham's point took them above Tottenham Hotspur, who will spend the three weeks of the international break rooted to the foot of the division.

United had spent the first few minutes of the game chasing lengthening shadows. Fulham played the ball about confidently and patiently. They evaded United's half-hearted attempts to press them until a ball was fizzed in to Gonzalo Garcia on the edge of the United box. Garcia snatched at his shot and dragged it wide but it was a chastening start for the visitors.

Lisandro Martinez deflected the ball past a helpless Senne Lammens in the Man United goal

Calvin Bassey wheeled away in celebration after his initial strike eventually led to the first goal

It was a tough watch for Manchester United's travelling fans, who saw a side devoid of energy

When United finally established a foothold in the game, they nearly took the lead. Lisandro Martinez ran on to a loose ball and hit a dipping swerving shot from 25 yards that was destined for the top corner until Bernd Leno launched himself through the air and tipped it wide.

United came close again midway through the half. Matheus Cunha stole the ball away from a Fulham defender as he tried to shepherd it out of play and pulled the ball back for Bruno Fernandes.

Fernandes clipped it towards goal but the ball rolled against the foot of Leno's right-hand post and dribbled away to safety.

United had made the best chances but Fulham had been the better team.

That dynamic shifted after half an hour when Garcia had a golden chance to put Fulham ahead but miskicked in front of goal as he tried to convert Alex Iwobi's cross. Lammens saved well when Sander Berge tried to convert the loose ball.

Then it was the turn of Josh King to go close. King should have been included in Thomas Tuchel's England squad after an outstanding start to this season but was overlooked. Everything about his play in this match showed why he should have been picked.

Fifteen minutes before half-time, he jinked past Luke Shaw with ease and rifled in a shot that Lammens kept out with his right boot.

In the midst of Fulham's missed chances, United hit the woodwork again. Cunha's shot from the edge of the area deflected off a defender and spun up into the air. It was looping over Leno until the goalkeeper got a hand to it and touched it on to the post. United were being outplayed but they were always in the game.

A minute before the break, Marcus Rashford volleyed over from ten yards out. At the other end, King went past Maguire and fell to the ground as Maguire's arm brushed him on his way through.

It was not a foul but nor was it the yellow card that referee Peter Bankes brandished at King.

Matheus Cunha's late deflected strike ensured Manchester United left with something

The second half started slowly but exploded into life just after the hour. Calvin Bassey wrestled the ball away from Cunha on the edge of the United box and unleashed a fierce left-foot drive. Lammens blocked it with his left leg but the ball rebounded to Martinez.

The Argentina defender could not react quickly enough to control it and it bounced off him and back towards goal. Lammens tried to clear it but got his feet in a tangle and deflected it into his own net. Martinez turned away in dismay.

United thought they had equalised minutes later. Bryan Mbeumo curled a shot goalwards and began to wheel away to celebrate before Leno pulled off a magnificent, flying one-handed save that preserved Fulham's lead.

United dominated possession after that but showed little in the way of cutting edge. It took a slice of fortune to drag them level. Fulham held on until two minutes from the end but then Cunha cut in from the left and fired in a shot. Leno had it covered but it deflected off David Affengruber's outstretched foot and bobbled apologetically over the line.

Sports.title: RIATH AL-SAMARRAI: It's all very well Howard Webb sending his VAR bunglers to the naughty step - but those that know him tell me 'back-stabbing' referee supremo must look in the mirror
Sports.content:
Matt Donohue and Blake Antrobus will have a sharper grasp of what it means to interfere with play this weekend. On account of their VAR blunders at the Manchester derby, Howard Webb has decreed they won’t have that option in the Premier League for the foreseeable future.

We know enough by now about their journey to the naughty step. But what about their boss? What about Webb?

How many of these malfunctions need occur before the guy in charge of refereeing takes a look closer to home?

He gave his opinion on Tuesday, which is to say he took a dim view of how his best official, Michael Oliver, saw a correct decision to disallow Erling Haaland’s winner overruled by his eyes in the sky. When Webb reviewed it all, he blamed Donohue’s ‘tunnel vision’ on Haaland and Antrobus was guilty of following Donohue down the same hole.

Neither of them factored for the obvious, that Enzo Fernandez was offside and interfering, and each of them will spend some time below ground as a consequence.

‘They'll not be officiating again until after the international break,’ said Webb.

Howard Webb may have a few questions of his own to answer if the Premier League refereeing standards keep slipping

Enzo Fernandez clearly interferes with play in the Manchester derby but it was missed by the VAR officials, who have now been stood down by Webb

I chatted over a few of these sentiments with a former Premier League referee on Friday and there was no disagreement about standing down the officials. Donohue, the VAR, and Antrobus, his assistant, had committed a cock-up in a high-profile game. Of course they should be benched for a while, we agreed.

But the issue was the man whose organisation put them there in the first place. That being the man who was also responsible for the training and refinement of Michael Salisbury, Lee Mason, John Brooks, Darren England and Dan Cook.

What do they have in common? They have all been in the VAR booth since Webb took over at what was then known as the PGMOL in late 2022 and they have all sat on that naughty step for human errors in their handling of the machine era. Salisbury has visited it more than once.

Errors will happen. That is fine. And it is also fine to view VAR as the worst encroachment in the recent history of the game; a joy-sucking, time-wasting, immensely flawed attempt to find a level of perfection that sport never needed and won’t be delivered. That’s my view and immediate abolition is my wish.

But so long as it exists, where is the accountability from Webb for its botched application in the Premier League? How many people have to be stood down for huge mistakes on his watch before Webb himself stands down?

To follow my conversations with those who have worked with him is to construct a complicated portrait. ‘He’s a clever man and he can be very charming,’ one former official tells me. ‘He can be very impressive, but he is also a master politician and will stab you in the back if it suits him.’

We can take those thoughts or leave them – refereeing is a competitive world. They can bitch and moan about a colleague as well as the best of us.

But other observations go deeper, namely around his key appointments, which include the import of Kevin Blom from the Dutch Eredivisie as performance coach and Hugh Dallas as manager of Pro Ref’s select group.

Erling Haaland celebrates the goal that should not have stood but that won the Manchester derby

Referee Michael Oliver takes his instructions from the VAR in Stockley Park

Dallas was fourth official in the 2002 World Cup final, so his credentials have merit; Blom is perhaps more famous in Scotland over a bad penalty decision that favoured Czech Republic in a Euro 2012 qualifier.

The latter is part of the tit-for-tat of football, but there is a perception in some quarters that they do not pose enough of a challenge to Webb’s leadership. In other words, who is keeping the boss in check?

As a former Premier League referee put it: ‘As ex-referees, we are asking: “Really, are you really surrounding yourself with these people?” It’s so Howard can be comfortable. I think he will always want people who he can be above.’

Only Webb will know if that’s true. But it is hard to deny that a vast amount of Premier League expertise has been lost to the migration of officials elsewhere once they leave the frontline.

Martin Atkinson refereed in the Premier League for more than 20 years, and then led the select group, but he is now the VAR manager for the Scottish FA. Jon Moss oversaw almost 300 top-flight games and left Webb’s PGMOL in 2024 – he is now head of refereeing at Football Australia. Mark Clattenburg presided over a Champions League final and today works on Gladiators.

All of them will have their reasons for being where they are and all of them dropped the occasional clanger. That’s football. That’s refereeing.

But it also looks a little like a drain of know-how that would doubtless help in the English game, where the quirks and rhythms are a unique challenge to officials.

I tend to doubt the idea that the VAR system is better implemented abroad, because statistics around the error rates across the major European leagues are fairly consistent.

Why is former referee Mark Clattenburg working on Gladiators and not helping out in the Premier League?

Martin Atkinson refereed in the Premier League for more than 20 years but he is now the VAR manager for the Scottish FA

I would also suggest that Webb is hardly the face of gross incompetence – one former colleague of his says that he is a better manager than his predecessor, Mike Riley, and worse at training referees.

Equally, some applaud the greater transparency he has pursued with video analysis on television; others say the referees ‘hate’ it.

It’s a tricky picture to study. It’s certainly far tougher to interpret than the one showing Enzo Fernandez interfering with play in front of the Manchester United goalkeeper. But one thing is clear – Webb cannot persist with the charade of blaming everyone except himself.

Sports.title: Pierre Sage appears to have saved his job at Crystal Palace for now after his well-drilled side played out a disciplined stalemate against Leeds, writes BOBBY MANZI
Sports.content:
Pierre Sage will be breathing a sigh of relief heading into the international break.

The pressure was on as Crystal Palace travelled to Leeds United with whispers suggesting Sage could become the first manager sacked if the performance was unpropitious.

In his post-match press conference, Sage admitted that he felt the pressure. ‘When I read social media, there is big pressure,’ Sage said. ‘I don’t care about it. I do my job honestly, I give my best with my skills and limits and at the end I have no regrets with what I do.’

At Leeds, they may not have won but their second positive Premier League result was a step in the right direction after conceding 11 goals in the first four league games.

Palace defended as a cohesive, disciplined unit - keeping a league clean sheet for the first time in the Sage era.

This was the second time this week Palace did not concede after beating Lech Poznan 4-0 in their maiden Europa League tie on Thursday. But the manner of those defensive performances were entirely different.

Palace were fragile defensively in Europe and offered chances a better attacking team would have taken. On Sunday, though, Palace were rejuvenated.

Leeds scarcely threatened as Palace nullified their frontline. Dominic Calvert-Lewin was denied from six yards after a fantastic stop from Walter Benitez, but aside from that, there were no real nervy moments.

Pierre Sage appears to have bought himself time as Crystal Palace manager

Chris Richards significantly improved against Leeds United after a slow start to the season

Takehiro Tomiyasu, who started at central centre-back and was a standout performer in the first half, was forced off at the break. Their control did not suffer, though, as Jefferson Lerma replaced him and Richards shifted into the middle.

That, in itself, is progress. Palace's back three has changed in every Premier League game this season and, as a result, they have lacked consistency and understanding.

But here, they won their duels and did not give the ball away as cheaply. Jaydee Canvot, who was dropped in the previous two games, improved drastically and made a vital interception in the dying minutes to prevent Calvert-Lewin from bombing through on goal.

Palace had planned to consider Sage's future at the beginning of the three-week-long international break. This performance, though, makes a managerial change implausible and unjustifiable.

The result should settle the nerves and fears. Offensively, Palace were laboured but a boring game with a solid defensive performance is exactly what they needed to restore confidence in the group.

In their five games this season, Palace have either matched or bettered their results from last term against the same opposition. Last term at Leeds, they could not handle the atmosphere and were thrashed 4-1. This time, they were fearless.

Even if Palace had lost at Leeds, sacking him would have been questionable. The offensive ideas are exciting, the defence has just struggled to click.

He has been trying to change the style of play, pressing higher and playing on the front foot and that has exposed the defensive weaknesses. Effective transformation cannot be achieved overnight, though. He requires time to integrate his ideas.

He came into a new job with two of his centre-backs signed in the final week of the window while the club did not purchase a replacement for Maxence Lacroix, relying on Axel Disasi on loan from Chelsea instead.

His other options were Richards, who struggled to settle without Lacroix's presence guiding him through games, and Canvot, a developing teenager who makes the occasional mistake.

For all the problems thrown Sage’s way, he has dealt with them calmly. He deserves time to implement his ideas. At Lens, he showed he can get a team competing above their perceived level, finishing second to PSG and winning the French Cup.

He is a talented, young and progressive manager. That was the right style of appointment in the summer and remains exactly what Palace need. Sacking him would have been premature and the response at Leeds, who are unbeaten this season, proved that.

Leeds should be aiming for Europe

Daniel Farke’s side, meanwhile, continued their impressive start to the season - remaining unbeaten after five games.

This was a far cry from the free-flowing Leeds played when they bossed Newcastle on Monday night. They were passive and crafted just one clear-cut chance against Palace’s resolute defence. But Farke admitted that it cannot be perfect every week.

‘It’s mixed emotions,’ Farke said. ‘We would have preferred to win but the reality is there are not 38 games with magic nights under the floodlights and champagne football where you overrun the opponent and score goals for fun.

‘Sometimes there are scrappy Sunday afternoons where we must dig in. I liked the clean sheet, extending the unbeaten run and the attitude to fight for every point where we tried to dig in.’

Daniel Farke admitted post-match that his side cannot play 'champagne football' every week after following up their 4-1 win against Newcastle with a goalless draw

His team did show defensive grit, too. Much like Palace, they were disciplined and made it tough for the opposition to break them down.

In goal, James Trafford made five saves and was key to securing a point.

Even though Leeds were heavily fancied, the result is overwhelmingly positive given they were not at their best but still managed to take something from the game. That is often the sign of a good team.

With nine English teams in Europe this season, Leeds should be contending for a European spot - taking advantage of their beneficial schedule while rivals slog through a 50-game-plus season.

The litmus test will come after the international break, though, with tough matches against Arsenal, Manchester United, Sunderland and Bournemouth in October.

Sports.title: Micah Richards reveals he would not have been able to cover England's World Cup game live on the BBC after the death of his dad without Mark Chapman
Sports.content:
Micah Richards has opened up on how his BBC colleague Mark Chapman helped him cope with the unexpected death of his father, Lincoln, on the day of England's semi-final against Argentina.

Richards, 38, was preparing to go on air with the broadcaster in Atlanta when he received a phone call from his brother informing him that Lincoln had died at the age of 66.

The former Manchester City defender went ahead with his punditry duties alongside Joe Hart and Wayne Rooney, aided by presenter Chapman.

He told The Sunday Times: 'On the day it happened my brother rang me, before the semi-final, and I’m going into it thinking how am I going to perform here? How am I going to act? I was on the phone to Chappers (Mark Chapman) for an hour. And he was saying, "Your dad would have wanted you to do it. This is what you’ve worked for since you’ve come into punditry."

'I didn’t want to tell Joe and Wayne, because I’ve known Joe since I was 17 and didn’t want to affect them, and Chappers said, "If in the first ten minutes you’re having a wobble let me know and we can just continue with the rest of the guys."

'If it wasn’t for him, I wouldn’t have got through it. One hundred per cent. And it was weird because when I’m on camera I’m sort of loud and obnoxious at times, but if you watch the footage I keep tapping my foot. I was just trying to hold it together.'

The former Manchester City defender revealed that he heard the news moments before going on air for the BBC's coverage of England's World Cup semi-final defeat by Argentina

News of Richards' heartbreak only emerged after the broadcast, which was watched by 24 million people, when he shared an emotional post on social media.

He wrote: 'Not long before going on air today, I received the awful news that my father Lincoln had passed away.

'His death was unexpected, and he has left us all too soon. He was my greatest fan. He barely missed a game my entire life.

'He would take me wherever I needed to go when I was a kid and he was the proudest parent possible during my professional career.

'It was so rare for him to not be by my side.

'I know how much watching England World Cup games means to everyone at home, and how the experience bonds families together across the generations, like nothing else.

'I know, particularly as a proud old-school Yorkshireman, Dad would’ve wanted the show to go on this evening. And so it did.

'Thinking of my siblings and all my wider family today as we remember my father Lincoln, my hero and inspiration.'

Micah Richards' father Lincoln, right, has died, the pundit said in an emotional social media post

Richards, whose middle name is Lincoln, has regularly praised the influence of his father – who came to the UK from St Kitts in the 1960s - on his career.

'I grew up in Chapeltown, a rough area of Leeds,' Richards said in 2007. 'There was all sorts of stuff – drugs and fighting. There is a point when you are 15 or 16 when you might want to get involved in it. There was definitely a temptation but I stayed grounded.

'I have been able to deal with all the stuff that has come my way. That's down to Dad. He's brought me up well. My Dad is a strong character. He is very principled. He's a Rastafarian. He has set standards for me.

'It's been great to have that sort of person behind me but at the same time I learned how to be my own man. Dad's always been here for me. He has missed only one game I have ever played in and that was my debut at Arsenal when I wasn't even been supposed to be in the squad.'

In 2023, Richards described his father as 'my rock and my hero' but said their relationship had changed after his dad and mother, Heather, separated.

In his interview with the Sunday Times, Richards described how his retirement from playing football had left his father, who he described as having found 'a purpose' following his career and attending his games, taking 'a turn for the worse'.

Sports.title: Furious Fulham boss Alvaro Arbeloa claims referees 'don't like Man Utd to lose'
Sports.content:
Furious Fulham boss Alvaro Arbeloa claims referees 'don't like Man Utd to lose'

Fulham are still without their first Premier League win under new boss Alvaro Arbeloa after being pegged back late on by Manchester United at Craven Cottage on Sunday afternoon

View 2 Images Alvaro Arbeloa was far from happy after Fulham's draw with Manchester United (Image: Getty Images)

Alvaro Arbeloa sensationally claimed referees 'don't like' Manchester United losing after Fulham's late draw. The Londoners looked on their way to their first Premier League victory under the Spanish coach.

‌



Lisandro Martinez had put through his own net to give Fulham the lead, only for Matheus Cunha's late deflected effort to ensure a share of the points.

‌



And while Arbeloa bemoaned his side's fortune for not being able to hold out for a much-needed win, he also took aim at the referees for not awarding a foul by Harry Maguire just seconds before United's equaliser.

‌



Arbeloa said: "We were so, so close. We were a little unlucky again but we know it was going to be difficult against a big team and we have seen what the referee has been doing through the match.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

‌



"There were so many things for them, you can see it in the foul by [Harry] Maguire. Every decision was for them. I knew after the game against Manchester City that they don't like Manchester United to lose.

"We were so, so close to our first victory that we are a little bit upset now. I think we did a good game.

"Obviously not an easy game for us, we were in the bottom position but we saw personality with the ball, we were brave. We had moments where we had to defend but in general we did a good game.

‌



"We wanted to control the transition and the counter attacks. We know they put too many people inside so we have to control the space behind our midfielders. They sometimes found the spaces, it is a difficult match against a big team and for me they will be near the top of the league by the end of the season.

View 2 Images Alvaro Arbeloa was left furious at the referee following Fulham's draw with Man Utd (Image: Getty Images)

"Now we have to find the first victory. If you see our first five games we have already played Man Utd, Chelsea, at Anfield, at Sunderland.

Article continues below

"Now we have an October that will be so important for us. We have shown the team we want to be and if we play in this way the victories will come."

Arbeloa now has a few weeks to stew on Fulham’s failure to secure victory against United, with the Premier League due to take a break due to the first international window of the season. Their next opportunity for victory is set to come in three weeks’ time as they take on newly-promoted Ipswich.

Sports.title: Premier League propose big Carabao Cup change in £1.8bn 'new deal for football'
Sports.content:
Premier League propose big Carabao Cup change in £1.8bn 'new deal for football'

The Premier League are offering the English Football League a 'new deal for football' worth £1.8billion, but they now want one massive change to the Carabao Cup

View 2 Images Premier League clubs wants changes to the Carabao Cup semi-finals (Image: Liverpool FC via Getty Images)

The Premier League reportedly want Carabao Cup semi-final ties to be decided over one match rather than two as part of a 'new deal for football'. A proposed agreement with the English Football League is said to effectively double the existing solidarity payment, which is divided among clubs across all three EFL divisions, to £1.8billion.

‌



It would be spread across 10 seasons, and both leagues are reportedly around £27million apart in negotiations. However, there is growing confidence of an agreement.

‌



Premier League clubs have unanimously approved the proposal. EFL sides doing likewise would avoid any involvement by the Independent Football Regulator (IFR).

‌



Andros Townsend delivers perfect response after being run over by pitch roller in freak accident READ MORE :

Richarlison takes to social media with clear message after Tottenham lose again READ MORE :

The Daily Mail reports that another condition of their additional funding would be to progress talks with the National League over new clubs earning League Two promotion every season. They cite sources that claim the Premier League wants to reduce its reliance on ownership funding for EFL clubs.

Controls on how these funds are spent are proposed, including a stop on any increases in player wages. The proposition also requires 15% of the funds to go towards infrastructure.

It also features a 'lifeboat fund' for clubs entering administration in future. They would be loaned £20million to continue paying essential creditors and operating.

‌



View 2 Images The Carabao Cup semi-finals could stopping being two-legged ties (Image: Paul Currie/Shutterstock)

The EFL want a tweak to their current divisional split of 80:12:8 between the Championship, League One and League Two. Despite the Premier League seeking no change, a change to 75:15:10 is being sought.

Under the new split, based on a mid-table finish, Championship clubs would receive £8.5million more, rising from £12.1million to £20.6million. That translates to a £1.3million uplift in League One, up from £2.5million to £3.8million, whereas League Two payments would grow by £700k, from £1.8million to £2.5million. A 2% increase in the Premier League transfer levy is to cover the increase, which would go from 4% to 6%.

‌



JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

The deal is around 17.5% of what all top-flight clubs earn from their collective broadcast rights. That is 6.5% more than the current level, but half of what the EFL initially sought.

EFL clubs were told about the proposal last week. They will make the final decision once it is ready for the league's board to recommend.

Article continues below

The deal has already been under discussion for six weeks now. It is said that the EFL prefers to wait until the IFR's State of the Game report, which is due to be published by them on 12 October.
