Garcia subsequently returned an adverse finding for ostarine following his 2024 victory over Devin Haney, which he also denied intentionally taking.

Both men were asked at the fight's press conference whether they had concerns that the other could use performance-enhancing drugs ahead of Saturday's contest.

Neither appeared keen to make it a central issue, with the focus instead returning to the fight itself.

Ryan Garcia, Benn's opponent, has also had controversy in his career over positive drug tests

Garcia has also questioned whether Benn's career has prepared him for this level of opposition, arguing that the Briton is taking a step too far by challenging for the world title.

JEFF POWELL IN LAS VEGAS An advance guard of a couple of hundred UK fight fans arrived here in time to see Conor Benn stage a public work-out three days before he challenges Ryan Garcia for the world welterweight title in the intimidating T-Mobile Arena. They kicked up a din as Benn went through a few minutes of snappy pad work in a temporary ring pitched between a bar waiting to serve them and the MGM Grand Casino’s sports book. While admitting he can’t wait to wolf down fish and chips after all the dieting to make the 147lbs welter limit he assured them: ‘I feel great and I’ll give my all to give you all a night to remember.’ But he refrained from removing his top to give them a glimpse of his body. Both he and Garcia looked sharp and calm in their brief appearances. The Benn faithful will be heavily outnumbered on Saturday night by the Americans and Mexicans rooting for King Ry but they are in good voice.

Benn's response was typically blunt. 'How is this too far? He quit against Tank Davis. He got outclassed by Rolly [Romero], and then got a world title shot with Barrios,' he said.

'Then there is me. Stepping up to fight the contenders up at middleweight, fight of the year up at middleweight, avenging my loss. Two big stadium shows. Just come off beating a two-time former world champion and having to make 147, which again I ain't made in four years in six weeks.

'What's he talking about? Ultimately, who cares what he thinks? I don't listen to quitters anyway.'

For all the talk, though, the immediate challenge is the scales. Benn has to get himself back down to a weight he has not made since 2022, before attempting to deal with one of boxing's fastest and most dangerous punchers.

He accepts it will not be straightforward, but he remains convinced the doubts surrounding him will only add to his motivation.

'If I'd listened to everyone that didn't believe in me, I'd be nowhere,' he said. 'But I continue to believe in me. And that's all that matters… you believing in yourself. I believe in me to get me to where I am right now, to revenge that loss against Eubank, to put on Fight of the Year against Eubank, to then fight for the WBC world title.

'I don't need nobody else to believe in me. Continue to doubt me because doubt fuels the fire.'

Sports.title: Katie Taylor is crowned undisputed champion for a THIRD time with unanimous decision victory over Flora Pili - as Irish boxing icon, 40, enjoys fairytale end to her career in front of 82,000 fans at sold-out Croke Park
Sports.content:
There will never be another night quite like this for Katie Taylor… or, for that matter, for boxing itself.

Under the lights at Croke Park, in front of 82,000 delirious fans, Ireland's greatest fighter walked into the ring for the final time and left it as a three-time undisputed world champion after defeating Flora Pili on points.

Taylor had dreamed of this moment for much of her life. She had spent more than a decade rewriting the history of women's boxing, collecting world titles, conquering America, avenging the only defeat of her professional career and becoming the undisputed champion not once, but twice.

But nothing could have prepared her for this.

The noise inside Croke Park was deafening as Taylor made her final walk to the ring, the 40-year-old receiving a hero's welcome before facing the undefeated Frenchwoman in the last fight of a career that has transformed boxing in Ireland and beyond.

And when the first bell rang, Taylor set about doing exactly what she had come to Croke Park to do.

Katie Taylor celebrated victory on her farewell fight to become a three-time undisputed champion

Taylor overcame the challenge of Flora Pili, who had been unbeaten in 12 fights as a professional

Taylor appeared in the ring with family and friends are wrapping up her career in style

From the opening round, she demonstrated her speed deploying a lightning-quick jab despite being 11 years older than her opponent.

It was in the second round Pili really felt Taylor's power after taking a strong right hand to the temple.

It got the fans excited but the Frenchwoman weathered the storm before receiving a slap across her face from her trainer in the corner as he urged her to 'wake up'.

Knowing she was down heavily on the scorecards Pili showed conviction in the seventh round but it was never going to be enough to topple the Irish champion.

As the tenth and final round rang in, both fighters touched gloves as a sign of respect. The crowd cheered their champion home as she drew the curtain on her career.

Taylor did everything she could to get the stoppage in the dying seconds of the fight but she had to settle for a points victory.

There was a moment after the final bell when Taylor simply stood and took it all in.

The noise, the tears, the Irish flags, the thousands of people on their feet inside Croke Park and the knowledge that this really was the end.

Taylor emerged to a stunning ovation at a sold-out Croke Park, with 82,000 in attendance

Taylor's husband Sean McCavanagh was among those watching on ringside at the venue

Westlife performed in the build-up to Taylor taking to the ring for the last time in her career

Michael Flatley was among the well-known faces in attendance on the historic night

She had wanted one final night. One final fight. One final chance to walk into the ring in front of her home crowd and remind the world exactly who she was.

She got all three.

Taylor leaves boxing as a three-time undisputed world champion, an Olympic gold medallist and one of the most important figures the sport has ever produced.

But her legacy cannot be measured in belts alone.

She changed women's boxing forever. She gave a generation of young girls a reason to believe that they belonged in a boxing gym. She carried Irish boxing on her shoulders for years and became a sporting icon far beyond the ring.

And perhaps most fittingly of all, she signed off where she had always wanted to be.

At Croke Park. In front of her people. With another world title wrapped around her waist.

The final chapter could not have been written any better.

Katie Taylor came home, became undisputed for the third time and walked away on top.

A champion to the very end.

Sports.title: Time is running out for Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury: AJ is still yet to sign Battle of Britain deal, reveals Frank Warren
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua has still not signed the contract, so the Battle of Britain against Tyson Fury remains in jeopardy.

Time is running out.

Promoter Frank Warren, who suggested that in reality boxing's longest hatching deal had to be finalised by this weekend, says: 'AJ hasn't signed yet.

'Tyson signed in January. He's training in Miami for the fight in early November and doesn't care where it takes place. '

The original agreement stipulated England, putting Wembley Stadium on alert.

But Netflix, the mega-paymasters for the broadcast, have joined their Saudi partners in insisting on New York's fabled Madison Square Garden so as to maximise US revenue.

Anthony Joshua (pictured) is still yet to sign the deal to fight Tyson Fury, Frank Warren has revealed

Warren (right) said Tyson Fury (left) has signed and is already in training for a potential bout

Joshua will need at least a two-month training camp for a fight of this magnitude and ideally nine to ten weeks.

It comes after Joshua was given 10 days to agree a deal on August 26 - seven days ago - with Warren previously warning: 'Unless AJ commits by the end of next week I'm afraid this will slip away like so many of those great fights which never happened.'

He added: 'At some point everyone has to say the most important thing is that it happens. Not this bulls*** about money.

'That everyone wants the fight. Does AJ really want it? I don't know. He's been through that tragedy of the car crash which killed two of his closest friends. Only he knows what he wants.'

Sports.title: Mercedes aims to end pole drought with upcoming Malaysia F1 upgrades
Sports.content:
Mercedes has confirmed its next big Formula 1 car upgrade will arrive at the forthcoming grand prix in Malaysia, where it hopes to get back into contention for pole.

The Silver Arrows is the runaway leader of the 2026 championship with a 145-point advantage over second-placed Ferrari, despite its last major upgrade package being Montreal in May.

Mercedes has instead preferred to fit minor race-specific updates whereas its nearest challengers Ferrari and McLaren have been significantly more aggressive with developments.

So although Mercedes won the first six grands prix, it has since won four of the last eight as McLaren and Ferrari have closed their respective gaps taking two wins each in that time.

But the German outfit is hoping to reestablish its dominance during the Malaysian weekend on 2-4 October, the race after Baku, as the Asian country replaces Bahrain to make its F1 return.

Speaking on the Nu Silver Arrows Radio Show podcast, trackside engineering director Andrew Shovlin said: “We haven't got much new coming to Baku, but actually that's a circuit that's more about drag than downforce.

“So the car was good in Monza, hopefully it will work well in Baku. But, you need a car that can have a good straight line speed.

Toto Wolff, Mercedes, James Allison, Mercedes, Andrew Shovlin, Mercedes Photo by: Sam Bloxham / LAT Images via Getty Images

“There's other things, though, you need in Baku, like the sort of street circuit nature, almost that Monaco-esque being able to deal with the low speed, keeping all the wheels on the ground.

“And then the updates, well, they're going to come Malaysia onwards and hopefully we'll make a decent step.

“I don't think we're going to be out front by miles, but hopefully we'll be back into a position where we can really go into qualifying, knowing that we're fighting for pole.”

Although Mercedes has won the last two races - Monza and Madrid - via the dominant Kimi Antonelli, it hasn’t actually claimed pole since the Italian went quickest at Spa in July.

So that is a run of four, three of which saw McLaren’s Lando Norris take pole, marking a far cry from the start of 2026 where the Silver Arrows took pole for each of the opening 10 rounds.

“Early in the season, we tended to go thinking, we have a car that if we do a really good job, it should be on pole,” added Shovlin.

“We should be fighting for a race win. Whereas now the margin between finishing first and finishing sixth is one or two tenths and it's difficult to predict because Monza is a unique track.

“It needs a car that's quite slippy with low drag and then new circuit like Madring couldn't be more different. But we just focus on getting the most out of the car and if we win, awesome.”

Sports.title: Cadillac F1 owners Mark Walter and TWG Global face class-action lawsuit
Sports.content:
Cadillac Formula 1 shareholder Mark Walter has officially become the subject of a class-action lawsuit, while a concurrent investigation into potential fraud between his insurance companies is ongoing.

The class-action lawsuit was filed in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida, and the complaint alleges that Walter used his firms - TWG Global, alongside Delaware Life Insurance and Group 1001 - to execute a scheme aimed at concealing federal investigations and diverting billions of dollars from policyholders' funds.

The lawsuit claims that insurance companies affiliated with Walter used money from annuity policyholders to finance a broader business network.

This network enabled the mogul to acquire stakes in sports franchises like the Los Angeles Dodgers and the Los Angeles Lakers, before expanding into motorsport through TWG Motorsport (a division of TWG Global) by acquiring Andretti Global and partnering with General Motors to launch the Cadillac F1 team.

Media outlets report that instead of maintaining low-risk investments, the insurers funneled approximately 42% of their assets - around $17 billion - into Walter’s private network of business interests.

The lawsuit was brought by 67-year-old Florida resident Ira Rosner, represented by law firm Robbins Geller Rudman & Dowd, who alleges that the insurance companies intentionally withheld key financial disclosures.

Valtteri Bottas, Cadillac Racing Photo by: Alex Bierens de Haan / LAT Images via Getty Images

USA Today reported receiving a response from a spokesperson for Group 1001 Insurance, who acknowledged awareness of the suit while emphasizing: "No court has ruled that Group 1001 Insurance or Delaware Life Insurance Company did anything wrong, and we intend to defend the case vigorously, consistent with our long track record of serving policyholders with integrity."

TWG Global plays a vital role in Cadillac F1's organizational structure, acting as both an investing partner and an operational entity for the team.

While the civil lawsuit does not directly halt track operations and no criminal charges have been filed against executives, the controversy raises questions about the future of Walter's sports holdings. Walter recently agreed to sell his stakes in both the Lakers and Premier League side Chelsea - the latter case a combined 25% holding with Todd Boehly, for which the pair have received almost $1 billion from private equity firm Clearlake.

Just this past August, amid rising scrutiny over Walter's business practices, the team's parent company took a firm stance on Cadillac F1's future, issuing a statement to deny any plans to offload its Formula 1 assets.

"TWG is not considering a sale of the Cadillac team or any other part of TWG Motorsport," the company stated categorically during the Dutch Grand Prix.

Sports.title: How Antonelli's luxury problem is causing Wolff and Mercedes grey hairs
Sports.content:
For better or for worse, there seems to be no slowing down Kimi Antonelli.

Just ask Pete Bonnington, who channelled his inner schoolteacher in Madrid as he relentlessly had to remind the 20-year-old Italian to pay attention to track limits.

Having benefited from an earlier virtual safety car on a circuit where overtaking proved impossible, all Antonelli had to do was to keep it clean until the finish line, with Max Verstappen and Lando Norris resigned to following him home.

Bonnington and Mercedes had already suffered a scare earlier in the race with what almost sounded like a prank call from the young Italian.

Antonelli: "Check the car!"

Bonnington: "Which corner?"

Antonelli: "No I didn't touch any wall, but the steering feels weird..."

But with five laps to go, despite little genuine pressure from behind, Antonelli did tag one of the many concrete walls lining the challenging Madring circuit. "I touched the wall on the entry to Turn 7," Antonelli yelled.

Despite being in control, it was another race where Antonelli had been dangerously flirting with the track limits, much to the dismay of his father Marco and team boss Toto Wolff. There's just no slowing Antonelli down.

"I just discussed it with his father and we were joking: 'What an idiot!'. No, that's just Kimi,” the Mercedes boss said after the race. “The white lines, we had to drum it into his head that he shouldn't go over the white lines. Even in Monza, he still went over the white lines and [risked] the car. And the same with track limits.

"At a certain stage, I said to him: 'Don't you see out of the car? Do we need to sit you that high up so that you have [avoid] those track limit things? We had a laugh about it.

"And today, six laps to the end or whatever it was, he says: 'Check the car, I just brushed the wall.' What?! He's causing us grey hair. But maybe he's like this and maybe that's what's making him so quick."

Wolff added: "He had to hit the wall again because he wants to go fast. Sometimes for me, he's an inch too cool."

Kimi Antonelli is giving Toto Wolff a few grey hairs Photo by: Anni Graf - Formula 1 via Getty Images

Antonelli's flat-out approach appears to be a trait that Wolff and Mercedes are going to have to live with for now, at least until it goes wrong one day. Could that day come when Antonelli starts thinking about the big prize at the end as he careens towards a maiden world championship?

Wolff is adamant that won't be the case, despite Antonelli being by far the youngest driver to ever be in that position. "I promise you he's not thinking about it," Wolff insisted. "The way this kid is able to compartmentalise and be the young kid and then get into the car and be the mature racing driver...

"If Kimi says to himself: 'I'm not thinking about the championship', then he's not thinking about the championship. We are also trying, the parents and myself, the team is saying: 'You know, this is not finished.'

"There are black swan events. They can come and you're losing something out of your hands when you didn't think it was possible to lose. So, he's not going to think about it. We're too grown up and mature for this. We think about worst-case scenarios. He doesn't think about it."

Building on the lessons of a troubled debut year in 2025, Antonelli feels he has the right support system around him to carry him through to the finish line, whether that be in Abu Dhabi or at an impromptu home race in Imola near his native Bologna.

Kimi Antonelli has a strong support network in the paddock Photo by: Sam Bloxham / LAT Images via Getty Images

"I’m lucky to have really good people around me," Antonelli explained. "I have an incredible team that supports me, a great family. Especially my dad is the one who keeps me on the ground. Especially when he sees that I might lose a little bit the way, he doesn’t [hesitate] to tell me off or to just tell me to come back to the ground.

"On my side, as I said many times, I just try to do my best every race, trying to really drive as fast as I can whenever I go in the car. And then we’ll see where we end up at the end of the year. But definitely I don’t want to over-complicate things or just drive worrying about championship or results. Just driving, doing my best."

Driving as fast as he can all the time, is certainly working for Antonelli right now. As far as his team is concerned, almost to a fault.

Sports.title: Former Mercedes F1 tech chief Elliott joins Alpine as CTO
Sports.content:
Alpine has appointed Mike Elliott as chief technical officer of its Formula 1 team, further bolstering the Enstone-based team's technical structure.

Alpine announced on Thursday that Elliott will "oversee the technical and engineering functions at the team's factory at Enstone" in what is a newly created position as CTO.

For the 52-year-old Briton, it presents a return to Enstone after serving as the team's principal aerodynamicist in its Renault and Lotus days.

Elliott then went on to join Mercedes as its head of aerodynamics, helping the team make a head start on the 2014 regulations. Elliott rose to the position of technical director and chief technical officer, trading positions with James Allison, before leaving the Brackley squad in 2023.

"He has a proven track record in the sport, having contributed to an impressive eight constructors' and eight drivers' championships," Alpine stated.

Pierre Gasly, Alpine Photo by: Sam Bagnall / Sutton Images via Getty Images

"Elliott's arrival at Enstone strengthens the team's technical capabilities as the team looks to build on the improved performances on track and close the gap to the top four teams."

Current executive technical director David Sanchez is understood to be reporting into Elliott, who is overseeing the entire technical area of the outfit.

After sacrificing last year, Alpine has made a strong start to the 2026 regulations, fighting Racing Bulls for fifth in the constructors' championship. The 2026 campaign is Alpine's first as a customer team of Mercedes.

Sports.title: Tsunoda's in-depth look at why he failed to master Red Bull’s F1 car in 2025
Sports.content:
It seems almost unfathomable for a title contender's team-mate to end up 17th in the Formula 1 drivers’ standings, yet that’s what happened to Yuki Tsunoda alongside Max Verstappen at Red Bull in 2025.

In a way, it was unprecedented – the closest modern example perhaps was Felipe Massa lying a lowly 16th eight rounds into the 2012 season while Ferrari team-mate Fernando Alonso comfortably led the championship, but the Brazilian somewhat turned the situation around.

Equally, Tsunoda’s case was unique. Having decided to release an underperforming Sergio Perez, Red Bull picked Liam Lawson over Tsunoda for a 2025 promotion, believing the New Zealander’s lack of experience would be offset by his allegedly higher potential.

Lawson didn’t get much time to prove himself. After two grands prix in which he was eliminated in Q1 and failed to score any points, he was sent right back to Racing Bulls, with Tsunoda finally getting his chance at the main team.

At the time, the Japanese was actually quite bullish about his odds of succeeding where so many others had failed.

“People often say Red Bull cars tend to have strong front-end grip. I personally love cars that turn aggressively, and in the past, I adapted my driving style to that kind of set-up,” Tsunoda said ahead of his Red Bull debut.

Liam Lawson, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Red Bull Content Pool

“Racing Bulls traditionally had cars that understeered a bit more, which was challenging for me at first, but I got used to it, and it eventually became my norm. Now, the key will be adjusting to Red Bull’s characteristics again, but considering my past experience, I’m not too worried about it.”

Perhaps he should have been. While Verstappen won eight grands prix – more than anyone, including 2025 champion Lando Norris – Tsunoda failed to take a single podium finish, with his highest result an underwhelming sixth in Baku; he scored 30 points to his team-mate’s 385 over their time together.

In 27 qualifying sessions (sprints included), Tsunoda made it to Q3 eight times, was out in Q2 on nine occasions, and was eliminated as early as Q1 on 10 occurrences. He outqualified his team-mate just once and was 0.6s slower on average.

So, what was the problem with Red Bull’s RB21 F1 car? To some extent, Tsunoda remains at a loss to explain it.

“Normally I'm able to understand the car, what I'm driving, what kind of characteristic,” Tsunoda detailed on the Beyond The Grid podcast, “but it feels like even after Abu Dhabi, I didn't know what kind of car I was driving. I still don't understand what was the issue and what things made me very struggle to learn about this car and get used to the car.

“I thought confidence was there, but some race I just somehow lost the confidence. I still don't understand the car, to be honest.”

Yuki Tsunoda, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Mark Thompson / Getty Images

Still, Tsunoda has fascinating insight to provide. He openly admits he refrained from tweaking his driving style, believing that’s just what works for him. However, he did end up trying out Verstappen’s set-ups – and that experiment just failed.

“One thing about myself: I have big enough ego to not change my driving style,” Tsunoda admitted. “I know what I'm doing in terms of driving and I believe in myself. So, I never try to change my driving style to another driver’s, even though the driver is competitive and fast.

“Obviously for Max, it's a different case. He's a world champion, he proves a lot of things and I still learn a lot of things from his driving.

“My core driving is the same. And at some time, probably the first year out of any years since I started, I thought about changing driving style and trying to do something similar to Max. But in my perspective, if I just look at data, I didn't really see a huge difference in terms of driving.

“What I did most – and what I think now was the biggest mistake last year – was to try to replicate the set-up, what he's doing; even knowing that sometimes, if I feel the car very oversteer, Max's [set-up] in theory makes the car worse, more sensitive in the direction change, or makes the car slide more.

"I tend to choose the set-up, even though I'm already struggling with oversteer. It can happen sometimes the opposite way as well: even though I'm struggling with understeer, his car is more understeer. I try to replicate that.”

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing, Yuki Tsunoda, Red Bull Racing Team Photo by: Zak Mauger / LAT Images via Getty Images

Tsunoda is not the first driver to unsuccessfully attempt to use Verstappen’s set-up. Alex Albon also struggled alongside the Dutchman, for a year and a half, in 2019-20.

Back in 2023, the Anglo-Thai reminisced in the High Performance Podcast: “[Verstappen] has quite a unique driving style, it’s not that easy to get along with. Everyone has a driving style; I would say my driving style is a bit more on the smooth side, but I like a car that has a good front end, so quite sharp, quite direct. Max does too, but his level of sharp and direct is a whole different level – it’s eye-wateringly sharp.

“To give people kind of maybe an explanation of what that might feel like, if you bump up the sensitivity [on a computer game] completely to the max and you move that mouse and it’s just darting across the screen everywhere, that’s kind of how it feels. It becomes so sharp that it makes you a little bit tense.”

This metaphor was brought up to Tsunoda, but he wasn’t convinced it was particularly relevant to the RB21. Asked if he could relate, the Japanese racer said: “Yes and no. First, the car is a lot different to when Alex was driving and I’ve never driven Alex's car.

“It's sensitive, but I didn't feel that sensitive. But at the same time, like I said, it was very up and down. Some tracks I'm driving more sensitive car than him, some tracks he was driving more sensitive. On average, probably he was driving a bit more sensitive car, more like a sharper car than me.

“What he was definitely better at was, even though the car was sensitive or even numb… In a corner, there's always one phase or one moment that the car naturally reacts to, or tries to kind of respect its own behaviour. You know what I mean? Like, always in the corner, as soon as I turn in or whatever, that car does its own thing. That can be like a sensitive, sharp rotation or, I don't know, the front slides or something. He’s able to use that and he can smell that kind of behaviour probably much faster than me. And he was able to maximise that kind of behaviour throughout the corner.

“It's not necessarily my driving style that I'm doing, but if I have that kind of moments, sharp turn-in or rotation or the front slide, I tend to force the car how I want to drive. I normally respect how the car wants to drive through the corner, or I’m able to use that kind of natural behaviour from the car. But I wasn’t able to use that ability much in the Red Bull.”

Yuki Tsunoda, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Zak Mauger / LAT Images via Getty Images

As soon as he first drove the RB21 in free practice at Suzuka, Tsunoda’s early optimism gave way to caution; he reported the car was “feeling a bit more tricky” than on the simulator.

With hindsight, it was a sign of the ordeal to come.

“Even though I said, yeah, I thought I had confidence, probably it was not enough, as much as the VCARB car that I drove for four years,” Tsunoda said. “Red Bull is still a car that was completely different, which I felt as soon as I stepped into that car in Suzuka.

“There's some confidence level I was able to build up, but to maximise that whole performance, I think that was probably something I was missing, and trying to find that confidence throughout the year.”

Tsunoda eventually found out in Qatar, at the penultimate round of the season, that he would not be retained as a race driver and would act as a reserve in 2026 – no huge surprise given his results, and the campaign had been so draining that the news actually was a relief to him.

“I still remember the moments,” he recounted. “Initially, what I got told was from Helmut [Marko, then Red Bull’s motorsport advisor].

“In the end, Helmut is the person that brought me into Formula 1, brought me even to the Red Bull junior programme. We were together since when I was 17, 18. I remember he was also pretty disappointed about that.

Yuki Tsunoda, Red Bull Racing, Helmut Marko, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Mark Thompson - Getty Images

“And when I got told, I still remember, I didn't feel that much of huge disappointment or devastated feeling.

"Obviously I was still disappointed and pretty sad that I'm not driving next year. But not as I expected because I don't know why, somehow in a way, I fought really hard. I fought more than ever in that 2025 year and even if I look back now, I don't have much regret. I gave everything.

“In a way, honestly, my heart was just saying, ‘Okay, now I can be relaxed’. Because it was so stressful, the second half of the 2025 season, where I fought hard with a lot of pressure. Like I was never able to kind of breathe out much.”

Sports.title: Autosport magazine: Antonelli and a Can-Am celebration
Sports.content:
Kimi Antonelli’s rise to become Formula 1 world championship favourite and a celebration marking 60 years of Can-Am feature in the October issue of Autosport, out today (17 September).

It’s not just his substantial points lead that makes Antonelli the likely 2026 world champion. His consistent level of performance, with a reducing list of apparent weaknesses as each week passes, makes him seem impregnable.

Antonelli’s remarkable victory from 19th on the grid at Monza was a brilliant demonstration of patience and speed when required. Yes, the strategy fell Antonelli’s way, but the win must have been a psychological hammerblow to George Russell.

The Briton is perhaps in the hardest position of all. If McLaren, Ferrari or even Red Bull can find a technical advantage and put on a charge – a challenge that Jake Boxall-Legge also explores in this issue – then Lando Norris, Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen can start racking up wins and eating into the gap, potentially with a team-mate to help.

But any Mercedes improvement will, of course, benefit both Russell and Antonelli. Russell will have to start consistently outperforming Antonelli – or hope the Italian has an unbelievable amount of misfortune.

As well as Stuart Codling’s look at the long wait for an Italian world champion and Antonelli’s challenge, we assess the role of the reserve driver in the modern era, and Ronald Vording listens to Honda’s chief engineer and trackside general manager Shintaro Orihara open up on the troubles Aston Martin’s engine partner has faced this season.

Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Federico Basile

It’s 60 years since the famous Can-Am series for big banger sportscars began and we celebrate the category that briefly outpaced F1 this month. Pete Lyons, Autosport’s Can-Am reporter from the period, outlines what made it so special, we recall a McLaren that proved unbeatable, and Gary Watkins argues that the championship’s second era shouldn’t be ignored.

Looking ahead, Tom Howard hears from the World Rally Championship’s new promoters to understand their vision for the future of rallying, while Marcus Simmons charts Ash Sutton’s inexorable charge to a fifth British Touring Car crown in our Donington Park and Croft debriefs.

Two very different machines also star in our 25-page National section: a rallycross supercar and a UK club racing icon set to return to competition at the Goodwood Revival.

Sports.title: Bruising F1 2026 will not be the end for Russell - Wolff
Sports.content:
Toto Wolff is confident that George Russell can overcome a bruising 2026 Formula 1 campaign and still become world champion in the future.

The Mercedes driver is second and 81 points behind his dominant team-mate Kimi Antonelli with just nine rounds remaining, meaning a maiden crown for the 20-year-old is a matter of time.

It comes despite Russell entering 2026 as the heavy title favourite as he maximised the W16 last year with fourth in the standings and 169 points ahead of seventh-placed Antonelli.

Very few expected Antonelli to make such a strong leap into his sophomore season after a very up-and-down rookie campaign, but he is the one to have capitalised upon the rocket ship Mercedes has delivered for 2026.

“You can have good races, bad races, good years and bad years, but we're talking about the driver that has won everything that you could have potentially won before,” said Wolff of Russell at the Spanish Grand Prix.

“Every single karting championship, Formula 3 in his rookie year, Formula 2 in his rookie year, went into the Williams. We're talking about the top driver.

“We need to find out what is it for him to be able to unleash that potential and of course, there's the psychological side. If you have a run like him this year, you're taking a beating.

“But the great ones, they recover. And I think that George has all it needs to fight for championships and even if that one has maybe sailed, there will be more.”

George Russell, Mercedes Photo by: Rudy Carezzevoli / Getty Images

The Spanish Grand Prix was where Antonelli took his second consecutive victory after Monza, which was particularly damaging for Russell as the Italian started 19th with his team-mate on the front row.

It has all led to Russell effectively conceding that “I don’t think I am in the fight” for the title, as eight-time race winner Antonelli is romping towards becoming F1’s youngest ever champion.

A high-pressure situation that Wolff doesn’t think will affect Antonelli, especially thanks to his support network that ensures he remains level-headed for the years to come.

“Kimi from his personality, so grounded, 100% racer, not distracted from anything outside, super family situation and that's why I see no risk that he's losing the plot because he's so dominant,” added Wolff.

Read Also: Formula 1 Russell and Hamilton concede F1 2026 title chances as Antonelli dominates

“Over the next few years, it's something that we will always have our discussions like we have now. What is it that could distract him? What is it that's good for him? What kind of environment he needs? That is the discussion we have.”

“I promise you he's not thinking about it. The way this kid is able to compartmentalise and be the young kid and then get into the car and be the mature racing driver, that's why if Kimi says to himself, I'm not thinking about the championship, he's not thinking about the championship.

“And we are also trying, the parents and myself, the team is saying, you know, this is not finished. There is black swan events. They can come and you're losing something out of your hand when you didn't think it was possible to lose. So he's not going to think about it.”

Sports.title: Haas confident of getting 2027 F1 budget closer to cap with new partner talks
Sports.content:
Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu says the team is making "positive" progress with his team's search for new sponsorship, as the American Formula 1 team seeks to start pushing its yearly budget towards the cap.

F1's smallest team, Haas employs just north of 400 people and has been operating well below the budget cap in both of its iterations. Although the team currently has a title sponsorship deal with Toyota's Gazoo Racing arm, which took over from money transfer company MoneyGram for this year, it is currently looking to further augment its sponsorship portfolio.

Rumours have surfaced that the team is in talks with BWT, currently Alpine's title sponsor, which will move on the team next year as Alpine has a new title partnership with fashion house Gucci planned for 2027. This is not the first time that Haas has been linked to BWT; the Austrian company was suggested as one of its destinations after it ended its deal with Aston Martin at the close of 2021, before it moved to Alpine in search of more pink livery space.

Earlier this year, Komatsu told Sky Sports that a lack of budget was stopping the team from increasing its headcount, and from improving its tooling and infrastructure, and that his job was to find more revenue by attracting new partners to the team.

Speaking over the Madring weekend, Komatsu provided an update and stated that the team was in talks with a few different prospective partners to help bring the team's budget closer to the $215 million cap.

"We're talking to so many prospects; it's getting there. I'd say very positive about next year's budget," Komatsu stated.

"It just helps massively. But I think slowly and surely we are getting our story out there and finding great people. So, yeah, it's good so far."

Asked about the BWT rumours, Komatsu stated that "we're not going to have pink cars, if that's what you are saying!"

Komatsu added that he was not looking to prospective future drivers to make up the shortfall, and that the team was still in a position where it could focus on selecting its 2027 line-up based on performance.

Ayao Komatsu, Haas F1 Team Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

Ryo Hirakawa, Leonardo Fornaroli, and Rafael Camara have been conducting tests in previous cars for Haas, as the team assesses potential future drivers; Komatsu estimated that there were five in the running, presumably including current incumbent Esteban Ocon (whose performances have improved of late) and Yuki Tsunoda.

Asked if any commercial factors would have a bearing, Komatsu stated that it would only enter the picture if he had two drivers who were largely inseparable in terms of pace.

"If it's within a tenth, for instance, very, very close, then affiliation package does come into play for sure. I don't think [that will be the scenario]. I think we can choose by performance; we haven't finished the whole programme yet.

"We really want two fast drivers because that's the best way to grow this team. It doesn't matter if it's two Ferrari drivers or two Toyota drivers or two McLaren drivers.

"I mean, Fornaroli, he's a McLaren driver, right? But honestly, it doesn't matter. Whoever is the fastest, that's the best for the team.

"Again, for everybody, 400 people working here, they need to know that we've got the best driver choice that we can get hold of so that these two drivers are getting the best out of the car. Imagine taking somebody half a second off, but extra money. That's not going to be very motivating.

"And also, one position in the championship. That's quite a lot of money, right? For us, like I said, I'm staying consistent. I've always said we take drivers by performance. That's what we're doing."

Sports.title: Ryan Garcia Delay Leaves Teofimo No Catterall Excuse
Sports.content:
Teofimo Lopez wants Ryan Garcia, but Ryan will not be available for several months. That gives Lopez time to satisfy his WBA obligation against Jack Catterall instead of protecting his position while Ryan takes another fight.

Ryan discussed returning against Isaac Cruz or Angel Fierro in December or January before targeting Teofimo around Cinco de Mayo. Teofimo does not need to spend that entire period waiting.

WBA president Gilberto Mendoza stated in July that the winner of the bout between Rolly Romero and Teofimo must face Catterall next. Catterall now wants that commitment enforced.

“I expect the WBA and Gilberto Mendoza to stand on business, keep their word and honour what was agreed. Like I say, I don’t ask for favours, just what was agreed and what I deserve,” Catterall posted on X.

The WBA may clarify Catterall’s position Monday. President Gilberto Mendoza announced that the championship committee’s decisions will be released then, although he did not identify the divisions involved. With Mendoza already committed publicly to making the Romero-Teofimo winner fight Catterall next, the welterweight ruling will receive immediate scrutiny.

The sporting argument is simple. Ryan can take his winter tune-up while Teofimo defends against Catterall. If both win, the May date between Ryan and Teofimo remains intact.

The business calculation explains the hesitation from Teofimo. Catterall is a southpaw who refuses to provide easy counterpunching opportunities. Teofimo looked erratic against Sandor Martin and Jamaine Ortiz when those southpaws denied him clean exchanges.

Catterall offers another difficult tactical night without delivering the massive financial return of a Ryan event

Avoiding Catterall brings problems. Teofimo would reach May after a long absence while Ryan arrives sharp from a recent winter outing. A dominant victory over Catterall proves Teofimo belongs at the top of the division and makes the bout with Ryan much easier to sell on pay-per-view. Sitting on the shelf also hands Ryan total leverage over purse splits, ring location, and weight terms. Ryan draws massive numbers regardless of who holds the belts. Teofimo needs Ryan to secure the biggest payday of his career.

If the WBA allows Lopez to stay idle while Catterall waits, the organization confirms its mandatory rules mean very little. Teofimo has ample time to make the defense. The only genuine obstacle is the fear that Catterall ruins the entire plan. If Matchroom and Catterall legally corner the WBA and demand an immediate purse bid, the chance of Teofimo vacating the belt is extremely high.

Teofimo knows by now the belt is secondary in this equation. Ryan draws massive gate receipts and pay-per-view buys whether a sanctioning body strap hangs over his shoulder or not. Ryan proved that against Gervonta Davis and Devin Haney, generating elite commercial numbers without needing sanctioning body validation.

For Teofimo, holding the WBA title is useful for billing, but holding onto it becomes reckless if defending it requires facing Catterall. Catterall’s ring movement and refusal to trade invite the exact difficulties that caused Teofimo problems against Jamaine Ortiz and Sandor Martin. A spoiler-style decision loss to Catterall destroys Teofimo’s leverage, ruins the Cinco de Mayo payday, and drops him completely out of the conversation.

Vacating the belt would be a calculated business move rather than a surrender. If Teofimo drops the WBA strap, he removes the obligation, avoids the stylistic trap Catterall presents, and walks straight into negotiations with Ryan based purely on his own name and promotional profile. Dropping the belt costs him sanctioning fees and a piece of hardware, but risking it against Catterall could cost him tens of millions of dollars. If the WBA genuinely threatens to strip him, expect Teofimo to drop the belt first and claim he outgrew sanctioning body politics.

Sports.title: Chris Eubank Jr. Trains With Paydays Waiting
Sports.content:
Chris Eubank Jr. is back on the heavy bag, flashing training clips that signal plans for another massive payday before 2026 closes out. While no deal is signed, Conor Benn and Hamzah Sheeraz sit as the two prime British pay-per-view options waiting for him at 168 pounds.

That gut on Eubank is not muscle. That is pure luxury padding bought by British pay-per-view receipts. To step into a ring with Benn, Hamzah Sheeraz, or any opponent dug up to face him, he will need to burn off significant excess baggage.

The immediate problem is whether Zuffa Boxing has any genuine desire to fund a third clash between Eubank and Benn. Zuffa invested heavily to stage Benn against Ryan in Las Vegas on September 12, only to watch Benn blown out in under two rounds. That defeat shattered the myth that Benn could hold his own against elite world punchers. Paying eight-figure sums to finance a third installment of a domestic soap opera makes zero business sense for Dana White and Zuffa.

Public interest in a third meeting is dead in the water. Hardcore and casual fans would recognize it immediately as a shameless cash grab between two celebrity fighters who operate on famous surnames rather than world-level achievements. Neither Eubank nor Benn has proven they can beat prime, dangerous opposition at the elite tier.

Writing another massive check for Benn to face an out-of-shape, 37-year-old Eubank produces zero return on investment outside of local UK curiosity. Zuffa targets global streaming metrics and brand dominance, not funding bloated purses for domestic nostalgia acts coming off bad losses. If Benn and Eubank demand the kind of money they made in their first two stadium meetings, White and Zuffa will tell them to go pound sand.

Matching Eubank with Hamzah Sheeraz brings its own commercial headaches. Sheeraz destroyed his standing with boxing fans when he gave up his WBO super middleweight belt rather than face Janibek Alimkhanuly. Abdicating a world title to protect a record leaves a terrible stain, removing any argument that Sheeraz is an elite attraction.

Sheeraz is not a pay-per-view needle-mover. He has shown zero natural charisma, no edge in interviews, and lacks the personality required to play a theatrical heel. Eubank can talk all day, but one man cannot carry a press tour if the other guy stands there like a statue giving generic media training answers. In the UK, you might scrape together a modest gate at an arena based purely on Eubank’s notoriety, but globally the event will do terrible business.

If Zuffa shuts the vault on a Benn trilogy, both men are trapped. Benn holds zero leverage, Eubank is carrying ring rust and visible weight, and Sheeraz brings minimal commercial draw outside the UK. The easy money built on family dynasties has run out, leaving both camps staring at cold market realities.

Chris Eubank Jr’s recent social media activity suggests a return could be near 🍿 pic.twitter.com/Tnr9QQhPQA — Ring Magazine (@ringmagazine) September 20, 2026

Sports.title: Anthony Joshua Won’t Stay With Usyk For Fury Camp
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua turning to Ben Davison to crack the Tyson Fury code is a flawed strategy built on outdated history. While Joshua balances visits to Oleksandr Usyk’s team in Spain and Derrick James in Texas, Davison’s presence in camp is being sold as an inside track on Fury. In reality, Davison’s playbook offers nothing useful against the Kronk fighter Fury became years ago.

Joshua recently spent time in Spain working around Team Usyk, yet he has returned to Davison’s gym in Essex while keeping ties with Derrick James open. Eddie Hearn has refrained from naming a single head trainer or confirming a permanent camp base, although he took steps to remove doubt surrounding Davison’s presence.

“I think in some capacity he’ll stay close to them,” Hearn stated regarding Joshua’s ties to Usyk’s team. “He’s always been, even when Ben wasn’t his principal trainer, working with him strategically, talking all the time. I think he respects Ben a lot. Obviously, there’s probably a feeling that Ben Davison knows Tyson Fury extremely well. I don’t know AJ’s final decision to where he’s going to locate his training camp, but Ben Davison will definitely be involved in that camp and that process.”

Davison’s familiarity with Fury cuts both ways. Fury knows how Davison schemes, how he sequences combinations, and how he reacts when a fight slips away from the whiteboard. Any blueprint reliant on years past will run into a fighter who knows the playbook just as well.

The bigger problem is that Davison worked with a completely different fighter. Davison guided the elusive version of Fury who completed a comeback and survived Deontay Wilder across twelve rounds in 2018. That fighter was a survival project built on light jabs, lateral evasion, and snatching rounds from the outside. Fury realized the limitations of that safety-first approach, parted ways with Davison in late 2019, and went to SugarHill Steward to resurrect the Kronk style.

Under Steward, Fury abandoned the backfoot bouncing, added twenty pounds of solid bulk, and committed to walking opponents down. He uses heavyweight bullying to control the ring: collar ties, framing with the forearms, turning opponents in the clinch, and dropping his upper body weight over their neck and shoulders. Davison never coached that style, never cornered Fury while he executed it, and was abandoned because Fury outgrew the light-hitting system Davison specializes in.

Preparing Joshua for the 2018 iteration of Fury is a trap. The modern Fury will not waste energy trying to outbox Joshua cleanly from the outside. He will lean his massive frame on Joshua, tie up his arms, and make every round an exhausting physical grind.

Consulting Team Usyk brings its own tactical contradictions. Usyk neutralized Fury using rapid lateral escapes, constant rhythm disruption, and cruiserweight agility. Joshua is a muscular, upright heavyweight who moves in straight lines. Forcing Joshua to mimic Usyk’s fluid footwork while executing Davison’s mechanical combinations will only leave him disjointed.

Trainer hopping has defined Joshua’s post-McCracken career. Moving through Robert Garcia, Derrick James, Davison, and Team Usyk points to a fighter looking for external solutions to internal doubts. When Joshua faces adversity, conflicting philosophies will paralyze him.

Joshua does not need a committee of trainers offering polite suggestions. He needs a single corner authority with absolute control over the strategy. If Joshua carries multiple voices into the ring, the hesitation will give Fury all the openings he needs.

The recent disaster with Moses Itauma against Filip Hrgovic exposed the exact same systemic flaws that showed up when Daniel Dubois ran right through Joshua at Wembley. Davison builds intricate, lab-tested game plans for the opening bell, but the moment a heavyweight fight turns into an ugly, grueling dogfight, his system breaks down.

Against Hrgovic, Itauma had everything going his way early, scored a knockdown, and swept rounds, yet the tank emptied completely because the conditioning foundation was not built for deep waters. When the crisis hit, Davison had no Plan B, telling a gassed 21-year-old to take deep breaths instead of giving him a practical survival strategy.

That identical corner paralysis was on full display against Dubois. Joshua walked out stiff, mechanical, and completely unprepared for a fighter charging forward with bad intentions. When Dubois clipped him in the first round, Davison looked lost. There were no adjustments to clinch, buy time, or change the target. Joshua was left wandering into right hands until the fifth-round finish.

The fact that Joshua kept Davison after the Dubois demolition shows a fighter desperately clinging to the comfort of Davison’s praise rather than demanding hard-nosed accountability. Joshua believes Davison holds the secret blueprint to beat Fury because Davison was in Fury’s corner years ago.

Relying on Davison to outscheme Fury is a massive tactical error. Fury knows Davison’s limitations better than anyone, which is why Fury left him for SugarHill Steward in the first place. If Joshua walks into a fight against Fury depending on Davison’s whiteboard tactics, he is walking into the exact same trap that cost Itauma his undefeated record and left Joshua flat on his back against Dubois.

Sports.title: Daniel Blancas Breaks Down Sergio Jimenez In Seven
Sports.content:
Daniel Blancas turned Sergio Jimenez into a stationary target Saturday night at Pechanga Arena in San Diego, breaking down the veteran with heavy body work before referee Thomas Taylor stepped in to halt the super middleweight bout at 1:38 of round seven. Jimenez absorbed clean punches without offering any real resistance, leaving Taylor with no choice but to wave off the scheduled 10-round contest on the Isaac Cruz vs. Nestor Bravo DAZN card.

From the opening bell, Blancas (16-0, 8 KOs) controlled the real estate. The Milwaukee fighter pumped his jab from long range, slipped away whenever Jimenez tried to close distance, and punished the 39-year-old puncher for following instead of cutting off the ring. Jimenez (17-2-1, 15 KOs) showed toughness, but durability proved to be his only asset. By the middle rounds, Blancas had taken away his legs with hard hooks to the ribs, creating openings at will until the finish in the seventh.

The opening round ended with both men trading past the bell, providing a brief flash of hostility to an otherwise disciplined boxing exhibition from Blancas. That minor scuffle did not alter the direction of the bout. Blancas went straight back to his jab in round two, steadily increasing his output to the midsection.

Jimenez came forward willingly, yet forward pressure without ring generalship meant little. He absorbed clean punches through the middle rounds without producing enough offense to make Blancas hesitate. The difference in hand speed, distance management, and lateral movement allowed Blancas to pile up points without taking serious risks.

The body punches did much of the quiet damage. The forward march of Jimenez slowed as the rounds passed, making his attacks telegraphed and easy to slip. Blancas stepped around him, reestablished his distance, and resumed punching before Jimenez recovered his balance.

After six one-sided rounds, the contest became an exercise in watching how much punishment Jimenez could endure. Blancas pressed the issue in the seventh, landing heavy combinations while Jimenez offered nothing back. Taylor saw enough, stepping between them to wave off the action.

Jimenez carried an imposing knockout percentage into the bout, but most of those early stoppages came against limited opposition. His previous defeat was a 10-round decision against Deon Nicholson in 2024. Against Blancas, he never came close to generating the firepower his paper record suggested. Blancas looked considerably longer, utilizing those natural physical edges with patience.

Trained by Jose Benavidez Sr., Blancas needed more than another safe distance victory against an opponent brought in to showcase him. He delivered the stoppage, forcing the issue until the referee intervened.

The win proved that Blancas can stay disciplined against a rugged opponent rather than abandoning his boxing technique in search of a wild finish. A step up in competition will reveal far more, because Jimenez lacked the tools to expose what lies beneath the polished exterior Blancas brings to the ring.

Sports.title: Ryan Garcia Gives Isaac Cruz One December Chance
Sports.content:
Ryan Garcia says a December offer is waiting for Isaac “Pitbull” Cruz after the Mexican pressure fighter stopped Nestor Bravo in six rounds Saturday night at Pechanga Arena in San Diego. The invitation comes with an ultimatum: accept it now or lose the opportunity permanently.

Cruz (29-3-2, 19 KOs) protected the payday by dropping Bravo twice and finishing him with a left hook. Ryan had wanted an impressive performance before committing himself, and Pitbull did enough to change his mind.

“Bravo, Pitbull proved me wrong tonight. Let’s do this in December. The offer is on the table,” Ryan posted on X. “I can tame a lion. I’m not too concerned about taming a Pitbull. I’ve already given the go to my attorney. If he rejects this time I will never give him another chance, you have my word.”

The deadline works in Ryan’s favor. Cruz fought on September 19, leaving him less than three months before a possible December return. He did not absorb prolonged punishment from Bravo, but an immediate camp leaves little time to recover or build a specialized plan for Ryan’s speed, height, and left hook.

Ryan (26-1, 22 KOs) fought only one week earlier, stopping Conor Benn in the second round. His shorter night and superior physical dimensions would allow him to begin preparing without making the same tactical overhaul required from Cruz.

Money and broadcasting may be harder to solve than weight. Cruz is aligned with Premier Boxing Champions and fought Bravo on DAZN, while Ryan carries enough commercial value to demand control over the purse, pay-per-view structure, and venue. Closing those details inside a tight negotiating window will test how serious both sides are.

Cruz also holds the interim WBC light welterweight title, while Ryan now fights at welterweight. If Ryan refuses to return to 140, Pitbull may need to climb seven pounds for the biggest payday of his career.

Ryan has applied public pressure and started the clock. Cruz preserved the opportunity against Bravo. Accepting it under Ryan’s timetable is the more dangerous part.

That ultimatum reads far more like an exit ramp than a genuine push to sign a contract. When a fighter publicly slaps a take-it-or-leave-it condition on an opponent alongside a rigid, short turnaround window, they are usually building an alibi for the public. If Cruz’s team asks for sensible terms, like more preparation time, a specific purse split, or a realistic weight agreement, Ryan can throw his hands up on social media, claim Cruz ran, and move on without taking the public blame.

Tactically and financially, Ryan has every reason to avoid stepping into the ring with Cruz right now: Cruz is an absolute nightmare style for Ryan. Ryan thrives at distance where he can set his feet, control the real estate, and wait for an opponent to lunge into his check left hook. What Ryan hates, and what Gervonta Davis showed so clearly, is relentless, suffocating infighting where an opponent digs into his body and refuses to give him breathing room.

Cruz does not respect perimeter posturing; he burrows his head into the chest, wings vicious hooks to the ribs, and turns bouts into phone-booth wars. Ryan’s habit of pulling straight back with his chin up when crowded is exactly the habit a wrecking ball like Cruz exploits. The risk-to-reward ratio makes no sense for Ryan. Ryan holds massive leverage as an independent draw, with enormous blockbusters waiting for him against Teofimo Lopez or a Devin Haney rematch. Those fights promise massive paydays with far less wear-and-tear style danger than a collision with Cruz.

Getting dragged into a grueling war with Pitbull risks a cut, an upset loss, or physical exhaustion that could sideline him and derail those nine-figure paydays.

By demanding Cruz jump into camp immediately for December under non-negotiable terms, Ryan creates an impossible bottleneck. If Cruz declines or asks to push the bout to early next year, Ryan gets to keep his bravado, declare he offered Cruz the shot, and safely pivot toward an easier touch like Angel Fierro while protecting his lucrative 2027 calendar.

Sports.title: Pitbull Cruz defeats Nestor Bravo
Sports.content:
Isaac “Pitbull” Cruz knocked out Nestor Bravo in the sixth round Saturday night at Pechanga Arena in San Diego, retaining his WBC interim light welterweight title. The Premier Boxing Champions card was promoted by Tom Brown’s TGB Promotions and streamed on DAZN.

Cruz (29-3-2, 19 KOs), 139 pounds, dropped Bravo (24-2, 17 KOs), 139½, during the opening round. Bravo tried to pull Cruz into a clinch while falling, beginning a foul-filled fight that kept referee Thomas Taylor busy.

Taylor deducted a point from Bravo for excessive holding in the second round. Another point came off in the fourth after Bravo threw Cruz onto the canvas.

Cruz ended the disorder at 1:30 of round six. A clean left hook landed on Bravo’s chin and left him seated on the canvas as Taylor completed the count.

Daniel Blancas Stops Sergio Jimenez

In the co-feature, Daniel “Ice Man” Blancas (16-0, 8 KOs), 166¾ pounds, stopped late replacement Sergio “Checo” Jimenez (17-2-1, 15 KOs), 166½, at 1:38 of the seventh round.

Blancas used his height and reach to control most of the super middleweight fight, although Jimenez had success during a spirited fourth round. Referee Ray Corona intervened midway through the seventh after Blancas landed a sustained series of punches without receiving anything in return.

Eumir Marcial Knocks Out Omar Huerta

Eumir Marcial (8-0, 5 KOs), 160½ pounds, knocked out Omar “La Bala” Huerta (15-2-1, 13 KOs), 159, at 1:08 of the third round.

Huerta threw a left as Marcial countered with a right to the chin. Marcial’s punch landed with greater force, dropping Huerta for the full count from referee Thomas Taylor.

Marco Verde Stops Guillermo Hernandez

Marco “Green” Verde (7-0, 4 KOs), 157½ pounds, stopped Guillermo “The G Warrior” Hernandez (7-1, 4 KOs), 160½, at 1:46 of the fifth round.

Hernandez received credit for a third-round knockdown when Verde lost his balance as their feet came together during an exchange. Verde recovered quickly and took control again.

A series of unanswered punches in the fifth persuaded referee David Soliven to stop the middleweight bout.

Undercard Results

San Diego super middleweight Lazaro Francisco Lorenzana (22-0, 13 KOs), 166½ pounds, earned an eight-round majority decision over Marcos “Zurdo” Vazquez Rodriguez (21-3-1, 10 KOs), 166¾.

Heavyweight Valerii Tadtaev (6-0, 5 KOs), 227½ pounds, knocked out Juan Silva (3-3, 3 KOs), 240½, in the opening round of their scheduled six-round bout.

Robert “El Pistolero” Guerrero (9-0, 4 KOs), 139¾ pounds, stopped Shawn Rall (4-8, 3 KOs), 139½, in the first round of a scheduled six.

Diego Luna (9-1-1, 6 KOs), 141¾ pounds, defeated Renny Viamonte Mastrapa (4-5-2, 2 KOs), 141, over four rounds.

Jimmy Lennon Jr. served as the ring announcer.

Sports.title: Isaac Cruz Knocks Out Nestor Bravo in Sixth
Sports.content:
Isaac “Pitbull” Cruz knocked out Nestor Bravo in the sixth round Saturday night, retaining his WBC interim light welterweight title at Pechanga Arena in San Diego. A clean left hook dropped Bravo onto his backside, where he remained as the referee completed the count.

The ending followed five rounds of punishment, holding and repeated fouls. Cruz (29-3-2, 19 KOs) attacked immediately and dropped Bravo with a left hook in the opening round. Bravo survived the follow-up barrage largely by grabbing Cruz whenever the champion moved within punching range.

Referee Thomas Taylor repeatedly warned Bravo about holding before deducting a point in the second. Cruz then scored his second knockdown of the fight as Bravo’s legs betrayed him again. The Puerto Rican challenger spent most of the round clinching and wrestling instead of mounting an attack.

The disorder continued in the third. Bravo landed multiple low blows that forced breaks in the action, but Taylor did not deduct another point. Cruz still controlled the actual boxing, landing the cleaner and heavier punches whenever Bravo released him.

Taylor removed another point from Bravo in the fourth after he threw Cruz to the canvas. The referee also warned Bravo that a disqualification would cost him his purse. By then, Bravo was doing little beyond fouling, holding, and trying to survive.

Cruz swept the fifth without scoring another knockdown. Bravo (24-2, 17 KOs) had no answer for the Mexican’s pressure and offered almost nothing that discouraged him from advancing.

The finish arrived in round six. Cruz stepped into range and buried a left hook on Bravo’s chin. Bravo fell backward into a seated position and showed no serious interest in beating the count.

This was never a competitive title fight. Cruz scored two early knockdowns, forced two point deductions and then produced the knockout that Bravo had spent most of the night trying to avoid. The victory keeps Cruz in position for another major fight at 140 pounds, including the lucrative Ryan Garcia bout he has been chasing.

Cruz used his post-fight interview to demand the lucrative fight he has been chasing.

“Hey Ryan, I am here. My next fight for you. Come on, Ryan. Come on,” Cruz told Ryan Garcia after the knockout.

Ryan named Cruz as a preferred opponent after stopping Conor Benn last week. Cruz did his part tonight by crushing Bravo, but the weight remains the obstacle: Cruz holds an interim title at 140 pounds, while Ryan has insisted his next major fight take place at 147.

Sports.title: Isaac Cruz vs Nestor Bravo: Live Scorecard and Results
Sports.content:
Daniel Blancas defeats Sergio Jimenez

Super middleweight Daniel “Ice Man” Blancas stopped Sergio “Checo” Jimenez in the seventh round Saturday night at Pechanga Arena in San Diego. The 6'3" Blancas controlled the early rounds with his jab, reach, and movement, preventing Jimenez from setting his feet. Jimenez forced his way inside during a spirited fourth round and landed several clean shots to Blancas’ head. Blancas regained command afterward and began sitting down on his punches as the 39-year-old Mexican offered less in return. The referee intervened in round seven after Jimenez absorbed another sustained attack. Blancas left the Pitbull Cruz undercard at 16-0 with eight knockouts, while Jimenez dropped to 17-2-1 with 15 knockouts.

Marco Verde stops Guillermo Amilcar Hernandez Saldana

Middleweight Marco Verde (7-0, 4 KOs) stopped Guillermo Amilcar Hernandez Saldana (7-1, 4 KOs) in the fifth round of their scheduled eight-round middleweight bout. The 24-year-old Mexican southpaw used his jab and footwork to control the distance from the opening bell. Hernandez pressed forward, searching for the single opening he believed would expose the 2024 Olympic silver medalist. Verde refused to trade recklessly and gradually increased the pressure as the fight reached the middle rounds. The referee stepped in during the fifth after Verde’s sustained attack left Hernandez unable to answer effectively. Verde handed the Canadian his first professional defeat while collecting the fourth stoppage of his young career.

Eumir Felix Marcial TKOs Omar Ulises Huerta

Middleweight Eumir Felix Marcial (8-0, 5 KOs) knocked out Omar Ulises Huerta (15-2-1, 13 KOs) in the third round of their scheduled eight-round bout. The Filipino Olympic bronze medalist opened the televised portion of the Cruz-Bravo card at Pechanga Arena in San Diego. Huerta pressed forward from his southpaw stance and tried to force Marcial into a physical fight. Marcial stayed composed, controlled the distance, and waited for an opening rather than trading recklessly. That opening arrived in the third round when Marcial landed a sharp counter right hook that dropped Huerta for the full count. The clean one-punch finish gave Marcial the quick win he needed before turning his attention toward the Asian Games.

Lazaro “El Rey” Lorenzana (21-0, 13 KOs) faced Marcos “Zurdo” Vazquez Rodriguez (21-2-1, 10 KOs) in an eight-round super middleweight bout at Pechanga Arena in San Diego. The non-televised preliminary contest matched two Tijuana-based fighters with contrasting styles. Lorenzana applied pressure behind combinations and body punches, while the 36-year-old Vazquez used his southpaw stance and experience to make the exchanges awkward. The heavily favored Lorenzana was attempting to build on recent decision wins over Luis Arias and Oliver Quintana. Vazquez brought durability but had produced mixed results against stronger regional opposition. The official winner, scores, and method had not been released when this update was filed.

Robert Guerrero Jr. (9-0, 6 KOs) overwhelmed Shawn Rall in the opening round of their scheduled six-round lightweight bout. The 19-year-old prospect wasted little time imposing his speed and power. Rall’s background in boxing and mixed martial arts did not help him slow the early attack. Guerrero forced the stoppage before the fight had a chance to settle into a rhythm. The victory gave “El Pistolero” another early finish on a PBC and TGB Promotions card. Guerrero continues building his own identity while carrying the name of his father, former two-division champion Robert “The Ghost” Guerrero.

San Diego’s Diego “Zorrito” Luna (8-1-1, 6 KOs) met Cuban-born Renny Viamonte Mastrapa (4-4-2) in a four-round light welterweight bout. Luna came in riding a six-fight winning streak and was heavily favored against Mastrapa. The local fighter had also displayed increased punching power during his recent run. Mastrapa was asked to halt that progress while fighting in Luna’s hometown. The contest was listed as completed on the preliminary portion of the Cruz-Bravo card. The official result had not been released when this update was filed.

Russian heavyweight Valerii Tadtaev (5-0, 5 KOs) faced Juan Silva (3-1) in a scheduled six-round contest. Tadtaev brought a perfect knockout rate and an aggressive pressure style into the ring. The 6'3" prospect had stopped Cristopher Bernal in the second round of his previous fight in May. Silva was attempting to become the first opponent to take Tadtaev the distance. Tadtaev was heavily favored to overpower him and add another quick finish. The official result had not been confirmed when this update was filed.

Ghana News.title: Government has improved sanitation in one-and-a-half years — Salaga South MP
Ghana News.content:
Member of Parliament for Salaga South and member of Parliament’s Select Committee on Sanitation and Water Resources, Zuwera Mohammed Ibrahimah, has rejected claims that little has been done to improve sanitation and water services under the current government.

Speaking to JoyNews’ Stephen Menash, she said the Committee’s ongoing field monitoring exercise had revealed visible improvements in several communities across the Volta and Oti Regions.

According to her, residents and local authorities have implemented sanitation interventions that are beginning to change conditions in some communities.

“I did say that I saw Nkwanta South before 2025 because I drive through Nkwanta South to my constituency, and I've seen Nkwanta South now. So anyone who says that they haven't seen improvement in the sanitation situation, maybe they are living in another world,” she said.

Ms Zuwera, however, acknowledged that the improvements do not mean the sanitation challenges have been fully resolved.

“In one and a half years, we've seen a lot of communities change. There will always be space for improvement. There will always be opportunity to do more. It never ends,” she said.

She said the Committee’s field engagements had also demonstrated that improving sanitation requires more than government investment, stressing the importance of behavioural change at the household and community levels.

One of the encouraging developments, she noted, was the attention some communities are beginning to pay to household waste management.

“The local assembly is where sanitation starts from, at the household level, before it becomes a national issue. If we are not able to manage it at the household level, then it becomes a concern,” she said.

The comments come as the Parliamentary Select Committee on Sanitation and Water Resources continues its nationwide monitoring exercise.

The Committee is engaging Metropolitan, Municipal and District Assemblies and assessing sanitation and water projects funded with public resources, as part of efforts to examine how such interventions are being implemented and their impact on communities.

While Ms Zuwera highlighted progress observed during the exercise, she stressed that sanitation remains an ongoing challenge requiring sustained investment and greater responsibility from households, communities and local authorities.

Ghana News.title: Nkwanta North Assembly to appear before Parliament over DACF sanitation spending
Ghana News.content:
The Nkwanta North District Assembly is expected to appear before Parliament’s Select Committee on Sanitation and Water Resources in Accra for further questioning over its presentation during the Committee’s sanitation monitoring exercise.

The Committee said it was dissatisfied with aspects of the Assembly’s presentation and wants clarification on issues raised during its assessment of nine assemblies in the Oti Region.

Member of Parliament for Salaga South and member of the Committee, Ibrahimah Mohammed Zuwera, said the Assembly would be invited back to provide further details.

She said the Committee had identified concerns with the presentation and would engage the Assembly further before reaching conclusions.

The issue forms part of a broader accountability exercise by the Committee to examine how Metropolitan, Municipal and District Assemblies (MMDAs) are accessing and using their District Assemblies Common Fund (DACF) allocations for water and sanitation.

Ms Zuwera said the exercise goes beyond determining whether assemblies have spent the funds, stressing that Parliament is also interested in whether the money is being used for its intended purposes and producing tangible results.

“Public funds are public funds. They are not funds for personal use,” she said.

Ms Zuwera also cautioned assemblies against attributing implementation challenges to delays in the release of the District Assemblies Common Fund where allocations have already been transferred.

According to her, the two quarterly DACF allocations for 2026 had been paid.

She therefore urged Metropolitan, Municipal and District Chief Executives and their respective teams to provide accurate information during the accountability exercise.

“The MCEs, the DCEs and their team [must] pay fidelity to the facts. That's the only way we can move forward,” she said.

The Committee’s exercise is intended to assess whether the 10% sanitation allocation from the DACF is being used for its intended purpose and whether the funding is translating into tangible improvements in sanitation.

Ghana News.title: Mourinho prints out ‘red card’ incidents after Real lose derby
Ghana News.content:
Real Madrid manager Jose Mourinho arrived at his post-match news conference carrying an A4 sheet of printed paper with screenshots displaying two incidents he believed should have resulted in Atletico Madrid dismissals.

Mourinho accused the officials of making key errors after Real Madrid were beaten 2-1 by Atletico Madrid, claiming the hosts should have been handed two red cards in the first half.

It was Real Madrid's second defeat of the season, having lost 1-0 to Real Betis earlier in September.

"We can skip the press conference because the story of the match is right here," Mourinho said as he showed media the printed images.

"Those were two clear red cards. Given the difficulties we faced afterwards playing 11 against 10, we can only imagine what 50 minutes of 11 against nine would have been like.

"So I'll just have to limit myself to hugging my players, who gave it their all and played a first half, showed great class and character, setting us up perfectly to win the second half."

Diego Simeone, in contrast, was ecstatic with the result and when asked to respond to Mourinho's refereeing rant, said he was always respectful of everyone else's opinions.

"I understand that we're in a privileged position with a lot of public scrutiny, as coaches, and whether it's Mourinho, [Hansi] Flick, [Manuel] Pellegrini, me, or anyone else, we need to be careful about what we say," he said.

"We have to know how to respect others, the referees, our colleagues and we all lose out. And when someone crosses that line of respect, it's not right - you can't cross that line."

I want to believe they are simply mistakes - Mourinho

Mourinho argued the two first-half decisions had a significant impact on the match, insisting his team had shown character despite the circumstances.

The first incident Mourinho referenced involved Real's Jude Bellingham and Atleti's Cristian Romero in the 37th minute, when both players challenged for a loose ball and the clash ended with Bellingham being shown a yellow card.

At the time, Mourinho pleaded with the referee for a red card to be shown to the Argentina international for dangerous foul play, because replays showed Romero made contact with his studs on Bellingham's knee. Bellingham's yellow card was retracted after a video assistant referee review and Romero was given a yellow.

The second was for a challenge by Atletico's Lee Kang-in on Fede Valverde, which Mourinho believed should have been a straight red card.

The Portuguese also questioned the appointment of the match officials, saying he wanted to believe the decisions were mistakes rather than deliberate.

"I want to believe they are simply mistakes, just as a coach makes mistakes, just as a player makes mistakes," he said.

Despite the defeat, Mourinho said he had no complaints about his players' commitment and praised their performance, particularly in the first half.

"I liked my team as a unit. Even in the first half I really liked them, and in the second half it was obviously very difficult to get the ball and to stop Atleti's possession. I liked their pride, I liked their determination, and it's a good feeling for me to not be disappointed in my players".

Mourinho also addressed the dismissal of Dean Huijsen, which resulted in a penalty for Atletico, admitting he had not yet watched the VAR replay.

The defeat leaves Real Madrid fourth in the league standings, with Atletico second - five points behind league leaders Barcelona.

Yet Mourinho was keen to stress that there was still a long way to go in the season.

"Under normal circumstances, it's not about how it starts, it's about how it ends," he said.

Atletico controlled the match - Simeone

Atletico manager Simeone rejected the suggestion the result would be overshadowed by the refereeing debate, saying his team had controlled the contest.

"The match I watched was an intense one, where I think we controlled it at all times," the Argentine said.

"We faced an opponent with incredible transitions and extraordinary players who obviously play for their team and do so very well. We controlled almost all the transitions they could have had."

Simeone described the derby as an intense match and praised his players' defensive organisation and collective effort against a Real Madrid side featuring several dangerous attacking players.

"I think we controlled the match at all times, through our teamwork, our defence, our collective effort, our group dynamics, and our play. Looking for where we could hurt them, which we knew was on the right side."

La Liga will resume on Friday 9 October following the international break.
