World.title: Remembering Olatunji Akinwande Braithwaite (1933-2016), By Chidi Anselm Odinkalu
World.content:
The contest for the presidency of Nigeria in the election on 11 August 1979 was between five candidates. Nnamdi Azikiwe of the Nigerian Peoples Party was born on 16 November 1904. On election day in 1974, he was over 74 years. Obafemi Awolowo of the Unity Party of Nigeria was over 70. He was born on 6 March 1909. Aminu Kano of the Peoples’ Redemption Party was born on 9 August 1920. He was 58. Shehu Shagari, the candidate of the National Party of Nigeria, was born 25 February 1925. He was 54. That was one year older than Waziri Ibrahim of the Great Nigerian Peoples’ Party who was born on 26 February 1926.

All of them were active in the politics of Nigeria before independence. Their average age in August 1979 was just under 62 years. The contest was in many ways a re-litigation of positions that all five had respectively canvassed over a period going back more than two decades previously.

The year before the election, in 1978, a new organisation threw itself into the contest for recognition as a political party in Nigeria. It called itself the Nigeria Advance Party. Organised under the imaginative acronym, NAP, this formation articulated an ideology of egalitarian humanism that was both fresh and refreshing.

Olatunji (Tunji) Akinwande Braithwaite, the founder of the NAP, was born on 17 September 1933. He was a lawyer. Early in his career, Tunji Braithwaite established a reputation as a courageous advocate for the public interest, prepared to put his professional skills at the disposal of endangered people and unpopular causes.

His causes were egalitarian. They included political participation anchored on a clear ideology as well as the protection of trade union rights. Less than two years into his legal practice, Tunji Braithwaite was on the legal team that represented Obafemi Awolowo in his infamous trial for treasonable felony. Afrobeat legend, Fela Anikulapo-Kuti, was his client.

When Tunji Braithwaite became a lawyer in 1961, Nnamdi Azikiwe was Nigeria’s Head of State; Obafemi Awolowo was the official leader of the opposition in the federal parliament; Waziri Ibrahim and Shehu Shagari were both ministers in the federal cabinet; and Aminu Kano was Deputy Chief Whip in the Federal House of Representatives.

When he founded the NAP in 1978, Tunji Braithwaite was 44. His application to the Federal Electoral Commission (FEDECO) to register the party for the 1979 election was ultimately unsuccessful. The Commission claimed that the political organization did not have sufficient footprint across the country.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Rather than deter him, the rejection seemed to inspire Tunji Braithwaite. Four years later, in 1982, FEDECO eventually registered NAP, bringing to six the number of political parties in the country at the time. The following year, Tunji Braithwaite joined the principals from 1979 as the sixth presidential candidate on the ballot.

Handsome, hirsute, and heterodox, Tunji Braithwaite represented the ambitions of a successor generation in 1983. His language was direct and his mantra was an appeal to build a country of equal citizenship for everyone. His central message was simple: “together we take the destiny of Nigeria in our hands.” In pursuit of this, he promised to rid the country of a pestilential generation of political “rats, mosquitoes, and cockroaches.”

The old machine politics was not about to allow him. The manufactured “landslide” of the ruling National Party of Nigeria saw to that in the 1983 elections. Three months after their return to office, Muhammadu Buhari, the soldier who formerly headed the Nigerian Army Corps of Supply and Transport, put the short-lived experiment in civil rule out of its misery on the last day of 1983.

Tunji Braithwaite was not done with the law or with improving himself. He returned to school and over the following three years acquired two graduate degrees, including a doctorate. He also became a published author in the field of legal philosophy.

In 1997, a 63-year-old Tunji Braithwaite was the first senior figure to challenge the design of military dictator, Sani Abacha, to impose himself on the country as an unopposed ruler. His courage eventually inspired others to step forward, including former Inspector-General of Police, Maigari Dikko Yusuf.

Upon the return to civil rule in 1999, the Independent National Electoral Commission eventually restored the registration of the NAP as a political party in Nigeria. In 2012, the Commission de-registered the party for not having won any seat in the election cycle.

By this time, however, ideology and the pursuit of the public good had fled from Nigeria’s politics. Political parties had become special purpose vehicles for grabbing and running away with power. Tunji Braithwaite was clear about his goals: “Who wants to win an election by bribery and all sorts of evils? I don’t want to win election through such means.” The problem, he argued, was that “the electoral system cannot, I repeat, cannot contain people with integrity.”

At his death on 28 March 2016, Tunji Braithwaite had been a lawyer and defender of the public interest in Nigeria for over 55 years. Along the way, he amassed a record of multi-dimensional impact with no need for the adornments of office or accoutrements of power. His entire armoury comprised his intellect, his values, and the force of his belief in the public good.

Amidst all this, he also found time to raise a family. Tunji Braithwaite was married to Grace Simisola Olubanwo Braithwaite, one of Nigeria’s most senior living medical doctors. Together, they raised five children, including one medical doctor and four lawyers.

The year 1933, in which Tunji Braithwaite was born, was significant abroad and at home. In January 1933, German President Paul von Hindenburg swore in Adolf Hitler as the new Chancellor of Germany. Two months later, on March 23 of the same year, Hitler enacted the Law to Remedy the Distress of the People and the Reich (so-called Enabling Act), which empowered him to effectively scrap the institutions of democracy. 20 days earlier, across the Atlantic, Franklin Delano Roosevelt was sworn in as the 32nd president of the USA.

In Nigeria, 1933 was an election year. It was the year in which the colonial government organized the third Legislative Council election. The first was in 1923. It was followed by another in 1928. In 1946, the Legislative Council comprised 46 members of whom 23 were ex-officio, 15 were appointed, four were nominated officials, and four were elected (three from the Colony of Lagos and one from the Colony of Calabar).

In the election in Lagos, Theophilus Adebayo Doherty was elected to the Council for the first time. He joined two re-elected members, Olawolu Eric Moore and Crispin Adeniyi-Jones. Within one year, however, many members of the Council, including the representatives for Benin-Warri and for the Oyo Province were replaced by colonial governor, Donald Cameron.

In Nigeria today, many will argue that the whimsical arbitrariness with which the colonial governor could appoint and replace members of the colonial Legislative Council is substantially replicated in outcome if not in remit in the unpredictability with which judges and courts today can now chop and change election outcomes with no regard to the will of the people.

What happened in Germany in the year of the birth of Tunji Braithwaite shows that democracy has the capacity to subvert itself from within. One of the defining controversies of the durable presidency of FDR was the ultimately unsuccessful effort to pass the Judicial Procedures Reform (Court Packing) Bill in 1937 and expand the composition of the Supreme Court of the United States. It was a dramatic illustration of the need to maintain firm boundaries in the delicate balance between the judiciary and democratic politics.

In Nigeria these days, it is clear that some judges are actively undermining the idea of government founded on the will of the people. But, if the life of Tunji Braithwaite taught any lesson, it is that citizens remain the ultimate source of legitimate power and that power that does not derive its source from their will always endangers both itself and the people. This is where Nigeria currently finds itself. In the year of the 10th anniversary of his passing and the 93rdanniversary of his birth, these are timely lessons to take to heart ahead of the 2007 elections.

Chidi Anselm Odinkalu, a lawyer, teaches at the Fletcher School of Law and Diplomacy and can be reached through [email protected].

World.title: NPFL Roundup: Enyimba sink to the bottom as Kano Pillars thrash Doma United
World.content:
Nine-time champions Enyimba are still searching for their first point of the 2026/27 NPFL season after suffering a third consecutive defeat, while Doma United remain top of the table despite losing heavily to Kano Pillars.

Enyimba’s difficult start continued at home as they were beaten 1-0 by Inter Lagos on Sunday.

Ezekiel Moses scored the only goal of the game in the 18th minute to condemn the Aba club to another defeat.

Enyimba are now the only team yet to pick up a point after three matches. They sit at the bottom of the 20-team table with a goal difference of -4.

Doma United, meanwhile, remain top despite their 4-1 defeat to Kano Pillars.

Abdullahi Musa opened the scoring for Pillars in the 20th minute before captain Rabiu Ali doubled the advantage 13 minutes later.

Ahmed Musa added a third in the 77th minute, while Nasiru Salihu also got on the scoresheet as Pillars completed a convincing victory.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Doma United remain top with nine points from four matches, two points ahead of Barau FC.

Kano Pillars moved into third place with seven points from three matches, level on points with Rivers United and Rangers International.

Plateau United also have seven points after four matches following their 3-1 victory over Shooting Stars.

After falling behind in the 15th minute, Jibrin Ibrahim put Plateau United back on level in the 50th before Seiyefa Jackson shot the home team ahead. Gideon Monday added a third in the 86th minute to send Shooting Stars back home empty-handed.

Abia Warriors secured their second win of the campaign with a 2-0 victory over Sporting Lagos.

Ikoi Etta broke the deadlock in the 88th minute before Emeka Obioma added a second in stoppage time.

Warri Wolves also recorded a narrow victory, beating Kwara United 1-0 through Ejike Ezekiel’s eighth-minute goal.

Nasarawa United and Rivers United shared the points after a 1-1 draw. Musa Yakubu converted a penalty in the 84th minute to earn a point for the Solid Miners.

In Owerri, there were plenty of goals as Rangers International overpowered Kun Kalifat 2-4 in the Oriental Derby

With three away wins in Lagos, Owerri and Aba, the 2026/27 NPFL season is increasingly unpredictable.

World.title: CANAL+, LALIGA sign anti-piracy agreement covering nearly 50 countries
World.content:
CANAL+ and LALIGA have signed an anti-piracy agreement covering nearly 50 countries across Europe, sub-Saharan Africa, and Haiti, as the broadcaster and the Spanish football league seek to strengthen their efforts against the illegal distribution of sports content.

The agreement, announced recently in Paris and Madrid, will see the two organisations share intelligence, coordinate enforcement strategies and accelerate action against illegal distribution networks operating across multiple territories.

The partnership brings together the anti-piracy technology, intelligence, and enforcement capabilities of both organisations to protect the commercial value of sports broadcasting rights.

Javier Tebas, President of LALIGA, said piracy had become a major challenge for the sports industry and required greater cooperation among rights holders and broadcasters.

“Piracy is one of the greatest challenges facing the future of sports, one that no organisation can tackle alone, which is why partnerships like this one are so important. By joining forces with CANAL+, we are bringing together technology, intelligence and operational expertise to protect the value of our competitions, defend the investment made by broadcasters and clubs, and ultimately safeguard the future of football.”

CANAL+ CEO Maxime Saada said the agreement reflected the broadcaster’s expanded efforts to combat illegal distribution of its content.

“The unprecedented scale of this partnership reflects the strategic importance CANAL+ attaches to the fight against content piracy. I am particularly pleased that our Group shares a common conviction with LALIGA, one of the sports leagues most committed to combating piracy: piracy undermines the entire sports ecosystem. By combining our anti-piracy expertise, we are significantly enhancing our ability to take action.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

All players in the sports industry, without exception, and more broadly all stakeholders in the audiovisual and creative industries, have a role to play in tackling the scourge of piracy. CANAL+ is fully assuming its responsibility, and this partnership is a call for all industry players to do the same.”

Focus on sports financing

CANAL+ and LALIGA said illegal broadcasts affect the wider sports ecosystem by reducing revenues that support professional and grassroots activities.

They said the impact extends beyond copyright infringement to investment in youth academies, clubs, audiovisual production and other areas dependent on sports media rights.

The two organisations described piracy as a growing challenge to the sustainability of sports broadcasting, particularly as illegal distribution networks operate across borders.

The new agreement is intended to enable faster identification of illegal services and better coordination of enforcement action across the territories covered by the partnership.

World.title: Wike-APC: Fights always end adultery, By Festus Adedayo
World.content:
Ancient Yoruba says, he who seeks to purchase only the fresh head and limbs of a tortoise will end up buying the whole creature — “Ẹni t’ó ńwá orí ahun láti rí; t’ó ńwá ẹsè ahun láti rà, onít’òhún á ra odidi ahun.” That ancestral wisdom, which carries the weight of Nostradamus’ predictions, captures the kernel of the tango between the 31-member Nigerian Progressive Governors Forum (PGF) and FCT Minister, Nyesom Wike last week.

The abrasive Wike arrived at the “Ìṣò L’ékụ-l’éja” — the herbalist’s stall of rats and fish, representing the 31 governors — and asked to buy only a tortoise’s head and limbs. In his guttural, impatient voice, Wike insists he wants no part of the full creature. But the Hope Uzodinma-led PGF is querying the logic of this impending transaction: If Wike’s Rainbow Coalition supports President Bola Tinubu’s return to office, it must go the whole hog and buy the tortoise whole. The PGF refuses to let an outside coalition weaken the ruling party or fragment grassroots loyalties ahead of 2027. Anyone who wanted its tortoise cannot be allowed to have its fragments.

That territorial war sparked immense political tension last week. PGF members filed out like wild cats — or enraged termites defending their mound. On Arise TV, APC chieftain Farouk Aliyu admitted Wike had caused massive distraction. When termites are confronted with external invaders of their territory, their fit of anger is synonymous with what you saw in the governors’ eyes last week. Wild cats’ fit is often very clear and unmistakable. Confronted with an interloper, their eyes narrow and dilate entirely. They look onto their target with a fixed, heavy-browed gaze, ready to pounce. Those days as kids, when we were playing in sand dunes and decision time beckoned, we sang: “The eyes of the leopard are red; the tail of the leopard is turgid!” – “Ojú ekùn ńpón, irù ekùn ńle!”

Yet, at their Abuja press conference, the PGF veiled its red eyes in diplomacy. Uzodinma was apparently afraid of the leopard and avoided naming it outright, even when Wike was the subject of the press conference. Who dares to peer a torch into the eyes of “Ògìdán, olóólà ijù” — the lone predator in the wild whose patterned spots is scarified by nature with tribal marks, and whose sharp claws mark its prey like an artist’s knife?

Still, Uzodinma found his footing: the PGF remains unequivocal that it will endorse no political alliance outside the official APC structure. It dismissed Wike’s Rainbow Coalition as a rude interloper. Aliyu reinforced this, insisting that APC will only sell the whole tortoise: the governors, not Wike, will run campaign structures in their respective states.

Wike would not hear of that. He promptly went deep down into the sewage, brought out chunky smelly faecal matter with his bare hands and pelted it on the PGF. Governors opposed to his Rainbow Coalition were “419-smart and politically lazy,” he said. If you didn’t hear it well, you’d think a motor-park tout was the protagonist. He singled out Kwara State governor, AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq and Uzodinma in an ad-hominem rain of abuses that signpost his garrulity and intolerance for the other person. Aliyu promptly called out his arrogance, urging him to watch his words and learn humility.

Beyond the insults, this friction highlights a deeper struggle for party control on the road to 2027. Stripped to its core, the exchange resembles the accusative howling between an adulterous woman and her liaison, something in the mould of a mistress and her partner washing their dirty linen in the public after a failed extra-marital fling. Rather than mere “shame,” the dynamics of traditional adultery aptly explain this drama. As Dadakuada bard, Odolaye Aremu, chanted: “Ìjà níí gb’ẹyìn àlè” — fights are always the end of adulterous flings.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

APC’s decision to bring a quarrelsome, voluptuous fling into its household in 2023 was bound to prove fatal. That liaison is akin to a man who takes a termagant — a woman always aggressively nagging, scolding and fighting to wangle her way through in her husband’s home (Pa-mí-nkú obìnrin tíí se orí bęnbę s’ókǫ) — as a consort. The end is predictable.

First, adultery is an affair kept secret until a messy spat exposes its squalid details. It is only when a messy fight ensues between the offeror and offeree — apologies to lawyers — that, in moments of exchanges of howling, its messy details unfurl. Outside of Aso Rock and Wike, no one knows the terms of agreement struck in 2023 between the philandering Villa and the PDP fling who is today in charge of the FCT. Second, a habit of illicit escapades as the APC has had in three years-plus with all manner of whores cannot but eventually lead him to an asínwín(madwoman); an àjẹ (a witch), or an òbùn (a filthy woman). In courting Wike, the APC’s hired farmhand (alágbàro) must have strangely acquired a field crawling with venomous snakes.

But the streetwalker the APC picked in 2023, with whom it has been in bed, has got her rewards. In the television interview, Aliyu said this much: “If you want to say that Wike has helped us, we accept that. But he has also been adequately compensated. The position of FCT minister is good and huge compensation in a political setting of this country.” Aliyu then concluded: “We don’t want either Wike or any other person from any other party to insult our leaders just because you have helped us.”

Adultery is abhorrent to political morality. In any sane polity, a figure who served as local government chairman, governor, and minister under an opposition political party and turning around to become a major-domo in the ruling party, is a bizarre arrangement. When you eagerly pick up a chattel discarded by another, you must ask why the original owner let it go. Did APC assume that the PDP which allowed Wike slid in the last months of 2023 was stupid? It is like finding a motionless buffalo stuck in a marsh (àbàtà) and excitedly pulling out a knife to skew its flesh, ignoring that its heavy filth might have caused its collapse.

If APC thought it found a humongous buffalo of Nyesom Wike’s monstrous size trapped in a puddle and picked it up, it apparently didn’t reckon that its overweight of dirt could have led to its fall. Couldn’t the Wike buffalo have been trapped by its own hubris? Now that the house is in commotion, no one should pity the APC for shouting “Eureka!” over a trapped buffalo find. If Wike was not poisonous to a peaceful PDP, would the original PDP have discarded its chattel?

Yoruba proverbs note that a half-cured lunatic has cyclic manifestations. In 2023, the APC was enchanted by Wike’s allure; now, it realises it carries a faggot infested with stinging bees on its head. From the way this pretty woman sitting comfy in its living room laughs when there is no joke, (apologies to Bob Marley) the huge problem that lay ahead is finally here.

The APC governors complain bitterly today about Wike’s gutter rhetoric. Another proverb exposes their ignorance of power dynamics. It says, if one’s mother’s lover is greater than one’s father, one must address him as ‘father’” (Bí àlè ìyá ẹni bá ju bàbá ẹni lọ, bàbá là á pè é”). The lover in this regard, who is spitting in the APC’s face, and who sees himself as greater than their father in Aso Rock, is Wike. They should either shut their mouths or allow him call their bluffs for free. Furthermore, don’t they know that a woman who destroys her previous home will not hesitate to turn her new home into a house of commotion? If Wike glibly destroyed his PDP for the peace of APC, would he hesitate to destroy an alien home? It reminds me of the tortoise who lifts up a morsel of food and his child opens her mouth to be fed with it. In reply, the tortoise asked her if he wasn’t miserly, how would the world name him ahun, the miserly?

For APC, Odolaye Aremu’s song captures its current travails: He sang, apparently sarcastically — The monstrous desire you craved is what you have now! — “Ohun t’óo l’óó dà, l’o dà yìí o!” Traditional folklore tells us that baby vipers eat their way out of their mother’s stomach: “Ọmọ inú ọká níí ṣe ikú pa ọká.” A party that covets unchecked bigness inevitably creates its own internal opposition and possibly, death. That is the bigness APC craved.

All said and done, he who brings the cripple to the shindig must take him back home. Aliyu and some other APC stalwarts have asked their Baba to quickly come back home. When he comes back from his photo-ops with French’s Emmanuel Macron, he must take his cripple back home. For the APC, that saying by the Yoruba — though extremely sexist and one of the weapons used by traditional Africa to under-price the woman — that a household where a bad-mannered woman gives binding instructions is a house on the verge of disintegration is trite. Wild trees will grow over it (Ilé tí obìnrin bá ti ńké atótó arére, títú ni ńtú, igi arère níí hù níbè kéhìn). How can a strange fling give instructions to children of a home? How can a strange house guest be allowed to run the home?

A Brother Called Judas: Is Charles Soludo Cain?

History records that the most fatal stabs always come from within oneself. In other words, there is a motif of proximity to stabs. Deepest wounds are often delivered, not by external rivals, but by those within the same household or friends.

On 22 September, 1828, the reality of the above dawned on the Zulu of present day South Africa. Afflicted by a strange psychosis that struck him after the death of Nandi, his mother, King Shaka Zulu went berserk. He ordered a year-long mourning of Nandi, forbade planting of new crops, banned milk from the kingdom and ordered the execution of pregnant women, as well as their husbands.

How does the kingdom handle this? Shaka’s half-brothers, Dingane and Mhlangana, as well as his induna, (chief advisor/attendant) Mbopha, had immediate answers. As Shaka’s army embarked on a military expedition northwards, the conspirators saw a loophole. While Shaka slept at his royal kraal in kwaDukuza, the trio caught him off guard, stabbing him fatally with their spears. As he lay dead, Dingane seized the reign of the Zulu Kingdom.

If that example is too alien, lost in the bowel of two centuries, let’s come home, to a contemporary example on the African continent. Thomas Sankara and Blaise Compaoré were what Yoruba call Kòrí-kòsùn — bosom, intimate and inseparable soulmates who shared an extremely close, deep bond. That bond was to later become one of the most famous real-life political fratricides on the continent. While Sankara was Head of State of Burkina Faso, he and Compaoré were not just ideological allies; they referred to each other as “brothers in arms.” In 1987, Compaoré orchestrated the fatal coup that got Sankara executed. He then took over power, while systematically legitimising his regime by deconstructing Sankara’s revolutionary legacy.

West African Mali empire epic griot recall themes of betrayal similar to the above. The epic goes thus: At the death of King Naré Maghan, his first wife, Sassouma Bereté and her son, Dankaran Touman, conspired against Sundiata Keita, Dankaran’s crippled half-brother. They did this out of envy and fear of Sundiata’s fame. An earlier prophecy had predicted Sundiata’s greatness. Both mother and son mocked Sundiata’s cripple state and then tried to eliminate him. The late King Maghan had in fact left a testament that the young, disabled Sundiata should take over the reign of the kingdom but Dankaran, who now usurped the throne, forced his crippled brother into exile.

Balla Fasseké, Sundiata’s devoted griot and advisor, took sides with Sundiata, leading to his exile, too, by Dankaran. In exile, Sundiata waxed stronger while, on the throne, Dankaran appeared to the people as a weakling. Then, when Soumaoro Kanté, Dankaran’s sorcerer, invaded Mande, out of fear, Dankaran fled. The void of a vacant monarchy led the Mande to send emissaries to Sundiata who, in a triumphant return, eventually became the king.

In both ancient and contemporary times, there is a huge literature of brothers stabbing brothers. From the biblical Cain killing his brother, Abel, out of jealousy of divine prosperity; to Julius Caesar being stabbed by his friend, Brutus, the literature drips of blood. Among the Igbo, there is a recurring motif of two brothers hunting or traveling together. One, the less-acclaimed/jealous brother plots to kill the other, so as to claim the crown or inheritance. Also in Igbo cosmology, extracting personal gains from one’s kinsman (Nwanne) at the expense of his life or well being, for personal gain, is considered a severe cultural transgression. Chinua Achebe’s literature is filled with such thematic warnings. He built a cultural archetype about fratricide as capable of breaking the fabric of Igbo community.

Again, traditional Igbo sees any attempt at breaking Umunna (kinship) values as cultural transgression. It questions the morality of exposing and externalising home-front disputes as tantamount to handing over one’s kinsman to external political adversaries.

From whichever lens you may look at it, though framed as fiscal transparency and Anambra State governor, Prof Charles Soludo, claimed he was “setting the records straight” by releasing his Anambra brother, Peter Obi’s alleged debt claims, what he did was actually Brutus stabbing Caesar, simplicita. It is fratricide disguised as governance audit. After he stabbed Caesar, Brutus’ defence, too, just like Soludo’s, was that it was done out of duty to the Roman state.

The above stab is also a replica of what happened between joint Roman Emperors and biological brothers, Caracalla and Geta. It is one of Roman antiquity’s most brutal accounts of sibling rivalry. It is dubbed the story of political fratricide and paranoia. Both brothers were born only eleven months apart. Their parents were Emperor Septimius Severus and Empress Julia Domna. Both brothers grew up in the palace with mutual childhood hatred, up until their adulthood.

A contemporary historian, Cassius Dio, recorded that both men serially clashed over sports, music, and social circles. Their father, in his bid to stabilise his dynasty, made them co-emperors. History recorded that while Caracalla was emperor in 198 AD, Geta was in 209 AD. In 211 AD, as he lay dying on his deathbed in Eboracum, modern York, Severus’ famous advice to his sons was, “Be harmonious, enrich the soldiers, and scorn all other men.”

On the throne, however, the hostility of the brothers paralyzed Roman governance. They then mutually divided the imperial palace into two. To avoid being poisoned, they fortified their doors with bodyguards and employed food-tasters. They even attempted to divide the Roman empire into two, a plan that was thwarted by their mother who tearfully asked if they wanted to divide her body, too. In December 211 AD, Caracalla decided to eliminate his brother. He arranged a fake reconciliation for their mother’s apartment, a place that would raise no suspicion and make Geta feel safe. There, Caracalla’s guards pounced on Geta and, as he fled to their mother’s bosom, clinging to her neck, he was stabbed to death nevertheless.

After killing him, Caracalla ordered what was called condemnation memory – a damnatio memoriae – which removed his brother’s name from every inscription in Rome, including his images. Any contrary effort, he decreed, was an offence against the Roman State. He also executed about 20,000 of Geta’s palace staff, supporters, friends, and political allies all over Rome.

What Soludo did last week in Anambra State is comparable to damnatio memoriae. Just as Brutus stabbed Caesar under the guise of “doing it for the republic” and administrative duty, on the on-going loan brouhaha, Soludo is Brutus and Caracalla rolled into one. Through Dr Law Mefor, his Commissioner for Information, Soludo disclaimed Obi’s self portrayal as loans-repellant during his time as Anambra State governor. Mefor, in a statement, said Obi left unpaid loans from eight different external borrowings, the total balance of which, at the official exchange rate, stood at ₦127.4 billion.

To me, the veracity or otherwise of both men’s claims on the loans is secondary. My questions to Soludo are: Since the man he claimed is his “good friend” — for whose sake he is stabbing his Nwanne — left office in 2007, has Soludo ever heard a word of the humongous broad daylight theft done on that friend’s behalf in his home turf? Has Soludo ever since then heard successors of his “good friend” talk about the loans he took while in office? Does he know that putting a shroud on his “friend’s” dirty linen was done in the spirit of their own brand of Umunna?

My concluding question to Charles Soludo will then be — is this newfound “Et tu, Brute?” spirit of his, which propelled the stabbing of his Nwanne — a result of an ambition to be president of Nigeria after his Anambra tenure, or, is Charles naturally a grumpy Cain and a betrayer Judas, who sold his predecessor for 30 pieces of shekels?

Festus Adedayo is an Ibadan-based journalist.

World.title: I need executive order from presidency to ban mining in problematic areas – Bago
World.content:
Governor of Niger State Umar Bago

Niger State Governor, Umaru Bago, has called for an executive order from the Presidency or the Federal Ministry of Solid Minerals Development to ban mining activities in locations identified as problematic across the state.

Bago made the call on Sunday during an interview on Channels Television’s Sunday Politics, following the deaths of 37 suspected illegal miners while in the custody of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps, NSCDC.

The governor said the state government required stronger intervention from the Federal Government because of limitations surrounding the enforcement of mining regulations.

Asked what his administration was doing about the presence of minors at mining sites, Bago said decisive action was needed to end the practice.

“I am in between the devil and the Red Sea because, as a governor, yes, it’s in my state. As a governor, I cannot just go and order the police or military to start shooting people or arresting people. As a governor, I can only make advocacy.

“But these people, because they have tasted the mining money, they cannot leave that side. We need decisive action. We need an executive order from the Presidency or from the Ministry of Mineral Resources to ban mining in certain locations where we have seen they are problematic. Once that is done, it can be enforced,” he said.

Bago said illegal mining had become a major challenge in Niger State, particularly with the increasing involvement of children in artisanal mining.

He expressed concern that the involvement of minors in mining was taking them away from school and exposing them to the dangers associated with mining activities.

The governor’s call came amid renewed scrutiny of mining activities in the state following the deaths of the 37 suspected illegal miners in NSCDC custody.

World.title: Troops rescue 2 kidnap victims, arrest 11 suspects in Plateau
World.content:
Troops of the Joint Task Force, Operation Enduring Peace (JTF-OPEP), have rescued two kidnapped victims and arrested 11 suspected kidnappers in Plateau.

Capt. Polycarp Oteh, the operation’s Media Officer, said this in a statement issued on Sunday in Jos.

Oteh said the operation, conducted on Saturday, followed credible intelligence on suspected kidnapping activities within Rayfield and other parts of the state.

He said the troops also recovered arms and ammunition during separate operations conducted in the state.

“Troops of Sector 1, Sub-Sector 12, deployed at Lamingo, successfully rescued two kidnapped victims and arrested 11 suspected kidnappers.

“They also recovered weapons during separate operations conducted in the early hours of Saturday,” he said.

According to him, the operations followed credible intelligence on kidnappers operating within Rayfield and other parts of Jos North Local Government Area.

“Acting on the intelligence, troops raided suspected criminal hideouts at Shere, Gwafan and Maza Hills, resulting in the arrest of 11 suspects,” Oteh said.

He said the rescued victims identified three of the arrested suspects as members of the syndicate allegedly responsible for their abduction.

The media officer said the troops also conducted cordon-and-search operations in communities across Bassa and Mangu Local Government Areas.

He said the operations led to the recovery of some weapons from the affected communities.

Oteh urged residents to support the military and other security agencies in tackling security challenges across the state.

World.title: Tinubu to First Lady at 66: You’re my truest friend
World.content:
By Johnbosco Agbakwuru

ABUJA — President Bola Tinubu has celebrated the 66th birthday of his wife, First Lady Senator Oluremi Tinubu, describing her as his “truest friend and confidante” and declaring that, if life gave him another chance, he would choose the same path that led him to her.

Tinubu, in a birthday message on Sunday, addressed the First Lady as “Oluremi mi” and wrote: “Today, I celebrate the woman who has walked beside me with patience, grace and uncommon courage.”

The President invoked Yoruba wisdom and scripture, quoting the proverb, “Ìyàwó rere ni adé ọkọ rẹ̀” — “A good wife is her husband’s crown” — and adding that the Book of Proverbs, which she knows “far better than I do,” also speaks eloquently of the worth of a virtuous woman.

Tinubu credited his wife with sharing his burdens and understanding him in ways few others could.

“The burdens that were mine to bear often found their way onto your shoulders. The thoughts I could not put into words somehow found their way to you,” he wrote.

He recalled her composure during difficult periods, saying: “In difficult times, when the future was uncertain, you stayed calm beside me and prayed with me. Through all these years, you have remained the one who truly understands me.”

The President also praised her honesty, particularly her willingness to tell him difficult truths.

“I call you my truest friend and confidante because you speak the truth plainly, even on the days I would rather not hear it,” he said.

“After a demanding day, you wait until we are alone before telling me what I need to hear. I have always cherished you for that honesty.”

Tinubu highlighted the First Lady’s role in shaping their family and faith life, saying their children and grandchildren had grown under the influence of her prayers, values of faith and kindness.

“Our home bears the lasting imprint of your devotion. Our children and grandchildren have grown beneath the shelter of your prayers. They carry your values of faith and kindness wherever life takes them,” he said.

The President also praised her public service and compassion, saying Nigerians knew her for her kindness, generosity and steadfast faith.

“I have watched you touch lives quietly and consistently, offering hope and support to those in need,” he said.

Tinubu traced her humanitarian activities from their years in Lagos to her current national platform.

“From the New Era Foundation during our years in the saddle in Lagos to the Renewed Hope Initiative today, your care has reached many young boys and girls, widows, elderly citizens, and women farmers across the country,” he said.

He singled out her advocacy for people affected by tuberculosis and other diseases, describing her as “a compassionate advocate and a determined champion.”

Tinubu further said his wife’s compassion transcended ethnic, regional and religious boundaries.

“I know the prayers you offer for people whose names you may never know. I also know many whom you have helped without ever meeting them. For you, compassion has never recognised the boundaries of tribe, region or religion,” he said.

Reflecting on their years together, the President said their shared experiences had strengthened their relationship.

“A long journey teaches a man the true value of a good partner. We have travelled a long road together. I think of the difficult decisions we talked through for hours and the sacrifices no one else saw. Laughter and prayer carried us through many of them,” he said.

Tinubu ended the tribute with a declaration of enduring love and commitment.

“If life returned me to the beginning, I would choose the same road that led me to you. Through every mile, my heart has always remained at home with you.

“Happy 66th birthday, my darling Oluremi. I pray that God Almighty will grant you many more years in good health and joy. May the years ahead bring you the same comfort and happiness you have so freely given to me and many others.”

World.title: Effurun attack: Keyamo fingers NDC thugs, vows action
World.content:
Festus Keyamo

By Omeiza Ajayi

ABUJA: Minister of Aviation and Aerospace Development, Festus Keyamo, SAN, has accused thugs loyal to the Nigeria Democratic Congress NDC of unleashing violence in his community in Effurun, Uvwie Local Government Area of Delta State, vowing to petition the Inspector-General of Police IGP this week over the incident.

Keyamo, in a post on his X handle, said he wanted “the world to see what the NDC’s thugs came to my community in Effurun, Uvwie LGA of Delta State, to do on Friday, 18th September, 2026.”

He alleged that the thugs “wrecked havoc on billboards pasted everywhere by Tompolo’s door-to-door Campaign Organisation, entered people’s shops with dangerous weapons and looted the shops.”

The minister lamented what he described as a double standard in public reactions to political violence, saying that “if it had been the other way round against the APC, the section of the bias Press and so-called human rights groups would have been screaming to high heavens, but since this happened, everywhere is mute.”

Drawing a comparison with an earlier incident, Keyamo said, “this is the exact point I made when I openly condemned the blockade of Peter Obi’s entourage from entering Benue State. But what happened in Benue is nothing compared to this.”

He described the situation as sickening, adding, “the double standards everywhere is sickening. The video is clear and the evidence is overwhelming. We have more evidence. The thugs were even accompanied by law-enforcement agents in their payroll.”

The minister, who described himself as the foremost political leader in the community, said he would not let the matter slide, stating, “I have warned everyone not to resort to self-help.”

He announced plans to escalate the matter to the police, saying, “I will be submitting a petition to the Inspector General of Police this week to thoroughly investigate this incident and bring all those found wanting to book (even against APC leaders, if anyone crossed the line).”

Keyamo also called for disciplinary action against law enforcement agents allegedly complicit in the incident, adding, “disciplinary action should also be taken against those law-enforcement agents in their midst that condoned the looting and destruction of properties.”

Keyamo further signalled a firmer resolve going forward, declaring, “some of us are now ready for the long haul!”

World.title: U-20 Women’s World Cup: Semi-final fixtures confirmed
World.content:
The semi-final line-up for the 2026 FIFA U-20 Women’s World Cup in Poland has been confirmed following the completion of the quarter-final fixtures.

Four teams — Italy, Spain, Colombia and North Korea — will compete for places in the final of the tournament.

Colombia secured the final semi-final spot on Sunday after edging Nigeria 1-0 in a closely contested quarter-final.

The South American side held on to its narrow advantage to end Nigeria’s campaign and book a place among the last four.

North Korea also advanced after defeating Canada 2-0 in their quarter-final encounter.

The two teams joined Spain and Italy, who had already secured their semi-final places following victories in Saturday’s quarter-final matches.

The semi-final action will begin on Wednesday, with Spain taking on Italy in the first encounter.

The second semi-final will see Colombia face North Korea, with both sides now two wins away from lifting the U-20 Women’s World Cup trophy.

Colombia vs North Korea
