He said that matters now because Canada is trying to put passenger trains back on a network that, in many places, was either removed or rebuilt for another purpose.

In Ontario, the province is preparing to restore Northlander passenger service between Toronto and northeastern Ontario, more than a decade after it was cancelled. The federal government meanwhile, is developing Alto, a new high-speed passenger railway between Toronto and Quebec City that would run largely on its own tracks.

Other communities are pushing for passenger rail to return, including on Vancouver Island, in Alberta between Calgary and Banff and in Cape Breton.

The power of owning the tracks

But Canada's railways have something airlines and trucking companies don't: control over the infrastructure they use.

Abandoned freight cars sit on overgrown tracks in a former shunting yard in St. Thomas, Ont., one of the remnants of the city's once sprawling railway network that linked major North American cities. (Colin Butler/CBC News)

"No one is going to build an alternative set of rails across this country under any circumstances," Perl said. "That's why they make the call on whether to put in or take out tracks in particular places."

In St. Thomas, CN has yet to restore the missing connection between London and Port Stanley.

"Even when the Canadian Transportation Agency orders them to do something they don't want to do," he said, "it can take quite a while, if ever, that they will go along with it because they have the ownership of that infrastructure."

Perl argues that kind of power has deep roots in the railway business and points to language the industry has given us.

"To 'railroad someone' is to take advantage and treat someone unfairly or unjustly," he said. "You don't see that with too many other industries."

World.title: Trump says proposed triumphal arch near White House would house drones, snipers
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President Donald Trump said on Sunday the triumphal arch he plans to build near Arlington National Cemetery in Washington would double as a "military complex" housing drones and snipers, as well as storing large quantities of ammunition.

The president cited national security concerns for the move, echoing the rationale offered for the roughly $400-million US ballroom complex being built on the site of the White House's former East Wing, which was demolished to make way for the project. He did not identify any specific threats.

The projects are part of Trump's ambitious effort to reshape Washington, including a push to add his name to the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. The plans have drawn criticism from preservationists and others who argue they could alter or diminish historic landmarks.

In a social media post, Trump said that at the "strong request" of the military he had agreed to turn the 76-metre arch "into a top grade Military Complex/Triumphal Arch, to house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage."

The White House and the Department of War did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

WATCH | Trump announces plans for arch: Trump says planned triumphal arch will house drones, snipers | Duration closed caption 3:18 U.S. President Donald Trump says his proposed 250-foot triumphal arch in Washington, D.C., will also serve as a military complex housing drones, snipers and ammunition. The announcement marks a significant change from plans previously reviewed by federal agencies.

The Federal Aviation Administration said last week that the arch would not pose a hazard to aircraft but would be required to have an "eternal flame" on top, clearing an aviation hurdle for the arch, which Trump proposed to mark the nation's 250th anniversary.

Aviation experts have raised safety concerns given its proximity to Reagan Washington National Airport, while veterans have sued to block the arch, arguing it would destroy the historic sightline between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.

The arch faces other legal challenges. Though the arch has received early approval from the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts, whose members were all tapped by Trump, a group of three veterans and an architectural historian sued, saying the project needs to be approved by Congress.

"The President's belated efforts to manufacture a national security justification for this project do nothing to cure its fundamental illegality," Nicolas Sansone, one of the attorneys representing the litigants, said Sunday. "Congress has not authorized the arch, and unless and until Congress does so, the project should not be permitted to move forward."

WATCH | Kennedy Center board votes to close after judge again blocks efforts to add Trump name to it: Kennedy Center board votes to close after failed efforts to add Trump name | Hanomansing Tonight | Duration closed caption 3:50 The Trump-aligned Kennedy Center board voted to close most of the performing arts venue just hours after a federal judge blocked the institution from returning President Donald Trump's name to the building.

The arch is proposed for a circle adjacent to the Memorial Bridge, which is a heavy traffic area as one of a handful of connecting bridges between the nation's capital and northern Virginia.

The project is one of several projects that the Republican president is pursuing to leave his lasting imprint on Washington. Among the others are the White House ballroom, renaming and renovating the Kennedy Center, refurbishing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and rebuilding a golf course in East Potomac Park that could significantly reduce the public's access to running and biking paths.

World.title: New Bluetooth tags let anyone track monarch butterfly migration in real time
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

For years tracking a tagged monarch butterfly relied on luck, on someone, somewhere along the migration route, finding the tiny sticker on a wing of the insect and reporting it.

This year Nature NB is using new technology that removes the guesswork entirely.

The organization deployed Bluetooth enabled tags on monarchs for the first time in New Brunswick this season, working in partnership with the Saint John Naturalist Club, Point Lepreau Bird Observatory and Environment and Climate Change Canada.

“It's a very exciting new chapter in the monarch conservation world in the Maritimes,” said Francie Morgan, program co-ordinator with Nature NB.

Francie Morgan holds a monarch fitted with a BluMorpho tag ahead of its release. (Submitted by Francie Morgan)

The tags, called BluMorpho tags, are solar-powered and weigh about 0.066 grams — a small fraction of a monarch's roughly half-gram body weight.

They attach to the butterfly's thorax using a dab of eyelash glue, with a small antenna running along the length of the abdomen.

Unlike traditional wing tags, which depend on physical recapture to generate data, theBluMorpho tags work through passive Bluetooth interactions.

Anyone with Bluetooth enabled on their phone who comes within 100 metres of a tagged monarch will automatically log a data point.

The BluMorpho tag weighs about 0.066 grams and is attached with a dab of eyelash glue. Details including capture time and sex are recorded before release. (Submitted by Francie Morgan)

“Download the Project Monarch app, scan for these tags and follow along on the journey of these monarchs,” Morgan said.

Jim Wilson, a birder and naturalist with the Point Lepreau Bird Observatory who has been tagging butterflies for years, said the shift is significant.

"The old method was simply to put a numbered wing tag on and hope somebody would find it or see it and report it between here and Mexico," Wilson said. "This is now online, you can go on there and find out where that monarch is."

Jim Wilson, Jean Wilson and Janet Kempster carefully tag a monarch at Point Lepreau Bird Observatory. (Submitted by Francie Morgan)

The technology was first used on monarchs in Canada last year through a partnership between Environment and Climate Change Canada and Birds Canada in southern Ontario.

Nature NB applied for funding once that pilot proved successful, receiving support from the Environmental Trust Fund of New Brunswick and 10 additional tags directly from the federal government.

The organization had hoped for 35 tags this season, but delays at the border have complicated things.

“Half of our tags are stuck at the border,” Morgan said. Nature NB expects to deploy 22 tags by the end of the season, with the possibility of 13 more if the remaining shipment clears in time.

Wilson said similar problems affected his team’s supply, and about eight of its 30 tags remain tied up in customs because of tariffs.

Early data has already offered new insight into monarch migration routes through the province.

Point Lepreau, which juts into the Bay of Fundy, has long been suspected as a key stopover point for monarchs before they continue down the Eastern Seaboard toward Grand Manan. The new tags have confirmed that pattern.

“We’ve already had three that have left there with the BluMorpho tags and ended up on Grand Manan,” Morgan said.

Program coordinator Brie Blair holds a monarch butterfly before it's release at Point Lepreau Bird Observatory. (Submitted by Francie Morgan)

Strong westerly winds this season also produced an unexpected result, three tagged monarchs ended up in Nova Scotia instead of continuing south, offering researchers new information about how wind conditions influence migration decisions.

“That would be some very new information," Morgan said. "We're waiting to see."

Wilson said tracking individual migration routes could help identify which natural corridors — mountain ranges, river valleys, coastlines — monarchs rely on most, allowing conservationists to prioritize protecting those areas.

“All monarchs need in their long trip to Mexico is the ability to find blooming plants from which they get nectar,” Wilson said. “If we know how and where they go over time, those roads can be preserved and hopefully enhanced.”

Anyone can follow the tagged monarchs by downloading the free Project Monarch app. Tags deployed in New Brunswick begin with the prefix PLBO, for Point Lepreau Bird Observatory.

By the end of the season, Nature NB expects 22 monarchs in the province will have been tagged with the new technology.

World.title: The highly strategic city that the Canada Investment Summit forgot
World.content:
Article content

This startles me; I still think of Sudbury as the poster child for Big Nickel. In the last world war, International Nickel and the Sudbury workforce supplied on the order of 95 per cent of Allied nickel. In February 1942, C.D. Howe told Sudbury nickel workers that if production there stopped, “the whole character of the war will be changed.” In the early 1960s, the same city put up a ring of civil-defence sirens and sent kids under their desks at school. We are happy to call the place strategic; we are less eager to pay for the roads that still move the metal.
