World.title: Prague and the 15-Minute City? Only for One in Seven Residents
World.content:
In the first year of the Friendly City Index, Prague ranked second among Central and Eastern European metropolises.

Yet only 13.82% of residents can reach most daily destinations – work, schools, shops, or healthcare – within 15 minutes. The best metropolises in the region remain closer to “30-minute cities.”



Young Czechs are closest to the ideal: 34% of those aged 18–24 said they can reach everyday destinations within 15 minutes. Middle-aged people, especially 45–54, scored the worst at 14.7%.

Smaller Czech cities outperform Prague. Olomouc (36%), Ostrava (29.7%), and Brno (21.8%) all ranked better in their categories. Compact urban structures and shorter distances explain much of this advantage. Polish cities also dominated the rankings, including Krakow, Szczecin, and Lublin.

Among metropolises, Warsaw leads with 15.9%. In other categories: Krakow (30.3%), Split (44%), Rijeka (53.3%), and Zadar (53.6%). Riga ranked worst at 9.8%, while Zagreb scored only 20%.

The smaller the city, the better the accessibility

Around 10–15% in metropolises, 30% in large cities, 40%+ in medium-sized cities, and over 50% in small cities. Even cities with metro systems like Prague or Bucharest show little improvement, confirming that compactness and urban structure matter more than infrastructure alone.

Transport habits

In Central and Eastern Europe, 46% rely on cars and 27% on public transport. In Czechia, the split is nearly even: 42.6% drive, 42.4% use public transport. Among 18–24-year-olds, more than half (51.1%) rely on public transport. Alternative mobility options such as bikes, scooters, and carsharing remain marginal.

Urban planner Peter Bednár explains: “The point is not that all journeys must be short, but that most daily activities can be done without a car. Achieving this requires higher density and a mix of functions. Without enough services and destinations nearby, the most practical walk still leads to the parked car.”

About the index

The Friendly City Index is an international survey on quality of life and urban development. In 2025, it covered 54 cities in nine countries with 4,500 respondents, including 500 in Czechia. The study was carried out by Syno International in partnership with Bolt.

World.title: Where to See Prague’s Best Autumn Colors Without Leaving the City
World.content:
Autumn in Prague does not have to mean a crowded walk across Petřín or a stroll through Stromovka.

Beyond the city’s best-known parks, forests, valleys and protected natural areas offer quieter routes where the changing season can be enjoyed without leaving Prague.

Many of these places are also surprisingly easy to reach. A tram, bus or train can take you close to the starting point, making it possible to plan a two- or three-hour walk without a car or a full-day trip.



Vinoř Park and the Satalice Pheasantry

In northeastern Prague, a marked trail links Vinoř Park with the Satalice Pheasantry through a narrow wooded valley.

The landscape is shaped by the Vinořský Stream, sandstone formations and small springs. Along the route, walkers can also come across traces of the area’s history, including rock carvings, the remains of an old hillfort and the entrance to a water cave.

The area is especially attractive in autumn, when old oaks and other trees turn yellow and brown. A long avenue between Vinoř and Satalice adds another distinctive feature to the route.

The official educational trail is about 3.5 kilometers long and takes roughly two hours. It starts near the Malá Obůrka pond and finishes close to the Chapel of St. Anne in Satalice. From there, buses and trains provide connections back into Prague.

Hvězda offers more than its main avenue

Hvězda Game Reserve is one of Prague’s better-known green spaces, but many visitors stay on the central avenue leading from Vypich to the white Renaissance summer palace.

The quieter parts begin once you leave the main route and head into the surrounding woodland.

Oaks, beeches and hornbeams dominate the reserve. According to Prague’s records, more than half of its forest stands are over 150 years old. Several notable beech trees date from plantings carried out after 1763, including a tree recognized as the oldest and largest beech in Prague.

A loop through the reserve can lead from the summer palace toward the pond and Světlička wetland meadow before returning along one of the smaller paths.

Dalejské Valley offers a different side of Prague

Prokopské Valley is familiar to many Prague residents, but the landscape continues west toward Řeporyje in the quieter Dalejské Valley.

Here, limestone cliffs, former quarries, open slopes and the Dalejský Stream create a landscape that changes frequently along the trail.

One option is to follow the green-marked hiking route from Řeporyje toward Hlubočepy. Rather than forming one continuous wall of autumn foliage, the valley combines yellow trees with exposed rock and brownish grass-covered slopes.

The area forms part of the northeastern section of the Bohemian Karst and is recognized for its geological features. Prague’s Nature Portal recommends following the valley along the stream.

Hostivař Forest Park changes after summer

Hostivař is closely associated with its reservoir and summer swimming, but the area takes on a different character once the bathing season ends.

The woods surrounding the water offer numerous walking routes, with more than 35 kilometers of paths and trails running through the forest park.

A shorter walk can follow the reservoir, while longer routes continue through woodland and meadows and pass the animal enclosure near the gamekeeper’s lodge. The Botič Stream Basin educational trail also crosses the area.

Autumn brings changing colors to the oak and larch trees, while the reservoir provides views that are particularly noticeable on cooler mornings.

World.title: New Dog Playground Opens in Central Prague with Agility Course
World.content:
Prague 1 now has its first public dog playground, giving dog owners in the city center a dedicated space for exercise and training.

The new facility is located on Ludvík Svobody Embankment, next to the Ministry of Transport’s traffic playground and close to Lannov Park. It has been open to the public since September 16.



At the center of the site is an approximately 92-meter-long agility course. It includes a tunnel, slalom poles, an A-frame and several jumping obstacles. The playground is freely accessible and does not require prior booking.

“Space in the center of Prague is very limited, so we want to use every suitable location to serve local residents,” said Kateřina Klasnová, Prague 1’s deputy mayor responsible for the environment.

The playground is currently unfenced, meaning dogs can enter and leave the area freely.

Some dog owners raised concerns about the lack of a fence during the opening, and Prague 1 said it would consider adding one.

An information board at the site explains the operating rules and provides instructions for using the agility equipment. The playground also has a waste bin and two dispensers containing bags for dog owners to clean up after their pets.

Responsibility for the site lies with the Prague 1 Department of the Environment. Visitors can report damaged equipment or other defects directly to the municipal district.

World.title: Emeli Sandé to Bring Her Biggest Hits to Prague at O2 universum
World.content:
One of Britain’s most acclaimed contemporary singers, Emeli Sandé, returns to Prague on November 3 for a special live concert at O2 universum.

The singer-songwriter will perform her best-known hits alongside music from her latest album, How Were We to Know.

Tickets are available through Ticketmaster and Ticketportal.

Select 2 tickets and enter promo code EXPATPRAGUE at checkout. You’ll only pay for 1 ticket.

Emeli Sandé’s biggest hits

Sandé became an international star with songs including Next to Me, Heaven, Read All About It, Clown and My Kind of Love, combining soul, pop and powerful vocals with deeply personal songwriting.

Her debut album, Our Version of Events, became one of the most successful British albums of its era and was the UK’s best-selling album of 2012. It also produced several of her biggest hits and established Sandé as one of the country’s leading vocalists.

She further cemented her place in British music history with performances at both the opening and closing ceremonies of the London 2012 Olympic Games.

In Prague, fans can expect a set spanning her career, including songs from her latest album, How Were We to Know. Released as part of a new chapter in her career, the album combines her distinctive soul influences with a contemporary pop sound.

ADONXS joins as special guest

Sandé will be joined by ADONXS, singer, songwriter and one of the newer names on the Czech and Slovak pop scene.

ADONXS represented the Czech Republic at the Eurovision Song Contest 2025, where he performed his song Kiss Kiss Goodbye. He has also released tracks including Wasted and Perfume, while his latest single, Cherry on Your Cake, continues his development as a songwriter and performer.

His appearance at O2 universum will open the evening before Sandé takes the stage.

Emeli Sandé live at O2 universum

The Prague concert will bring together Sandé’s most recognisable songs with material from her more recent work, giving audiences the chance to hear her signature voice in a live setting.

With hits that have become familiar to audiences around the world, the concert offers a chance to revisit songs such as Next to Me, Heaven and Read All About It, while discovering the latest direction of her music.

World.title: EU Citizens Can Vote in Czechia’s October Elections: Here’s How
World.content:
EU citizens living in Czechia can vote in the country’s municipal elections this October, but those who are not already registered will need to take action before election day.

The elections will take place on October 9 and 10, with voters in Prague choosing representatives for both the Prague City Assembly and their local municipal district.

EU citizens aged 18 or over who have permanent or registered temporary residence in Czechia can vote in municipal elections. However, they must be registered in the relevant electoral register.

Registering to vote

The deadline for registration is October 7, but the civic initiative Volby pro všechny recommends registering as soon as possible.

Its EU Voter Registration Tool generates the necessary application form and explains how to submit it to the relevant municipal or district office.

Registering early also means voters should receive their ballot papers at home before election day, giving them time to understand the unfamiliar Czech voting system. Those who register closer to the deadline will receive their ballots at the polling station.

There is also an important option for those who miss the registration deadline. According to Volby pro všechny, EU citizens will have a special possibility this year to register directly at their polling station on election day, provided they bring the required identification and proof of residence.

Find your polling station

Voters cannot simply choose any polling station. Their home address determines where they can vote.

The Polling Station Finder allows residents to enter their address and find the correct polling place. It can also create a calendar reminder for election day.

Voters should bring a valid ID or passport and the relevant Czech residence document.

What will Prague residents vote for?

Prague voters will cast two votes: one for the Prague City Assembly, covering the capital as a whole, and one for the council of their municipal district.

For those unfamiliar with the division of responsibilities, Volby pro všechny has created a “Who Does What?” quiz explaining which level of local government deals with different issues.

The organization has also published an overview of political parties and groups and is preparing a quiz that will allow users to compare their answers on policy questions with the positions of Czech political parties.

A guide in 23 EU languages

Volby pro všechny has also prepared a seven-step checklist for EU citizens, available as a downloadable PDF in 23 EU languages.

For EU citizens who have never voted in Czechia before, the resources provide a straightforward way to check their registration, find their polling station and understand what to expect on election day.

World.title: Prague Unveils Future Metro Stations in Nusle and Náměstí Míru
World.content:
Prague’s future Metro Line D has taken another step toward becoming a reality, with new preliminary designs released for two stations planned along the route.

The Prague Public Transit Company (DPP) has presented renderings of the future Náměstí Míru interchange and Nusle station, offering an early look at how the new metro line could change the city’s underground transport network.

The images do not represent the final appearance of either station. DPP plans to select the architectural solutions through a two-stage competition, which will focus on the design of the interiors and the public spaces around the stations.

DPP intends to organise the competition in two stages, using a workshop format. The winning designs are expected to be selected within 18 months of signing the contract with the competition organiser. Preparations for that contract are currently underway.

Náměstí Míru station will connect Metro Lines A and D

The future Náměstí Míru station is planned beneath Sázavská Street, approximately 40 metres underground. It will be built using underground mining methods and will feature a single-vault design with an island platform.

The new station will be located above the existing Line A station, creating a new interchange between the two metro lines.

The design includes two vestibules equipped with escalators and a third access point with an elevator. The renderings show the planned exits towards Vinohradská, Francouzská, and Sázavská streets, as well as an elevator entrance on Korunní Street.

Metroprojekt has also presented a possible design for the outlet of a ventilation shaft in Riegrovy Sady. The structure will form part of the station’s technical infrastructure, although its final appearance may change following the architectural competition.

New Nusle station will serve Náměstí Bratří Synků

The second station featured in the new designs is the future Nusle station, which was previously known as Náměstí Bratří Synků.

The station will be built using cut-and-cover construction methods, with its island platform located approximately 13 metres below ground level. It is planned between Náměstí Bratří Synků and Otakarova Street.

Plans also include an underground parking garage for local residents above the station.

The new renderings show the proposed station entrances on Náměstí Bratří Synků, the northern vestibule beneath Otakarova Street, and the planned completion of the existing urban block.

When will Prague’s Metro Line D open?

Construction of Metro Line D began in 2022 with the section between Pankrác and Ryšánka. Work on the following section, extending towards Nové Dvory, began in June 2026.

The Pankrác–Nové Dvory section is planned to be the first part of the new metro line to open to passengers. DPP currently expects the section to enter service in the second half of 2032.

World.title: Two New Squares and a Tower Planned Around Holešovice Station
World.content:
The area around Prague’s Nádraží Holešovice station is set for a major redevelopment after the international architectural competition for the site was won by Czech studio Chybík + Krištof.

The winning proposal envisions turning the current transport hub and surrounding brownfield into a new urban district, with two public squares, improved connections between public transport services and a new high-rise building designed to become a landmark.



The redevelopment covers roughly eight hectares around the station. Its aim is not only to add new buildings, but also to reorganise one of Prague’s important transport nodes and connect it more closely with the surrounding neighbourhood.

The competition jury selected the proposal by Chybík + Krištof as the winning design.

From transport hub to urban district

Nádraží Holešovice is currently one of Prague’s major transport interchanges, but much of the surrounding area has traditionally been used primarily for transport and other infrastructure.

The redevelopment is intended to change that. Alongside new construction, the project places emphasis on making transfers between different modes of public transport easier and fully accessible.

The project forms part of the wider Nové Holešovice development, which brings together the Prague Public Transit Company and private investors.

CPI Property, EP Real Estate, Penta Real Estate and AKIPIA are among the companies involved. The City of Prague and Prague 7 municipal district are also participating in the project.

World.title: ČokoFest to Bring Three Days of Chocolate to Galerie Harfa
World.content:
Chocolate lovers will have plenty to discover in Prague this October as ČokoFest 2026 returns to Galerie Harfa for three days of tastings, workshops, competitions and sweet treats.

The festival will take place from October 16 to 18, 2026, at the shopping center in Prague 9. Admission is free.



Now in its 14th year, ČokoFest brings together Czech and international producers, including established chocolatiers and smaller makers.

Visitors will be able to sample and buy a wide selection of chocolates and confectionery, including handmade and bean-to-bar products, pralines, cakes, cookies and macarons.

The festival will also feature a range of less conventional chocolate and sweet specialties. Among the offerings will be a chocolate fountain, chocolate kebabs, chocolate-covered fruit, as well as chocolate-infused wine and beer. Other products on sale will include jams, liqueurs, syrups, dried fruits, honey products, coffee and tea.

Exhibitors from several European countries will join Czech producers, giving visitors the opportunity to discover different chocolate styles and specialties while shopping at international sales stalls.

ČokoFest will also feature a program of activities for both adults and children. Visitors can take part in tastings, competitions and creative workshops, while children can enjoy a dedicated zone and entertainment from performers dressed as popular children’s characters.

Cooking demonstrations will be another part of the program, with chefs from local restaurants sharing their experience and showing visitors how to prepare various sweet treats. Some workshops will also focus on chocolate-making techniques that can be tried at home.

The festival is designed as a family-friendly event, with activities taking place throughout the three days. In addition to tasting and shopping, visitors can watch pastry chefs at work, take part in competitions and learn more about the production and preparation of chocolate and other confectionery.

Opening hours:

Friday, October 16: 2:00–6:00 p.m.

Saturday, October 17: 10:00 a.m.–6:30 p.m.

Sunday, October 18: 10:00 a.m.–5:00 p.m.

World.title: Europe’s diesel crisis deepens as prices hit record highs – Hungary feels the pressure
World.content:
Europe’s diesel crisis is putting fresh pressure on drivers, businesses and farmers as disrupted oil supplies push fuel prices higher. France recorded a new diesel price record on Sunday, while European wholesale prices have also surged. Hungary is feeling the effects too, but the government has opted for targeted financial support rather than bringing back a nationwide fuel price cap.

Diesel is particularly important to the wider economy: it powers freight transport, agricultural machinery and much of the equipment used in construction and industry. When its price rises, the consequences can eventually extend beyond filling stations to the cost of transporting food and other goods.

The latest price increase comes as fighting in the Middle East and damage to Russian refining infrastructure continue to disrupt international fuel supplies.

Diesel prices reach record levels

France provided one of the clearest signs of the worsening situation on Sunday, 20 September. According to an AFP analysis of prices displayed at more than 8,700 filling stations, the national average diesel price reached almost EUR 2.41 per litre, breaking a record set just one day earlier.

Petrol has also become more expensive in France. The widely used SP95-E10 grade averaged more than EUR 2.17 per litre on Sunday, while SP98 exceeded EUR 2.28.

The pressure is not confined to France. Reuters reported on Friday that European diesel futures had reached approximately EUR 183 per barrel during the week. That is a wholesale market price, rather than the amount motorists pay at the pump, but it illustrates the strain on fuel supplies.

Some French filling stations have experienced temporary shortages, although the French government has rejected suggestions of a nationwide supply crisis. Elsewhere, governments are considering or introducing measures to ease the impact on consumers. Germany, for example, has announced a temporary fuel tax reduction equivalent to approximately EUR 0.17 per litre, due to take effect on 1 October.

Why is diesel becoming so expensive?

Refineries turn crude into diesel, petrol and other fuels, and several important sources of refined products have been disrupted by the conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine.

According to Reuters, diesel exports from the Middle East fell by more than 50% between March and August. Russian output has also been affected by repeated attacks on refineries, while restrictions on Russian exports have added to pressure on the international market. Together, these developments have reduced the supply available to importing countries.

Europe is particularly exposed to disruption in the trade in refined fuels. Reuters reported earlier this month that interruptions to Middle Eastern exports had cut the region’s supplies of diesel and jet fuel, leaving inventories at a 12-year low.

If you missed it: Fuel prices soar in Hungary: Diesel hits 4-year high – what does the government say about fuel price caps?

Hungary: No return to protected fuel prices

Hungarian motorists are also paying more for fuel. According to Holtankoljak.hu , the national average price on Friday, 18 September, was HUF 709 per litre for diesel and HUF 635 for 95-octane petrol. Prices can vary between filling stations.

The Hungarian government, led by Prime Minister Péter Magyar, has decided against reintroducing the previous fuel price cap. The decision reflects concerns that forcing prices below market levels could lead to supply shortages.

Instead, they have opted for targeted support rather than reinstating protected fuel prices. Eligible diesel car owners are set to receive HUF 5,000 per month until the end of the year, while farmers can reclaim the excise tax on diesel. However, these measures do not cap pump prices, leaving Hungarian motorists exposed to further fluctuations in the European fuel market.

More details: Hungary reveals new diesel subsidy details: Who gets EUR 55 and when will payments begin?

World.title: Ukraine could store fuel in Hungary as MOL and Naftogaz strike deal amid Russian attacks
World.content:
Ukraine could soon have additional fuel storage facilities on Hungarian territory under a new agreement between MOL and state-owned energy company Naftogaz. The two groups have signed a memorandum to develop storage capacity near their shared border, as repeated Russian strikes put Ukraine’s domestic fuel infrastructure at risk.

Naftogaz announced the agreement on Sunday, 20 September. The proposed facilities would store petroleum products in Hungary for the needs of the Ukrainian market, according to acting chief executive Serhiy Fedorenko.

The memorandum was signed at the Carpathian Economic Forum, held as part of the inaugural Carpathian Eight (C8) summit. The Ukrainian news agency Interfax reported the announcement on Sunday afternoon.

Why does Ukraine want to store fuel in Hungary?

Naftogaz says continued Russian attacks on Ukraine’s fuel infrastructure have made alternative supply routes and additional storage capacity increasingly important.

“Diversifying supply routes and creating additional storage capacity outside the strike zone is a matter of stability for the entire market,” Fedorenko said in a statement shared by Naftogaz on Telegram .

Locating storage facilities on the Hungarian side of the border could allow Ukraine to maintain some fuel reserves beyond the reach of attacks on infrastructure within its territory, while keeping them close to the Ukrainian market.

The project could therefore provide another option for managing fuel supplies if domestic storage or distribution facilities are damaged. However, the companies have not yet announced how fuel would be transported to and from the planned site.

Fedorenko said the development could improve the reliability of supplies for Ukrainian consumers and support cross-border energy infrastructure between Ukraine and Hungary.

If you missed it: Budapest and Kyiv face sharp criticism from the Russian Embassy over alleged secrecy and unfulfilled promises

When could the MOL–Naftogaz fuel facilities be built?

The companies have signed a memorandum of understanding, meaning construction has not yet been announced. There is no confirmed opening date, investment figure or planned storage capacity.

The announcement concerns petroleum products, including refined fuels, rather than natural gas. Further details are also needed on the facilities’ precise location, financing and future operation.

The agreement was reached during the C8 summit, held in western Ukraine on 18–20 September. The new regional initiative brings together Ukraine, Hungary, Poland, Slovakia, Romania, the Czech Republic, Austria and Serbia, with energy security, logistics and cross-border cooperation among its priorities.

If the project proceeds, Hungary would provide a new location for fuel storage serving Ukraine. For now, the memorandum marks the beginning of the proposed development rather than the availability of additional fuel reserves.

Featured image: MolGroup

World.title: Time to get your jackets out: Cold front to bring a sharp temperature drop to Hungary next week
World.content:
A cold front will sweep across Hungary on Sunday night, bringing strong winds and a sharp drop in temperatures. Daytime highs will fall to around 20°C for much of next week, while some sheltered areas could see temperatures approach freezing overnight, according to HungaroMet’s forecast released to MTI on Sunday.

The change will be most noticeable early in the week, when gusty winds and occasional showers could disrupt the otherwise sunny weather. Conditions are expected to become calmer and warmer by next weekend.

Strong winds and showers to start the week

On Monday, 21 September, the cloud associated with the cold front should clear southern and eastern Hungary during the morning, giving way to several hours of sunshine. Brief showers are most likely in the north-east, where isolated thunderstorms could also develop.

North-westerly winds will strengthen across much of the country, with stormy gusts possible in some areas. Daytime temperatures are expected to reach 18–24°C.

HungaroMet has also warned that Monday’s thunderstorms in the north-east could bring gusts of 60–75 km/h, potentially accompanied by small hail or ice pellets.

Tuesday will remain mostly sunny between passing clouds, although isolated showers and thunderstorms are still possible, particularly in the north-east. Strong north-westerly winds will affect large parts of Transdanubia and central Hungary.

The cold front-caused temperature drop will become more noticeable: afternoon highs are forecast at 16–20°C, while temperatures could fall to around 4°C overnight in colder, sheltered locations.

Hungary Weekly Briefing is out: Orbán’s new campaign, motorway deal and a possible break with Russian gas

Chilly mornings ahead, but sunshine will return

Wednesday is expected to bring plenty of sunshine, with only a few clouds and a chance of a brief shower in eastern or north-eastern Hungary. Daytime temperatures will reach 18–22°C, but some sheltered areas could approach freezing before sunrise.

Thursday will see a temporary increase in cloud cover from the west and north-west. Rain will be more likely in western Hungary, with highs of 17–23°C. Another cold morning is expected, particularly in places protected from the wind.

Friday should be mostly sunny, with only isolated showers. Early-morning temperatures will range from 3°C to 10°C, before rising to 18–23°C in the afternoon.

What will the weekend weather be like in Hungary?

The outlook for Saturday and Sunday, 26–27 September, is more settled. Saturday should be dry and mostly sunny, with lighter winds and afternoon temperatures of 19–24°C.

Sunday is also expected to be sunny and dry. After morning lows of 5–13°C, temperatures could climb to 20–25°C, bringing a milder end to the week.

The forecast is based on HungaroMet’s weekly outlook provided to Hungarian news agency MTI on Sunday, 20 September. Travellers and residents should check the latest official forecasts and weather warnings as conditions may change.

World.title: Orbán government took on EUR 13.7 billion in extra motorway costs citing Ukraine war, minister says
World.content:
Hungary’s previous government committed the state to at least HUF 5 trillion (EUR 13.7 billion) in additional motorway concession costs, citing the economic consequences of the war in Ukraine, according to Transport and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy. In a statement published on Sunday, he questioned why taxpayers were made to bear these risks under a contract signed months after the Russian invasion had begun.

“The money the Hungarian state intended to pay to Lőrinc Mészáros and László Szíjj’s company under the overpriced and unlawful concession agreement could have filled 46 lorries with HUF 20,000 banknotes,” Vitézy wrote.

The minister detailed the controversial arrangement in a Facebook post on Sunday, following the government’s announcement that it would seek to terminate the 35-year motorway concession agreement.

At the centre of the dispute is a December 2023 amendment signed by former cabinet minister Antal Rogán. Vitézy said the Orbán government agreed to cover a substantial share of the private motorway operator’s rising construction and financing costs, citing the economic consequences of the war in Ukraine.

The minister questioned the justification for the decision, pointing out that the original contract had been signed on 17 May 2022 — almost three months after Russia invaded Ukraine.

According to Vitézy, the compensation mechanism alone increased the state’s projected payments by at least HUF 5 trillion over the contract’s lifetime.

As we previously reported, the 35-year agreement covers the operation, maintenance and development of a substantial part of Hungary’s motorway network until 2057. The contract was awarded to MKIF, a company linked to businessmen Lőrinc Mészáros and László Szíjj. According to the government’s calculations, total payments under the concession could reach HUF 23.2 trillion.

The HUF 5 trillion figure refers to additional projected contractual costs, not money already paid out by the state.

Why did the Orbán government assume the extra war-related costs?

The December 2023 amendment introduced a mechanism known as war-related investment cost compensation, intended to address higher construction prices and interest rates resulting from the economic consequences of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

It was made possible by an emergency government decree, which treated the prolonged economic effects of the war as circumstances that could not reasonably have been foreseen when certain contracts were signed.

Vitézy questioned this justification, pointing out that Russia invaded Ukraine on 24 February 2022, almost three months before the original concession agreement was signed. He argued that a long-term concession should normally require the private operator to assume substantial commercial risks rather than passing them on to taxpayers.

Government questions motorway operator’s profits

The minister also criticised the financial structure of the arrangement, arguing that it allowed MKIF’s owners to retain profits while transferring a significant share of cost increases to the state.

He noted that the amendment was introduced approximately 18 months after the original agreement, at a time when, according to him, the operator had not yet built any new motorway sections.

Vitézy described the arrangement as one that protected the profits of Mészáros and Szíjj while leaving taxpayers exposed to rising costs. The government has argued that the contract is overpriced and contains provisions that violate procurement rules. Following its review, it announced on 18 September that it would initiate steps to end the arrangement.

The European Commission has also initiated infringement proceedings against Hungary over concerns about the concession’s compliance with EU procurement rules, including its duration and the allocation of operating risk.

What happens to the motorway contract now?

The government’s decision has already prompted a response from MKIF. As we wrote on Saturday, the company warned that statements questioning the agreement’s validity could affect its financing arrangements. MKIF also reserved its contractual rights and potential legal claims, although it has not announced that it has filed a lawsuit.

The motorway operator has disputed the government’s interpretation of the contract. Its chief executive, Tamás Németh, has maintained that the company bears significant risks under the concession.

The Tisza government is seeking a negotiated termination of the agreement, although Vitézy has indicated that a legal dispute could follow if the parties fail to reach a settlement.

For now, the concession remains in force, and neither the terms of its termination nor its potential financial consequences have been settled. Vitézy also announced that he would discuss the motorway concession in more detail in an interview on the Kontroll YouTube channel at 6 pm on Sunday.

World.title: A royal gift that never reached King Charles III: Hungarian defence minister investigates
World.content:
Hungary’s defence minister, Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi, has raised questions about an unusual military purchase originally linked to King Charles III’s 2023 coronation. The gift never reached London, but the Hungarian army still paid millions of forints for it. The minister now wants to know what happened to the purchase and how much it ultimately cost taxpayers.

The unusual purchase was detailed in a Facebook post published by the minister on Sunday, 20 September . According to Ruszin-Szendi, the previous defence leadership had planned to present the British monarch with an exclusive, four-horse Esterházy-style carriage as a ceremonial gift.

However, the plan was abandoned after the British royal family informed guests that only symbolic gifts should be brought to the coronation.

The carriage nevertheless remained part of Hungary’s military procurement records. Publicly available data from 2023 list the purchase of a specially commissioned Esterházy carriage, raising questions about its intended use after the London trip was cancelled.

How much did the coronation carriage cost?

According to the figures presented by Ruszin-Szendi, the carriage itself cost HUF 10.25 million excluding VAT, or approximately HUF 13 million including tax. Another HUF 5 million was spent on harnesses and ceremonial uniforms.

The vehicle, decorated with Hungary’s coat of arms and national colours, remained in the country. However, its subsequent use and the full costs associated with the purchase have yet to be clarified.

Caption: After renovation. The ceremonial carriage originally intended as a gift for King Charles III. Photo: Facebook / Dr. Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi

The minister raised several questions: What military purpose was the carriage intended to serve after the original plan was abandoned? How long did it remain unused? Was it subsequently modified, and if so, when and why? He also wants to establish the total amount paid by Hungarian taxpayers.

If you missed it: Man throws wine at Hungarian PM Péter Magyar during harvest festival – VIDEO

Defence minister questions priorities behind purchase

In his statement, Ruszin-Szendi acknowledged that the Hungarian Defence Forces carry out ceremonial duties, including supporting national and military celebrations and preserving military traditions.

Still, he questioned whether these responsibilities justified purchasing such an expensive carriage, and stated that defence spending should prioritise military readiness, properly equipped personnel and the development of Hungary’s armed forces.

He presented the purchase as one of several decisions made under the previous defence leadership that his ministry intends to examine.

Another unusual Hungarian gift to King Charles III

The carriage story follows a separate controversy involving two Hungarian Lipizzaner horses sent to the British royal household in 2024. The horses, Nelson and Iveco, were selected as part of the original gift arrangements for King Charles III. They were subsequently transferred to the Royal Mews under a loan agreement rather than a completed donation.

Earlier this month, Hungary’s agriculture ministry acknowledged that it had sent a letter concerning the termination of the loan. The ministry later said the wording had been incorrect and clarified that Hungary did not intend to bring the horses home.

Here’s the full story: Hungary admits “embarrassing blunder” over King Charles III’s Lipizzaner horses – updated: another twist

Wider review of military spending continues

The carriage purchase is part of a broader review of contracts and procurement decisions made under Hungary’s previous defence leadership.

Ruszin-Szendi said his ministry would continue examining questionable spending decisions from the past four years. He also indicated that legal action, including filing criminal complaints, would follow where the findings justified such steps.

World.title: Budapest gold scam: Elderly victims allegedly drugged, cheated out of millions worth of gold
World.content:
Three members of a family have been arrested in Budapest after defrauding elderly people out of hundreds of millions of forints through an illegal gold-buying business.

Police say one victim was given a drink that caused him to lose consciousness, while another was tricked into signing away a property worth HUF 145 million. Investigators also seized nearly HUF 200 million worth of gold.

The Budapest Police Headquarters (BRFK) released details of the case on Sunday, 20 September. According to the official police statement, the suspects, aged 28, 50 and 53, ran an unauthorised gold-buying business in Újbuda, Budapest’s District XI.

They allegedly attracted customers by offering prices well above market value. Once people entered the premises, however, the suspects reportedly used deception, intimidation and other methods to obtain their valuables for far less than they were worth.

The victims were mainly elderly people, with the suspects allegedly adapting their methods to each person’s circumstances.

Elderly man loses consciousness, wakes up without his gold

One of the most disturbing cases involved a 71-year-old man who visited the business carrying gold worth more than HUF 10 million.

According to police, the suspects offered to drive him home so they could purchase additional valuables he had left there. Before leaving, however, they allegedly gave him a drink containing an unidentified substance. The man lost consciousness and later woke up injured in the street. His gold jewellery had disappeared.

In another case, the suspects allegedly approached an elderly man on the street, claiming they wanted to buy his property. After gaining access to his home, they reportedly stole valuables and documents, and later persuaded him to sign papers supposedly related to his deceased wife’s inheritance proceedings.

Instead, the man was tricked into signing a life annuity agreement, through which the suspects acquired a property worth approximately HUF 145 million. Ownership was subsequently registered in the name of one of their relatives.

If you missed it: Man throws wine at Hungarian PM Péter Magyar during harvest festival – VIDEO

Gold bars melted down, customers pressured into accepting less

Other victims were reportedly lured to the business with attractive offers for their gold. Once the gold bars had been handed over, the suspects allegedly melted them down and then claimed the metal was of poor quality. They offered only a fraction of the originally promised price.

Customers who wanted their gold back were refused. Police say some were kept at the premises for hours, facing pressure and feeling outnumbered and eventually, desperate to leave, they accepted payments tens of millions of forints below the initial offers.

In some cases, the suspects allegedly cut jewellery into pieces before a sale had been agreed, allowing them to classify it as scrap gold and offer a much lower price.

Police seize nearly HUF 200 million in gold

Investigators from Budapest’s District XI police station arrested the three family members on 15 September. All three were questioned on suspicion of fraud committed as part of a criminal group and as a regular business activity.

During searches, officers discovered and seized gold bars, jewellery and other gold items with an estimated value of nearly HUF 200 million. The suspects were taken into custody, and a court subsequently ordered their pre-trial detention.

The investigation is ongoing, and the three suspects are presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

World.title: Nearly one million people affected by dementia in Hungary – but many cases could be prevented
World.content:
Dementia affects nearly one million people in Hungary, including patients, relatives and carers, while research suggests that up to 45% of dementia cases could potentially be prevented or delayed. Ahead of World Alzheimer’s Day on 21 September, experts have warned that families bear much of the burden of caring for people with the condition, with limited support from the state.

An estimated 200,000–300,000 people in Hungary are living with dementia, according to experts interviewed by Hungarian news agency MTI. The condition affects approximately 10% of people aged over 65, although comprehensive national data remain unavailable.

Including relatives and carers, the total number of people affected is estimated to approach one million, roughly one-tenth of Hungary’s population.

Zoltán Hidasi, an associate professor at Semmelweis University’s Department of Psychiatry and Psychotherapy, explained that Alzheimer’s disease is the most common cause of dementia, accounting for an estimated 70–80% of cases.

Dementia is not a single disease but a group of symptoms involving a decline in cognitive abilities severe enough to interfere with everyday activities.

Could nearly half of dementia cases be prevented?

According to Ágnes Eszter Melcherné Kázár, a general practitioner and head of the Feledhetetlen Foundation, international research suggests that approximately 45% of dementia cases could potentially be prevented or significantly delayed.

The figure is consistent with the 2024 Lancet Commission on dementia prevention, intervention and care, which identified 14 potentially modifiable risk factors throughout life.

These include high blood pressure, diabetes, obesity, smoking, excessive alcohol consumption, depression, physical inactivity and social isolation.

The commission also highlighted two less widely recognised risk factors: high LDL cholesterol in middle age and untreated vision loss later in life. Experts emphasise that prevention should begin long before old age. Education, regular physical activity, a balanced diet, maintaining social connections and managing cardiovascular conditions can all contribute to reducing risk.

If you missed it: Magyar government plans to hike tobacco taxes, sending cigarette prices sharply higher

When should memory problems become a concern?

Hidasi explained that occasional forgetfulness does not necessarily indicate Alzheimer’s disease. Memory performance naturally varies between individuals, while stress, anxiety and fatigue can also affect the ability to remember names or recall where everyday objects have been placed.

Dementia is progressive, although its rate of development varies considerably. Some people experience a gradual decline over many years, while others deteriorate more rapidly.

Early diagnosis is particularly important because some conditions that cause cognitive impairment, including certain vitamin deficiencies or hormonal disorders, may be treatable.

People experiencing concerning memory problems should first consult their GP, who can arrange further neurological or psychiatric assessment if necessary.

Although Alzheimer’s disease currently has no cure, newer treatments have emerged. The European Union authorised lecanemab in April 2025 and donanemab in September 2025 for certain patients with early-stage Alzheimer’s disease. These medicines can slow cognitive decline in eligible patients but do not reverse the condition, and their use is subject to medical restrictions and safety monitoring.

Hungarian families carry much of the burden

Beyond the medical challenges, dementia places a substantial financial and emotional burden on families. Melcherné Kázár told MTI that dementia is frequently diagnosed relatively late in Hungary, often when patients have already reached a moderate or severe stage.

People with moderate dementia may still be capable of basic self-care but often require assistance with household tasks and financial matters. In more advanced cases, relatives may need to provide help with eating, washing and other essential daily activities.

The foundation’s head criticised the limited availability of state support, noting that family members sometimes sacrifice their employment to care for relatives.

She also highlighted the absence of a comprehensive national dementia strategy and dementia registry in Hungary. According to the expert, recognising cognitive impairment within the country’s disability support framework and making dementia a public health priority would be important steps towards improving care.

The warnings come ahead of World Alzheimer’s Day, observed internationally on 21 September to raise awareness of Alzheimer’s disease, other forms of dementia and the challenges faced by patients and their families.

World.title: Can farming survive Hungary’s growing drought crisis? New documentary reveals the stakes
World.content:
Hungary’s Great Plain is facing an increasingly severe water crisis, threatening the livelihoods of farmers across the region. A new documentary explores how changing agricultural practices and restoring the landscape’s ability to retain water could help communities adapt to prolonged drought.

The situation is particularly alarming in the Homokhátság, a sandy region between the Danube and Tisza rivers, where falling groundwater levels and deteriorating soil conditions are making traditional farming increasingly difficult. For local farmers, adapting to the changing climate is becoming a matter of economic survival.

These challenges are at the centre of a new WWF Hungary documentary, premiered online by 24.hu. The final instalment of the three-part series brings together scientists and a local farmer to examine whether agriculture can remain economically viable as water becomes increasingly scarce.

A region losing its water

The Homokhátság has been struggling with water shortages for decades. Climate change, alterations to the natural landscape, intensive water use and drainage infrastructure have all contributed to its deterioration.

As we previously reported, less than 3% of Hungary’s arable land is irrigated, leaving farmers particularly vulnerable to prolonged drought. A recent policy study also estimated that the record-breaking drought of 2022 caused more than HUF 1 trillion in damage to Hungarian agriculture.

According to an earlier instalment of the documentary series, approximately 6–8 billion cubic metres of groundwater have been lost from the region over the past 15 years. Wells are drying up, while increasingly prolonged dry periods are putting additional pressure on agricultural production.

The consequences extend beyond individual farms. As soils lose moisture and vegetation deteriorates, the landscape becomes less resilient to further drought. WWF Hungary has warned that water scarcity is threatening both agriculture and local livelihoods, making changes to water management and land use increasingly urgent.

Hungarian farmer warns: current methods are reaching their limits

The documentary features farmer Zoltán Szabó, who describes the difficulties of maintaining profitable agricultural production under increasingly challenging environmental conditions. His experiences illustrate why farmers may need to reconsider practices that have shaped their businesses for years.

“We have reached our limits. From here, things can only get worse. If we want to maintain current production levels, we must build up our soils, not destroy them,” Szabó says in the film.

The documentary also features hydrogeologist Judit Szőnyi, ecologist Csaba Tölgyesi and geographer János Rakonczai, who examine the region’s problems from different scientific perspectives.

Rather than focusing exclusively on irrigation, the experts explore how agricultural practices could help retain moisture, protect soil quality and make better use of the water already available in the landscape.

Related: Hungarian agriculture, as we know it, is nearing the end – but researchers already have a plan

Could regenerative farming help save the Great Plain?

Among the approaches examined in the film are regenerative agriculture, minimal soil disturbance and the cultivation of more drought-tolerant crops. Maintaining healthy soils is particularly important because their structure and organic matter influence how effectively they absorb and retain moisture.

The documentary also considers whether some areas should move away from intensive crop production towards grassland management or extensive livestock farming.

Such changes would require farmers to adapt their business models, but could offer alternatives in places where conventional production is becoming increasingly difficult. Water retention is another central issue. The series’ previous episode highlighted community-led initiatives that seek to keep water in the landscape rather than allowing it to drain away rapidly through existing channels.

Some projects have already demonstrated how previously dry areas can recover when water is retained, with wildlife returning to restored habitats.

A documentary about Hungary’s changing landscape

The three-part series was developed under the MOSAIC project, which examines how land-use decisions can better account for climate change and biodiversity.

Its first episode explored the causes of the Homokhátság’s water crisis, while the second focused on practical solutions and community action. The newly released final instalment shifts attention to farming and the difficult choices facing those who depend on the land.

By combining scientific explanations with personal stories, the filmmakers aim to show not only what Hungary risks losing, but also how changing agricultural practices could help preserve the region for future generations.

World.title: EU President to Skip Serbia and Bosnia on Balkan Tour
World.content:
The European Commission announced on Friday that President Ursula von der Leyen will miss Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina during her trip to the Western Balkans between September 30 and October 2, citing upcoming elections in the two countries.

“In light of the upcoming parliamentary and general elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in Serbia, the president intends to visit these countries at a later date,” a Commission spokesperson, Arianna Podesta, said on Friday.

During the trip, von der Leyen will visit Albania, Kosovo, Montenegro and North Macedonia where she will meet leaders and look at EU-funded projects.

After the EU announcement, Serbia’s President hinted that looming elections were not the only reason for the no-show – hinting at her recent criticism of his administration.

“Ursula von der Leyen is far too wise and intelligent a woman to have any illusions about, or to be unaware of, public opinion in Serbia. So I’m sure she knows very well… [but] let’s not get into that,” Vucic said.

Von der Leyen and other EU officials have condemned Serbia’s government over the glorification of the convicted Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladic, whose funeral in Belgrade on September 7 was attended by ministers and high officials both from Serbia and Bosnia’s Serb-led entity, Republika Srpska.

“I was horrified by the pictures from Ratko Mladic’s funeral in Belgrade last week. He committed the most atrocious crimes against humanity. Glorifying war criminals simply has no place in the European Union,” von der Leyen said on September 16. Serbia is an EU candidate state.

A day after Mladic’s funeral, von der Leyen also wrote on X that “the elements of official support and the presence of some senior Serbian officials at the funeral are deeply regrettable”.

Earlier in September, EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos cancelled her planned visit to Serbia, the day after Mladic’s body was transported on a government plane to Belgrade, where it was met by officials and an army honour guard.

Early parliamentary elections will be held in Serbia on October 25. President Vucic called the elections after a year-and-a-half of anti-government protesters demanding snap elections.

The elections will be Vucic’s most challenging test since he came to power in 2012. The main rival to his ruling Serbian Progressive Party, SNS, is the Student List, a political list formed by Serbian students who have been protesting since November 2024, following the deadly collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad.

Bosnia and Herzegovina will hold presidential ​and parliamentary elections ‌on October 4.

World.title: Week in Review: Campaigns, Crackdowns and Clan Wars
World.content:
Wildfires have blazed across the Balkans over the last couple of months amid another scorching summer. Around the Albanian coastal city of Himara, they forced evacuations, destroyed homes and olive groves.

The Albanian government has identified the growing threat from wildfires as an expected consequence of climate change. But there’s a lack of readiness and coordination to confront the challenge, experts are warning.

World.title: Discontent Simmers in Kosovo as Protesters Denounce Hague War Crimes Verdict
World.content:
The KLA War Veterans’ Organisation, which staged Friday’s protest, called for the dismissal of Justice Minister Donika Gervalla, the repeal or amendment of the Law on the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, unlimited funding for the defence of the four former KLA leaders in their upcoming appeal against the verdict, and the engagement of top international experts for their defence.

Hysni Gucati, head of the organisation, accused minister Gervalla of submitting evidence for the case to the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague.

“We are telling [Prime Minister] Albin Kurti to remove these people from the government starting today; he should not keep them in the government. People who collaborate with the enemy are enemies of my nation, and we do not want them among us,” Gucati said.

“Donika Gervalla has still not come forward to apologise,” he added. Gervalla has not commented publicly about the allegation so far.

World.title: Fining Bosnia’s Parties for Campaign Violations Won’t Deter Them, Expert Warns
World.content:
The unprecedented fines imposed this week by Bosnia’s Central Election Commission won’t stop ruling parties from exploiting state resources to secure votes, Dario Jovanovic, project manager of the fair-elections campaign group Pod Lupom, told BIRN on Friday.

“Parties in Bosnia view these fines as a minor, predictable cost of doing business,” Jovanovic said. “When a ruling party controls millions in public budgets, a few thousand euros will not stop them from exploiting state resources to secure votes.”

The state Election Commission imposed unprecedented penalties exceeding 100,000 euros during a single session in Sarajevo on Thursday, heavily targeting major political entities for premature campaigning and abusing public resources ahead of the polls on October 4.

The primary target of Election Commission’s sanctions was the Alliance of Independent Social Democrats, SNSD, the Bosnian Serb ruling party led by Milorad Dodik.

The SNSD, which holds power in Bosnia’s Serb-led entity, Republika Srpska, was directly fined about 41,900 euros, while individual sanctions against its candidates brought the party’s total penalty to 52,700 euros, effectively accounting for over half of the entire session’s fines.

The regulatory body cited multiple severe violations of Bosnia’s Election Law, focusing on the unlawful exploitation of public infrastructure projects for partisan gain and the illegal use of children for political marketing.

Dodik himself was personally fined around 4,600 euros over an Instagram post in which he took direct credit on behalf of his party for taxpayer-funded public works. A member of the state parliament, Sanja Vulic, was fined 4,100 euros for inaccurate media statements and premature campaigning during a television broadcast.

The financial sweep extended beyond the SNSD. The Drasko Stanivukovic – Safe Srpska Movement coalition received the second-highest cumulative penalty, of some 13,000 euros. Following the ruling, Stanivukovic, mayor of Banja Luka, the main city in Republika Srpska, criticised the decision.

“They are fining us simply for doing our jobs and presenting infrastructure projects to the citizens,” Stanivukovic stated to media. “These decisions are rigid and politically targeted to diminish our campaign visibility.”

Other penalised entities included the Social Democratic Party, SDP, which was fined 8,700 euros, and Nedeljko Stevandic’s United Srpska, at 7,200 euros.

Major political entities from Bosnia’s other entity, the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, including the Party of Democratic Action, SDA and a five-party Croat coalition, were also hit with financial sanctions.

With voters set to elect the state’s tripartite Presidency and entity parliaments in less than three weeks, the watchdog’s latest financial targeting represents an aggressive institutional effort to enforce compliance in a highly polarized race.

World.title: Greece Mourns Margarita Papandreou, Pioneering Feminist
World.content:
Margarita Papandreou with her three sons Photo: Nikos Papandreou/Facebook.

Greek feminist and author Margarita Papandreou, who was the wife of prime minister and centre-left PASOK party founder Andreas Papandreou, died in Athens on Friday. On September 20, she would have turned 103 years old.

Margarita (Margaret) Chant-Papandreou, originally from the US, studied journalism and pursued postgraduate studies in Public Health. Her name became linked to one of the most prominent political dynasties in Greek history, as well as to a series of significant reforms regarding gender equality.

She was the second wife from 1951 to 1989 of Andreas Papandreou; together they had four children, including former PM George Papandreou and PASOK MEP Nikos Papandreou.

“Margarita Papandreou linked her name to the struggle for women’s rights and social progress,” stated PASOK’s current leader, Nikos Androulakis.

Margarita met Andreas in the US in 1948 and the couple moved to Greece in 1961. Following the military takeover and Andreas’s arrest in 1967, she campaigned for his release. They left Greece for Sweden, and then Canada, returning to Greece after the fall of the military junta in 1974, when Andreas announced the founding of PASOK.

Margarita did not remain in her husband’s shadow; in 1976, alongside other women, she founded the Women’s Union of Greece, a women’s non-profit.

She played a pivotal role in promoting, drafting and passing legislation that improved the social status of Greek women. Key measures included the introduction of civil marriage in 1982, the abolition of the dowry system, the legalisation of divorce by mutual consent, the right of women to retain their maiden names after marriage in 1983, and the legalisation of abortion in 1986.

In her book, Love and Power, she recounted her turbulent relationship with her husband – marked by infidelity, their acrimonious divorce and his subsequent marriage to a younger woman.

Her son, Nikos Papandreou, wrote in the preface: “She may have stood by the side of the Greek politician who transformed Greece – Andreas – but she also created and led the country’s most significant feminist movement, the one that exerted the greatest influence regarding women’s rights in Greece.”

World.title: Turkey Arrests Fund Managers Over Stock Market Manipulation Scandal
World.content:
Turkish authorities arrested four suspects on Friday, including investment fund board members, and imposed travel bans on 51 others, as part of an investigation into alleged manipulation of the stock market, Justice Minister Akin Gurlek announced.

Courts have also imposed precautionary measures on accounts and other assets linked to those under investigation, to prevent their transfer, Gurlek said.

“Those who exploit the sweat, labour and savings of our citizens will be held accountable before the law,” he added.

Turkey’s Capital Markets Board, SPK, has filed criminal complaints about alleged manipulative transactions in several funds and listed shares.

In a separate investigation, a court ordered access blocked to 246 social media accounts accused of publishing speculative material capable of causing fear or panic among investors.

Another investigation by prosecutors in Istanbul’s Bakirkoy District has resulted in 16 arrests over social media posts allegedly intended to manipulate capital markets, Gurlek said.

Turkish Interior Minister Mustafa Ciftci on Thursday said operations related to the stock market investigation would continue, suggesting further action is likely.

On Thursday the SPK ordered the liquidation of 130 funds managed by seven portfolio management companies after liquidity problems contributed to sharp market losses.

Trading on Istanbul Stock Exchange was temporarily suspended on Wednesday after the benchmark BIST 100 index fell by more than 6 per cent, triggering a market-wide circuit breaker.

Estimates of the combined size of the 130 funds differ.

According to Reuters, their assets are worth around 21.4 billion US dollars, involving about 353,000 investors. CNBC-e puts the total at about 19.8 billion US dollars and the number of investors at more than 514,000.

Liquidation does not mean that the investors’ money has been confiscated. Instead, banks are being tasked to deliver citizens’ money in these funds. Is Bank has been appointed to handle the liquidation of funds managed by Tera Portfoy, while state-owned Ziraat Bank will oversee funds belonging to the six other managers.

The proceeds will be distributed to investors according to their holdings. However, investors may not recover the last reported value of their holdings, as the final amount will depend on prices achieved when the assets are sold.

The crisis intensified after regulatory changes targeted risks associated with funds concentrated in thinly traded shares.

“It has been observed that some funds have caused price movements that cannot be explained by the financial realities of companies,” the SPK said on Thursday, adding that the new measures were aimed at preventing market manipulation and increasing transparency.

World.title: Expelled by Greece’s Ruling Party, Ex-PM Samaras Plots His Revenge
World.content:
At the beginning of September, former Greek prime minister Antonis Samaras seized on a newspaper report that users of the online platform of the Greek health service were allowed to specify gender options beyond ‘Male’ and ‘Female’, to include ‘Other’ and ‘Undetermined’.

Samaras was expelled from Greece’s ruling New Democracy party last year, and still bears a grudge.

He promptly took to Facebook to accuse the conservative government of promoting a “woke agenda” and echoed erroneous claims that school textbooks were depicting families with same-sex parents.

“The only thing ‘undetermined’ here is the extent of the ideological shift within the ruling party,” Samaras wrote. Greek families “need support, not redefinition”, he claimed.

World.title: EU Should Not Turn a Blind Eye to Montenegro’s Bloody Clan War
World.content:
When Montenegro declared independence in 2006, it identified EU and NATO integration as its strategic priorities. The country applied for EU membership in 2008, accession negotiations began in 2012, and NATO membership followed in 2017.

Yet, beneath the language of democratisation and Europeanisation lies a far less reassuring reality: a country where rival organised crime clans have waged a conflict for more than a decade, with dozens of people murdered, including innocent bystanders – and where allegations of links between criminal groups, police officers, and senior judicial figures have repeatedly surfaced

The question is not merely why Montenegro has struggled to defeat organised crime. It is why this conflict appears to have become increasingly peripheral to the European Union’s public assessment of the country.

The origins of Montenegro’s interclan war are generally traced to a dispute involving the disappearance of almost 200 kilograms of cocaine in Valencia, Spain, in 2014. What followed was a violent confrontation between two criminal groups based in the coastal town of Kotor – the Kavac and Skaljari clans. Most of the country’s organised crime groups eventually aligned themselves with one of the two rival groups.

Kotor itself became a symbol of the problem. The UNESCO World Heritage Site and historic home of both clans was described by then Interior Minister Goran Danilovic as a “hostage town.” Investigations subsequently alleged the existence of surveillance networks used by criminal gangs and the disclosure of confidential police information to members of the Kavac clan.

World.title: Croatian Prices Rise Once Again in August
World.content:
September the 20th, 2026 – Croatian prices rose once again this August, with restaurants, housing and fuel in particular all climbing up.

The prices of goods and services for personal consumption, measured by the consumer price index, in August 2026 compared to August 2025 (on an annual basis) were on average higher by 4.2%, while compared to July 2026 (on a monthly basis) they were on average higher by 0.4%.

Morski reports that when observed according to the main groups of the ECOICOP classification, ver. 2, on an annual basis, the largest increase in consumer prices on average was recorded in the groups Transport, by 13.5% (contribution to the increase of +1.88 percentage points), Housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuels, by 10.8% (+1.62 percentage points), Restaurants and accommodation services, by 6.1% (+0.34 percentage points), Health, by 5.1% (+0.14 percentage points), Alcoholic beverages and tobacco, by 3.9% (+0.19 percentage points), Insurance services and financial services, by 3.6% (+0.07 percentage points), Personal care, social protection and miscellaneous goods and services, by 2.8% (+0.14 percentage points), Information and communication, by 2.7% (+0.16 percentage points), and Recreation, sport and culture, by 2.4% (+0.09 percentage points). The increase in prices on an annual basis was mitigated by a fall in prices in the groups Clothing and footwear, by 5.1% (contribution to the fall of -0.36 percentage points), Education services, by 2.0% (-0.01 percentage points), Food and non-alcoholic beverages, by 0.6% (-0.16 percentage points), and Furnishings, household equipment and routine household maintenance, by 0.3% (-0.02 percentage points).

According to the main components of the index (special aggregates), an increase in prices on an annual basis was recorded in the components Energy, by 17.6%, Services, by 7.2%, and Food, beverages and tobacco, by 0.1%, while a fall in prices is observed in the component Industrial non-food products excluding energy, by 1.3%. An increase in prices on a monthly basis was recorded in the components Energy, by 3.9%, and Services, by 0.1%, while a fall in prices appeared in the components Industrial non-food products excluding energy, by 0.9%, and Food, beverages and tobacco, by 0.2%.

The prices of goods and services for personal consumption, measured by the harmonised index of consumer prices, in August 2026 compared to August 2025 (on an annual basis) were on average higher by 3.7%. Compared to July 2026 (on a monthly basis) they were on average higher by 0.3%.

World.title: FlixBus Expands Network to 258 Destinations in Croatia
World.content:
September the 20th, 2026 – The popular coach service FlixBus has expanded its already enviable network to 258 destinations in Croatia.

Croatia is an important part of the Flix Europe East region, and Central, Eastern and Southeastern Europe are among the areas with great potential for further development, says Michal Leman from Flix. Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that a decade of FlixBus operations in Croatia has now officially been marked. The company began providing services back in 2016 in four Croatian cities and in cooperation with four bus partners, and today in the wider Flix network it has more than 258 connected destinations in Croatia and 390 cities across Europe.

Michal Leman, Vice President Europe East of Flix, emphasises that the anniversary is not only a look back. “Croatia is now entering a new chapter in which we want to further develop domestic and international connectivity, in cooperation with our local partners. Croatia is an important part of the Flix Europe East region, and Central, Eastern and Southeastern Europe are among the areas with great potential for further development.

We therefore see the future not only in new lines, but in even stronger partnerships, better connected markets and a greater number of opportunities for passengers,” Leman says. In the first ten years of operations, FlixBus in Croatia has transported 16.3 million passengers, and the growth of the network is best shown by the connectivity data: the number of direct connections to and from Croatia increased from 375 in 2016 to 4,471 in 2026.

The number of bus partners simultaneously rose from four to 15, while during 2026 FlixBus records an average of around 9,100 departures per month. Today a total of 128 lines operate from and to Croatia. Ten years of development has not meant only an increase in the number of lines and destinations, but above all growth in opportunities for passengers – from a greater choice of destinations and travel times to stronger linking of Croatian cities with neighbouring countries and the rest of Europe.

From the very beginning Croatia, was part of a wider story of regional connectivity. Only a year after entering the Croatian market, in 2017, FlixBus expanded to Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia and Slovenia, thereby laying the foundations for stronger connectivity of Central and Southeastern Europe. Flix sees particular potential in Southeastern Europe, where stronger domestic and international connectivity can further bring individual markets closer together, but also better connect them with the rest of the European network.

World.title: The Croatian Bell Tower That Offers Views into Three Countries
World.content:
September the 20th, 2026 – There’s a Croatian bell tower hidden away in an old Istrian town which, on clear days, offers spectacular views into three different countries.

A trip to the gorgeous old settlement of Buje is a perfect combination of history, untouched nature and excellent gastronomy, and nearby are the Momjan castle and the unusual Istrian desert of Piski. Putni kofer/Ivana Vasarevic writes that for all their abundant beauty, very few parts of Croatia look as fairy-tale-like as the interior of Istria. Astonishingly beautiful towns surrounded by untouched nature never cease to delight us, and one of them is certainly Buje. Situated on a fertile hill, in the firm embrace of centuries-old vineyards and olive groves, this Istrian gem was already inhabited in the Bronze Age and today has around 3,000 inhabitants. It is only 13 kilometres from the crystal-clear Adriatic Sea (Umag), and the Slovenian border is also very close.

the guardian of buje

Picchio4ever, Daniele Kovacic – Opera propria

Its ancient population once lived in a fortified hillfort, of which there are as many as about 20 remains in Buje and the surrounding area! A labyrinth of paved streets full of charm will take you to the core of the old town and Freedom Square, where the magnificent Church of St. Servulus and the 15th-century bell tower will greet you. From it, in fine weather, there is a fantastic view of as many as three neighbouring countries: Slovenia, Italy and Austria. This beautiful bell tower is one of the tallest in Istria, and given that it stands at 222 metres above sea level, it was once a lookout and watchtower, so it received the nicknames guardian of the town and watch of Istria. In addition, its image also adorned the town seal from the 13th century.

IT wAS FIRST MENTIONED IN DOCUMENTS AS EARLY AS 981 AS CASTRUM BUGLE

And there is also the bell tower that proudly stands next to the Church of Our Lady of Mercy (St. Mary of Mercy). It dates from the 17th century, is 22 metres high, is adorned with a clock, and at its base there is a characteristic passageway, opposite which is the ethnographic museum. At the same time, in the aforementioned church you can see the sculpture of Our Lady of Mercy, one of the most beautiful wooden statues in Istria. In the Iron Age, the wider area around Buje was inhabited by the Histri, the first documented people to settle on the Istrian peninsula, and the Romans also had their colonies in Terra Magica. In the Middle Ages a fortified medieval town developed, and it is first mentioned in documents, i.e. in a charter of the German-Roman Emperor Otto II, as early as 981 as Castrum Bugle.

THE MAGNIFICENT TOWER wAS ONCE PART OF THE VENETIAN WALLS

At the beginning of the 15th century the entire Buje area came under the rule of the Venetian Republic, and over the next four centuries the magnificent bell tower, the impressive Church of St. Servulus (the town’s patron saint) and the town loggia, which was located on Freedom Square, were built there. To this day, the Tower of St. Martin, which was part of the Venetian walls, has been preserved from that period. And after the fall of the once mighty Venetian empire in 1797, the French, the Austro-Hungarian Monarchy and the Kingdom of Italy successively ruled in Buje. After the end of the Second World War, the town and its surroundings ended up in the Free Territory of Trieste. Its status was settled only in 1954, when it was agreed that the northern part of the Territory, Trieste and the surroundings, would belong to Italy, and the southern part, including Buje, to the then Yugoslavia.

THE ETHNOGRAPHIC MUSEUM iS HOME TO AN OLIVE PROCESSING PLANT AND AN OLD BLACKSMITH’S WORKSHOP

If you find yourself in Buje, also take a look at the aforementioned ethnographic collection in the local museum, which preserves handicrafts of folk material culture from the entire Buje area. It is located in a magnificent four-storey building, and tools, furniture and everything that made up a typical old household, once oriented towards agriculture and ancient crafts, are exhibited in it. Down in the basement, you will find a blacksmith’s workshop and an old olive processing plant, i.e. a press, millstone and stone vessels with wooden lids in which olive oil was stored. Traditional Istrian cuisine and valuable pottery items are exhibited on the first floor, and the greatest attraction of this part of the museum is the hearth, the lifeblood of every Istrian household.

NEARBY LIE THE MEDIEVAL MOMJAN CASTLE AND THE ISTRIAN DESERT OF PISKI

The second and third floors are reserved for a loom and antique carved chests in which clothes and other personal items were kept. In addition to all of the above, the third floor is often used for occasional exhibitions of an ethnographic and historical character. Near Buje are also the picturesque settlement of Momjan with its imposing medieval castle above the Dragonja River and the Istrian desert of Piski, a unique natural phenomenon, i.e. marl dunes, one of the greatest attractions of northwestern Istria that really looks impressive.

tHE HOME OF BEER MISU!

Momjan – Fraxinus Croat

And after sightseeing this magical little town, it is time to explore the wine and olive oil roads of the Buje area. Enjoy the delicious Istrian cuisine and excellent wines, but also the excellent local beer that has been produced since 2013 at the San Servolo brewery in Buje. Only four ingredients are responsible for its perfect taste: barley malt, hops, yeast and natural water from the St. John spring, which is located in the valley of the Mirna River. In the pub you can also taste dishes such as beer soup or beer misu.
