BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 20. The Grape and Wine Festival continued today in Shamakhi.

The festival was held on the grounds of the viticulture and winemaking complex of Şirvan şərabları LLC in the village of Meysari, where various wine brands were represented with their own pavilions. Guests had the opportunity to visit the pavilions and taste different types of viticulture and winemaking products.

Visitors learned about the traditions of viticulture and winemaking and also took part in various entertainment and show programs.

During the event-filled day, guests enjoyed performances by our Eurovision representative Dilara Kazimova, Teymur Suleymanbeyli, People's Artist Zulfiya Khanbabayeva, as well as DJ Kamon.

Entertainment activities for different age groups added a special touch to the festival program throughout the day. Visitors took part in various competitions and quizzes.

The Organizing Committee presented certificates to the organizations represented at the festival.

The festival's youngest guests were not forgotten either. A children's entertainment area, an interactive program for children, and activities with animators were organized at the venue.

The festival was organized by the Shamakhi District Executive Authority, Abqora restaurant, and the Nasimi Gardens complex.

The festival aims to promote local grape and wine production, increase the export potential of wine products, and inform the general public about the history of viticulture and winemaking in Azerbaijan, as well as the work being carried out in this field.

World.title: Massacre site concerns halt plans for regional Victorian dog park
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

A proposed dog park at Robinvale's Centenary Park has been put on hold after traditional land owners said the area contains Aboriginal ancestral remains.

Brothers Uncle Brendan Kennedy and Uncle John Kennedy said the area, traditionally known as Bumbang, is a ceremonial, massacre and repatriation site for the Tati Tati people.

Uncle Brendan said the Tati Tati people have always known about its significance.

"It's not new knowledge, and it didn't spring up just because they wanted to build the dog park," he said.

"It's obvious that the investigations weren't thorough by whoever investigated the cultural significance of the area."

According to the two men, the last recorded Tati Tati ceremony held at the site was in 1892 and was witnessed by Annie Carrington, a woman who lived at the Bumbang estate as a girl.

In the 1960s, Ms Carrington recounted what she had seen to local historian Kaye Gross, who later shared the account in a letter to Uncle John.

The Kennedy brothers provided the letter to Swan Hill Rural City Council more than 15 years ago as part of a submission opposing a proposed rezoning of Centenary Park.

The letter had stopped that project at the time, but has since gone missing.

"We gave that letter to former Swan Hill councillor, Bill McGinty," Uncle Brendan said.

"We had First Peoples — State Relations investigating the Swan Hill Council about where that letter is and … Swan Hill Council doesn't have that letter.

"But we do know that letter did exist."

Council unaware of history

At the request of the state cultural body First Peoples — State Relations, Swan Hill Rural City Council has paused works at Centenary Park while investigations are undertaken.

Stuart King says it is disappointing to have the project halted after going through the proper processes. (ABC News: Sarah Buchecker)

Mayor Stuart King says the council was not aware of the site's history before work began, and that council had followed the required process and had an approved cultural heritage management plan for the dog park.

"Going through the process … to get a cultural heritage management plan done, we would expect that those issues would be identified through that process," he said.

"It came as a bit of a surprise to us."

Cr King said it was disappointing to have projects halted after going through the proper processes.

Heritage concerns investigated

First Peoples — State Relations has confirmed work in the area has been stopped until the matter is resolved.

A Department of Premier and Cabinet spokesperson said the government was working with the Swan Hill Rural City Council and Traditional Owners to investigate.

Uncle John and Uncle Brendan have also contacted Deputy Premier Gabrielle Williams to order a cultural heritage audit regarding the Cultural Heritage Management Plan submitted as part of the dog park proposal.

A decision regarding the audit is due in the coming weeks.

The Kennedys say they do not want any further works happening at the site.

"We definitely don't want a dog park built right on our repatriation site or on this ceremonial site," Uncle Brendan said.

They would like to see the area preserved and revegetated with native food and medicine plants, alongside cultural information about its Tati Tati history.

Uncle Brendan said protecting the site was important for future generations.

"We're trying to protect our heritage here," he said.

World.title: Short-stay owner ordered to pay compensation after refusing guide dog user
World.content:
A Queensland man has been ordered to pay compensation to a legally blind woman he kicked out of his short-stay house for having a guide dog.

Brendan Farrugia appeared before the Queensland Civil and Administrative Tribunal after being caught on tape refusing service to Moreton Bay woman Janice Whittle.

The tribunal ordered Mr Farrugia to pay $3,500 to Ms Whittle for breaching Queensland's anti-discrimination laws.

Mr Farrugia told 612 ABC Brisbane he had "made a mistake" and would follow the tribunal's orders.

Ms Whittle used smart glasses to secretly record her confrontation with Mr Farrugia outside Sunny's Piece of Paradise in Agnes Water in December 2024.

Loading...

The video, which was shown during the hearing, shows Mr Farrugia refusing to allow Ms Whittle into the property because of her guide dog.

In the video, he tells Ms Whittle that he would not have allowed her to book accommodation in the first place if he had known she had a guide dog.

During the exchange, Mr Farrugia tells Ms Whittle he had a "no pets" policy and she would need to pay a $100 cleaning fee if she wanted to stay.

In Queensland it is illegal to refuse service to a guide dog user and also illegal to charge additional cleaning fees because of a guide dog.

Mr Farrugia said he had made an honest mistake, and asked 612 ABC Brisbane to "please leave me alone".

"It happened, I made a mistake, let's move forward," he said.

"I'm a business owner, doing what I can, in these challenging economic times."

Mr Farrugia was given until September 28 to pay the money.

This tribunal case follows criminal proceedings in which a Magistrates Court fined Mr Farrugia $2,800 for breaching the Guide, Hearing, and Assistance Dog Act over the same incident.

Not putting up with it any more

Ms Whittle said she bought the smart glasses because she had been repeatedly refused service in restaurants, hotels, airports and other venues.

Janice Whittle says it was a long and exhausting bureaucratic battle. (612 ABC Brisbane: Kenji Sato)

"I've been abused pretty much all my life and I've never stood up for myself," Ms Whittle said.

"Well, things change.

"I couldn't put up with it anymore and I want people to know it's against the law to refuse a guide dog."

An important precedent

Human rights lawyers from Basic Rights Queensland provided legal advice to Ms Whittle during her civil hearings.

Practice director Sam Tracy said guide dog users faced this kind of discrimination on a daily basis, but it almost never reached a court.

Sam Tracy says these cases rarely end up in court. (ABC Radio Brisbane: Kenji Sato)

"This is a very significant case in regards to disability discrimination in Queensland," Mr Tracy said.

"We don't often see decisions where compensation is reached, they're often settled.

"This case represents not only a significant use of the protections under state law, but also under anti-discrimination law."

World.title: Live: ASX set to slide despite Wall Street edging up and lower oil prices
World.content:
Australia's largest lender, CBA, is the latest bank to bring forward its forecast for an RBA rate hike in September.

It had previously forecast a move in November.

The switch follows a similar move by the Westpac, the second biggest lender, on Friday.

CBA's head of Australian economics Belinda Allen said the context of the September meeting, recent RBA communications and market pricing were all supporting the case to move earlier than had been anticipated post the surprise July CPI print.

"The risk sits with the need to tighten monetary policy further beyond September given the inflation backdrop, but it is not an easy decision to push monetary policy further into restrictive territory," Ms Allen said in a note this morning.

On Friday, Westpac's chief economist Luci Ellis changed the bank's stance noting a recent escalation in the RBA's communications pointing to the "upside risks to inflation appeared to be materialising".

However, Ms Ellis said she expected the RBA vote for a hike would not be unanimous.

The ANZ is now the only one of the "Big Four" retail banks still forecasting the RBA's next move, a hike, in November.

Over the past week, senior RBA officials have focussed their public comments on inflation with Deputy Governor Hauser and Assistant Governor Hunter raising concerns about the entrenched nature of the problem.

But it was Governor Michelle Bullock at the House of Representatives Standing Committee on Economics on Friday that appears to have caused the CBA to bring forward their forecast.

"Given market pricing there was a chance the Governor could provide a more balanced assessment around inflation and growth given her role of balancing the views of the staff and the Board," Ms Allen said. "But instead, the Governor noted 'some of these upside risks to inflation appear to be materialising' and commentary around inflation remained hawkish."

The market is now placing the chances of a September rate hike at 90%.

However, the CBA and Westpac are at odds over the RBA board's likely vote, arguing that it expects a unanimous decision.

World.title: Calls grow for mental health service in Victorian town 'left out of the mix'
World.content:
Since 2022, Stacey Kelly has regularly taken a five-hour round trip on public transport to access mental health treatment and services in Ballarat.

The Horsham mother of three lives with depression, anxiety and depressive psychosis, and the treatments she requires are not provided in her home region.

She is one of many Wimmera residents calling for a mental health facility in Horsham, so residents can access services and treatment closer to home.

"I [travel to Ballarat] because I wish to be alive," Ms Kelly said.

"It's an inconvenience in the fact that it takes a whole day to go and have the treatment and come home again."

She said it would be "incredible" if a facility existed in Horsham where she could receive treatment after work, minimising the impact on her everyday life and keeping her closer to family and friends.

"When I first started treatment, I was away for seven weeks," Ms Kelly said.

"So, I was away from family and friends and anyone who was giving me support.

"It just had a huge impact emotionally, financially, and stability-wise.

"We are one of the biggest areas that has high suicide rates and mental illness, and we have no capacity to support these people."

Ms Kelly meditates every day. (ABC News: Nethma Dandeniya)

Push for a 24/7 service

Horsham Rural City Council is pushing for the local mental health facility to operate 24 hours a day.

"It's actually a real concern that we haven't got anything here in Horsham that's 24-hour care close to home for the people that need it," Mayor Brian Klowss said.

Horsham is the region's largest population centre and referral hub, but there is no local inpatient unit.

Instead, the acute inpatient bed base is in Ballarat, two hours away from Horsham and even further for residents in smaller Wimmera towns.

Currently, if someone presented after hours to the emergency department at the Wimmera Base Hospital with a mental health issue, there would be no one in the ED with a mental health qualification to respond to their needs.

The most likely outcome is that the person would be connected with a telephone triage service based in Ballarat.

Mayor Brian Klowss is pushing for Horsham to get a 24/7 mental health facility. (Supplied: Rural Press Club of Victoria)

Cr Klowss said about 400 people from the Wimmera were admitted or transported to Ballarat Hospital annually for mental health-related issues.

"I think we've just been left out of the mix … I think there's a real, genuine need for this service," Cr Klowss said.

Brian Klowss says about 400 people from the Wimmera region are admitted or transported to Ballarat Hospital annually for mental health-related issues. (ABC: Dominic Cansdale)

Concerning data

Mental Health Victoria chief executive Phillipa Thomas said some areas across the Wimmera had "really stark" rates of mental health distress and illness, which were disproportionately higher than the rest of the state.

Data from a Western Victorian Primary Health Network report last year showed rates of emergency department presentations for mental health and behavioural disorders for Horsham were 2.15 times higher than Victoria's average.

Rates of avoidable deaths from suicide and self-inflicted injuries in the Wimmera over the five years to 2021 were also significantly higher than the state average.

"If you look at the distribution of mental health services across Victoria … it is impossible to ignore the fact that the needs of that community are not served in the same way as other parts of the state," Ms Thomas said.

A 'black spot'

Member for Lowan and shadow minister for mental health Emma Kealy agreed there was a "huge gap" in mental health services in the Grampians and Wimmera region.

"It's simply not viable just to have the proverbial ambulance at the bottom of the cliff."

Emma Kealy says there's a big gap in access to mental health services in the Wimmera region. (Supplied: Emma Kealy)

Uniting Vic.Tas Head of mental health Linsie Davies said a mental health and wellbeing officer who could help address multiple barriers would benefit people in the Wimmera.

"We regularly see and hear stories about people losing their homes, relationships, jobs and sadly lives as people fall through the cracks because there have been delays in receiving mental health treatment," she said.

A spokesperson for Grampians Health said there were currently no plans for a 24/7 inpatient mental health facility in Horsham.

A Victorian government spokesperson said people in the region could already connect with crisis assessment, treatments and other supports through the Grampians Mental Health and Wellbeing service.

It's safe to say the government aren't fans of the opposition's vow to cut tax on fuel when the global price of Brent crude oil averages $US100 a barrel over two weeks.

"It's an unfunded, uncosted promise from [Angus] Taylor," Finance Minister Katy Gallagher told ABC's Radio National Breakfast this morning.

World.title: With this 'little bit', households can help tackle organic waste problem
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Every drop makes an ocean is a motto sustainable-living champion Benjamin Head wants everyone to be guided by.

From food scraps and garden clippings to paper, cardboard, old bottle caps and packaging material, the 62-year-old puts to use materials many of us throw out as general rubbish.

Over more than two decades, Mr Head has made his suburban home on the Gold Coast a waste ecosystem of its own and has seen his rubbish pile progressively shrink.

Queensland lagging behind organic waste goals Green food and garden organic bins — known as FOGO bins — have been heralded as the answer to diverting organic materials away from landfill, but Queensland is falling behind on its goals.

"It's gradually getting less and less," he said.

"I get a bit more money in my pocket and we leave the Gold Coast in a better place for our future generations.

"Think before you toss. Look in the bin and see if there's anything of value and pull that out, it doesn't take very long, and put that into a separate bin or bucket."

Mr Head said his farming background gave him a head start with integrating the circular-economy model into his daily life, but recycling habits could be adopted by anybody, and on any scale.

His process is simple: most leftovers from the kitchen table and cooking go into a large backyard composting bin and some to feed the chickens.

Benjamin Head is passionate about educating people on how to compost and recycle better at home. (ABC News: Michael Lloyd)

Cane mulch, grass clippings, flowers and leaves are added to the composting mix, along with shreds of paper and cardboard.

The product is a nutrient-rich soil, which Mr Head puts back into the garden to grow a variety of fresh organic fruit and vegetables, saving money on the grocery shop.

"We have 300,000 tonnes of [residual] waste [annually] in the Gold Coast; we have 680,000 people," he said.

"If we can get everybody to do a little bit, then we're heading in the right direction."

Organics infrastructure lacking

What Mr Head does forms part of a much larger goal by government to reduce the amount of waste sent to landfill and to improve recycling rates.

Queensland's latest waste strategy, released in June, sets a target of reducing residual waste, collected from statewide red bins, by 65 per cent in the next decade.

Addressing food and garden waste is a top priority under the plan. Half of the state's total landfill waste comprises organics, which, upon decomposing, produce the dangerous greenhouse gas methane.

Organic waste makes up 50 per cent of what goes into red rubbish bins across Queensland each year. (ABC News: Michael Lloyd)

However, just 11 of Queensland's 77 councils provide a kerbside green bin service for garden waste and only some provide FOGO bins for food and organic waste, by request. These are concentrated in the state's south-east.

It is also in this region where the strategy has set the biggest landfill-reduction target of 70 per cent over 10 years.

Council-led initiatives, such as the Advanced Resource Recovery Centre (ARRC) on the Gold Coast, have introduced programs incentivising residential organic recycling.

"That's an opportunity for residents of the Gold Coast to get low-cost home composting and worm farms available," ARRC CEO Grant Gabriel said.

"It's important that all Australians think about what goes into your green bin and, if any of that can be turned into home composting to make their gardens more healthy, where they're growing roses or fruit out of there, there's an opportunity for everyone to really bring that circularity into their home."

Grant Gabriel says resource recovery is equally about the role of households, developing the end market for recycled goods, and landfill alternatives. (ABC News: Michael Lloyd)

The waste strategy also recognises the need to provide additional funding for organics-processing infrastructure, including green bins, and support for activities such as home composting and community composting.

Mr Gabriel said to improve the overall resource recovery rate, the amount of total waste reused, recycled or turned into energy, it was also important to have conversations about developing the end market for recycled products, and invest in landfill alternatives like waste to energy.

Push for top-down messaging

Circular-economy expert Bel Chellingworth said, when it came to managing organic waste at home, many residents were restricted by a lack of space.

Labor's broken promise on plastic recycling Industry groups say they were left blindsided by the federal government's decision to scrap mandatory standards for packaging.

"I lived in a rental unit and I had a small household, so I had a worm farm, but it couldn't cope with everything that even I produced in one week," she said.

"And it was really only when my council introduced the food waste bin that I could put all of my food waste out of landfill and into the worm farm and the bin as a combination."

Ms Chellingworth said larger-scale home composting could be a highly effective solution for residents living in regional areas and those with larger backyards.

However, she said the onus of improving recycling rates and better waste management ultimately fell on national policymakers.

Bel Chellingworth says Australia falls behind other OECD countries in terms of circularity rates. (Supplied)

"We certainly need to see some consistent messaging and some consistent assistance from the federal government down to the states and territories and then down to councils," she said.

The federal government earlier this month quietly stalled changes promised in 2023 to mandate more recycled material in packaging and has also abandoned its goal to roll out green bins for all Australian households.

World.title: Winless Bombers, Saints and Magpies AFLW coaches under pressure
World.content:
The AFLW has passed the midway point of this year's home-and-away season, with some expected storylines and some surprises.

With all the twists and turns, here's what fans are talking about the most.

Will pressure come on coaches without a win?

It's the question fans could be heard right around the boundary fence asking on Sunday afternoon: "Will Essendon win a game this year?"

The Bombers recorded their sixth straight loss, this time against Gold Coast by 41 points, which raised some doubts about the future of head coach Natalie Wood.

Natalie Wood is the inaugural coach of Essendon. (Getty: Michael Willson/AFL Photos)

Last year, Essendon finished 14th with four wins and eight losses, but escaped a lot of scrutiny due to a high injury toll taking the blame.

This year, fans expected better. Against the Suns, the only goal came off the boot of Emily Gough.

But they're not the only ones. St Kilda remains without a victory and with a percentage of just 36.5.

It's the sixth season head coach Nick Dal Santo has been at the helm, over which time he's taken the team to one finals campaign (last year, in which it lost an elimination final to Adelaide by 44 points).

This year, they lost to Geelong by 85 points in round two, North Melbourne by 92 points in round five, and managed just one goal against Sydney in round three.

Then at Collingwood, the inaugural AFLW side continue to struggle for success, with another year down the bottom end of the ladder.

Sam Wright took over as head coach ahead of the 2024 season and quietly re-signed until the end of 2027 last week. It came amid media reports of player concern about the lack of direction in the club's AFLW program.

Wood and Dal Santo are both out of contract at season's end.

This is Nick Dal Santo's sixth season as head coach at St Kilda. (Getty: James Wiltshire/AFL Photos)

In 2022, Carlton launched an independent review into its AFLW program after managing just six wins across two seasons. The club then signed Mathew Buck as coach and rose to become a genuine finals contender.

Many are now starting to ask whether it's time Collingwood, Essendon and St Kilda do the same.

North are no longer a top of the ladder

Hawthorn's Friday night win over two-time reigning premiers North Melbourne sent shock waves through the AFLW competition.

The Kangaroos were on a 32-match winning streak — the longest in AFL/VFL/AFLW history — and had gone undefeated since 2023, a total of 1,020 days.

Hawthorn ended North Melbourne's 32-match winning streak. (Getty Images: Emily Barker)

Carlton had got close to them the week before, going down by just 10 points, and many thought Melbourne might be the ones to break the run in round seven.

But then came along the Hawks in humid Cairns, where a clutch Lucy Wales goal in the dying minutes of a hard-fought four quarters changed the narrative of the season.

The unbeatable Kangaroos were beaten and the premiership race was blown wide open.

Less than 24 hours later, Melbourne put its foot down against Carlton to remain the only team undefeated this season and take the top spot on the ladder.

Umpiring an issue

One consistency across all leagues and codes, no matter the gender or sport, is fans having a gripe with umpiring or refereeing decisions.

But AFLW fans may have a better leg to stand on than most.

This season, Ray Chamberlain, who retired from the AFL at the end of 2024 after 389 games, returned to help officiate and mentor the next generation of umpires in the AFLW.

He wasn't alone, with the AFL putting a call out to retired umpires to make a return in the women's game, which former AFL-listed umpires such as Jordan Bannister and Chris Donlon answered.

Ahead of the season, Chamberlain said he was happy to help because there was "a need there".

"You want to do it well and you want to support what they're doing," Chamberlain told SEN.com.au.

The state leagues are still the primary pathway for umpires wanting to make into the AFL, which has its finals campaigns running concurrently to the AFLW's start of the season.

With a lot of umpires prioritising the state leagues, there was a dearth of experienced umpires to officiate the AFLW and there was a desperate need for mentoring and development.

Who saw this coming from the Dogs and Suns?

While many of the top eight were predicted by pundits at the start of the season to be finals contenders — Melbourne, North Melbourne, Geelong, Sydney, Carlton and Hawthorn — two teams on the rise that have surprised fans have been the Gold Coast Suns and the Western Bulldogs.

The Suns have lured some big-name recruits in recent years, including premiership players Anne Hatchard and Lily Mithen.

But much of their rise this year has come off the back of teenagers.

Ava Usher of the Suns has been impressive this season. (Getty: Janelle St Pierre/AFL Photos)

The teams has enjoyed the fruits of the Suns Academy, with graduates Ava Usher, Alannah Welsh, Sunny Lappin, Georgia Davies, Mikayla Nurse, Dakota Baron and Bronte Parker all catching the eyes of the competition. And they've helped steer their side to four wins and two losses.

Meanwhile, things have started to click at the Kennel under Tamara Hyett, with the Dogs also sitting at 4-2.

The Dogs have struggled in recent years, and they finished in 12th place last season. But, buoyed by an extremely strong pre-season, they launched into this year with gusto.

Credit to them, they stuck to the plan even when external scrutiny came. Now they pose a serious threat to the teams coming up against them. All this work has been led by captain Isabelle Pritchard, forward Emma McDonald and midfielder Jess Fitzgerald.

The Western Bulldogs have been on the rise in 2026. (Getty: Paul Kane)

There is still a lot to play out in the remaining half of the home-and-away season, particularly with Richmond and Fremantle knocking on the door of the top eight.

But one thing is for sure: It's got an ending a lot less clear than when the year started out.

World.title: Hundreds recruited to help foster kids visit birth families in NSW
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Thousands of children in foster care are improving ties with their birth families, as part of an overhauled supervision system in New South Wales.

More than 300 specialist workers have now been recruited by the Department of Communities and Justice to accompany children on supervised family visits.

These Family Time visits can vary widely in setting — from picnics and sports events, to theme parks and zoos.

Kylie Stone is among the recent recruits, whose own childhood experience of family separation motivated her to join the team.

She grew up in outer-western Sydney, where her father grappled with addiction and went to prison when she was aged 11.

"I just remember waiting for all my letters to come or waiting for phone calls and wanting to go and see my dad," she said.

Photos and letters from Ms Stone's childhood. (ABC News: Gavin Coote)

Now, Ms Stone is determined to make a difference to other families' lives in her old neighbourhood.

One of her proudest moments in the job involved a young mother and her child who had been removed from her care while she sought treatment for an addiction.

"I started working with her when her baby was three months old. We shared her first Easter, her first birthday, her first Christmas together," she said.

"There were days that she did struggle and she's like, 'I don't know if I can do this', and she's actually now gone through final orders and she's getting her little girl back.

"Honestly, it gives me goosebumps."

Ms Stone says supervised contact creates a "space place". (ABC News: Gavin Coote)

Ms Stone acknowledges while permanent family reunification is not always feasible, supervised contact provides a "safe place" to build connections and ease the impact of separation.

Supervised family visits have long been a feature of the state's foster care system, but previously they were run by caseworkers in the private sector.

It was a system that Families and Communities Minister Kate Washington argued was plagued by poor training and a high staff turnover, which would often make it a distressing experience.

"When a different person was turning up to their door every single time, they didn't know the child, they didn't know the families," she said.

Ms Washington said bringing the program in-house had ensured there was rigorous oversight and training of workers.

There is also a strong focus on making sure Family Time workers are culturally-matched, and to date, almost 20 per cent of the team identifies as Aboriginal.

Family Time visits can take place in a range of locations. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

Growing focus on Aboriginal kinships

One of the new program officers is Cody McGrady Miller, a Gomeroi and Wonnurua man who was 12 years old when he was removed from his mother's care by caseworkers and police.

He and his sister were placed in the care of his great-aunty in south-west Sydney, and said the turnover of casework teams "make it really difficult".

"Back then, there was not much understanding around Aboriginal kinship systems and the way in which our communities support children," he said.

Family Time worker Cody McGrady Miller was removed from his mother's care at 12. (ABC News: Brigitte Murphy)

Now he works with the Family Time team in Tamworth, and has led efforts to ensure supervised visits are culturally appropriate.

"For us as Aboriginal people, I think that connection is one of the most significant parts of culture, and with the lived experience, I feel like that I can really contribute to ensuring that there's a better experience for children and young people in care," he said.

Building a 'legacy' for families

Nicholle Andreuzza says "beautiful venues" with activities can have a positive impact. (ABC News: Gavin Coote)

Supervisors typically write detailed reports after each visit, which is often used for family law or court proceedings.

But Nicholle Andreuzza from the Department of Communities and Justice said there had been a move away from the "clinical" approach to supervising family visits.

"What we're seeing now is beautiful venues," Ms Andreuzza said.

"We're seeing kids and mum and dad at soccer fields with the support of their Family Time work, we're seeing kids having experiences like ice skating, we do some visits in home when safe to do so."

Ms Andreuzza said the Family Time workers also played an important "legacy" role, by taking pictures during the visits.

"So for kids when they get older … they're able to look at photographs and look at all of the positive moments that they've had with their mums, dads, brothers, sisters, uncles, aunties," she said.

World.title: Opposition leader claims proposed fuel excise cut won't add to inflation
World.content:
Opposition leader claims proposed fuel excise cut won't add to inflation

Opposition leader Angus Taylor has pledged to halve the fuel excise, and insists it will be fully funded and won't add to current inflationary pressures.

World.title: Australia news live: Anthony Albanese travels to US; seventh intergenerational report to be released; Donald Trump says arch to be ‘military complex’
World.content:
Finance Minister Katy Gallagher has called the Coalition’s planned automatic cut to the fuel excise an “unfunded, uncosted” bad idea, as she reiterated the government was not planning further cuts to the petrol tax.

“If you also look back and see all the other range of promises [the Coalition] have made since the election, there are hundreds of billions of dollars in unfunded promises, and this adds to that list. This is not something that we have been considering,” Gallagher told ABC Radio National this morning.

Finance Minister Katy Gallagher. Alex Ellinghausen

Gallagher said the government changed the fuel excise immediately following the war in Iran but has shifted to providing more permanent cost of living supports to avoid “one-off arrangements”.

The Coalition’s proposal would halve the fuel excise when Brent crude oil traded at over $US100 ($140) per barrel averaged over a fortnight. The cut would last for three months and then be readdressed when the period ended. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor framed the policy as “a relief at the bowser”.

Gallagher said the government was not considering further cuts to the excise. Income tax cuts, Medicare funding, and additional medicines on the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme represented longer lasting cost of living support.

“Our decisions have been built and baked into the budget to make sure that that cost of living help is permanent. You know, the sooner this war in the Middle East stops, the better,” Gallagher said.

World.title: Inglis and Ellis shine to steer Australia to one-wicket win over Zimbabwe
World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket Inglis and Ellis shine to steer Australia to one-wicket win over Zimbabwe Nick Said September 21, 2026 — 6:44am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Josh Inglis scored his second ODI century and Nathan Ellis his highest score in the format with an unbeaten 36 from 44 balls as Australia claimed a dramatic one-wicket victory over hosts Zimbabwe with a ball to spare in Harare on Sunday (local time). When Ellis was joined at the crease by number 11 Spencer Johnson (7 from 13 balls), the tourists needed 27 runs to reach their victory target of 272, something the pair managed at a run-a-ball to take their side to the win. Josh Inglis celebrates his century. AP Photo/Wonder Mashura Zimbabwe will rue Wessly Madhevere dropping Ellis in the penultimate over when he could have sealed victory for them, as he then failed to defend nine runs in the final over when Ellis hit a six off the first ball. Australia, who rested several of their regulars for the tour, claimed the series 3-0 and now move on to South Africa for three ODI fixtures that begin in Durban on Thursday.



“Great game of cricket,” Australia captain Mitchell Marsh said. “I thought Zimbabwe probably deserved to win, but the boys got the job done at the end there and that was fantastic to see. “We’re aware we need to keep improving as a team. I thought the way we played over the three matches, albeit today we got lucky, but there’s lots of positive signs with our group. We’ve got some young talent which is exciting for the future.” Australian captain Mitch Marsh with his teammates after winning the ODI series 3-0. AP Photo/Wonder Mashura After the home side elected to bat first, Zimbabwe’s innings was anchored by an unbeaten 81 from 72 balls by captain Sikandar Raza, to go with half-centuries for Craig Ervine (59 from 79 balls) and Innocent Kaia (55 from 66 balls). Kaia retired hurt with a hamstring injury, with the score on 148 for three, as he could no longer run between the wickets.



Australian bowler Nathan Ellis. AP Photo/Wonder Mashura Seamer Ellis was also the pick of the Australian bowlers with 3-50 in his 10 overs. Related Article Test cricket ‘There’s a reason I’m still here’: Labuschagne’s vow in fight to save career Australia were always up with the run rate in their reply but when openers Travis Head (6) and Marsh (8) fell early, it set the tone for an innings where they lost wickets at regular intervals. But Inglis scored a superb 103 from 102 balls as he struck 11 fours, with the next highest scorer Ellis on his unbeaten 36.



Zimbabwe all-rounder Brad Evans was the pick of the home bowlers with 4-47 in 10 overs. “I thought 280-290 was par with the bat so to make a game out of 272 was a great effort,” Raza said. “As a captain I’m really proud. Plenty to learn. I’d rather have a game like that than for the Aussies to just chase it down in 40 overs.” Reuters

World.title: Germany’s Merz stumbles on after another big election defeat. But for how long?
World.content:
WorldEuropeWorld politics Germany’s Merz stumbles on after another big election defeat. But for how long? James Crisp September 21, 2026 — 6:08am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Friedrich Merz, the pugnacious, stubborn German chancellor, has come out fighting in a desperate attempt to save his chancellorship. The leader who promised to transform his country’s fortunes when he took power last year suffered another bloody nose at the ballot box from the Alternative for Germany (AfD) on Sunday. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz speaks to media at the CDU party headquarters in Berlin. AP Photo/Markus Schreiber The hard-right party won state elections in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, taking 37 per cent of the vote, according to the first exit poll. It was not the crushing victory the AfD won earlier this month in the other east German state of Saxony-Anhalt, but Merz’s conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) still took a beating, and his leadership could be on the brink.



Merz’s approval ratings stand at just 10 per cent, with voters weary of his brusque, tough-guy management style, which persists even as he fails to stop the rise of the AfD and deliver on key manifesto pledges. Related Article Analysis

World elections Election shockwave: Meet the smiling new leader set to bring hard-right upheaval to Germany The irony is that some CDU insiders blame their Social Democratic Party (SPD) coalition partners in the federal government for slowing Merz’s reforms aimed at rebooting Germany’s struggling economy. The chancellor appeared contrite after the Saxony-Anhalt result and made an uncharacteristic and unconvincing promise to listen more to voters. Mecklenburg-Vorpommern is a smaller state, with just under 1.6 million people, but the timing, and that of the state elections in Berlin on the same day, was dangerous.



In the capital, voters handed the hard-Left Die Linke a 24.5 per cent victory over the CDU on 20 per cent. The AfD came third, with 16 per cent, the exit poll said. There have been murmurs of discontent within the CDU, a party not accustomed to replacing its leaders less than two years after coming to power. Germany as a whole is not used to palace coups after 16 years of Angela Merkel. But Merz’s predecessor, the SPD’s Olaf Scholz, also did not see out his full term; his coalition collapsed because of infighting. ‘German Burnham’ required Merz had been on manoeuvres in the days running up to Sunday’s elections.



He cancelled his planned appearance at the UN General Assembly. Party insiders insisted a leader, derided by some as a foreign-policy chancellor, a charge also levelled at former British prime minister Keir Starmer, was needed in Berlin. AfD members, including candidate Enrico Schult (second from left), speak to supporters at the party’s election evening gathering as Merz appears on a TV screen behind. Getty Images Before the exit polls dropped, Merz held a behind-closed-doors meeting with senior party members to challenge them to continue backing him. If they do not, he will demand they name a successor. The front-runner is Hendrik Wüst, North Rhine-Westphalia’s minister-president, who is viewed as Germany’s answer to Andy Burnham. But he has state elections in April, and missing them to take on the big job is an idea frowned upon by many in a decidedly old-fashioned and stuck-in-its-ways CDU.



Merz’s pressure has already brought some results, including a letter of muted support from eight state leaders, including Wüst, who claimed that Europe, faced with a surge in support for populist parties, needed a strong and stable Germany. Related Article Analysis

UK politics Farage says Britain is broken and only Reform can fix it. Now the pressure is on to deliver He can also rely on the fact that his party knows that changing the chancellor will require the SPD’s agreement, which could demand a slowdown of much-needed reforms in return. Merz is also attempting to strike a crowd-pleasing note to shift the narrative of a month of three bruising elections. He is planning measures to cap the soaring price of petrol amid record diesel prices and has softened his position on early retirement. But he remains almost fatally tone-deaf. His hopes for new laws that would force people to post online under their real names seem misguided, as voters are far more concerned with the cost of living.



His chances of survival depend not on his political skills but on his party’s risk-averse nature and a German political system that makes it difficult to remove a sitting chancellor. With the CDU not enduring the historic humiliation of falling below 5 per cent, Merz will pray that a period of intense political pressure around the three state elections will now begin to subside. On the point of being knocked out, he is hoping to hang on long enough to be rescued by events. The Telegraph, London Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

Beyond those three, trying to identify a “surprise packet” is the next task. Brownlow Medal contenders Marcus Bontempelli, Nick Daicos and Bailey Smith. Think Hawk Jai Newcombe, Gawn’s teammate Kysaiah Pickett, Izak Rankine, Tim Taranto and Ollie Dempsey. Yes, even Dempsey and Taranto. Surprise packet: Izak Rankine’s hot form late in the season could push him to a high spot on the leaderboard. Why is Nick Daicos so favoured? “Ladies and gentlemen, please put your hands together for this year’s Brownlow medallist … Nick Daicos.”



Those are the words you will almost certainly hear on Monday night. Perhaps the biggest question now is – at what stage of the count will the Collingwood star be confirmed as a first-time medallist? Will Daicos reach the unbeatable stage at round 20, still with a month of votes to be counted? Or will the 23-year-old dynamo, the hottest of hot favourites, have to endure a nervous flutter or two in the final few rounds? In either case, it will be Daicos on the podium with a glass of champers not long after, and almost certainly with a winning total in the 40s. Daicos was, unsurprisingly the pre-season Brownlow favourite. After polling 28, 38 and 32 votes in the past three seasons, he was the obvious pick. Those tallies have given him two second-placed finishes (behind Matt Rowell and Patrick Cripps in 2025 and 2024 respectively). In 2023 he was probably the most unlucky, finishing only three votes adrift of winner Lachie Neale as he took the competition by storm for the first time but injury impacted his finish to the home-and-away season.



The other great question surrounding Daicos is exactly how many votes he will accrue. Cripps’ ridiculous and record-breaking season two years ago (45 votes – eight ahead of Daicos) could easily be toppled. Getting to the 50-vote mark is not outside the realm of possibility. Amid the Brownlow prognostications and permutations, Daicos is variously tipped to finish with anywhere between 38 and 52 votes. A readjustment of votes from The Age footballer of the year award (where five players are given a score out of 10 each game), has Daicos reaching 43 votes. The AFL website’s Brownlow predictor lands on Daicos with 47 votes, with the next player a whopping 13 behind. He is also the unanimous choice of our experts. (Scroll down to see who they think will finish second and third, and their wildcard choices.) Any way you look at it – the medal is Daicos’ to lose.



Thus, the other intrigue on Monday night is the chase for second spot. Who should you lean towards? Daylight might be the best answer. Related Article Scoop in September

AFL 2026 Scoop in September: Why the Tassie stadium could be bigger than we thought The biggest victim of the Daicos juggernaut is fellow vote-magnet Marcus Bontempelli. At age 30 and surely with seasons of footy still to come, “the Bont” is tracking to become the greatest Brownlow vote-winner in history. The Bulldog is likely to reach third spot on the table (behind Gary Ablett jnr and Patrick Dangerfield) this year. Nothing is guaranteed in footy, and perennial contender Bontempelli might never win Charlie. A significant change to the Brownlow happened this year as the AFL allowed umpires to access statistics upon request. The league is trying to avoid perceived voting blunders by tinkering with the system. In deciding on the 3-2-1 votes for each match, the umpires can now ask for stats in 16 categories to help their judgment. Champion Data projections have Isaac Heeney polling in 12 games with five three-vote performances. Heeney is one of five Swans players suspended for breaching the club’s behavioural standards on the night of the Pullman hotel scandal.



The five are eligible to win the Brownlow but are not allowed to attend. Wanganeen-Milera figures prominently in Champion’s predictions, but interestingly not in the tips of our experts. Eagle-eyed Brownlow followers will try to assess how this affects voting patterns. The change might mean there’s less chance of a “bolt-from-the-blue” winner, such as West Coast’s Matt Priddis in 2014 or even Rowell last year. “With the new voting model, which allows umpires to review the post-game statistics, we forecast that the Brownlow will now heavily skew towards favourites in the future. This may make winners like Matt Rowell, who was $17 last year, more unlikely,” says TAB’s senior AFL trader Bart Kennett.



Time will tell what it means for the Brownlow long-term. But, don’t worry, you’ll still hear “N. Daicos, three votes” many times on Monday night. Here are the latest odds Nick Daicos $1.01

World.title: Forget the grand final, this is the hardest week in rugby league
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Opinion Forget the grand final, this is the hardest week in rugby league Roy Masters Sports Columnist September 21, 2026 — 5:22am

September 21, 2026 — 5:22am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Preliminary finals are to a grand final what a nervy, fumbling first date is to a comfy, content wedding anniversary. It’s edgy expectation versus partial fulfilment. The penultimate weekend of a season, where four teams fight for the right to advance to the Big Dance, often has players and coaches nervous and uptight. They are aware that a tiny slip-up could end their season days short of what could have been a premiership. Loading Grand final teams tend to be more relaxed, some clubs simply secure at having already achieved their place in history. “Players can lose their edge going from a prelim to the grand final,” says Storm coach Craig Bellamy. Even the most vigilant coach can’t counter the doorman whispering to grand final players before kick-off, “No matter what happens today boys, you have done the club proud.”



It follows that a defeat in the preliminary final can be more devastating than losing a grand final. Bellamy, coach of more preliminary and grand final teams than anyone over the past quarter-century, has been more gutted after losing preliminary finals than I have seen him after narrow defeats in deciders. In 2011, after the Warriors won in Melbourne, he isolated himself from everyone, desperately desolate. His team had been expelled from the previous year’s competition as punishment for salary cap cheating, stripped of all honours and a galaxy of star players. A grand final win would have been redemption for all the world to see. “That was the worst,” admits Bellamy. Melbourne captain Christian Welch with coach Craig Bellamy in 2023 after losing the preliminary final to Penrith. NRL Images Ten years later, a Storm winger dropped the ball with the line wide open, and it was the Panthers who advanced to the grand final against the Rabbitohs. The Panthers were still a little fragile, relying on a Stephen Crichton intercept to launch their dynasty. It denied Bellamy the one prize which eluded him – successive premierships – and he fumed at the front of the bus during the silent journey to the team’s Queensland COVID base where they had been isolated almost all season. As coach of St George in 1984, I felt a one-point loss in the preliminary final more than a one-point loss in the grand final the following year. Lose a grand final, and you can console yourself with having had the experience. Also, the disappointment is ameliorated if your two lower-grade teams win, as the Dragons did in 1985. Lose a preliminary final, and you walk away with nothing. Many a player has declared after losing a preliminary final, “I won’t watch the grand final.”



Yet, paradoxically, the culture both in the NRL and the AFL says there is only one winner in a season. Every team that failed to stand on the dais on grand final day is a loser. So how can losing a prelim be more devastating? It’s the opportunity missed factor, the nagging feeling that if you reached the big day, you would have won. It hurts more when, throughout the season, your team has dominated the team it could have met in the decider. Perhaps coaches feel the loss of preliminary finals more than players. Young players at the top clubs believe they will be back the following year. Many never are. After four straight premierships, Nathan Cleary and the Panthers were hit with preliminary final pain in 2025. Getty Images Melbourne’s Christian Welch won a grand final in 2020; lost grand finals in 2016, 2018 and 2024 and lost preliminary finals in 2021 and 2023. He counts losing grand finals as far more devastating. “Having to stand on the field watching the premiership rings being handed out, you picture yourself in their position on the stage singing the team song,” he says.



Related Article Analysis

NRL 2026 The secret to DCE’s 424-game career? A ‘goldfish memory’, Ted Lasso and Dolphin days “You are so physically close to your lifelong dream but in reality, closer to the boys who won the spoon a month earlier. You can feel the euphoria of the winners; they are 10 metres away from you. A grand final loss is just so much more confronting and visceral, whereas a prelim loss you can justify in your head that you weren’t that close to premiership glory.” One thought I can’t reconcile in my head is how today’s NRL champions don’t display the prime trait of their generation. The social scientists insist the Gen Z population is the most risk-averse generation in history. They fear failure, yet today’s dressing shed disappointment is like non-stick cookware. Maybe it’s the attack-focused nature of today’s rules that promotes the rocks-and-diamonds players, such as Reece Walsh and Scott Drinkwater. It follows that these preliminary finals may not be the nervous, mistake-dreading encounters they were in the past. Still, the bunker plays to the textbook Gen Z fear. The lottery luck of some of the decisions sees players concede “12-point tries”. That is when a try is denied and the opposition scores immediately afterwards. An NRL official, not authorised to speak publicly, says an incorrect bunker ruling followed by an opposition try occurs far more than is reported.



The psychiatrist’s riddle is relevant to this weekend’s finals in terms of the focus on the Sydney crowd turnout and the number of teams that progressed from week one with zero or minimal recent experience in the play-offs. Is the stadium half full or half empty? The Dolphins will ride the emotions of preliminary finals week for the first time. Getty Images Will the newcomers be contenders or pretenders? To continue the analogy at the top of this column, will the teams like the Dolphins be nervous first daters or relaxed anniversary celebrants? By contrast, Penrith’s nucleus of playmakers are now in their seventh successive preliminary final. Maybe they will reach the altar a fifth time, but the bunker has a habit of being the disruptive, uninvited guest at a wedding. World.title: Opposition leader claims proposed fuel excise cut won't add to inflation
World.content:
Opposition leader claims proposed fuel excise cut won't add to inflation

Opposition leader Angus Taylor has pledged to halve the fuel excise, and insists it will be fully funded and won't add to current inflationary pressures.

World.title: Australia news live: Anthony Albanese travels to US; seventh intergenerational report to be released; Donald Trump says arch to be ‘military complex’
World.content:
Finance Minister Katy Gallagher has called the Coalition’s planned automatic cut to the fuel excise an “unfunded, uncosted” bad idea, as she reiterated the government was not planning further cuts to the petrol tax.

“If you also look back and see all the other range of promises [the Coalition] have made since the election, there are hundreds of billions of dollars in unfunded promises, and this adds to that list. This is not something that we have been considering,” Gallagher told ABC Radio National this morning.

Finance Minister Katy Gallagher. Alex Ellinghausen

Gallagher said the government changed the fuel excise immediately following the war in Iran but has shifted to providing more permanent cost of living supports to avoid “one-off arrangements”.

The Coalition’s proposal would halve the fuel excise when Brent crude oil traded at over $US100 ($140) per barrel averaged over a fortnight. The cut would last for three months and then be readdressed when the period ended. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor framed the policy as “a relief at the bowser”.

Gallagher said the government was not considering further cuts to the excise. Income tax cuts, Medicare funding, and additional medicines on the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme represented longer lasting cost of living support.

“Our decisions have been built and baked into the budget to make sure that that cost of living help is permanent. You know, the sooner this war in the Middle East stops, the better,” Gallagher said.

World.title: Inglis and Ellis shine to steer Australia to one-wicket win over Zimbabwe
World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket Inglis and Ellis shine to steer Australia to one-wicket win over Zimbabwe Nick Said September 21, 2026 — 6:44am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Josh Inglis scored his second ODI century and Nathan Ellis his highest score in the format with an unbeaten 36 from 44 balls as Australia claimed a dramatic one-wicket victory over hosts Zimbabwe with a ball to spare in Harare on Sunday (local time). When Ellis was joined at the crease by number 11 Spencer Johnson (7 from 13 balls), the tourists needed 27 runs to reach their victory target of 272, something the pair managed at a run-a-ball to take their side to the win. Josh Inglis celebrates his century. AP Photo/Wonder Mashura Zimbabwe will rue Wessly Madhevere dropping Ellis in the penultimate over when he could have sealed victory for them, as he then failed to defend nine runs in the final over when Ellis hit a six off the first ball. Australia, who rested several of their regulars for the tour, claimed the series 3-0 and now move on to South Africa for three ODI fixtures that begin in Durban on Thursday.



“Great game of cricket,” Australia captain Mitchell Marsh said. “I thought Zimbabwe probably deserved to win, but the boys got the job done at the end there and that was fantastic to see. “We’re aware we need to keep improving as a team. I thought the way we played over the three matches, albeit today we got lucky, but there’s lots of positive signs with our group. We’ve got some young talent which is exciting for the future.” Australian captain Mitch Marsh with his teammates after winning the ODI series 3-0. AP Photo/Wonder Mashura After the home side elected to bat first, Zimbabwe’s innings was anchored by an unbeaten 81 from 72 balls by captain Sikandar Raza, to go with half-centuries for Craig Ervine (59 from 79 balls) and Innocent Kaia (55 from 66 balls). Kaia retired hurt with a hamstring injury, with the score on 148 for three, as he could no longer run between the wickets.



Australian bowler Nathan Ellis. AP Photo/Wonder Mashura Seamer Ellis was also the pick of the Australian bowlers with 3-50 in his 10 overs. Related Article Test cricket ‘There’s a reason I’m still here’: Labuschagne’s vow in fight to save career Australia were always up with the run rate in their reply but when openers Travis Head (6) and Marsh (8) fell early, it set the tone for an innings where they lost wickets at regular intervals. But Inglis scored a superb 103 from 102 balls as he struck 11 fours, with the next highest scorer Ellis on his unbeaten 36.



Zimbabwe all-rounder Brad Evans was the pick of the home bowlers with 4-47 in 10 overs. “I thought 280-290 was par with the bat so to make a game out of 272 was a great effort,” Raza said. “As a captain I’m really proud. Plenty to learn. I’d rather have a game like that than for the Aussies to just chase it down in 40 overs.” Reuters

World.title: Germany’s Merz stumbles on after another big election defeat. But for how long?
World.content:
WorldEuropeWorld politics Germany’s Merz stumbles on after another big election defeat. But for how long? James Crisp September 21, 2026 — 6:08am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Friedrich Merz, the pugnacious, stubborn German chancellor, has come out fighting in a desperate attempt to save his chancellorship. The leader who promised to transform his country’s fortunes when he took power last year suffered another bloody nose at the ballot box from the Alternative for Germany (AfD) on Sunday. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz speaks to media at the CDU party headquarters in Berlin. AP Photo/Markus Schreiber The hard-right party won state elections in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, taking 37 per cent of the vote, according to the first exit poll. It was not the crushing victory the AfD won earlier this month in the other east German state of Saxony-Anhalt, but Merz’s conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) still took a beating, and his leadership could be on the brink.



Merz’s approval ratings stand at just 10 per cent, with voters weary of his brusque, tough-guy management style, which persists even as he fails to stop the rise of the AfD and deliver on key manifesto pledges. Related Article Analysis

World elections Election shockwave: Meet the smiling new leader set to bring hard-right upheaval to Germany The irony is that some CDU insiders blame their Social Democratic Party (SPD) coalition partners in the federal government for slowing Merz’s reforms aimed at rebooting Germany’s struggling economy. The chancellor appeared contrite after the Saxony-Anhalt result and made an uncharacteristic and unconvincing promise to listen more to voters. Mecklenburg-Vorpommern is a smaller state, with just under 1.6 million people, but the timing, and that of the state elections in Berlin on the same day, was dangerous.



In the capital, voters handed the hard-Left Die Linke a 24.5 per cent victory over the CDU on 20 per cent. The AfD came third, with 16 per cent, the exit poll said. There have been murmurs of discontent within the CDU, a party not accustomed to replacing its leaders less than two years after coming to power. Germany as a whole is not used to palace coups after 16 years of Angela Merkel. But Merz’s predecessor, the SPD’s Olaf Scholz, also did not see out his full term; his coalition collapsed because of infighting. ‘German Burnham’ required Merz had been on manoeuvres in the days running up to Sunday’s elections.



He cancelled his planned appearance at the UN General Assembly. Party insiders insisted a leader, derided by some as a foreign-policy chancellor, a charge also levelled at former British prime minister Keir Starmer, was needed in Berlin. AfD members, including candidate Enrico Schult (second from left), speak to supporters at the party’s election evening gathering as Merz appears on a TV screen behind. Getty Images Before the exit polls dropped, Merz held a behind-closed-doors meeting with senior party members to challenge them to continue backing him. If they do not, he will demand they name a successor. The front-runner is Hendrik Wüst, North Rhine-Westphalia’s minister-president, who is viewed as Germany’s answer to Andy Burnham. But he has state elections in April, and missing them to take on the big job is an idea frowned upon by many in a decidedly old-fashioned and stuck-in-its-ways CDU.



Merz’s pressure has already brought some results, including a letter of muted support from eight state leaders, including Wüst, who claimed that Europe, faced with a surge in support for populist parties, needed a strong and stable Germany. Related Article Analysis

UK politics Farage says Britain is broken and only Reform can fix it. Now the pressure is on to deliver He can also rely on the fact that his party knows that changing the chancellor will require the SPD’s agreement, which could demand a slowdown of much-needed reforms in return. Merz is also attempting to strike a crowd-pleasing note to shift the narrative of a month of three bruising elections. He is planning measures to cap the soaring price of petrol amid record diesel prices and has softened his position on early retirement. But he remains almost fatally tone-deaf. His hopes for new laws that would force people to post online under their real names seem misguided, as voters are far more concerned with the cost of living.



His chances of survival depend not on his political skills but on his party’s risk-averse nature and a German political system that makes it difficult to remove a sitting chancellor. With the CDU not enduring the historic humiliation of falling below 5 per cent, Merz will pray that a period of intense political pressure around the three state elections will now begin to subside. On the point of being knocked out, he is hoping to hang on long enough to be rescued by events. At age 30 and surely with seasons of footy still to come, “the Bont” is tracking to become the greatest Brownlow vote-winner in history. The Bulldog is likely to reach third spot on the table (behind Gary Ablett jnr and Patrick Dangerfield) this year. Nothing is guaranteed in footy, and perennial contender Bontempelli might never win Charlie. A significant change to the Brownlow happened this year as the AFL allowed umpires to access statistics upon request. The league is trying to avoid perceived voting blunders by tinkering with the system. In deciding on the 3-2-1 votes for each match, the umpires can now ask for stats in 16 categories to help their judgment. Champion Data projections have Isaac Heeney polling in 12 games with five three-vote performances. Heeney is one of five Swans players suspended for breaching the club’s behavioural standards on the night of the Pullman hotel scandal.



The five are eligible to win the Brownlow but are not allowed to attend. Wanganeen-Milera figures prominently in Champion’s predictions, but interestingly not in the tips of our experts. Eagle-eyed Brownlow followers will try to assess how this affects voting patterns. The change might mean there’s less chance of a “bolt-from-the-blue” winner, such as West Coast’s Matt Priddis in 2014 or even Rowell last year. “With the new voting model, which allows umpires to review the post-game statistics, we forecast that the Brownlow will now heavily skew towards favourites in the future. This may make winners like Matt Rowell, who was $17 last year, more unlikely,” says TAB’s senior AFL trader Bart Kennett.



Time will tell what it means for the Brownlow long-term. But, don’t worry, you’ll still hear “N. Daicos, three votes” many times on Monday night. Here are the latest odds Nick Daicos $1.01
