World.title: Forget the grand final, this is the hardest week in rugby league
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Opinion Forget the grand final, this is the hardest week in rugby league Roy Masters Sports Columnist September 21, 2026 — 5:22am

September 21, 2026 — 5:22am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Preliminary finals are to a grand final what a nervy, fumbling first date is to a comfy, content wedding anniversary. It’s edgy expectation versus partial fulfilment. The penultimate weekend of a season, where four teams fight for the right to advance to the Big Dance, often has players and coaches nervous and uptight. They are aware that a tiny slip-up could end their season days short of what could have been a premiership. Loading Grand final teams tend to be more relaxed, some clubs simply secure at having already achieved their place in history. “Players can lose their edge going from a prelim to the grand final,” says Storm coach Craig Bellamy. Even the most vigilant coach can’t counter the doorman whispering to grand final players before kick-off, “No matter what happens today boys, you have done the club proud.”



It follows that a defeat in the preliminary final can be more devastating than losing a grand final. Bellamy, coach of more preliminary and grand final teams than anyone over the past quarter-century, has been more gutted after losing preliminary finals than I have seen him after narrow defeats in deciders. In 2011, after the Warriors won in Melbourne, he isolated himself from everyone, desperately desolate. His team had been expelled from the previous year’s competition as punishment for salary cap cheating, stripped of all honours and a galaxy of star players. A grand final win would have been redemption for all the world to see. “That was the worst,” admits Bellamy. Melbourne captain Christian Welch with coach Craig Bellamy in 2023 after losing the preliminary final to Penrith. NRL Images Ten years later, a Storm winger dropped the ball with the line wide open, and it was the Panthers who advanced to the grand final against the Rabbitohs. The Panthers were still a little fragile, relying on a Stephen Crichton intercept to launch their dynasty. It denied Bellamy the one prize which eluded him – successive premierships – and he fumed at the front of the bus during the silent journey to the team’s Queensland COVID base where they had been isolated almost all season. As coach of St George in 1984, I felt a one-point loss in the preliminary final more than a one-point loss in the grand final the following year. Lose a grand final, and you can console yourself with having had the experience. Also, the disappointment is ameliorated if your two lower-grade teams win, as the Dragons did in 1985. Lose a preliminary final, and you walk away with nothing. Many a player has declared after losing a preliminary final, “I won’t watch the grand final.”



Yet, paradoxically, the culture both in the NRL and the AFL says there is only one winner in a season. Every team that failed to stand on the dais on grand final day is a loser. So how can losing a prelim be more devastating? It’s the opportunity missed factor, the nagging feeling that if you reached the big day, you would have won. It hurts more when, throughout the season, your team has dominated the team it could have met in the decider. Perhaps coaches feel the loss of preliminary finals more than players. Young players at the top clubs believe they will be back the following year. Many never are. After four straight premierships, Nathan Cleary and the Panthers were hit with preliminary final pain in 2025. Getty Images Melbourne’s Christian Welch won a grand final in 2020; lost grand finals in 2016, 2018 and 2024 and lost preliminary finals in 2021 and 2023. He counts losing grand finals as far more devastating. “Having to stand on the field watching the premiership rings being handed out, you picture yourself in their position on the stage singing the team song,” he says.



Related Article Analysis

NRL 2026 The secret to DCE’s 424-game career? A ‘goldfish memory’, Ted Lasso and Dolphin days “You are so physically close to your lifelong dream but in reality, closer to the boys who won the spoon a month earlier. You can feel the euphoria of the winners; they are 10 metres away from you. A grand final loss is just so much more confronting and visceral, whereas a prelim loss you can justify in your head that you weren’t that close to premiership glory.” One thought I can’t reconcile in my head is how today’s NRL champions don’t display the prime trait of their generation. The social scientists insist the Gen Z population is the most risk-averse generation in history. They fear failure, yet today’s dressing shed disappointment is like non-stick cookware. Maybe it’s the attack-focused nature of today’s rules that promotes the rocks-and-diamonds players, such as Reece Walsh and Scott Drinkwater. It follows that these preliminary finals may not be the nervous, mistake-dreading encounters they were in the past. Still, the bunker plays to the textbook Gen Z fear. The lottery luck of some of the decisions sees players concede “12-point tries”. That is when a try is denied and the opposition scores immediately afterwards. An NRL official, not authorised to speak publicly, says an incorrect bunker ruling followed by an opposition try occurs far more than is reported.



The psychiatrist’s riddle is relevant to this weekend’s finals in terms of the focus on the Sydney crowd turnout and the number of teams that progressed from week one with zero or minimal recent experience in the play-offs. Is the stadium half full or half empty? The Dolphins will ride the emotions of preliminary finals week for the first time. Getty Images Will the newcomers be contenders or pretenders? To continue the analogy at the top of this column, will the teams like the Dolphins be nervous first daters or relaxed anniversary celebrants? By contrast, Penrith’s nucleus of playmakers are now in their seventh successive preliminary final. Maybe they will reach the altar a fifth time, but the bunker has a habit of being the disruptive, uninvited guest at a wedding. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: Women-only startup founders got 5.94 percent of venture capital in 2025
World.content:
Women-only startup founders received less than six cents in every venture capital dollar invested in New Zealand last year, despite a sharp rise in funding.

New data from the Aotearoa Centre for Enterprising Women at the University of Auckland Business School shows women-only founding teams attracted $14.75 million in disclosed investment from venture capital firms in 2025, more than triple the $4.59m raised the previous year.

Their share of total disclosed capital more than doubled, from 2.9 percent to 5.94 percent, but the gap remained significant.

Male-only founding teams received $172.35m, or 69.42 percent of disclosed capital, while mixed-gender teams received $61.17m, or 24.64 percent.

Gender Investment Gap co-founder Jenny Rudd said the improvement was encouraging, but the headline number was still too low to celebrate.

"When we look at women-only founded startups, it's doubled from about 3 percent last year to 6 percent," she said. "Which is great when it's doubled, but it's not really meaningful enough yet to get excited about."

Rudd said women-only founding teams accounted for about 12 percent of all deals but received about 6 percent of the money.

"That tells us that we're getting half the amount for our deals that everybody else is getting."

She said women-led startups often generated more revenue on less investment capital, but unconscious bias could still shape what investors saw as a safe bet.

"People who are deploying venture capital dollars, also largely men, see people that look like them as safe and what success looks like," Rudd said.

Contented co-founder Hannah Hardy-Jones said she and co-founder Lucy Pink raised $4.1m this year, but only after bootstrapping the company to $1m in annual recurring revenue.

She said that gave them a stronger position when they finally spoke to investors.

"We had proved ourselves before actually raising capital," Hardy-Jones said.

Hardy-Jones said earlier fundraising conversations had shown how differently women founders could be treated.

"The questions that I was asked as a founder were very different. It was all around competitors and risk, whereas my male counterparts were not fielding those sorts of questions. It was always around vision and ambition."

The research suggests the funding problem continues past the initial stages.

Women-only teams accounted for 17.6 percent of pre-seed investments and 15 percent of seed investments, but 7.5 percent of bridge investments.

None of the Series investments captured in the 2025 dataset went to women-only founding teams.

Hardy-Jones said more women needed to be visible in the startup ecosystem, and entrepreneurship should be taught earlier.

"The more women that are put into the space and given these opportunities, the more that evens out," she said.

Rudd said venture capital firms also needed to think about what they signalled publicly.

Rudd said if a fund's website or communications mostly showed male-led companies, women founders could decide it was not really for them.

"I didn't approach most of the VC firms when I was raising capital because I was like, they're not really designed for me," she said.

World.title: Should schools ban students from doing cartwheels?
World.content: Research on gymnastics injuries in children and teenagers shows wrist sprains, arm fractures and concussions are among the most common injuries. But this research does not tell us how likely children are to get hurt doing cartwheels or handstands in school playgrounds.

World.title: Person seriously hurt at 400-person Castle Street student party
World.content:
A person has been hospitalised after a large student party on Dunedin's Castle Street.

Castle Street is notorious for parties - being home to many University of Otago students.

The Otago Daily Times reported up to 400 people were at the party - and it was in celebration of "school reunion" day.

The ODT said one person was taken out of a flat with a head injury.

Hato Hone St John said it was called to the incident at 10.34am on Sunday.

"We responded with one rapid response vehicle. One patient was assessed at the scene and was transported to Dunedin Hospital in a serious condition."

In a statement, Dunedin Police said it was aware of - and monitored - the event.

"Inquiries into the circumstances of the incident are ongoing."

The University of Otago told The ODT the party was not organised by the university.

World.title: The electorate where a parrot trainer, a former All Black captain and a DJ want your vote
World.content:
What does a meteorologist, a parrot trainer, a former All Black captain and a DJ have in common?

They're all vying to be the next MP for Tukituki in Hawke's Bay. The bellwether seat is currently held by National MP Catherine Wedd, who is up against five newcomers.

Over their morning coffee in Havelock North, some locals in the Tukituki electorate have their minds made up already.

"I'm very comfortable with who the candidates are and yes, I know who I'll be voting for - the people who focus on the economy," said one man.

"To be honest I'm going to go with ACT or TOP. I'm not supporting the current prime minister and I've always been a right-wing voter all my life," said another.

One woman told RNZ she'd usually give both votes to Labour, but that's unlikely this time around.

"The Labour person, whoever it is, for around here isn't very visible so I'm a bit disappointed in that. Not too sure who I'll give my vote to in the electorate, but the party vote will probably go to Labour."

Others are feeling rather unsure.

"There's a lot of uncertainty. I don't like either of the two main parties so where are we going to go?" said a local pensioner. "And certain candidates I'm not fond of. I don't know... it could be very interesting seeing what happens."

"I'm concerned," said another voter. "Concerned because the polls and what they're showing. Not sure I believe the polls, but it creates that degree of uncertainty,."

Taine Randell. RNZ / Alexa Cook

The Tukituki electorate takes in Hastings, Havelock North, Flaxmere, Clive and Ōtāne, as well as the coastal settlements of Haumoana, Te Awanga, Ocean Beach and Waimārama.

Six very different candidates are vying for the job in a historically blue seat that flipped to red in 2020 when Labour's Anna Lorck won.

Former All Black captain Taine Randell, who was a student at Lindisfarne, has stepped into the political contest for New Zealand First.

"We've got a few issues in New Zealand and I don't have a great deal of confidence in the people that we've got there that they are going to solve those issues, so with my experience I'm going to throw my hat in the ring and see if I can do better."

His key priority is economic growth.

"There's no progress without growth. Through my experience in small and medium businesses, from zero employees up to 120, that's where the potential is for growth in New Zealand. We've just got to make sure they stop getting punished by banks, energy companies and out-of-control Government regulation."

Something people might not know about Randell, who played 52 tests for New Zealand, is that in 2008 he was working as an oil broker in London right before the global financial crisis happened.

"My wife and I decided we were coming back to New Zealand, so I made sure I'd been paid and then handed in my resignation. It turned out to be the same day that Lehman's bank went bust. The biggest insolvency in the history of mankind - talk about good timing," he laughed.

Rachel Ward. RNZ / Alexa Cook

Putting up giant billboards of her face on fences is all rather new to Opportunity candidate Rachel Ward.

"I'm not sure you ever get used to that," Ward said.

The mother of two has resigned from her conservation job managing Cape Sanctuary to dip her toes into politics because she's frustrated about the "conservation bureaucracy and environmental short-sightedness of the current coalition government".

"It's just too important and I have a really strong gut feeling that this is what I should be doing, if I can make things better for our environment and for my kids in the future."

As well as being able to do back flips on the trampoline, she's also New Zealand's only certified parrot trainer.

"I do have a business in Australia that is a parrot behaviour and training business - it seems wacky and out there, but in Australia one in three people have a pet parrot - and they're all pretty naughty and bite and do all sorts of things."

Ward wants to focus not only on protecting the environment, but also on unifying New Zealanders.

"There are policies and bills going to Parliament that are dividing our country... it really upsets me, and we can do so much more together when we celebrate our differences and culture.

"Watching politics around the world and the division... we don't need to be like that and we don't need to follow that trajectory."

Dan Scott. Supplied

Labour's candidate for Tukituki is 22-year-old meteorologist Dan Scott.

"I grew up in Hawke's Bay and I've been watching, especially since the cyclone hit, and I've been really concerned that there's not been the investment or the thought put into what the people of Hawke's Bay really need and deserve," he said.

His campaign is focused around healthcare, the cost of living, climate change adaptation and jobs. The closure of the McCain factory in Hastings really struck a nerve with him.

"I'm really worried there is no planning from Government in terms of how to follow that up. It's crucial we have food processing continue in Hawke's Bay so we can still have food from New Zealand growers and not rely on imported items."

Asked what's something people don't know about him, his response is unexpected.

"I have always had a fear of public speaking growing up... the fact I've managed to turn that around and run for Parliament might give people a bit of a surprise."

If successful, Scott plans to split his time between Hawke's Bay and Wellington, where he works as a meteorologist and forecaster.

Mark Longworth. Supplied

The fourth political newcomer for Tukituki is Green Party candidate Mark Longworth. The natural medicine grower lives in Central Hawke's Bay and is a former DJ.

Longworth said he decided to stand for Parliament after feeling uninspired by the options at last year's local elections.

"If I couldn't cast a vote for my values from what was on offer, I felt it was important for those votes to go somewhere... to be counted and do more good.

"No option wasn't good enough for me so I felt the need to put my hand up for the general election."

He has three priorities.

"Grow the Green Party vote, get more people enrolled to vote, especially our rangatahi, and make this coalition a one-term government."

Rob Douglas. Supplied

ACT's Rob Douglas is standing again for Tukituki, after having a run at the job in 2023.

He's a property valuer in Hawke's Bay, and told RNZ he is not aiming for the electorate vote.

"I'm not asking people in this election to actually vote for me personally, I'm asking the voters of New Zealand to give their party vote to ACT.

"We've got two really clear objectives - we're trying to lock Labour out and unlock NZ's potential."

A little-known fact about Douglas is that he struggled at school.

"Against all my objections at school I was given a lot of remedial reading... it's made a real difference in my life.

"I now write valuation reports for a living, something I couldn't have done without that base knowledge I picked up then. I feel it's so important for Kiwis to get the opportunity to get that core knowledge."

A billboard for Catherine Wedd. RNZ / Alexa Cook

Incumbent National MP Catherine Wedd is hoping she'll keep the job come 7 November.

"It's been an absolute privilege to represent Hawke's Bay Tukituki for the last three years and I feel we have a lot more to do," she said.

Her main priority for the region is the economy, as she wants to see more growth in the farming and horticulture sectors.

"That's why I've been a really staunch advocate for water security. We're one of the only regions in the country without large-scale water storage. If we can get that in Hawke's Bay it will unleash so much potential for the district and the region."

Something people might not know about the MP is that she used to work as a journalist for 1 News and the BBC.
