World.title: National MPs don't like supermarket break-up policy - David Seymour
World.content:
David Seymour responds to supermarket policy announcements Morning Report Download MP3 8m

The ACT Party says National MPs have been coming to them "exasperated" by their own party's policy to break up the supermarket duopoly.

But National's leader is pushing back, saying the policy will be based on a review of the evidence and presents an opportunity for small businesses.

Last week, National promised to split Pak'nSave from New World and Four Square, subject to an independent Commerce Commission assessment of the plan, which echoes one put forward by New Zealand First back in April.

Meanwhile, Labour is promising to outlaw price-gouging for a range of essentials and to split up Woolworths and Foodstuffs' retail and wholesale businesses, while the Greens have vowed to force Woolworths and Foodstuffs to sell some of their stores and wholesale operations to the government.

ACT leader David Seymour called it a "race to the bottom… to beat up the supermarkets the most".

Shoppers at Costco in West Auckland. Stuff / Abigail Dougherty

While acknowledging "clearly things are more expensive", he told Morning Report it was not clear supermarkets were making excessive profits nor that any of the proposed solutions would make groceries cheaper.

"The most important question is well what else will these policies do? And the effect on New Zealand business, both inside and outside the country, people's willingness to invest and innovate - which by the way, is what we actually need if we want higher wages and a more affordable life - is terribly chilling. Because once you start with one industry, the first question is who's next?"

The Woolworths-Foodstuff duopoly has an 82 percent market share. The government's efforts to attract a third nationwide chain have so far come to naught, though US bulk discounter Costco opened its first New Zealand store in West Auckland about four years ago, and has plans for more.

Labour's Arena Williams discusses new supermarket policy Morning Report Download MP3 7m

Seymour said Costco only agreed to come here when it was granted a five-year exemption to new rules requiring supermarkets to supply other retailers at wholesale prices.

"They said if that's the rule in New Zealand, 'We're out.' So they were given an exemption from that. And I think that nicely illustrates that regulatory uncertainty and exactly the kinds of policies that every other party is now proposing in a kind of hysteria to be seen to be the toughest beating up on one sector, actually can drive away exactly the kind of investment that we need."

Seymour questioned if any of the parties proposing radical solutions were "absolutely sure" they knew "what the right market structure is for groceries in an island nation of 5 million people spread along a mountain chain at the end of the world's supply chain".

Labour's commerce and consumer affairs spokesperson Arena Williams. Sam Rillstone

"We've been doing this in New Zealand for too long. I mean, Jacinda [Ardern, former prime minister] said we're being fleeced by the petrol stations, we had to go with the farmers for a while, landlords were the baddies at one point, so we put more taxes and regulations on them. The banks have been in for a good beating, now it's the supermarket.

"There's only 5 million of us, guys. We've got to stop and actually start asking, well, how do you get the kind of investment and innovation that leads to more competitive offerings, higher wages and better prices?"

Seymour said there had been an "unprecedented wave of National MPs" - at least five, that he knew of - which had approached ACT with concerns about their own party's policy.

"We can understand the Green Party - they always want to do crazy stuff, but the National Party for a long time has given people reassurance that this is a place where you can actually own something, and if you do a good job you can sell and maybe even make a profit - but not always.

"It's hard enough to do business as it is in any country without worrying if your own government's going to attack you."

'Massive opportunity' for small businesses - Luxon

Christopher Luxon discusses supermarkets, AI and the Warriors Morning Report Download MP3 6m

Nearly 500 owner-operators of Foodstuffs supermarkets signed open letters to National leader Christopher Luxon expressing concern about the policy.

Asked if he expected such a pushback from businesses, Luxon said his policy was "not about business, it's actually about the fact that we believe in competition".

"We are very pro-business and we're also pro-competition. And actually, the owner-operators, the 400-500 that are in that Foodstuffs group, are incredible.

"It's actually a sector I worked in for 18 years... I can't think of a single [other] market that has 82 percent market share with two players. I mean, other 5 million people countries I operated in around the world would have three to five operators, typically.

"It's a market in New Zealand that has a 4 percent margin. I mean, many countries around the world would have 1.5 to 2 percent ... there's an excess profit being made every day, and it's about then not just jumping to a populist easy answer."

He said politicians should not be "going off and intervening in a market like this in an ad-hoc way".

"We're now handing it over for six months to the Commerce Commission, with all of their economists, with all their deep competition experts... if it is [the right way forward], we move forward with it. It may well be that Foodstuffs decides to do it voluntarily. It may well be that we have to mandate that happening... if [the Commission] decide not to do it, then we won't be doing it."

Luxon pleaded ignorance of National MPs calling for Seymour to stop the policy.

"I'm not aware of that. I'm just saying to you, caucus backs the policies. MPs will have concerns as they do on all our policy areas, and we discuss those and we raise those in our caucus meetings, as we should."

He said different reports suggested different gains, with some pointing to a 3.5 percent reduction in grocery prices in a year, and others 5 percent lower after six years.

The change could be an opportunity for small businesses, he suggested.

"You could, for example, see owner-operators starting to have two stores or more stores, they could create new formats... for many small businesses across New Zealand, who want to provide products and services into the supermarkets, this is a massive opportunity."

Labour's proposed fix

Labour commerce and consumer affairs spokesperson Arena Williams told Morning Report breaking the wholesale dominance the duopoly has over smaller retailers was key to bringing down prices.

"The two major grocers have locked in their market power with not only suppliers but with small grocers as well, by dominating the market not only in retail but also in wholesale. We're going to stop that."

The Commerce Commission's market study in 2022 recommended against this separation.

"What they identified with that model was that there were two problems with it," Williams explained, saying Labour's new plan - three years in the making - fixed those.

Labour announces new supermarket policy Morning Report Download MP3 4m

One was a "guaranteed route for retail grocers to be able to access from the wholesalers [without] relying on the wholesalers themselves to come up with the solution within their own businesses that would allow for that".

"And they also identified some problems with the way that supplies are bought essentially by only two buyers with huge market power over them. We've also fixed that… That's what's taken us three years, but we're certain that this is the model which won't see prices rise in the short-term, like the one proposed by National, and it's the one that's best understood by the market, so we can get underway quickly."

Another plank of Labour's policy is to ban price-gouging.

"Anyone who is price gouging will need to stop that," Williams said. "There is evidence in the Commerce Commission's market study in 2022 that supermarkets were making excess profits of $1m a day. Within that, there will be prices which are higher than they would otherwise be in a competitive market.

World.title: Fonterra raises farmgate milk price
World.content:
Fonterra has increased its 2026/27 milk price forecast and narrowed its forecast price range, following improvements at recent Global Dairy Trade (GDT) auctions.

The co-op said the revised new season farmgate milk price forecast was $9.50/kg of milk solids, with a new range of $8.50-$10.50/kg.

It's still down from the opening forecast of $9.75/kg announced in May and a wide range of $8-$11/kg, but an improvement from the earlier price drop announced in July.

Chief executive Richard Allen said the increase in the milk price midpoint is supported by recent improvements in global commodity prices.

"Since our last update in July, GDT auction results for key commodity products, particularly whole milk powder and skim milk powder, have improved. Globally, we continue to see strength in demand.

"This improving outlook reflects continued delivery from our focused execution across our B2B businesses. Geopolitical volatility remains and, with only two months complete, previous seasons tell us that things can always change."

World.title: Forest and Bird calls for fast-tracked coal mining application to be declined
World.content:
*Correction: This story has been updated to clarify the independent fast-track panel, rather than the EPA, found gaps in the conservation plan.

Forest and Bird is calling for a fast-tracked coal mining application to be declined after the fast-track panel found gaps in its conservation plan.

The independent panel has sent a letter to mining company Bathurst asking for more information about its application to mine coal from Buller's Denniston Plateau.

It has asked the company to be more specific about how it would protect the area's wildlife, which includes protected lizards and insects.

RNZ has approached Bathurst for comment.

"There were some shortcomings in their plan for lizards," Forest and Bird's regional conservation manager Scott Burnett said.

"The Department of Conservation's best practice for lizard management is to salvage more than 80 percent of the lizards from a site before development occurs. In Bathurst's application they expect that fewer than one percent of lizards can be feasibly salvaged, so that's a massive scale difference there.

"Likewise, the avatar moth, which recently won bug of the year, it's only found on the Denniston Plateau, and a number of the sites where it has been found are within the mine footprint. The entomologist who discovered the avatar moth, Brian Patrick, feels that if the mine is to go ahead the moth will go extinct."

Burnett said he was pleased the panel had gone back to Bathurst to ask for more information.

"Outside of our overarching concerns around the failings of fast-track, this is an example of the process working as intended," he said.

One expert fears this moth will go extinct if the mine goes ahead. CC BY 4.0 Brian Patrick

"We would ultimately like to see the application declined. We know that is not likely, given the permissiveness of the regime, but we would also like to see really robust conditions in place both to protect wildlife and also to ensure New Zealanders don't foot the bill for future cleanup."

Buller District Council mayor Chris Russell said he supported Bathurst's application and believed it should be granted, but also noted it was important to consider the environmental impacts.

"The effects on ecology and water quality, along with acid mine drainage, rehabilitation and the project's long-term obligations, must be properly tested," he said.

"[But] the significant economic and social consequences of closure must be given the same consideration."

He noted the project would maintain jobs for at least 390 people, the vast majority of which lived in Buller.

Burnett disagreed with that argument.

"This is very much pitched as a jobs versus nature argument. The Buller community outwardly support the mine going ahead to protect jobs in Westport," he said.

"This occurring in 2026 in a climate and biodiversity crisis, where people feel like their best recourse is to double down on short term jobs that cause this environmental harm... [that] is a failure of national and local leadership."

Russell said the final decision belonged to the panel.

World.title: Meet the teens training to play for the Tasmania Devils
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The Tasmania Devils AFL team has secured a coach, is on track to build a stadium and is training its up-and-coming players as the state prepares to join the national football league in 2028.

Some of the Devils' first official players are likely to be sourced from interstate, but the Tasmanian club is looking to its homegrown talent as the foundation to field a strong side for the future.

Through its pathways program, about 420 young people from areas around Launceston, the North West and Hobart already train regularly to develop their potential as AFL and AFLW players.

Prince trains with the Tasmania Devils' Launceston hub, which supports young talented footballers to develop their AFL potential. (ABC News: Duncan Bailey)

Fifteen-year-old Launceston local, Prince, is part of the program and trains four times a week, splitting his sessions between the Devils and his local football club.

He said being considered for a future AFL career was a "dream come true", and that he was motivated by his family's refugee journey from Sierra Leone before he was born.

Prince's family migrated from West Africa to Tasmania before he was born. (ABC News: Duncan Bailey)

"[My family] went to a refugee camp in Ghana … where my brother and sister were born … and then [to] Australia," he said.

"It requires a lot of resilience to migrate and raise multiple kids in a different country.

" That work ethic has been passed on through my upbringing and I just really want to work hard at my sport to give back to [my family]. "

Loading...

Coby, 15, is a fellow Tasmania Devils pathways player who almost left football behind after a loss in his family.

Playing in the AFL had been his dream since watching a football game at the MCG when he was six years old.

He said getting the call to say he had made the pathways team was "one of the happiest days" of his life.

Coby says his Nan's passing has inspired him to push on with chasing his AFL dreams because she was his biggest supporter. (ABC News: Duncan Bailey)

"But when my Nan passed away, I thought, 'How am I going to overcome this and do what I usually do without my biggest supporter?'" he said.

"Then I realised, if I quit I would never know how good I could be.

"Now I want to be the best that I can be [for her] … hopefully that's going as far as the AFL."

Devils set sights on AFLW

The Tasmania Devils pathways program also focuses on creating a competitive AFLW side for the state.

Lilanni plays in the Tasmania U18 Talent League side. (ABC News: Duncan Bailey)

Lilanni, 17, plays in the Tasmania under-18 talent league side and is draft eligible this year.

She hopes to join her sister, Fremantle Dockers' player Tunisha Kikoak, in the AFLW ranks.

"When I first touched the ball I [knew I] wanted to be in the draft and be an AFLW player like my sister," she said.

Lilanni said the increased focus on women's football across the country had led to better development for young female players.

"There's more opportunities for the girls that I play alongside [than before] and there's more chances to grow as a player," she said.

Brad Cox-Goodyer is AFL Tasmania talent pathways skills acquisition coach and says the Devils are building a strong side ahead of their debut in 2028. (ABC News: Duncan Bailey)

AFL Tasmania talent pathways skills acquisition coach Brad Cox-Goodyer said the Devils had already been working to develop individual talent.

"We're in our third year now and it's exciting … [we] get better every year and [are] hoping to get more kids playing for the Tassie Devils," he said.

World.title: SCG madness and Plugger's point: The Swans-Bombers prelim, 30 years on
World.content:
When Dale Lewis recalls being at the Sydney Swans in the 1990s, it certainly was not all about big games and big crowds.

"We're training, doing preseason out of the showgrounds next door [to the SCG] and one of the days, the Big Day Out was on at these showgrounds. We had to walk the oval, arms linked like we're in a search party checking for needles and shit in the grass before we trained," he says.

"The Swans weren't popular. We were having crowds of 5,000 people. I jumped the fence one day to get the footy for a boundary umpire.

"I've got a great mate … his brother used to come, and he used to love it because he could sit anywhere, and he cracked the shits when we started getting good because he had to go buy a ticket and couldn't get a decent seat and sit where he wanted to."

It all changed in the mid 1990s, when the Swans went from the basement to the penthouse.

With three straight wooden spoons between 1992 and 1994, they went from winning one game in 1993 to four wins in 1994 and eight wins in 1995, then a surge to 16 wins and top of the ladder in '96.

A finals win over Hawthorn put them in a home preliminary final against Essendon at a heaving SCG, 30 years ago today.

Swans utility Troy Luff had gotten his opportunity that season. Originally from Traralgon in Victoria, he grew up attached to a footy like most kids, then he and his family moved to Nelson Bay near Newcastle.

He was spotted while kicking goals for fun in the Hunter, but struggled to make a mark with the Swans under Ron Barassi.

Then new coach Rodney Eade changed everything as Luff became a permanent fixture in the side.

Troy Luff got his big opportunity for the Sydney Swans in 1996, and he rode the momentum to the prelim. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

"It was more excitement rather than pressure," Luff says.

"If we lose, we lose. We got this far, but everyone just went out there and enjoyed themselves, and the results came our way."

Lewis agrees.

"None of us saw it coming, but by Christ it was addictive once you started to win, especially at home," he says.

"Because I think that was the year we started. We ended up winning 22 or three in a row at the SCG as the run got going. You started to get a feeling about it.

"And once we'd beaten Hawthorn in that first qualifying [final], the expectation was why not?"

In 1992-93, the Swans lost 26 games in a row.

Lewis, drafted against his preferences in 1990 by Sydney, was out the week they broke the run against Melbourne and ended up playing in 33 consecutive losses. He tried to leave Sydney in 1994, but ended up staying.

In 1995, a series of important arrivals arrived, none bigger than the famous bookends, Paul Roos and Tony "Plugger" Lockett.

The former St Kilda superstar Lockett had won his third Coleman Medal (and first in Sydney) in 1996, booting 114 goals in the home-and-away season.

Former Fitzroy key position player Roos brought skill, leadership and experience.

Now they and the Swans were a win away from a grand final.

The game

It was fierce, frantic footy early doors. Not a heap of composure was shown, with lots of scrubby kicks under pressure, aiming for territory rather than accuracy.

Early in the game, Essendon was looking for James Hird, who - along with Michael Voss of the Brisbane Bears - would win the Brownlow Medal two days later. Hird kicked long from 60, and Steven Alessio marked before converting from 20 out.

Soon after, Lewis marked, then tripped over Hird and was crunched in a tackle. Hird grabbed the ball and scored. Swans fans were livid, but Essendon led by two goals.

The Swans tried kicking to Lockett, but Essendon cleared – their movement was better, and Hird earned a free on 50. He went long, Justin Blumfield came down with it and ran around to kick Essendon's third.

Sydney could not take a trick. Lewis grabbed the ball in the centre square and quickly went long again in Lockett's direction; in the end, Jason Mooney kicked a point to make it 3.1 to 0.1.

Hird came off the ground with blood streaming from his left cheek after he and Andrew Dunkley contested a ball, the Swans defender roughing the Bombers star as he lay on the ground with Dunkley on top of him.

A Barry Young point extended the lead, then Gary O'Donnell took possession and went long to Che Cockatoo-Collins, who marked and drilled it from inside 50. Seven minutes left, Bombers by 25.

The Bombers were dominating clearances, and Damien Hardwick set up Mick Symons for a contested mark, but his kicking radar was off. The Swans' forward forays were like chaos balls compared to the Dons.

Dale Lewis's long-kicking, strong marking style made him an important player for the Swans against the Bombers. (Getty Images: Mandatory Credit: Allsport Australia/ALLSPORT)

Another series of points, then Wade Chapman marked a Stuart Maxfield kick near horizontal at half-forward. His kick came, and Lewis drifted in from the side for a great mark. He kicked it, and the Swans trailed by 19 at quarter time.

"Part of your job is to kick goals and everything else, but to take a big mark," Lewis says.

"That was in front of the Ladies Stand too, I think. A mad, mad Swans house there. Always nice to do that."

Luff says the Swans had built up confidence during the season.

"There was never an attitude of, 'Oh geez, they've got three goals on us, we're going to lose this.' We were like, 'No, no, we'll get that back.'''

Tough night for Essendon's Lloyd

On the Essendon side of things, forward Matthew Lloyd was playing a prelim in game 16 of his career, at just 18 years old.

Drafted at 16, thanks to a one-off change of the rules due to draft concessions for the new Fremantle side, Lloyd was highly touted.

He kicked three on debut against the Crows in 1995 before playing a couple of finals as a schoolboy.

In 1996 he kicked another seven against Adelaide, and then just before finals he booted three against the Swans at the MCG.

"I was playing local footy in 1993, Western Jets in '94, and then suddenly I'm playing as a 17-year-old in '95. So yeah, it all happened so fast, but I was very driven," Lloyd says.

"[The focus] was all footy, footy, footy. I was 78 kilos, and I actually ended my career at 92 to 94 kilos.

"So I was out of my depth physically. I did kick three on debut, and I kicked three in the first [1995] final, so I had some good moments."

Matthew Lloyd kicked three against the Swans in August 1996, but he struggled in the cauldron of an SCG prelim a month later. (Getty Images, file photo)

Fast-forward to the prelim in 1996; it was a different story.

"I just felt like the SCG, where I hadn't played before, the crowd was on top of you, it was loud, and it was physical," Lloyd says.

"I was a very nervous type. I had a big fear of failure. I wasn't able to get my hands on the footy; it was more the atmosphere in that stadium and some big Sydney players too that I was playing on [that was intimidating]."

In the second quarter, Sydney was trying to hit back, and narrowed the gap through goals to skipper Paul Kelly and Daryn Cresswell. The lead was four points.

Lloyd was scrambling to make an impact. Nearly halfway through the quarter, a big Mark Harvey kick was bouncing towards the boundary at half-forward.

Mark Bayes and Hird were running one way, and Lloyd was racing out of forward 50. As Lloyd recalls, what happened next was "quite innocuous" as he tried to bump Bayes.

"You bump someone, and instead my elbow came back into my side. It took my breath away, and I felt winded. I played out the rest of the second quarter, but I felt like I was deteriorating health-wise," he says.

A review of the video does not suggest there was a huge problem – Lloyd kept launching himself into packs, although if you were keeping your eye on him rather than the ball, he was taking longer to get up each time.

"It's all a bit of a blur for me because I remember I couldn't concentrate; I couldn't really take in the half-time address [from Kevin Sheedy]," he says.

"I was losing colour in my face and body. I said to the club doctor, 'I'm not feeling very well', and they decided to have me start the third quarter and see how I was feeling after five minutes.

"I'm not sure how long I was in the third quarter where I eventually came off … but they knew to get me to hospital at that point."

Lloyd went to emergency at a Kings Cross hospital.

"I just remember lying there still in my full Essendon kit of the football jumper, the shorts, socks, and boots I presume, and just pain, just in so much pain," he says.

He was given morphine, and the pain subsided a little.

"They asked me to hop, and I hopped, and I said, 'I actually feel a bit better,'" he says.

"I can't remember what they thought it could have been, but they said, 'He's right to go back to the hotel.'"

Swans making a run

Back at the SCG, things were improving for Sydney.

After those two early goals, the Swans sensed an opportunity. Derek Kickett kicked from the right pocket to the square for Lockett to mark and goal. The crowd erupted and Sydney led by two with 9:26 left in the half.

Another scrambled ball was toed toward goal by Lockett, only for Sean Denham to palm it away like a goalkeeper.

Somehow Lockett got it out to Luff, who kicked the goal and Sydney led by eight. It was pandemonium at the SCG.

"From memory, he burst through and pushed someone out of the way, then handballed it to me at the top of the square and I snapped the goal," Luff recalls.

"And you just get pumped; it helps you keep building from moments, whether it's a good tackle or a good spoil [or a goal]."

Misses by Barry Young and Hird brought the margin back to six.

The play was getting faster and more chaotic, and the ball pinged in and out of 50 for Sydney. A kung-fu style kick from Luff found Greg Stafford, who ignored a furious Plugger before Cresswell snapped his second. Swans led by 12 at half-time.

Early in the third, a Lewis kick found Lockett near the point post – he marked then stumbled and fell over. His kick hit the post.

On the ABC Radio broadcast, commentator Peter Longman said: "He's done some good things, Lockett, but if he were a racehorse they'd be checking him out behind the barriers and declaring him a non-starter, I feel sure."

Teammates knew Lockett was in pain.

"An 80 per cent Plugger is better than not having him in the side at all, even 70 per cent Plugger. He was just that good," Luff says.

The back-and-forth continued, with a kind of stalemate.

Luff snapped over his shoulder, but it bounced out 15 metres wide of the posts. Luff then got the tap to Kelly, who took two steps and snapped for a Sydney goal. Cue huge chants from the red and white faithful.

Utility Troy Luff contributed to the Swans' historic prelim challenge, setting up a goal and kicking one of his own. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

"I started in defence when Paul Roos was injured. I'd play centre-half-back. Andrew Dunkley was injured, I'd play full-back. Plugger was out, I'd play full-forward. So I just played any role the team needed [including ruck]," Luff says.

There were 41,731 at the SCG that night – and they were totally fired up, making the noise of a much bigger crowd.

"David Murphy used to tell me before that year, 50,000 people, you can just hear your teammate. [With a] 75,000 crowd, you can barely hear your teammate," Lewis says.

"Anything over 85, 95,000, you can't hear your teammate, and you can't even feel yourself get hit. Such is the noise and the adrenaline; you don't even know what's happening.

"The messaging was always, [finals are] going to be quicker, it's going to be faster, it's going to be harder. And none of it's bullshit."

Just when Swans fans might have been feeling a little confident, the Bombers had a forward 50 stoppage; the tap went to Harvey, and then O'Donnell, who kicked from 35 and the lead was 13 points.

But Sydney went down the corridor, and Lewis marked. A huge roar greeted his goal, and a fan leapt the fence and ran next to the umpire to do a tandem goal signal. He then got out of there quick-smart.

At 19 points down, the Bombers were not done. Dean Wallis marked in the pocket, then Sydney gave away 50. Dunkley was in the umpire's face – Wallis goaled, then confronted the Sydney full-back.

The Bombers won the next clearance, and Alessio found Hird in the square to score. With 3:00 left in the term, it was a seven-point game.

In the final minute, Alessio marked around 50 – and converted. A quarter to go, Sydney led by a solitary point, 8.7 to 8.6.

Troy Luff recalls Swans coach Rodney Eade urging players to keep things tight to start the final quarter at the SCG. (Getty Images, file photo)

"I remember Rocket (Rodney Eade) just saying that we needed to shut that down at the start of the last quarter, not go out and try and kick a goal," Luff says.

"If they got the first goal, they've kicked four in a row, and they may have gone on with it. But if we just shut that momentum down, play a bit defensive to start with, then once the game settles, then we [can] go out and attack."

Only three of the 16 goals kicked had been to the left-hand end. The Bombers would be kicking to that end in the final quarter.

Early on, O'Donnell fed Che Cockatoo-Collins, who burst down the right. His kick found Hird, and the Essendon champion slowed, then raced forward and snapped. The umpire scampered around. The Bombers had their early goal.

With 18:27 left, Essendon led by five. Everyone was tiring, and play was largely stuck between the arcs. Time ticked slowly; after a series of misses it was 9.9 to 8.9.

The tension was rising. Essendon's Denham might have cracked a rib; Sydney's Michael O'Loughlin hurt his knee. He came off and returned, still limping.

From a boundary throw 40m out, Harvey handballed to a running Symons.

ABC's Peter Longman was left incredulous:

"He's put it through! The Bombers lead by 12 points! Symons, a duffer from a standing start, has a checkside kick from 35m out and he's put it through – and he might have put the Bombers into the grand final next week!"

The Bombers led by 12, 4:09 on the clock.

The final minutes

Lewis had a sick feeling, wondering if this was how it would finish.

"Something you've wanted so bad as a kid, as a senior footballer, as an AFL player, it's within your grasp, but you can't touch it … It hits you in the gut real hard. I'm not going to lie to you, that was a shit feeling when he kicked that one," he says.

The runner told Lewis to drag Hird to full-forward because Sydney needed goals.

"So I hightailed it out of there," Lewis recalls.

Essendon hacked it forward; Adam Heuskes cleared to Kelly. He found Maxfield, who was chased through the middle, taking two bounces as the roar built. A kick from 60 to Hird and Lewis – and Lewis grabbed it and kicked the goal. Six points, 2:48 left.

It got even more frantic, the ball stuck in the middle. The Swans cleared, and it went to Simon Garlick, then Chapman, then Maxfield to Lockett, who played on but didn't go for goal, opting to kick inside to Cresswell. Cresswell marked then lay down, cramping.

He got up and kicked it, and with 89 seconds left, the scores were level.

Cresswell raised his arms skywards. The Sydney Airport curfew was still half an hour from kicking in, but the roar erupting would have matched a take-off from Mascot.

The clock ticked down, a ball-up with 1:02 left, no real progress.

The play was ferocious as players collided. The ball went inside 50; Swans couldn't mark. Blumfield cleared it desperately, and Chapman marked to the right of the centre square. He back-pedalled, then kicked high to the left side of 50.

From stage right came Tony Lockett to pluck it from the sky and draw every single decibel from surrounding suburbs with 17 seconds left.

He was 52 metres from goal, with an injured groin, and no other options. The clock ran down.

"The video shows me walking past him as he's about to line up to take the shot. I've just turned around to him and said, 'All you have to do is get it over the line. Doesn't matter what it is, just get it over the line,'" Luff recalls.

The siren's gone, the crowd's collective blood pressure had spiked into the stratosphere, but Plugger had it.

Loading...

Everyone watched the ball fly towards goal. Was it there? A point was enough; out on the full or short meant extra time.

The roar gathered. The umpire fired out one finger to signal a behind, and absolute bedlam ensued at the SCG. The Bombers were distraught. The Swans were ecstatic.

Sydney vs Essendon AFL preliminary final Sept 21, 1996 (SCG) SYDNEY: 10.10 (70) def ESSENDON 10.9 (69) Goals: Sydney: D Lewis 3, D Cresswell 3, P Kelly 2, T Lockett, T Luff Essendon: J Hird 3, S Alessio 2, J Blumfield, C Cockatoo-Collins, G O'Donnell, M Symons, D Wallis Crowd: 41,731

It was over. Two seasons removed from the wooden spoon, the Swans were in their first grand final since South Melbourne's infamous "Bloodbath" decider against Carlton in 1945.

Lewis recalls the feeling when Lockett took the grab.

"Call it presumptuous, but the moment he marked it, I knew we were going to play in a grand final," he says.

What about Plugger's groin, the distance, the pain, the effort required?

"None of it became relevant because he's Tony Lockett," Lewis says.

"We would pick him from anywhere, any angle, any distance. Because that's what he does. Not only was it his job, but the belief we had in him when he had the ball in hand, kick a goal or convert and finish was just amazing."

The aftermath

Sydney's Tony Lockett pushed himself to the limit for the most important behind of his career that put the Swans in the grand final. (Supplied: AFL Photos)

Luff was quick to the party.

"We're like, 'That's going to score.' And then the excitement hit us. And I was one of the first ones to jump on Plugger, and then everyone else just piled on top," Luff says.

"And what I do remember is Plugger on the bottom going, 'Get off me, get off me.' He was so sore from his groin that everyone jumping on didn't help his cause.

"Then [we] got up and we're like, 'We're in the grand final. We're in the grand final.' It was ecstatic. It was fantastic."

Lewis turned to Stafford in the square to find he was already off running.

"I get in a bit late on the pile on, and all I can do is pat a few blokes … because I was too busy celebrating down the goal square looking for a bit of love from teammates who'd already done the bolt," he says.

Dale Lewis says the surge of euphoric Swans fans onto the SCG after the 1996 prelim was the precursor of the "Buddy moment" in 2022. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Michael Willson)

The euphoric crowd of Swans fans surged onto the ground.

"That's the precursor to the Buddy moment [Lance Franklin's 1,000 goals] in terms of the crowd getting on the ground at the SCG," Lewis says.

"You didn't want to get off [the ground], but you wanted to get off because you wanted to get into that little room downstairs and soak it all in with each other and just go, 'F***, how good is this. We're in one.'"

Lloyd's dream turns 'nightmare'

Back at the Bombers team hotel, Matthew Lloyd was in his room with his parents. Players were coming in, but the morphine was wearing off.

Once people had gone, Lloyd asked his parents to help him to the bathroom, where he passed blood.

Essendon's Dr Bruce Reid came, and Lloyd says he was "rolling around in bed, just the worst pain of my life." Reid asked him if he had shoulder pain.

"I stopped for a second, and I said, 'Yeah, really strong shoulder pain.' I remember him saying, 'Get him an ambulance. He's got a ruptured spleen,'" Lloyd recalls.

Scans showed a large tear in his spleen, and a litre and a half of blood. It could have been fatal if left longer. As scary as this was, Lloyd had to come to terms with what it meant for his footy career.

"I knew going into this game, the reserves had qualified for the grand final," he says.

"I thought, 'Well, I'm going to play in that because I qualify for that or I'm going to play in the AFL grand final,' and then it turned into my nightmare."

Lloyd lost eight kilos, was bedridden for a time and could not do anything physical for three months. But in 1997 he burst out with a 63-goal season.

"I lived and breathed footy, no interest in going to parties," Lloyd says.

"My dad played 29 games for Carlton, and from the moment I was three or four, I had a footy in my hand, and it's all I ever wanted to do … and I was no different with my rehab; I was willing to do anything to play AFL footy."

That determination saw Lloyd finish as Essendon's top goal-kicker and eighth in VFL/AFL history, with 926 majors.

While Lloyd was suffering through a ruptured spleen, the other Bombers were dealing with a season cut short.

He says the players filing through his hotel room that night let him know coach Kevin Sheedy had exploded like never before after the game.

Lloyd was told Sheedy was pointed in his criticism of the team and of individuals, not just for the loss but for the way they lost and a perceived lack of toughness.

Three years later, a dominant Bombers team came up against Carlton and lost in the prelim. Lloyd says it still hurts today.

"In 1999, [Sheedy] was very different. He [went], 'OK, how I'm going to go to sell to these boys the hurt and what we're going to do in 2000 and this should steel us for 2000.' But in '96, he wasn't like that."

Essendon, including Lloyd, had to wait until 2000 for the flag, as they tore through the AFL going 24-1, including three finals by a ridiculous combined margin of 230 points.

For Sydney's Dale Lewis (centre), the ultimate grand final success eluded him, but the prelim win remains unforgettable. (Getty Images)

For the Swans, the euphoria became a magic grand final week and a dream first quarter and a half – but then the Kangaroos put their foot down, and North ran away with it to win by 43 points. Lockett kicked six, but it wasn't enough. Sydney had to wait until 2005 for the drought to break.

Luff, Lewis and Lockett never won a flag, although Plugger made history with an untouchable 1,360 goals.

It is now 30 years, but Dale Lewis, for one, has not forgotten that night.

"I can see it now. I get a little bit emotional about it," he says with a slight crack in his voice.

"I can see that [night]. I can see the looks in a couple of guys' eyes. I know who I turned to. You look at it, and you go, 'Unbelievable'."

World.title: From career crossroad to grand final, Erasmus 'stoked' he stayed with Dockers
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Nine rounds into the 2025 AFL season, Neil Erasmus was at a career crossroad.

The midfielder had played just 25 games since being drafted ahead of the 2022 season, and struggled to force his way into a stacked Fremantle midfield.

He was behind Caleb Serong, Andrew Brayshaw, Jaeger O'Meara and Nat Fyfe in the pecking order, and was playing a lot for Peel Thunder.

"There was [a chance of me leaving] and a little bit around just wanting a fresh start," Erasmus said.

"There's only so many times you can play sub and come in and out of the team and I was just looking for a bit more continuity.

"The potential for that elsewhere was probably luring me a little bit."

Neil Erasmus played just 39 games in his first four years in the AFL, before becoming a central part of the Dockers side this season. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

The 22-year old found form, and a spot in the Dockers side in the second half of the 2025 season, playing 13 more games including the elimination final loss to Gold Coast.

He ultimately signed a three-year deal with the club though until the end of 2028.

"Having some deep thoughts and conversations towards the back end of last year and playing the last couple of games and finding my feet a little bit, and really just enjoying my time made the decision pretty easy," Erasmus said.

"The club's been amazing and obviously stoked that I did stay in the end."

Grand final bound with mates

The decision to stay couldn't have worked out any better for Erasmus, who has played every game this year for the Dockers, and will run out on the MCG in the club's second-ever grand final.

A childhood West Coast Eagles fan, Erasmus is now all purple.

"To be honest, in my draft year, I probably went to being a bit indifferent," he said.

"A few of my favourite players stopped playing for the West Coast, obviously retired and when you get to be interviewed by so many different clubs you kind of see how they go about it and I really respected the way Freo went about it."

Jye Amiss was selected in the same draft as Neil Erasmus, along with Matthew Johnson. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

Along with Erasmus, the Dockers selected Jye Amiss and Matthew Johnson in the 2021 national draft, and then took Karl Worner at the rookie draft.

All four have become key parts of Fremantle's charge to the grand final, though playing alongside Johnson holds a special place.

"I played cricket and footy with him and against him from a really young age. It's pretty cool to be lining up with him," Erasmus said.

The Dockers progressed to the decider with a stirring come-from-behind win over Sydney at the SCG, and the scenes in the rooms after the game drove home the scope of the achievement.

"There was a lot of emotion post-game and almost more around the staff, you just feel so happy for them," Erasmus said.

"They've been working here for a lot longer than me personally and it's just great that they can get a bit of that success."

Erasmus said he was particularly happy for two club stalwarts in Paul Salis and Gary Ingraham.

"They talk about the 2013 flag and that team never used to miss a kick at training, like, all the time," he said.

"They just absolutely love it and it's just so cool to be able to give them the opportunity to get back there."

World.title: Aussies claim one-wicket win over Zimbabwe to sweep ODI series
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Josh Inglis has scored his second ODI century to help Australia claim a dramatic one-wicket victory ​over Zimbabwe with a ball to spare in Harare.

Nathan Ellis also played a key role in the successful run chase, posting his highest ODI score with an unbeaten 36 from 44 deliveries.

When Ellis was joined at the crease by number 11 Spencer Johnson (7 from 13 deliveries), the tourists needed 27 runs to reach their victory target of 272.

They managed to achieve this at a ​run-a-ball to guide Australia to ‌the win.

Zimbabwe will rue Wessly Madhevere dropping Ellis in the penultimate over when he could have sealed victory for the hosts.

Madhevere then failed to defend nine runs in the final over when Ellis hit a six off ‌the first ball.

Australia, who rested several of its regulars for the tour, claimed the series 3-0 and ⁠now move on to South Africa for three ODI fixtures.

"A great game of cricket," ​Australia captain Mitchell Marsh said.

"I ‌thought Zimbabwe probably deserved to win but the boys got the job done at the end there and that was fantastic to see.

"We're aware we need to keep improving as a team. I thought the way we played over the three matches, albeit today we got lucky, but there's lots of ​positive ‌signs with our group.

"We've got some young talent which is exciting for the future."

After the home side elected to bat first, Zimbabwe's innings was anchored by an unbeaten 81 from 72 ⁠balls by captain Sikandar Raza, to go with half-centuries ‌for Craig Ervine (59 from 79 balls) ‌and Innocent Kaia (55 from 66 balls).

Kaia retired hurt with a hamstring injury, with the score on 3-148, ‌as he could no longer run between the wickets.

Seamer Ellis was also the pick of the Australian bowlers with 3-50 in his 10 overs.

The Australians were always up with the ‌run rate ​in their reply, but when ⁠openers Travis Head (6) and Marsh (8) fell early, it set the tone for an innings where they lost wickets at regular intervals.

But Inglis scored a superb 103 from 102 balls as he struck 11 fours.

Zimbabwe all-rounder Brad ⁠Evans was the pick of the home bowlers with 4-47 in 10 overs.

"I thought 280-290 was par with the bat, so to make ‌a game out of ‌272 was a great effort," Raza said.

"As a captain, I'm really proud. Plenty ​to learn. I'd rather have a game like that than for the Aussies to just chase it down in 40 overs."

Reuters

World.title: Alex de Minaur fires as Aussie pair clicks in Davis Cup triumph
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Alex de Minaur has returned to form to seal Australia's Davis Cup progression, with the hosts beating Poland 3-1 in Brisbane also thanks to some earlier doubles brilliance.

The world No.9 found top gear on Sunday at Pat Rafter Arena, beating Kamil Majchrzak 6-3 6-3 to clinch a 3-1 result that sends Australia into the Cup's penultimate round next year.

With his backhand and serve firing, de Minaur followed up his 57-minute annihilation of Maks Kasnikowski on Saturday with another therapeutic response to a disappointing second-round US Open exit earlier this month.

Earlier, Max Purcell's scintillating tiebreak tennis alongside rock-solid Rinky Hijikata swung their doubles match, and the tie, in Australia's favour.

The pair's 7-6 (7-3) 6-3 defeat of Jan Zielinski and Karol Drzewiecki followed the win and the loss posted in singles by de Minaur and James Duckworth respectively on Saturday.

Purcell, on the comeback from a controversial 18-month anti-doping ban, turned the match on its head after a tight first set progressed to an inevitable tie break.

He drilled a backhand return to win the opening point on the Polish serve, then produced a pair of aces to shoot the hosts clear 3-0.

De Minaur wins Davis Cup opener After a long and winding road to Brisbane in 2026, Alex de Minaur rides a partisan home crowd to an impressive victory in the first rubber of Australia's Davis Cup tie against Poland.

An unforced error from Poland was followed by two more Purcell winners, and he then held his nerve on a series of low volleys to eventually clinch the set.

Hijikata then held impressively and, after missing two break-point chances, nailed a forehand return to nab the match's only service break.

That was all Australia needed, with the composed pair energising the sold-out Pat Rafter Arena to secure a pressure-relieving victory in 77 minutes.

Australia's win followed a shock loss on the road to Ecuador earlier this year that plunged it into the must-win encounter against Poland.

The Aussies still need to win next year's qualifying round, against an opponent still to be decided, to progress to the finals in Italy in November, 2027.

AAP

World.title: Lions star to challenge grand final ban, Hawks duo handed massive fines
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The Brisbane Lions will challenge a one-match ban handed to Lachie Neale, which would rule the two-time premiership captain out of the AFL grand final.

Neale was offered the suspension after being charged with striking during the Lions' controversial nine-point win over Hawthorn in Saturday night's preliminary final at the MCG.

Hawks fans throw bottles at umpires Hawthorn fans are condemned for their behaviour after the siren following a heart-stopping preliminary final against the Brisbane Lions at the MCG.

Meanwhile, Hawks pair James Sicliy and Tom Barrass have been fined $10,000 and $5,000 respectively for abusing umpire Hayden Meyer following the frenetic finish to the match.

Neale's off-the-ball incident involved a gut punch to the Hawks' Jack Ginnivan in the first quarter.

Vision showed Ginnivan wrestling with Lions forward Eric Hipwood, before Neale jogs over and hits the Hawks player with a left-handed punch to the stomach.

It was graded intentional conduct, medium impact and body contact.

Within minutes of the AFL releasing the match review findings on Sunday, the Lions confirmed they will challenge the ban.

Neale will front the tribunal but, if unsuccessful, will miss Saturday's grand final against Fremantle at the MCG.

New match review guidelines state intentional strikes to the stomach are automatically graded as medium impact rather than low, resulting in one-match bans.

Lachie Neale has won two flags with the Lions. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: Robert Cianflone)

Neale may attempt to lean on the "exemplary record" clause to clear himself for the grand final.

He has never been suspended in his 320-match career and could use the same clause that helped Scott Pendlebury escape suspension for his bump on Adelaide's Josh Worrell this season.

Under AFL regulations, "a player with an exemplary record may argue that their good record constitutes exceptional and compelling circumstances".

Players can no longer use the so-called "good bloke" defence that helped Brisbane's Charlie Cameron overturn a ban in 2024.

Neale's other option is to attempt to have the impact grading reduced, though that route would be unlikely to be successful.

A suspension would also mean Neale may have played his final match for the Lions.

The 33-year-old, who has twice won the Brownlow Medal, is expected to make an off-season move to Collingwood as a free agent.

Neale and Harris Andrews were co-captains when the Lions won the 2024 and 2025 premierships.

Should the Lions defeat the Dockers, they will match the feat of the club's 2001-03 squad, which won three straight flags.

James Sicily was fined $10,000 by the AFL. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Sicily and Barrass were handed their massive fines for misconduct after their heated conversation with Meyer immediately after the final siren.

It followed a controversial finish, in which a holding-the-ball free kick paid against Hawthorn's Jarman Impey gifted Brisbane's Hugh McCluggage the match-clinching goal in the dying stages.

Sicily and Barrass were not offered an early plea.

The AFL determined the fixed financial sanction for abusive language towards an umpire was inadequate, and so charged Sicily and Barrass under the "other misconduct'' provision.

Hawks midfielder Jai Newcombe was cleared over his first-quarter contact with Neale in a collision that involved opponents pushing the two players into each other.

ABC/AAP

World.title: Crows prevail in fiery AFLW clash with Lions
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Brisbane's wait to ignite its AFLW season will continue, as an ugly moment contributed to its nine-point loss to Adelaide.

Last year's grand finalists entered Sunday's clash at Springfield Central Stadium to find form after suffering their third loss in four games with a five-point defeat to West Coast last Saturday.

But an outburst in the third quarter by Lions defender Lily-Rose Williamson, wrapping her arms around the neck of Teah Charlton inside the forward 50, severely damaged their chances.

The midfielder scored from the ensuing free kick and the Lions didn't recover until late in the final term as the visitors secured a 5.9 (39) to 4.6 (30) victory.

The Lions (2-4) were left stunned as the Crows held them goalless in the first quarter while kicking two majors of their own.

But Brisbane stepped up as midfielders Orla O'Dwyer and Shanae Davison slotted settling goals to reduce the visitors' lead to two points at half-time.

Do you have a story idea about women in sport? Email us abcsport5050@your.abc.net.au

The visitors restored their advantage when forward Hannah Munyard poked the ball through the middle before Charlton scored.

Crows forward India Rasheed grabbed a major, but teenager Asher Fearn-Wannan and midfielder Catherine Svarc kicked consolation goals.

Suns surge to victory, Tigers survive Giants comeback

The Suns notched a third-straight AFLW win with victory over the Bombers. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Gold Coast's band of youngsters have strengthened their grip on a third AFLW finals berth, beating Essendon by 41 points at Windy Hill.

The Suns have surprised many this season after starting the campaign as one of the more youthful and inexperienced sides in the league.

Their 7.9 (51) to 1.4 (10) win over Essendon on Sunday was their third consecutive victory and moved them into fifth spot, just four points behind second-placed defending champions North Melbourne.

Gold Coast's defence was resolute in the blustery conditions, and the Bombers did not score a point until late in the second quarter.

At the same time, the visitors were dominating territory and snagged three goals courtesy of a trio of players all aged under 21.

After leading by 20 points at half-time, Suns forward Anne Hatchard and midfielder Charlie Rowbottom added their names to the scoresheet, before Emily Gough found the Bombers' only major late in the third period.

The visitors grabbed another two goals in the final term to complete the win.

Defender Niamh McLaughlin (33 disposals, 506 metres gained) and Rowbottom (36 disposals, one goal) were busy for Gold Coast (4-2), while Hatchard and Havana Harris scored two majors each.

The loss kept the Bombers (0-6) winless, although midfielder Madison Prespakis was outstanding with a game-high 38 disposals

North's record winning streak over after shock loss to Hawks North Melbourne has lost for the first time in almost three years, with the two-time defending AFLW premier falling to a shock 7-point defeat to Hawthorn in Cairns.

At Manuka Oval, Richmond survived an almighty scare to claim a stirring 9.14 (68) to 10.1 (61) win over a pinpoint-accurate GWS.

Fresh off a 15-point win over St Kilda last Sunday, the Tigers (4-2) raced out of the gates and led by 16 points at quarter-time in Canberra.

Richmond continued to run riot in the second term, booting five goals in 12 minutes to balloon their advantage to 55-18 at the main break.

But the Giants completely transformed after half-time, scoring six majors, including a double from Georgia Garnett, to give themselves a glimmer of hope at three-quarter time.

Leading by eight points, the visitors sprayed a flurry of opportunities wide, but their defence held off the Giants' desperate attack to claim the win and go equal with the Suns on victories.

Finals hopes are fading for the Giants (1-5), but midfielders Alyce Parker (27 disposals) and Rebecca Beeson (23 disposals, two goals) were prolific, while Garnett finished with three goals.

Forward Gabby Seymour (16 hit outs) posted a career-best three majors for Richmond, while Olivia Wolmarans also had three goals.

At Moorabbin Park, West Coast notched a second win of the season with an 11-point victory over St Kilda.

The Eagles kicked on after a tight first half, with key forward Amy Franklin kicking two goals.

Ella Roberts was industrious in midfield for West Coast, completing 25 disposals, as her side rose to 13th with the 5.6 (36) to 3.7 (25) victory.

AAP/ABC

World.title: AFL bans loom for bottle-throwing Hawks fans
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The AFL has condemned the behaviour of Hawthorn fans and warned they face minimum five-year bans if identified after they "crossed the line" throwing bottles at umpires.

The match officials had bottles thrown at them from the stands as they walked off the MCG playing arena following the Hawks' nine-point loss to the Brisbane Lions in Saturday night's preliminary final at the MCG.

"The AFL and MCC [Melbourne Cricket Club] security will work with Vic Pol to identify the bottle throwers directed at the umpires last night," the league said in a statement.

"If identified they will be banned from games and the stadium for a minimum five years.

"The passion for footy is unmatched in Australian sport, however, what transpired last night by a number of individuals was dangerous and crossed the line."

At the heart of Hawthorn's collective rage was a holding-the-ball free paid against Jarman Impey in the last minute of the match.

Hawks fans throw bottles at umpires Hawthorn fans are condemned for their behaviour after the siren following a heart-stopping preliminary final against the Brisbane Lions at the MCG.

It was the most controversial of a succession of contentious umpiring calls during the game.

Brisbane's Hugh McCluggage then kicked the match-clinching goal, which put the Lions in front by three points.

Hawks players James Sicily, Tom Barrass and Jack Ginnivan had a heated conversation with the umpires immediately after the full-time siren.

Sicily ($10,000) and Barrass ($5,000) have since been fined by the AFL.

On Saturday night, Hawks coach Sam Mitchell said he did not know about Sicily, Barrass and Ginnivan speaking to the umpires, but he was aware of the bottles being thrown onto the ground.

"At the end of the game, part of me wanted to break down in tears, part of me wanted to scream with rage, part of me wanted to throw chairs, you don't know how to react," Mitchell said post-match.

"So when you're in the stand, you need to continue to be feeling that emotion, because that's why we love it, but how it manifests itself. We shouldn't be throwing things on the field and doing those types of things.

"But the passion in the stand and the passion of the game is why we love it so much, so I hope that for the vast majority it was felt responsibly."

Bottles and cans could be seen on the playing area after the match. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: James Wiltshire)

On Sunday, Premier Ben Carroll condemned the behaviour, telling reporters that it was not the "Victorian way".

"I think these people should be made an example of," he said.

"This could have had catastrophic injuries if one of those bottles or cans hit an umpire on the head.

"You've always got to respect the umpire's decision."

AFL Fans Association president Ron Issko said he understood the passion, disappointment and frustration of Hawthorn supporters, but denounced their throwing of objects at the umpires.

"It is never, ever an excuse to throw bottles or cans on to the ground or at the umpires. What we saw was an ugly look for our game," he said.

"There is an even more serious concern when objects are thrown towards people.

"A bottle, or can, could cause a serious injury to a player, umpire, security staff, ground staff or another spectator.

"When a bottle is thrown towards an umpire and comes close to hitting them, that crosses an even more serious line.

"No-one should have to fear being struck by a projectile simply because they are doing their job."

AAP

Tech.title: No Dogs in Space is back to feed your need for obsessive music history
Tech.content:
In August, I wrote about my love of the music history podcast No Dogs in Space, but mourned the fact that there hadn’t been a new episode in over two years. Little did I know that hosts Carolina Hidalgo and Marcus Parks were gearing up to announce the show’s return with season four, Punk 2.0. The first episode premiered this week, part one of a series on the New York Dolls, a band near and dear to my heart as a native Staten Islander, home of frontman David Johansen.

For the new season, Hidalgo and Parks decided it was time to get back to basics. Part of that was that they felt punk rock was where their passion and expertise were strongest. Parks said that they “wanted to go all over. I wanted to do Beethoven at one point,” but that “we realize like what we do best is tell a punk story, right? Not the punk story, but a punk story.“ But also, they said, that’s just where the most interesting stories are. After spending enormous amounts of time translating German into English for their experimental rock series, they realized that, often, the story behind the bands boils down to ”art school kids fucking around.”

There were a number of reasons why the new season took so long to come together. But one of the biggest is that the duo made a few false starts. Early on, the plan was to tackle the DC punk scene. Hidalgo told The Verge that “we worked on it for over six months” and that they planned to launch the series with Bad Brains. “And then we look into them,” Hidalgo said, “and they’re like, incredibly homophobic. Like, fire and brimstone … A lot of No Dogs bands like, they’re problematic, but that was like a really tough one to focus on.”

The two then attempted to do a series that covered the DC as a whole — “never do that,” Hidalgo warned. Parks said that “it just kept swelling larger,” listing off a number of acts that may not have been part of the DC punk scene, but were important foundational elements, like Chuck Brown and go-go. The two even mused that Georgetown University’s WGTB radio might be worthy of a series all on its own. But ultimately, “when you try to put all of them together, you can’t. You just can’t put all of these stories together,” Parks said. “And after eight months of working on it … we eventually had to admit defeat.”

The effort wasn’t a total waste, however. They did get a two-part series on Link Wray out of it that will premiere later this year.

Obsession is their superpower. Image: Marcus Parks / Carolina Hidalgo

Like any season of No Dogs in Space, part of the fun is the weird sidequests and rabbit holes that Parks and Hidalgo go down. During the New York Dolls series, Hidalgo became obsessed with Mott the Hoople. The band is best known for their David Bowie-penned hit “All the Young Dudes,” but their story is a fascinating one. Hidalgo says lead singer Ian Hunter “was just a guy digging ditches. And then he got a call from a friend who said, ‘Hey, there’s a band, and like, they’re not very good, and they need a new lead singer,’ and so he just showed up.” Hunter also wrote “Cleveland Rocks,” which was covered by The Presidents of the United States of America and became the theme for The Drew Carey Show.

Parks says he became obsessed with drag queen Jackie Curtis. “It could be argued that the punk style that is often credited to Richard Hell probably actually originated with Jackie Curtis,” he said. He also shared a story about how Curtis once “went out on to [their] windowsill… like Batman, inching like Batman” to get into the apartment of a recently deceased neighbor to steal her clothes before the coroner came.

It’s these sorts of tangents that make No Dogs in Space so compelling. “We live our lives in like a state of obsession,” Parks said. “Obsession really is, it is kind of our superpower. And we were both recently diagnosed with autism and discovered that that’s just who we are. That’s the superpower that we get.“

If you’re wondering where to start, the new series on the New York Dolls is as good as any. The Dolls were a protopunk and glam act that played an important role in building the NYC scene. But I also can’t recommend the series on the Replacements, Dead Kennedys, or Joy Division enough. You can listen to the new season of No Dogs in Space now on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or anywhere else you find fine podcasts. Or, for the first time, the show will be posted on YouTube as full video episodes.

Tech.title: No one is surprised that Nvidia’s Jensen Huang thinks AI fears are overblown.
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

The man who may stand to make the most money from the AI boom seems to think he knows better than anyone else, including researchers who have studied and worked on AI for decades. In an interview with CBS Sunday Morning, he claimed there was a “0% chance” of AI being the end of the world. He also said of people sounding the alarm about the dangers of AI that, “Scaring people is unnecessary. It is irresponsible.”

He also claims that calls from CEOs like Anthropic’s Dario Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman to slow down the development of AI are “not grounded in science.” He even argued that there was no need for new rules, laws, or guidelines, in the face of several high-profile cases in which models escaped containment and hacked other companies.

It’s not surprising that Huang was dismissive of the dangers posed by rogue AI and concerns about selling chips to China, or that he adamantly opposed new regulation. He is the CEO of the world’s most valuable company and number seven on Forbes’ list of the richest people in the world. Just as importantly, his wealth has skyrocketed from an estimated $21 billion in 2023 to over $192 billion in 2026. Any hiccup in the unchecked expansion of the AI industry could slow his ascent.

is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

The president posted on Truth Social that he wanted to appoint an “AI czar” to lead a new “AI force.” He made the announcement amid growing calls from across the political spectrum and even within the industry to pump the brakes on AI development. He posted that his administration “will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry. Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows!”

In the rambling post, Trump said that data centers were “wealthy and prestigious” and claimed without evidence that they raised salaries, lowered taxes, and made for safer streets in the communities in which they were built. He also related the AI Force to his creation of the Space Force, which he claimed was a “tremendous SUCCESS.”

The president gave no timeline or further details about the AI Force nor who might be tapped to lead it. Though he insisted that “Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!” for the position of AI Czar.

Tech.title: A24’s reputation is on the line with the SCP Foundation movie
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

After the success of Backrooms, it looks like A24 is trying to cash in on yet another internet horror craze with a new installment in the V/H/S horror anthology series set in the SCP Foundation universe. But as soon as it was announced, the backlash started, and V/H/S: SCP already appears to be on shaky ground.

SCP is a creepypasta that, like Backrooms, originated on 4chan. The fictional SCP (Special Containment Procedures) Foundation documents, captures, and contains paranormal or supernatural anomalies. It’s a sprawling story told primarily through wiki entries that mimic documentation you might file while working at a government agency. It’s sci-fi cosmic horror by way of bureaucratic nightmares. It’s the sort of material ripe for a monster-of-the-week style anthology.

But, unlike Backrooms where A24 worked with the creator of a YouTube series popular within the Backrooms community, it does not appear as if the studio tried to engage the SCP community at all. The SCP Foundation Wiki, the official home for all things SCP, posted a statement following the announcement of the film that read, “We have not had any communication with the filmmakers, producers, or distributors for this project, despite our best efforts, and to the best of our knowledge they have not made any efforts to contact us.”

DrEverettMann, an SCP Foundation Wiki Admin, told The Verge that, “We have made several attempts to contact them since the announcement of the project but haven’t received a response.”

This isn’t just about generating goodwill with fans, either. SCP is an organized community effort with licensing rules. The SCP Foundation is organized under a Creative Commons license, specifically CC BY-SA 3.0, a ShareAlike license. That means, while anyone can distribute or create works based on SCP, it must also allow anyone to copy, redistribute, or create derivative works based on theirs. That would make making money on a feature film extremely difficult.

A24 made several serious missteps following the release of Backrooms, angering fans by filing copyright claims against other Backrooms creators, before withdrawing them after director Kane Parsons intervened. So, A24 and its partners at Image Nation Studios and Spooky Pictures have been eager to clarify that they are not asserting exclusive rights to the SCP universe. A24 declined to comment, but Monique Levine, a spokesperson for Image Nation and Spooky, told The Verge that “A24’s worldwide rights pertain to the specific film project being produced.”

The problem is, under the license used by the SCP Foundation, nobody can claim exclusive rights to any SCP material. Creative Commons’ CEO Anna Tumadóttir told The Verge that, “Anyone can use works available under Creative Commons ShareAlike (CC BY-SA) license, even commercially,” but that, “Adaptations must be released under the same terms as the original,” and “unless a separate agreement is reached with the copyright holders, a studio-produced film like this would need to be released under CC BY-SA 3.0 or a compatible later version, with attribution to the original creators, and without exclusive distribution rights. Anyone else would remain free to redistribute or stream it under the same terms.”

As Paul Szynol, a law professor at the University of Michigan and Villanova, told The Verge, while “anyone — A24, Netflix as well as you, me, and all of our cousins” are free to make an SCP film and release it in theatres, “the studio wouldn’t be able to stop anyone else from making adaptations of its film,” or redistributing it. And, as he points out, that “would be an extremely unusual business model for a major studio.”

SCP’s DrEverettMann agreed. The license “wouldn’t prevent the film from being shown in theaters, nor would it prevent theaters from charging admission as usual,” he said. But “whether it would be practical to release the film under traditional distribution methods is a trickier question.”

Mann expanded, “The fact that anyone is able to distribute a CC BY-SA-licensed work means that the usual theatrical exclusivity wouldn’t apply. It is not possible for anybody to have exclusive rights to a film distributed under a CC BY-SA license … We don’t know how many people would choose to pay to see a film in theaters when they could legally download it at home for free.”

This leaves A24 with a few options. It could simply carry forward with the project as is and worry about the legal problems later. But as Tumadóttir points out, “CC licenses, including ShareAlike, have been enforced in courts around the world, when needed.” And Szynol concurs, saying, “In that case, A24’s version of the film would be unauthorized and infringing. Basically, it would be the death of the project.”

It seems more likely that A24 and Spooky Pictures will abandon the SCP branding, while still taking “inspiration” from the source material. It’s a tactic others have taken with commercial works, like with the novel There is No Antimemetics Division written by SCP Foundation contributor QNTM.

Another option would be to release the movie under the ShareAlike license and hope that it could still recoup production costs even without being able to claim rights. It would be the boldest move, but perhaps the least likely outcome.

Tech.title: Humans, not rogue AI, are still the biggest cybersecurity risk to energy systems
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Before recent high-profile hacks raised the specter of AI possibly “killing all humans,” our energy systems were already disturbingly vulnerable to cyberattack — and the risk is growing.

“We were always prey. We were just kind of surviving at the appetite of our predators,” Joshua Corman, executive in residence for public safety and resilience at the Institute for Security and Technology (IST), told me last year. At the time, I was preoccupied with a Department of Homeland Security warning that Iranian actors and sympathizers could target the US with cyberattacks.

Last week, I called Corman up to chat about recent incidents of rogue AI agents orchestrating their own complex cyberattacks. Even AI executives are talking about whether the technology they’re building could grow so out of control that it triggers an apocalypse. If there is now a 10 percent chance of artificial intelligence one day killing all humans, as some AI developers warn, surely there’s a chance it could knock our lights out in the meantime?

“Any sociopath that wants to [attack] is now more powerful than they used to be.”

But when I spoke to Corman and other cybersecurity experts, they were still more worried about generative AI in the hands of bad actors than they were about rogue agents. As tech companies race to build ever more powerful AI models, utilities will similarly have to shore up their defenses — no matter who or what initiated the attack.

“It’s literally any sociopath that wants to [attack] is now more powerful than they used to be,” Corman tells me. “This has been a force multiplier and continues to grow.”

Much of our critical energy infrastructure — keeping the lights on in our homes, food cold in our refrigerators, and life-saving devices working in hospitals — was never designed to connect to the internet. The lifespan of a power plant is typically decades long. The average age of a nuclear reactor in the US is about 44 years. They weren’t constructed with today’s cybersecurity risks in mind, making them easy targets for hackers.

Eventually much of this infrastructure did connect to the internet. It’s been difficult to fix any resulting cybersecurity vulnerabilities ever since. Some of the companies that originally designed the equipment still in use in the power sector have gone out of business, leaving no one behind to develop a software patch for those orphaned devices. Even when there is a patch available, applying it in a timely manner is another challenge. Unlike IT software upgrades, operational technology (OT) systems that control physical machinery for critical infrastructure might only be designed to apply updates once each quarter or year. Smaller utilities might also lack the resources, staffing, and know-how to use the latest defensive measures.

“The true difference from AI is that it’s letting adversaries move more quickly — but it’s very challenging for those defending the infrastructure to match that pace,” says Sophie McDowall, a research associate at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies’ Center on Cyber and Technology Innovation.

Related The AI Superintelligence Slowdown

Intent is a key factor when assessing the risks posed by generative AI. When an OpenAI model managed to break out of the company’s training parameters to attack AI lab Hugging Face, “Some of the sophistication and the capabilities and just what we saw in that were really eye-opening and in a sense terrifying in terms of how effective they were,” says Rob Denaburg, cybersecurity program senior manager at the American Public Power Association, which represents community-owned utilities across 2,000 municipalities.

But Denaburg points out that even in the Hugging Face hack and similar instances of AI agents breaking into systems they were never supposed to target, the rogue agents remained focused on fulfilling their training goals. If someone was to train a model to carry out an attack on energy infrastructure and agents broke out of the sandbox in that scenario, it would probably be a bigger concern for a utility. Again, that involves human adversaries with malicious intent.

Historically, adversarial nation-states were largely considered the biggest cybersecurity threat to critical infrastructure. “They’re going to be more disciplined,” Corman says, and more capable of undertaking a sophisticated cyberattack. Now, AI is making it easier for less-skilled adversaries to launch an effective assault.

“A bad-actor human can use these tools to be better than they naturally would be to attack things they normally didn’t know how to … because whereas they may not know OT protocols and OT networks and OT strategies, the LLM has read the manuals and does know what to do,” Corman says.

Utilities have to be more prepared, and defensive strategies are similar regardless of who the bad guy is. “AI or not, it is at the end of the day, still a cyberattack,” Denaburg says. “Even though AI can help an adversary maybe chain vulnerabilities together and automate some of the process going from initial access to exploit … as long as you can stop them in one spot, they can’t carry out that attack.”

Power companies can follow a range of best practices to safeguard critical infrastructure. Some of them are non-cyber solutions, like ensuring systems can switch to manual operations when needed or in some cases pulling back on how interconnected this infrastructure is in the first place. Increasingly, “in the face of the AI stuff, they’re starting to realize if we can’t protect it, disconnect it,” Corman says.

“They’re offering support for a problem that they are partially causing.”

Governments and the companies developing advanced AI models hold responsibility, too, McDowall says. It was a positive step, she notes, that OpenAI CEO Sam Altman recently met with utilities to discuss securing power grids. But there’s a lot more they could do to prevent disaster, she says. “They’re offering support for a problem that they are partially causing,” while failing to adequately control their own technology advancements, McDowall tells The Verge.

And while there are regulatory guardrails for research and development when it comes to nuclear technologies and hazardous materials, there aren’t yet the same policy safeguards for AI. “This is a technological scientific development that could cause potential risk to critical infrastructure systems, that can cause potential threat to human life. And so there does need to be restrictions,” McDowall says.“I recognize that we also don’t want to limit development, but there’s no reason that we can’t drive research forward while also doing it responsibly.”

She points out that there’s a dearth of research into how AI might be used to improve cybersecurity for energy systems — particularly beyond just red teaming to discover vulnerabilities.

Earlier this month, OpenAI pledged $1 billion toward subsidizing training and access to new models that are supposed to help defend critical infrastructure.

“In the coming months, AI-enabled cyber attacks will become far more widespread and sophisticated as models around the world become increasingly capable,” OpenAI said in the September 3 announcement. “Frontier AI can help defenders move faster.”

But Corman cautions against relying on friendly AI agents to fight off the malicious ones. They could both be hard to control in the sensitive confines of an OT system for critical infrastructure.

“It’s also really dangerous to introduce too much change too fast in an OT environment,” Corman says. “Now we have an AI bull fighting another AI bull in an OT china shop.”
